Don Joaquín Velázquez de León, Advocate of Causes in the Royal Audiencia of Mexico, formerly Public Professor of Mathematics in the Illustrious University, and Literary Member of the Royal Cantabrian Society of the Friends of the Country, gave this opinion.

M O S T E XC E L L E N T L O R D.

T he volumes which were brought to me by Your

command, bearing this title, Elements of the Newer Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri — when I had turned through them, I wondered at the Author’s labor, diligence, alacrity, brevity. For it is scarcely credible to say how much he himself, how learnedly, how vigorously he has labored to instruct Youth in Philosophy (in a philosophy that truly deserves to be called by the name of philosophy)! So far, indeed, are these School Institutions themselves from thrusting upon us anything adverse or hostile either to morals, which ought to be kept uncorrupted, or to the most holy laws, that in my judgment (if I may be permitted to discern anything,

¶ being

PDF 10

being not altogether indifferently versed in these matters) this way and method of teaching Philosophy agrees very closely with the true and genuine one, often adopted by most distinguished Men, and such as the Spanish Universities among our countrymen have long since followed in these times by Royal command. This being so, Most Excellent Prince, there is no reason why the publication of these Elements in print should be forbidden. Such, at least, is my opinion. Given at Mexico, on the day after the Nones of September, in the year of the Lord 1774.

Joaquín Velázquez

de León.

¶ N. B. There follows the same Approbation, translated by its Author, by verbal order which His Excellency was pleased to give for the purpose.

PDF 11

H aving seen the Books which, by superior

command of Your Excellency, were sent to me with this Title: Rudiments of the Modern Philosophy, by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, I admired the labor of the Author, his diligence, his comprehensiveness, and at the same time the concision with which he writes. Indeed, it can scarcely be believed what a variety of things the Father Doctor has taken up, with how much erudition, and how earnestly he has undertaken this labor in order to instruct Youth in a Philosophy that well deserves this name! And these School Institutions are so far from including anything opposed either to the Laws of the Kingdom or to the integrity and purity of morals, that, on the contrary, in my opinion (if I may give one in these subjects, in which I am not without some experience) this method of teaching Philosophy agrees closely with the true one, which has always been desired by the Authors of better doctrine

¶2 and

and taste, and which at this time has already begun to be put into practice in the Universities of our Spain by order of the King Our Lord. Wherefore I find nothing, Most Excellent Sir, to hinder the printing and publication of this Work. So I judge it. Mexico, September 6, 1774.

Most Excellent Sir.

Joaquín Velázquez de León.

MOST HONORABLE LORD

Don José Ignacio Bartolache y Díaz de Posadas, Doctor of Medicine, for a four-year term holder of the Prime Chair of the same Faculty in the Illustrious University of Mexico, and Literary Member of the Royal Cantabrian Society of the Friends of the Country, wrote this.

JUDGE. T hat old answer of some Sage, I know not whose

(to one asking what boys ought to learn), that they ought, in short, to learn what would be of use to them as Men: this I wish wholly to make my own, and I solemnly profess it, now that I have read through these Elements of the Newer Philosophy, compiled by the Rev. Father Dr. Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Secular Priest of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, for the use of the American Youth of the Schools, and have followed them almost syllable by syllable. Wherefore, since the Author, a man diligent above most, has excerpted nearly everything from all the best writers for the sake of instructing Youth rightly, has composed it and written it out briefly, while I myself have come upon nothing that is out of harmony with the orthodox faith,

or

or that is foreign to a Christian Philosopher, I judge it most equitable, and that it will be useful, that these pages be committed to the Press. Given at Mexico on the day before the Ides of September, 1774.

Dr. José Ignacio Bartolache.

Father Don José Henríquez, Professor of Sacred

Theology, Secular Priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri of San Miguel el Grande.

A t the bidding of the Congregation of San

Miguel I have striven with all my might to read through, with the greatest attention I could, these two volumes whose title is Elements of the Newer Philosophy. I feared, however, lest I should judge of this work more from prejudice and from my esteem for its most distinguished Author (with whom I had long since begun to live in the closest intimacy) than by right and deservedly. But I frankly confess that I gave myself wholly to playing the part of a supercilious censor, not of a fulsome and shameless praiser. And so, after I had long and much considered what in the end I ought to write on this account and lay before the Conscript Fathers of our Family, behold, these few things came to mind, which will serve in place of a censure. First, indeed, that our countryman, Father Doctor Don Juan Benito, has hit the nail on the head, in that under the name of Philosophy he has brought together for the benefit of the young not an empty fallacy, by deceiving, but a doctrine of the first utility, by teaching. For these Elements

of

PDF 16

of the Newer Philosophy seem to me to embrace, with wonderful brevity and clarity, and likewise in wonderful order, whatever the English, the French, the Dutch, the Italians and the Spaniards, earnestly intent upon philosophical matters through long decades of years, have searched out. The young beginner will certainly find here a great many things duly treated which he would seek elsewhere in vain; unless, having grown older, he devotes himself strenuously for the rest of his life (which happens to very few indeed) to Philosophy and to books, of which we have no great supply. But if anyone should compare those little questions so often debated, On Prescissions, On the Being of Reason, On the Appetite of Matter, On the Categorematic Infinite, or others far emptier still, which the Author knowingly and prudently passed over, with the disquisitions he has briefly written out On God, One and Existing, On the Immortality of Souls, On Virtue, On Duties, and on many others of that kind: he will, by Hercules, perceive which of them are better able to pave and smooth the way both to the right instruction of boys and to Sacred Theology. And truly, so the matter stands. For neither the right Instruction of boys, nor the duties of civil life, nor the science of corporeal nature, nor the best arts (nay, not even the cobbler’s,

although

PDF 17

although it is commonly held the most illiberal of all), nor finally Sacred Theology, can be helped or increased by those very trifles which we have mentioned above. Let men, then, otherwise most grave, cease to weep whole days and nights over the burial of the Summulae and the Categories, and over the felled Porphyrian Tree, as though it were all over with the commonwealth, with themselves too and their children, with altars and hearths. This is most ridiculous, and is to be met not with much bile but rather with phlegm, that is, with laughter. Wherefore my opinion is this: that the Fathers of our Congregation ought in no way to hinder these volumes from being committed to the press, since the Author has most diligently excerpted from every side, compiled and explained a doctrine both sound and useful; and that it will be of advantage and profit to the young men who will apply themselves to Philosophy among us, I for my part in no way doubt. Given at San Miguel el Grande, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, in the Year mdcclxxiv.

José Henríquez de Rivera.

prepared for the use of the Salesian College by Father Don Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra y Dávalos, Deputy Priest of our Congregation and Rector of the same College, have been examined by our order, and nothing is found in them out of harmony with right morals, or contrary to the Faith, to Religion and to the Royal Ordinances, but rather they are judged most apt for governing morals, for defending the Faith and Religion, and finally for instructing Youth in a wholesome and useful Philosophy, we grant permission that they be committed to the press, if it shall so seem good to those to whom the rest pertains. ¶ N. B. The names of the most learned Doctors and Fathers have been written down in precisely that order which the Illustrious University of Mexico has hitherto observed, so that (saving the precedence of the Faculties and Sciences) he who is prior in time is also prior in right and in place. As for the Sacred Families of the Orders, exactly the same custom has been retained as is publicly observed in Academic Disputations. We acknowledge, meanwhile, that some most distinguished Men, on account of their dignity and their ornaments of honor, some more eminent than others, ought perhaps to have been listed otherwise: which was not ours to do, nor indeed a thing to be done rashly.

To

PDF 24

Juan Benito Díaz de Gamarra sends greetings and his lucubrations.

Y our cause, all of you, is at stake, young men of most ex‐

cellent talent, fitted beyond other nations for the Sciences. It is your cause that is now at stake. For I did not wish these pages to be written for, or dedicated to, learned Men who think they have attained Philosophy, such as it is, by the labor of two years (and not very strenuous labor at that); nor to those who all day long pronounce from the School’s lectern, as from a tripod, on matters exceedingly difficult and not equally well known to themselves (*). But to you, young men, who are now for the first time approaching these sacred rites, and who are about to enter, when at length it may be allowed, the citadel of human Philosophy, than which nothing can be more delightful.

To you, great hope of our Country, I submit these Institutions of the Newer Philosophy, excerpted, very briefly indeed, from here and there; and I would give you far other things, and a good many of them, were the course of the Schools not so short, which by custom you must run through. But come, and since it was for your

sake

(*) The renowned Melchor Cano, bk. VIII of De locis theologicis.

PDF 25

sake that this task and labor were undertaken, hear in a few words what I have accomplished in writing, or at least have attempted.

First of all, then, I commend to you again and again the History of the Philosophy you are entering upon, set down rather briefly at the very threshold of the Institutions. Read it through, turn it over, meditate on it, and weigh in your minds how important it will be for learning Philosophy itself thoroughly, correctly and in due order. For if you do not know what Philosophy is, under what Authors it was born, how far and in what esteem it was held among our forebears, what its fortunes were, what its progress, what its way and method of teaching, it cannot possibly be that you will not err shamefully at every turn. And no kind of error, in my opinion at least, is more to be guarded against and avoided than that of those for whom this alone counts as true philosophy, what they themselves learned as beardless boys; everything else they hold as nothing, as though it were the empty dreams of a sick man’s fancy. For which reason they are deservedly laughed at.

Others, however, and indeed very many in these times, are so delighted both by Aristotle and, above all, by what, under the name of so great

¶¶¶ a

PDF 26

a Man (for we freely admit that he was certainly a very great man), is commonly peddled in the Schools, that they seriously affirm that nothing fitter or more convenient could ever be found for sharpening the little wits of boys, and for teaching Sacred Theology eloquently and learnedly, than those everlasting exercises, the disputes and logomachies On Universals, On the Being of Reason, On Substantial Forms, On the Union and the Whole Composite, and six hundred others of that kind, by which minds are indeed tortured and worn down; but I fear they grow no sharper for the pursuit of wisdom and for the best disciplines, at which all our strength and thought ought to aim, as at a target. And what profit, pray, will those utterly empty interpretations of the Mahometans Avicenna, Averroes, Alfarabi, and the rest of the Arab throng be able to bring to the true religion, to the Church of Christ, and finally to Sacred Theology? No doubt the venerable Fathers of the Church, our forebears, now Fathers Conscript among the dwellers in heaven, Dionysius the Areopagite, Ephrem, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Athanasius, Epiphanius, both Gregories, Chrysostom,

Basil,

PDF 27

Basil, Leo, Hilary, Prosper, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, did not themselves also either defend the Church, or discourse on Theological matters, or rout the profane innovators, the Heretics. On the contrary, they did so above all: for their golden volumes bear witness to it. And yet one would look for Aristotle there in vain. Not that these very great men were ignorant of dialectic and syllogisms, or ordered them banished altogether when matters of the very gravest weight were to be treated or debated: a thing which, had it been done, would have been done quite rashly and heedlessly (yet it was not done by them), and which we would by no means imitate, since the subtleties of syllogisms do not so greatly displease us. But, as I judge, admonished by the saying of Paul, where he says: Beware lest any man cheat you by philosophy, and vain deceit, these most Holy Men resolved, in holiness, to treat all those things which pertain, by God’s revelation, to holiness of life and to everlasting beatitude: from which, assuredly, the whole Philosophy of the Heathen is all but alien. Let them cease, therefore, to deafen our ears, and even to tear us and ours to pieces with abuse, who think they cannot approach Sacred Theology

¶¶¶2 until

PDF 28

until they have called whole hundreds of petty questions into contest. Unless perhaps these men (as I strongly suspect, and grieve) are pursuing not, after all, Sacred Theology, which is an altogether divine science, but the smoke and shadow of Theology, having embraced a cloud for Juno, as the proverb has it.

But surely, you will say, St. Albert, surnamed the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas (to say nothing for the moment of St. John Damascene), St. Bonaventure too, and the other Theologians of the more recent age, Most Wise Men, admirable for counsel, maturity and character, Peter Lombard, Scotus, Alexander of Hales, were much given to disputation, and did not disdain laborious questions, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle: and because they often attributed very great authority to this Philosopher, no one could rightly reproach such great Men on that account, as though they were Philosophers of a lower bench and Theologians of little eloquence. Are not these things most certain, and set before the eyes of all, clearer than noonday itself ? I grant it. But since mention of this matter

has

PDF 29

has come up, and it calls for circumspect and well-considered speech, let us, if you please, pursue the matter in order.

As for St. Thomas (for of all the others I must speak afterwards), no mortal ever embraced more, none more skillfully, more learnedly, more temperately, none more briefly, all the things that seemed to bear upon Sacred Theology, or could in any way be referred to it. Immortal God! what genius the Man had! what abundance in disputation! how constant, how great his diligence in unrolling the volumes of the Sacred Page! how he revered the Holy Fathers of the Church! how incredible and almost divine that acumen of his altogether Angelic mind in discerning the most difficult things! what candor in writing, what method in teaching, what severity in judging! You might truly say (as Cicero had said before, in a matter not very unlike) that the books of St. Thomas Aquinas, and especially that Theological Summa, though all should roar against it, far and greatly surpass the libraries of all the Theologians, both in the abundance of the greatest matters and in the strength of authority. For St. Thomas

brought

PDF 30

brought into Theology, with his immortal and more than Sallustian brevity, more things, exceedingly learned and most worth knowing, than most others even desired. And this outstanding praise of St. Thomas as a Theologian remains, and will remain as long as learning is held in honor. But if at times (for I return to the point from which I had digressed) he is wont in disputing to attribute authority to Aristotle, he did so unwillingly indeed, where Sacred Doctrine was in question. Unless you would have it that so great a Man was so dull of wit, so inept too and heedless, that what he had deliberately laid down in the preceding pages, namely in Art. VIII of Quest. I, about diminishing the authority of all save that of divine revelation, made to the Apostles and Prophets who wrote the Canonical Books, he himself afterwards weakened on purpose by his own example. But if the question concerns St. Thomas not as Theologian but plainly as Philosopher, remember that it is not now that Thomas Aquinas, the light and ornament of the Church, but a Heathen Philosopher (lately made pious from impious), Aristotle by name, who is making trouble for you, a trouble which will amount to next to nothing.

For

PDF 31

For how few do not know that the Angelic Doctor did indeed purge the Peripatetic Philosophy, stained everywhere with six hundred errors, but that he did not on that account wish what remained to be firm, ratified, and in a word sacrosanct, except what unconquered reason urged? Where, then, are those who have so often arraigned us for attacking or injuring St. Thomas? Perverse men, for whom it would have been far better to have spent strenuous effort in reading St. Thomas, which is the last thing they do, than, sitting idle, out of utter sloth, to make a mockery and a jest of things they do not even touch, or at least do not grasp. But enough of this.

I come now to the rest: namely Sts. John Damascene, Antoninus, Albert, Bonaventure, Doctors most illustrious within the memory of man, Scotus, Hales (for the Bishop of Paris had been of another mind), do not spurn questions, that is, those doubtful controversies much agitated in the Schools, nor syllogisms, nor Aristotle. And do we, then, spurn them, or declare war on the disputations of the School? Assuredly

the

PDF 32

the thing speaks for itself: we too have humored our age, and our Masters, who are held in great esteem among our countrymen, embracing questions, syllogisms, and finally Aristotle himself, where he seemed to judge rightly; but all of it, as far as our strength and our want of skill allowed, soberly, prudently, temperately. For the very pursuit of brevity, which ought to have been our whole care and concern, would have compelled us to restrain the pen, even had it otherwise been worth the trouble to write much more, lest we overwhelm our young recruits.

And since we have set forth enough so far, by way of our defense, lest anyone (as usually happens) should take our silence for a bad conscience, it remains for us to add briefly something about the plan of our work. And first, we present to you a philosophy that is not the common one, set down in a style a little more polished than that in which it is commonly taught, and that both as concisely as could be done and also as plainly as possible, and complete in every respect: so that I would be persuaded that I had done something like a marvel, had not nearly everything come from all the best

Philosophers

PDF 33

Philosophers of the newer age, culled with great labor and likewise with the utmost fidelity. This alone I rightly claim for myself, judging that no ordinary diligence was needed even for that very task: and therefore that you, young men, will one day render me no small thanks, if not while I live, then at least when I am dead. For what? I turned over more than a hundred volumes, and not carelessly either, before I set my hand to writing these Elements. I surveyed everything with my own eyes; I resolved to grow pale over papers day and night, so as to provide for our Youth. What more? My leisure [if God, Best and Greatest, leaves any to those who labor without rest for Christ Jesus], my home in my sweet Country; money, a sum large enough, which I have spent; and, what mortals are wont to hold dearer, my reputation and the good opinion of my name (since I am arraigned before the ignorant crowd as guilty of overthrowing Philosophy and the ancestral religion of our forefathers): all these I have valued, to be sure, but only so far as to judge that your instruction and training were to be held of greater worth, or rather by far the greatest.

But in truth, it is a newer philosophy that I myself

¶¶*¶ bring

PDF 34

bring forward. And why should I not bring it forward? But it is wholly heretical, they say, and was long ago raised up from the lowest seats of Erebus and Orcus, such, namely, as is found among foreign nations, where

The guilds of flute-girls, the quack-druggists,

Beggars, actresses, buffoons, all that breed, while they indulge their own wit too freely, while they strive to overturn the Church of Christ from its foundations, as though about some other business, these very men, together with the Peripatetic School, corrupt, ruin and go about to destroy the orthodox faith, the Christian religion, and the morals held most holy for so many centuries now.

Is it so indeed? O splendid, watchful, excellent guardians of the Church! Of course Aristotle, whom you worship as the god of philosophy, was orthodox after all, he was outstanding in piety and religion. But what is the point of saying more about these things now? Each man, as a rule, defends his own philosophy, received from his forebears, as if it were some household gods, and would grieve most bitterly to see them attacked, conquered, plundered.

I warn and adjure you, therefore, young men, that none of you, from the course once begun of these Institutions and of the newer Philosophy,

be

Benito Jerónimo Feijóo, whom he holds up to ridicule on the ground that he had praised some of the Moderns named above without discrimination.

where truer things will not be at hand. Detractors of this stamp, querulous, difficult, more frivolous even than anyone could imagine men of mature mind to be, whom riding on a reed, and nuts, and odd-and-even no longer delight: these, I say, do not listen to. For they are tiresome and empty.

But if, finally, they object to us that it is useless for these extracts of ours to be published for the benefit of Youth, since other Institutions, already made public in print, are not lacking: let them show, I beg, where at length one may find (what we have long and much sought) a newer doctrine, in a manner not at all at odds with the Schools, and both very briefly delivered and also sufficiently plain, open, arranged in order, adorned, and (what matters most) likely to be useful in the rest of life (*).

It

It grieves me, though, that these Institutions of mine are to be printed in type that is smaller, and yet neither uniform nor elegant: a thing that has befallen me against my will and to my reluctance, owing to the poverty of the printing trade in this part of the world and to the shortness of time. But you will readily forgive, not a fault indeed, but the fact that the volumes display something unsightly and awkward, looking forward to more accurate, more correct, more handsome ones from day to day, if it please the Powers above, which I for my part promise you.

Go on, then, young men, as you have begun, and together with me render the greatest thanks you can to our most illustrious Lord Prelate of Michoacán, Don Luis Fernando de Hoyos y Mier: because, with most munificent benevolence toward us, he, a Man to be looked up to, brought his mind, lofty indeed and most ready for every good thing, to take singular and ever more diligent care of the order of studies in this Most Illustrious College of St. Francis de Sales; because he not only approved the Institutions of the newer philosophy, long since delivered to you by me from our Academic chair, but even celebrated them with praise; and because, most kindly

§. I.

The origin and progress of Philosophy from the creation of the

world to the coming of Christ our Lord.

hilosophy means the same as Study, or Love of Wisdom. “Wisdom, 1

P moreover, is (as Tully says, following the opinion of the ancients (a)) the

knowledge of things divine and human, and of the causes by which these

things are held together.” For in Philosophy, things pertaining both to God and to

other things placed outside God are examined, namely with the help of natural rea‐

son, and their causes are derived, by a well-ordered consequence complete according

to its own laws, from principles either altogether certain or highly probable. Those

who seek it are named Philosophers, a name retained all the more carefully ever since

the modest answer of Pythagoras, as we shall say later.

2 Adam, the first parent of mankind, is said to have received from Almighty

God, without any labor, a Philosophy complete in every respect. But when, as

Purchot says (b), for violating the law of God he

¶¶¶¶ had

(a) Bk. 2 of On Duties.

(b) In the Preface to his Institutiones Philosophicae, from which we have excerpted, with a few

changes, some things that pertain to this first part of the History of Philosophy, as also the rest from

p. 2

had been expelled from the garden of delights in which he had been placed, then, given over to the darkness of ignorance among the other penalties of sin to which he became subject, he dragged all his posterity with him into that darkness. Hence almost no traces of that excellent and heavenly gift remained in men’s minds, when some, shaking off the sloth of the rest, moved by admiration of the most beautiful things and taught by frequent observation of particular effects, which is called experience, set about restoring it from its foundations with every effort and zeal.

3 It is agreed among nearly all, moreover, that the study of natural science and of the liberal arts flourished above all in Greece; but what Diogenes Laertius says in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, that Philosophy was born in Greece just as men themselves were, is altogether foreign to the truth. For, to pass over what Josephus says (c), that the grandsons of Seth observed the order of the Heavens and the courses of the stars, “and, lest their discoveries should slip out of men’s knowledge, since Adam had foretold a general destruction of the World, the one by fire, the other by flood, set up two columns, one of brick, the other of stone, and carved their discoveries on both, so that if the brick one should perish in the flood, the stone one would survive and give men the means of learning”: to pass over these things, I say, which are commonly known (although they were for the most part unknown to the Heathen), no one will indeed deny that the Patriarchs and leaders of the Hebrews, such as Abraham, Moses and others, were instructed in the science of natural things, just like Solomon, King of the Jews, who, as the Sacred Scriptures testify (d), “treated about trees from the cedar that is in Libanus, unto the hyssop that cometh out of the wall: and he discoursed of beasts, and of fowls, and of creeping things, and of fishes.” This moreover is certain from the testimony of the Heathen themselves, that the Assyrians and Chaldeans were laudably versed in Astronomy, invited, namely, by the flat and open region they inhabited, from which they could freely observe the courses of the stars. Hence Tully (e) records that the Chaldeans excelled in the knowledge of the stars and in the shrewdness of their minds.

4 From the Assyrians and Chaldeans, moreover, as Josephus witnesses (f), Arithmetic was carried by Abraham to the Egyptians, who, compelled by necessity, likewise studied Geometry: since, as Proclus reports, the boundaries of their fields were so confounded by the annual flooding of the Nile that they could not afterwards be distinguished without Geometry.

5 Finally, from the Egyptians, at once to the Phoenicians and to the Greeks across

the

(d) Bk. III of Kings, ch. 4.

the sea, Geometry was carried; which Thales of Miletus, namely, learned in Egypt

and brought into Greece, as Diogenes Laertius himself narrates in his life.

6 Therefore we must not credit Philosophy to the Greeks alone: but just as

among them there arose men excelling in ingenuity and in the knowledge of natural

things, who were first called Wise Men, afterwards Philosophers, so the other nations

too had their own interpreters and teachers of truth: among the Hebrews, indeed,

the Rabbis; of Babylon and Assyria, the Chaldeans; among the Persians, the Magi;

among the Indians, the Brahmans, or Gymnosophists; nay, even on the shores of the

farthest East, among the Chinese, there were cultivators of the human disciplines and

of the liberal Arts, among whom Confucius is most celebrated, who is therefore

called the Chinese Philosopher. Likewise among the Egyptians the Hierophants flour‐

ished, and among the Gauls the Druids.

7 The chief glory of Philosophy, however, is attributed to the Greeks because

they applied themselves more diligently to each of its parts, and, having arranged it

as it were into a kind of body, handed it down to posterity in their Writings.

Wherefore the more illustrious sects of Philosophers, of which mention is made in

the Schools, are to be traced back to the Greeks.

§. II.

The More Illustrious Sects of Philosophers. 8

A sect, moreover, is a certain multitude of men which, in some way cut off and di‐

vided from others, follows a certain kind of doctrine under some Leader. Hence

it was named secta either from secando [cutting] or from sectando [following].

9 Further, the first Philosophers of the Greeks are divided into two sects, namely

the Dogmatic and the Academic.

10 The Dogmatic sect comprises those Philosophers who contend that they

have attained the truth, at least in most things; and it is in turn twofold, the Ionic

and the Italic.

11 The leader of the Ionic sect was Thales, called the Milesian, either because he

had as his native city Miletus, which is the capital City of Ionia, or because, al‐

though he was of Phoenician origin, he was enrolled, as some relate, among the

Citizens of Miletus. Apollodorus, in Diogenes Laertius’s life of him, records that he

was born in the first year of the 35th Olympiad, and died in the seventieth year of

his age. That first year of the 35th Olympiad, moreover, is the year 639 before the

common era of the Christians, and 3365 from the founding of the world. (*) Thales

was followed by Anaximander,

¶¶¶¶ 2 Anaximenes,

(*) An Olympiad is a space of four years. The first Olympiad was celebrated in the year of the

world 3250.

p. 4

Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Heraclitus, Democritus, and others, all of whom made the Philosophy of their master illustrious, and carried it down as far as Socrates and Plato.

12 The chief of the Italic sect was Pythagoras of Samos, who, having been a disciple of Pherecydes the Syrian, and having traveled through Egypt and Babylonia for the sake of acquiring learning, at length betook himself to Italy, in the time of Servius Tullius, King of the Romans; and at Croton, not far from Tarentum, he devoted himself to Philosophy for about twenty years; and having afterwards gone from there to Metapontum, as Justin testifies (g), he died there in the 4th year of the 70th Olympiad. By him the name of Philosopher was first used. For when, passing through the Peloponnese, he was asked by Leon, Tyrant of the Sicyonians, or of the Phliasians (Sicyon and Phlius, moreover, were cities of the Peloponnese), what he professed himself to be, he answered that he was a Philosopher, that is, one devoted to Wisdom; using, namely, a more modest appellation, says Diogenes Laertius in the Proem to the Lives of the Philosophers, in order to beat down the arrogance and pride of the Greeks, who proclaimed themselves Wise Men: because God alone can truly be called Wise, whereas men are rather to be named lovers of Wisdom than Wise.

13 Among others, the doctrines of Pythagoras were embraced by Timaeus of Locri, Archytas of Tarentum, Philolaus of Croton, Parmenides and Zeno, both of Elea, the latter of whom is called the author of Dialectic by Diogenes Laertius, and Melissus of Samos: all of whom gave their chief attention to Physics, or natural science, right up to the institution of the old Academy, whose Chief was Socrates; at which time the Philosophers, following the example of Socrates, turned their minds from Physical things to the science of morals.

14 The Academic sect took its name from the Academy, that is, from a wooded place situated in a suburb of Athens, which a noble hero, Academus by name, had consecrated to the exercises of the Philosophers. The Philosophers of this sect withheld all assent; they affirmed nothing whatever: and the sect itself was in turn divided into the old, the middle, and the new Academy.

15 The Chiefs of the old Academy were Socrates and his disciple Plato. Hence the old Academics were called by the same token Platonists, and also Sceptics, or Inquirers: because, although they judged truth to be unknown, they nevertheless did not despair of finding it, and therefore devoted themselves constantly to the inquiry after it. They were also called Pyrrhonists, from Pyrrho, an Academic.

16 Socrates was born in Attica in the 4th year of the 77th Olympiad, according to Diogenes Laertius in his life; that is, in the year of the world 3536 according to Ussher’s calculation. He died, however, in the 1st year of the 95th Olympiad, in the seventieth year of his age. “It was he who first, from things hidden (as Tully says (h)) and wrapped up by nature herself, in which, before him, all

the

(g) Bk. XX of the Histories, ch. 4.

(h) Academic Questions, bk. 1.

p. 5

the Philosophers had been occupied, called Philosophy away and brought it to common life, so that it should inquire about virtues and vices, and in general about good and evil things; and he held that heavenly things were either far removed from our knowledge, or, even if they were known as fully as possible, still contributed nothing to living well. In nearly all the discourses which were written down, variously and copiously, by those who heard him, he disputed in such a way that he affirmed nothing himself, refuted others, and said that he knew nothing, except that very thing.”

17 Crito, Aristippus, Cebes, Xenophon, Euclid and others were followers of Socrates. But among them all Plato the Athenian was eminent, who also succeeded Socrates in the Academy and, keeping to his method, affirmed nothing, but, as the same Tully says (i), “in his books many things are argued on both sides, everything is inquired into, nothing certain is said.” Plato, moreover, had among his other disciples Aristotle, afterwards the Chief of the Peripatetic sect, and his own adversary.

18 After the death of Plato and of Speusippus, the other successors of Socrates in the Academy cast off that timid method of philosophizing; and, having passed over to the party of the Dogmatics, they established a threefold Sect, that of the Peripatetics, of the Stoics, and of the Epicureans.

19 The Peripatetics glory in Aristotle as their master. He was born at Stagira, a town of Macedonia, about the year of the world 3621, namely in the first year of the 99th Olympiad, his father being Nicomachus and his mother Phaestis, and in his seventeenth year he heard Plato. When he had been trained in the Philosophical disciplines for full twenty years and his master had been taken from among the living, Aristotle betook himself to Hermias, tyrant of the Atarneans in Mysia; and having stayed with him for three years, he set out for Macedonia to instruct Alexander, and, after spending eight years with him, returned to Athens. Here, since he found Xenocrates, the successor of Speusippus, in the Academy, he chose for himself the Lyceum (a place in the suburb, which had been built by Pericles so that he himself might train newly levied soldiers in it in the arts of war); and since in that station he discoursed on philosophical matters while walking about, it came about that the School was called Peripatetic, from its custom of walking about.

20 Strabo is our authority (k), and the Writers of the History of Philosophy agree wonderfully with him on this, that Aristotle handed over his writings and his Library to his disciple Theophrastus, to whom he also left his School; and that Theophrastus likewise bequeathed by will both his own books and Aristotle’s to Neleus of Scepsis, who had been a hearer of him and of Aristotle, as Diogenes Laertius testifies (l). Neleus, therefore, carried that Library over to the town of Scepsis, and at his death left it to his heirs, unlearned men. But they, when they learned of the zeal of the Attalid Kings, to whom Scepsis

was

(k) Bk. 13 of the Geography.

(l) In the life of Theophrastus.

p. 6

was subject, in seeking out books from every quarter to furnish the Library of Pergamum, buried their own in the ground lest they be carried off; and there they lay a long time, abandoned and, as it were, entombed. At length, dug up by the successors of those men, damaged and gnawed by damp and by moths, they were sold for a great sum of money to Apellicon of Teos, a man more devoted to books than to learning. Apellicon, for his part, after an unskilled restoration of the eaten-away parts, transcribed the books into new copies, which nevertheless still teemed with very many faults, and with very many gaps also left unfilled.

21 But immediately after the death of Apellicon his library, which was at Piraeus, was carried off by L. Sulla, as Plutarch records in his life, and taken to Rome, where a certain Grammarian, Tyrannio, asked to be allowed the use of the Aristotelian books; and, having obtained this permission, he himself corrupted a great many things in them, and shared copies with a certain Andronicus of Rhodes, by whom, after they had been likewise interpolated, they were at length brought out into the light. From this it is more than sufficiently clear that the books of Aristotle were wretchedly defiled and full of gaps in many places, so that no one can affirm for certain which are the words of Aristotle himself, and what Apellicon supplied, what Tyrannio and Andronicus. Whoever wishes to know more of this, let him read Stanley (m). We pass on to the rest.

22 The Leader of the Stoics was Zeno of Citium, that is, a native of Citium, a town of Cyprus, who at Athens, in the Portico, taught the doctrines of a severer Philosophy, with great celebrity of name, about the 130th Olympiad.

23 The Epicureans were so called from Epicurus, the Patron of this sect, who in the gardens where he held his gatherings expounded the tenets of Democritus, which he had made his own. He died in the second year of the 127th Olympiad, in the year 3735 after the founding of the world, having lived 72 years. Lucretius, twelve years younger than Cicero, wrote out the Philosophy of Epicurus in Latin verses divided into six books. Epicurus is censured by Tully (n) for having despised Logic, but far most of all because “he tore Religion up by the roots from the minds of men, abolishing it, together with the immortal Gods, in reality, while leaving the Gods in words.” We add this one thing: that the School of Epicurus lasted, in a continuous succession and with a rare agreement, down to the age of Augustus, fourteen Masters filling a space of 237 years.

24 Meanwhile, however, the method of Socrates had been revived by Arcesilaus about the 120th Olympiad, whence he himself is named the Chief of the second, or middle, Academy. He, moreover, added this to the opinion of Socrates: that he not only affirmed with Socrates that nothing is known, but contended that nothing whatever can even be known. Hence the new Academics were also called Acataleptics, as if you were to say, men who professed that they could comprehend nothing at all.

On the Eclectic Philosophy, and on Philosophy after the Birth of

Christ.

26

T his Philosophy is called Eclectic by the Greeks, Elective by the Latins. This man‐

ner of philosophizing is explained by Clement of Alexandria when, after dis‐

coursing at length in praise of Philosophy, he adds that he had declared all this not of

the Stoic Philosophy, nor of the Platonic, nor of the Epicurean or the Aristotelian;

but whatever things have been rightly said by these sects, which teach justice togeth‐

er with pious knowledge, this whole selection, he says, he calls Philosophy (o). As if

(as Stanley adds (p)) “he judged the study of those who do not hesitate superstitiously

to swear by the words of a single master not worthy even of the name of Philosophy.”

The Eclectics, namely, imitate the bees, which (these are Seneca’s words (q)) “wander

about and pluck the flowers fit for making honey, then arrange whatever they have

brought in, and distribute it through the combs, and, as Virgil says:

……………………the liquid honey

They pack, and swell the cells with sweet nectar.”

27 The Chief of this Philosophy was Potamon of Alexandria, and this manner of

philosophizing (for this method of philosophizing cannot come under the name of a

Sect) had hearers who had won illustrious fame. Men renowned for Holiness also

strove to defend the Eclectic philosophy with especial zeal, foremost among them

Clement of Alexandria and Gregory Thaumaturgus, having professed it, namely, for

no other reason “than that they might draw from many sects the truth which could

not be found in one”; which Lactantius intimates, affirming at the same time that “all

those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discov‐

eries of their forefathers, and, like cattle, by others

are

(q) Letter 85.

p. 8

are led; nor do they think it possible either that they themselves should be wiser, because they are called the younger, or that those others should have been foolish, because they are named the elders (r).”

28 In the following ages after the coming of Christ, the doctrine of Plato always held first place until about the eighth century of the Church, and very many of the Holy Fathers consecrated their study and their vigils to it. Among the Latin Fathers it was most diligently cultivated by St. Augustine, who, being of a most penetrating wit, illustrated it in many parts and happily employed it to refute the errors of the Heathen and to assert the truth of the Christian Religion.

29 As for the Aristotelian Philosophy, it is certain that in the first ages of the Church it never held any dominion; nay rather, the Holy Fathers derided it with countless reproaches. These may be read in the celebrated Petavius (s). Their file is led by St. Justin Martyr (or whatever other Christian Doctor wrote the book entitled The Overthrow of Certain Aristotelian Doctrines). Clement of Alexandria follows, writing thus (t): “But it will not be irksome to recall also the Peripatetics, the father of whose sect, understanding nothing about that Father who is Supreme, teaches very many errors.” Irenaeus, Bishop of Lyons (u), refutes two things received from Aristotle, namely hair-splitting talk and subtlety, by which the simplicity and candor of the Christian Faith are corrupted. This very thing is censured in Aristotle by Origen (x), Lactantius Firmianus (y), Eusebius of Caesarea (z), Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria (a), Basil (b), Gregory of Nyssa (c), Ambrose (d), John Chrysostom (e), Augustine (f), and Jerome (g), who testifies that the Arian heresy borrows the streams of its argumentations from the fountains of Aristotle; which St. Ambrose (h) also confirms, saying: “For thus we know that the Arians rushed headlong into perfidy: they abandon the Apostle,

they

p. 9

they follow Aristotle.” Gregory Nazianzen too (i) laments that the captious arguments of the sophists and the depraved artifice of the Aristotelian art had crept into the Church like certain Egyptian plagues. St. Augustine addresses the Pelagians thus (k): “Your heresy has been brought to this, that your followers groan that no Dialectician Judges from the Schools of the Peripatetics are to be found in the Church by whom you might be acquitted.” St. Vincent Ferrer exclaims querulously (l) that Aristotle and Averroes were vials of the wrath of God poured out upon the waters of Christian wisdom, whence they were made bitter as wormwood. Whoever wishes more, let him read the celebrated Guido Grandi. Let us follow our History.

30 The Western Provinces, meanwhile, presented a far different face of things. For the Arabs, toward the end of the eighth century and the beginning of the ninth, having previously subdued very extensive regions and obtained dominion far and wide through Africa and Spain, revived the doctrine of Aristotle, rendered from Greek into Arabic and from Arabic into Latin and illustrated with commentaries, and brought it into the public schools; and this system indeed held them for nearly five hundred years, the understanding of the Greek and Latin languages being almost buried along with it. This method of philosophizing, brought by the Arabs into Spain, migrated to the English and the French and was spread far and wide; then the eloquent and richer style of Plato’s discourse began to be neglected and dialectical acumen to flourish, the interpreters of Aristotle zealously pursuing a subtle, minute, contentious, excessively talkative manner of discoursing: among whom are reckoned as chief Avicenna, Alfarabi, Alkindi, but easily the prince of all Averroes of Córdoba, called by the singular title of the Commentator. Hence was born the disputatious and contentious Philosophy, which brought barbarism of speech with it into the Schools, and was called Scholastic, because it has been in use in the Schools down to our own times; although it has met with varied fortune at different times, and if I had a mind to draw out my discourse on it at greater length, whole volumes of Brucker and others would have to be copied out by me; we shall, however, touch on some chief points.

31 In the year 1209, by Decree of the Council of Paris, the principal books of Aristotle were burned and the reading of them forbidden. In the year 1591 Francesco Patrizi urges Gregory XIV to remove the Philosophy of Aristotle from the Schools of Christians. Afterwards Peter Ramus defended Theses at Paris against the doctrine of Aristotle. Then John Pico della Mirandola attempted to restore the Pythagorean Philosophy, Bessarion and Marsilio Ficino the Platonic, Caspar Scioppius the Stoic, Bernardino Telesio that which is called the Parmenidean.

32 Some establish Lanfranc, Archbishop of Canterbury, as the Founder of the Scholastic Philosophy. Others, among them Naudé, trace its first origin back to St. John Damascene, from whom it came down to the Latins,

¶¶¶¶¶ Peter

(i) Oration 26.

(k) Against Julian, bk. 6.

(l) In the celebrated Grandi, in the Diacrisis against the Philosophia Novo-Antiqua.

p. 10

Peter Abelard and his disciple Peter Lombard. It is divided into three ages, of which the first, in the opinion of some, began about the middle of the eleventh century and was carried down to the middle of the twelfth. At that time there flourished Abelard; Lombard, called the Master of the Sentences because he expounded the sentences collected from the ancient Fathers; Gilbert de la Porrée, Peter Comestor, and John of Salisbury. The second period runs to about the year 1330; it was made illustrious by the geniuses of Albert the Great, St. Thomas Aquinas, and St. Bonaventure. The third lasted until letters and the arts were restored; in which age Durandus, Ockham, and Cardinal Pierre d’Ailly were renowned.

33 Among the Scholastics, or new Peripatetics, three more illustrious sects are reckoned: namely those of the Thomists, the Scotists, and the Nominalists. The first follow as their leader St. Thomas, born in the year 1224 in the Castle of Aquino, who afterwards professed the Rule of the Order of Preachers, and on account of the purity of his morals and the excellence of his doctrine was justly and deservedly distinguished with the title of the Angelic Doctor. Among the Thomists are celebrated Dominic of Flanders, Francisco de Vitoria, the Most Illustrious Melchor Cano, Domingo de Soto, Medina and very many others, whom it would take long to recount.

34 The second School acknowledges as its chief John Duns, who, whether he was a Scot by country (a surname that is still given to him even now and is carried over to the sect founded by him), or was born at Dunstan in Northumberland, or in the village of Duns in Ulster (for the Writers are not agreed about this), entered the Order of Minors and flourished chiefly at the beginning of the fourteenth century. His subtle wit, and the Wisdom answering to it, brought forth the title of Subtle Doctor; and both together brought it about that, while he held the Theological Chair at Oxford, thirty thousand Scholars and more flocked together to hear him. Among the followers of Scotus there excelled Francis of Meyronnes, who had received the doctrine while his Master was still living, John Punch, Bartholomew Mastrius, Martin Meurisse, and Claude Frassen, a celebrated Scotist, who was taken from among the living in the eleventh year of this century (m).

35 The third sect is that of the Nominalists, who contended that names and words are the object of Logic, and whose Doctor was William of Ockham, English by nation, of the Order of Friars Minor, and a disciple of Scotus. The Scholastics are also divided into Realists and Nominalists. The matter of this disagreement, moreover, was furnished by the treatment of universals, since the former contended that universal natures exist, as it were, in reality, while the latter affirmed that they are constituted only in words.

§. IV.

(m) Wadding, in the Bibliotheca Minorum.

p. 11

§ . I V.

Innovators in Philosophy who Revived the Ancient Doctrine.

36

A bout the middle of the seventeenth century Galileo, the excellent

Mathematician of the Grand Duke of Tuscany (n), shook off the yoke of the

custom grown inveterate in the Schools and tried new paths. Following in his

footsteps, very many Men outstanding in learning restored the Mechanical

philosophy.

37 Pierre Gassendi, Royal Professor of Mathematics in the Academy of Paris,

was born in the year 1562. He put together a system of the Epicurean Philosophy,

rejecting those things which could not well be reconciled with Religion. And in‐

deed the tenets of Epicurus as emended by him so commended themselves to

the Learned that from this eminent restorer the Gassendist sect arose.

38 Certain men devised a new kind of Philosophy, called the Philosophy of

the Christians. Of their number is Thomas Burnet in the Sacred Theory of the Earth,

where he busies himself with interpreting Moses, but most wretchedly distorts

the Mosaic narrative. To him must be joined the Theory of Whiston; both of

these, however, were refuted by learned Men. To the same class belong Edmund

Dickinson in his Physica vetus et nova, and John Comenius in his Physica ad lumen

divinum reformata. His hypotheses were for the most part retained by Johann

Bayer in the Work entitled Ostium et atrium naturae.

39 At this point mention must now be made of the restored Philosophy of

the Chemists, and of those who as it were dug it out of the ashes, cultivated it,

and rendered this discipline Experimental, by laboriously scrutinizing nature, sub‐

jecting bodily things to trials, and putting useful experience in place of the sterile

speculations of others. That the origin of metallurgical Chemistry is most an‐

cient is shown, among others, by the celebrated Boerhaave (o). Paracelsus is said

to have revived the Chemical art, chiefly among the Germans, whence he is also

called the Father of the Chemists. That part of this discipline which comprises met‐

allurgy was cultivated, after Georg Agricola, by Lazarus Ercker, Joachim Becher

and Johann Kunckel. Chemistry was made useful to Medicine and Physics by

Boyle, Slare, Homberg, Geoffroy, Lémery the Younger, Hoffmann, and the cele‐

brated Hermann Boerhaave, who brings forward these and others.

¶¶¶¶¶ 2 §. V.

(n) Born at Pisa in the year 1564.

(o) Elements of Chemistry, vol. 1, pt. 1, On the History of the Art.

p. 12

§ . V.

The Newer Eclectic Philosophy, with Bacon of Verulam as its

Author.

40

O f the newer Eclectic Philosophy, namely of that which has gained not only ap‐

provers but also cultivators, the parent is held to be Francis Bacon of Verulam,

born in England in the year 1561. Others throughout England, stirred by the lead of

this Man, cultivated the Philosophy sketched and shaped by him. The chief were

Boyle, Wilkins, Willis, Christopher and Matthew Wren, from whom the Royal

Society of England took its origin, founded under Royal auspices in the year 1660.

And this Eclectic manner of philosophizing held sway among the English almost

until the times of Newton, by whose authority it passed into a sectarian one.

41 The same thing happened in France: for Descartes, born in the year 1569, af‐

ter he had passed through the philosophical course in the College of La Flèche and

had completed journeys through various provinces, published the system of his

doctrine that he had worked out, and found adversaries by far the fiercest, but also

adherents and vigorous champions, who, spread far and wide, formed a sect named

Cartesian from the name of its Author. Among these the chief are held to be

François Bayle, Antoine Le Grand, Jacques Rohault, Nicolas Malebranche, D. de

Molières, Hartsoeker, Purchot and others. This, however, must here be noted: that

by the lead, or the example, or the counsel of Descartes the manner of philosophiz‐

ing was changed, and the Mechanical sect flourished.

42 In England, as far as the Cartesian manner of philosophizing had penetrated,

another Philosophy was inaugurated by Isaac Newton, who was brought into the

light in the forty-second year of the last century; and it afterwards passed into a

sectarian one, and is today defended with great zeal by very many. That eminent

Man, namely, rejecting the hypotheses of Descartes and conjectures of every kind,

established new rules of philosophizing, holding that nothing ought to be admitted

in Philosophy except what either experiments or reasons invincibly demonstrate.

He set out the foundations of his doctrine partly in the excellent work which he

entitled Mathematical Principles of Philosophy, illustrated with Commentaries by the

most celebrated Le Seur and Jacquier, partly in the Opticks. In these he everywhere

uses the greatest moderation, professing that natural things are considered by him

only mathematically, and that their physical causes are not inquired into: wherefore

he made use of certain general terms, by which he designated abstract notions after

the manner of Geometers.

43 This sect numbers celebrated Men, men who for their skill in experimenting

and

p. 13

and in making calculations are especially illustrious: so that it is for this reason called

Newtonian from the name of its Author, but Mathematical on account of its method of

treatment. It is pleasing, for honor’s sake, to name in particular Keill, Roger Cotes, ’s

Gravesande, Musschenbroek, Clarke, MacLaurin, Jurin, Desaguliers, Krafft; and, to

say nothing of others, the theory of Newton finds plain favor with the more recent

Astronomers.

44 In Germany an Eclectic-Exotic kind of Philosophy unfolded itself through

Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, born at Leipzig in the year 1646. He praised the

Scholastics’ manner of philosophizing; and, having undertaken to restore to its for‐

mer standing their authority, hitherto shaken and all but trampled underfoot, he also

touches in his works on what pertains to rational and moral Philosophy; but he ac‐

complished greater things in the higher Mathematics.

45 He published a natural Philosophy mixed with the principles of Descartes,

comprising it in two little books, a New Physical Hypothesis and a Theory of Abstract

Motion; he was, moreover, the first to lay down the distinction of forces into living

and dead, and to teach that the former must be estimated in a far different way from

the latter. In Metaphysics he showed himself exotic in the highest degree, by intro‐

ducing the principle of sufficient reason, asserting monads and a pre-established harmony,

and defending the perfection of the world far too much. The principles of Leibniz were

cultivated by Christian Wolff, famous in this our age for the volumes he has pub‐

lished, in which he comprised universal Mathematics, Logic, Metaphysics, Ethics and

Physics. I do not care to list the adherents of either of the two, since they have nei‐

ther greatly distinguished themselves by their writings nor propagated the doctrine

more widely.

§. VI.

The Efforts of the Moderns in Cultivating the Parts of Philosophy.

46

I t remains for us now to weave together the history of those who, after the restora‐

tion of the study of letters, whether within private walls or by the combined

labors of many, emended and illustrated particular parts of Philosophy. In doing this,

the names chiefly of the Moderns will be brought forward, including those Authors

whom we have so far placed in no sect; at the same time, however, it will be neces‐

sary to recall to mind those also whose efforts have already been made plain before.

47 Rational Philosophy, besides Lorenzo Valla, Rudolph Agricola, Juan Luis Vives,

Bacon, Descartes, Gassendi and Hobbes, whom their differing periods set apart,

some more widely, others less, was taken up for emendation by Peter Ramus, born in

France in the year 1515, with such success that the Ramist Dialectic commended itself

exceedingly to many

on

p. 14

on this account, that, rejecting empty subtleties, it referred that discipline to the use of the courts and of life, and above all to the reading of the ancient Writers. Hence it came about that it gained both numerous disciples and eminent men as patrons: in France, Omer Talon; in Germany, Franz Fabricius, Sturm, Chytraeus.

48 Among the Cartesian Writers on Logic there stand out the Author of the Art of Thinking (L’Art de penser), whether he was Arnauld or someone else (p), and Malebranche, who treated at length the art of seeking the truth. There were also those who deduced the precepts of Logic from Mathematical principles; a work of this kind was published by Erhard Weigel, entitled in this form: Analysis Aristotelica ex Euclide restituta, etc. Likewise Walther von Tschirnhaus, in the book whose title is Medicina mentis. To the same class belongs the Logic of Christian Wolff, which he composed by the Mathematical method, illustrated with higher examples. Those Writers on Logic who seem to deserve the name of Eclectics are generally reckoned to be these: John Locke; Christian Thomasius; Mariotte; Poiret; Jean Le Clerc; Jean- Pierre de Crousaz; Andreas Rüdiger; Fortunato da Brescia; Antonio Genovesi; the celebrated Luís António Verney, who also published at Valencia a Method of Studying under the feigned name of Father Barbadiño; Honoré Fabri, Dominique Buffier, Noël Regnault, Cochet, and others.

49 Metaphysics and Logic, since they lend each other mutual service, have been joined together by most of the authors of Logic just indicated. Morhof says that Descartes and Honoré Fabri were reformers of Metaphysics; he then brings forward Henry More’s Enchiridion Metaphysicum and Thomas White’s Euclides Metaphysicus, and in the latter he censures the method. Finally, he commends the little book of Juan Luis Vives On First Philosophy. As for others, a great many may be counted who treated parts of this discipline. Ontology, Cosmology, Psychology and natural Theology were expounded in ample volumes by Wolff, following the doctrine of Leibniz. Nor were the studies of others lacking, although they pursued these several subjects in a somewhat different way, and also less expressly. Among the rest there were renowned Clauberg, Du Hamel, Le Grand, Régis, Buddeus, Le Clerc, Purchot, Corsini, Cudworth, Clarke, Nieuwentyt, Derham, and all those who, by fighting against the Atheists, deserved best of natural Theology. To their number must be joined, more recently, the celebrated Antonio Genovesi. The doctrine, moreover, of first truths, as a particular part of Metaphysics, was unfolded as vigorously as it was elegantly and skillfully by the celebrated Verney and by Father Buffier.

50 But some have abused this most excellent and most useful part of Philosophy, while either, granting too much to the soul and to ideas, they rushed headlong into

Idealism,

(p) Some say the Author of this work is Nicole, others D. de Trigny, others several men of Port- Royal.

p. 15

Idealism and Egoism, like fanatics and enthusiasts; or while, on the opposite side, not separating the mind from the affection of the body, and wrongly disparaging the excellence of the noblest being, they entangled themselves in the foul error of Materialism. Most impudently, and at the same time most unskillfully of all, this matter was handled by Benedict Spinoza, whom one may call an abortive vagabond of Philosophy, and something viler than a man.

51 Many increased moral Philosophy by their writings, but not all advanced it equally as its dignity deserved. For Hobbes and Spinoza indeed contaminated this doctrine with principles full of poison. As for the rest, namely Montaigne, Grotius, Pufendorf, Buddeus, Selden, Heineccius, Cumberland, Wolff and others, what is to be thought of them beginners must necessarily learn from their own masters in this discipline. Here again the most learned Buffier performed excellent service, comprising a treatise On Civil Society in four books, to which he added his remarks on the moral doctrine of Aristotle, Cicero, Gassendi, Pufendorf, Silvain Régis, Pierre Charron and the Scholastics. The Ethical precepts of the rest, such as Du Hamel, Purchot and Corsini, are in any case in everyone’s hands. Likewise the celebrated Genovesi comprised Moral philosophy in the Work entitled Diceosina: ovvero Filosofia del Giusto, e dell’Onesto.

52 The Mathematical disciplines, bound to Physics by an intimate agreement and serviceable to the life and society of men, have been cultivated by a great many of the Moderns. It is by no means our purpose to review them one by one, since we know that this has been done, among others, by the celebrated Wolff (r). We shall bring forward only the chief ones, and those who cannot be unknown to a Philosopher.

53 And of Astronomy, indeed, there were eminent restorers in the fifteenth century of Christ: Georg Peurbach; Johann Regiomontanus; Copernicus; Tycho Brahe, famed for his arrangement of the world system; Kepler, Galileo; Huygens; Hevelius; de la Hire; Newton; Cassini, etc. It would take long to bring together all those who developed the various parts of Mathematics. Among others, these too claim a place here: Christopher Clavius, Paul Guldin, Scheiner, Grimaldi, Claude Milliet de Chales, Riccioli, D. de la Caille, D. Clairaut, Guido Grandi, Father Cametti, Abbot of Vallombrosa, and D. La Lande, who last of all, but above all, has treated of Astronomical matters.

54 Finally, with how great accessions the Studious searchers of Nature have enriched natural Philosophy cannot be defined in a few words. For who could comprise in a page the manifold discoveries, the perfection added to the discoveries of the ancients, the number, manner and elegance of the experiments, and in them the accuracy, the attention, the selection? We shall briefly sketch both the restorers of Physics and the new form of this discipline.

After

(r) Elem. of Mathematics, vol. V.

p. 16

§. VII

55 After those already named before, namely Bacon, Gassendi and Descartes,

there followed exceedingly illustrious Men: Galileo of Florence. He undertook to

treat the doctrine of motion by a clear method; he demonstrated the weight of the

air, or held up a light to the others for discovering it; to him is also attributed the dis‐

covery of the Astronomical telescope, of the sunspots, and of the Satellites of Jupiter,

although others will have it that the former were detected earlier by Father Scheiner,

the latter by Simon Marius.

56 This master of his was followed in advancing Physics by Evangelista Torricelli,

from whom the use of tubes adapted to measuring the weight of the air took its ori‐

gin. What shall I say of the remaining discoverers and discoveries? Andrea Cesalpino,

Chief Physician to Clement VIII, Supreme Pontiff, illustrated Physics by having de‐

tected, or explained, the circulation of the blood, although the English attribute this

to Harvey, others to the Spaniard Gómez Pereira, others to others.

57 Pecquet, in the last century, first detected the receptacle of the Chyle. And

how much did others toil in the various parts of natural science? Boyle, Digby,

Homberg, Lémery, Boerhaave in Chemistry; Grew, Sam. Morland, Camerarius,

Vaillant, Morison, Hermann, Ray, Rivinus, Tournefort, Linnaeus in Botany? Indeed

Mariotte, by means of trials made on motion, on plants, waters, colors, etc.; Pascal,

by investigating the weight of the air and weighing the equilibrium of liquids;

Newton, by his optical observations and the bringing of Geometry over to natural

science; Otto Guericke, by the invention of the air pump, won great light for Physics

and for themselves a matching name in the republic of letters. To say nothing now of

the efforts of Richer, of both Cassinis, of Picard, Maraldi, Maupertuis and his

Companions; of the microscopical secrets of Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Power,

Hartsoeker, etc.; of the Electrical experiments of Jallabert, Watson, Waitz, Bose,

Nollet, Musschenbroek, Franklin, Beccaria, Paulian; of the various studies of

Hauksbee, Fermat, Carré, Petit, Sauveur, Malézieu, Ramazzini, Dodart, Santorio,

Feuillée, Hales, Cotes, Ozanam, Desaguliers, Borelli, Malpighi, Redi, both Bernoullis,

Varignon, Hermann, Bülfinger, Poleni, Euler, Grandi, Teichmeyer, Krafft, Verdries,

Sturm, Wolff, and very many others, whose memory will very often recur in the

Physics.

The Academies of Sciences, Usefully Established.

58

F urther, how great are the accessions that natural Philosophy owes to the

Academies of Sciences, not one of the learned is unaware. Nor

is

p. 17

is it our intention, however, while we present these, to list all the Gymnasia and public Schools established in various places from Charlemagne onward; still less does it please us to enumerate the private little gatherings of a few, which were, namely, of short life and hardly fitted for the public utility. The name of Academy was given, while Paul II, Supreme Pontiff, governed the Church, to the College of those residing at Rome who had undertaken some restoration of the fallen ancient learning.

59 In the same city celebrated Academies afterwards opened, namely: that of the Humorists, founded by Paolo Mancini, a Roman nobleman, so called from the rain falling from the clouds, because this was their Emblem, with the motto Redit agmine dulci [it returns in a sweet stream]. The other was that of the Lynxes; they took this name from the gift of the Lynx, which excels in sight, so as to intimate their perspicacity in scrutinizing the works of nature; and this Academy, founded either by Federico Cesi or by Angelo, son of Federico, cultivated chiefly Chemistry, and produced illustrious men, Galileo Galilei, Fabio Colonna, and others. There were likewise several Colleges at Rome, such as those of the Ordinati, the Delfici, the Incitati, the Partenii, the Rinnovati, etc. (s); at Venice the Veneta Academy flourished, and also another, of the Incogniti. At Padua the Academy of the Eterei took its origin from Scipione Gonzaga; another comprised the Animosi Academicians. Nor did the other parts of Italy lack their Academies: at Naples, Siena, Ravenna, Ferrara, Verona, Milan, Bologna, etc.

60 In Tuscany, at Florence, besides the Academy of the Bran-Sifters, or della Crusca (so named because in their disputations the Academicians separated the purer flour, namely the food of minds, from the bran, that is, from errors, being nevertheless intent with their chief care on imparting elegance to the Italian language), there shone forth the Experimental Academy, or del Cimento, by the munificence of Leopold, Grand Duke of Tuscany: by which it came about both that outstanding Philosophers were associated in it, and that spirit, aids and opportunities for setting up experiments were furnished to the Academicians. Britain followed the example when, about the year 1663, the Royal Society of England was erected at London by the authority of King Charles II. France, stirred by the rise of the Academies of Italy and England, and moved also by the happy successes of her own (namely of the French Academy (Académie Françoise), instituted in the year 1637 by Louis XIII through the agency of Cardinal Richelieu, and likewise of the other Academy, of Sculpture and Painting, which unfolded itself in 1664), saw the Academy of Sciences born under the auspices of King Louis XIV in the year 1666, which in the year 1699 received a new rule by the King’s will. In Germany, although a beginning of the German College of the Curious of Nature was made in the year 1652, it must nevertheless be confessed that it long remained stuck in its infancy, on account of the distance between its Colleagues, the lack of patrons, etc.

¶¶¶¶¶¶ 61 For

(s) Giovanni Ferro, in the Theater of Emblems.

p. 18

§. VIII

61 For this reason the Emperor Leopold the Great in 1670 added spurs to the

Academicians, holding out to them the hope of his patronage, so that they might de‐

vote their efforts to promoting this business. And indeed the studies of the Academy

of the Curious of Nature answered the wishes of so great a Prince; for in that same

year, namely 1670, they began to publish the Miscellanea Curiosa. In the year 1690 an

Academy of Philosophers was formed at Bologna, who were to share among them‐

selves the sciences pertaining to Mathematics and Physics; it afterwards, in the year

1712, took on another face through the favor and gifts of Count Marsigli, and was

named the Institute of Sciences and Arts of Bologna. Frederick, King of Prussia, estab‐

lished the Academy of Berlin; Peter, Emperor of Muscovy, that of Petersburg. In our

own Spain, moreover, besides the Royal Academy of Seville and the Cantabrian, there

is no lack of others for the cultivation and increase of the Sciences and Arts. Now,

what and how great advantages have flowed, chiefly into Physics, from the

Academies established by the favor, liberality and care of Princes, and what are to be

expected hereafter, is easily seen. The former the books of the Physicists declare; the

latter the industry, sagacity and ardor of the Academicians promise.

The Institution of Literary Journals.

62

W hat, finally, do we judge it to be that the newer Physics owes to the institution

of Journals, or literary acts? In the sixty-fifth year of the last century (for be‐

fore this the learned world lacked these aids) a man of great mind and most zealous

for the promotion of letters, Monsieur Sallo, Senator of the Supreme Court at Paris,

formed the plan of preparing universal Journals; this he himself also first carried out,

and he entitled the work Diarium Eruditorum (Journal des Sçavans). In the year 1666

the celebrated Gallois took over the author’s labor, laboriously compiling the Journal

continuously week by week up to the year 1674; and it was afterwards carried on by

the celebrated de la Roque. The History and Memoirs of the Royal Academy of

Sciences (Histoire & Mémoires de l’Académie des Sciences) are communicated annually to

the learned world.

63 Next, in the first year of this century, under the auspices of the Duke of

Maine, the Acta Trivoltiensia (Mémoires de Trévoux, pour servir à l’Histoire des Sciences, &

des beaux Arts) began to appear. Italy too, in the year 1668, published learned Journals

(Giornale de’ Letterati). In Germany certain men of letters from the Electorate of

Saxony, with joint labor, produced about the year 1682 the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig,

or Journals. Holland, not suffering its own industry to be found wanting here,

brought out at Amsterdam in the year 1684 the Excerpta Reipublicae Literariae

(Nouvelles de la République des lettres).

64 In

p. 19

64 In the thirteenth year of this present century the Diarium Literarium (Journal Litteraire à la Haye) appeared at The Hague, several men joining their labors. I pass over the transactions of the English Society (Transactions Philosophiques), published from the year 1665; the Literary Journals of Great Britain at the beginning of this century; the Bibliotheca Germanica, published in the year 1720, or the literary History of Germany and its Regions. In the year 1737 there began to be brought out in our Spain el Diario de los Literatos, an excellent work indeed; and would that it had been carried on down to this day.

65 Nor do I mention the Acta of the Institute of Bologna, the Petersburg and the Swedish, the Learned Mercuries (les Mercures Sçavans), etc. In this class must be placed the monuments of those who have collected the History of nature; the way being led (after the example of Aristotle and other more ancient writers) by Gaius Plinius Secundus, or the Elder, who, famous in the age of Vespasian and Titus, compiled thirty-seven books of natural History; he was followed by Solinus and Dioscorides; likewise by Claudius Aelian, author of seventeen books of the History of animals, in the time of the Emperor Hadrian. With these, I say, leading the way, the following treated this subject: Conrad Gesner, born in Switzerland in the year 1516, a distinguished Physicist and Philologist, and for this reason given the surname of the German Pliny, who, besides other things, comprised a History of animals in four volumes; Rembert Dodoens, born in Brabant in 1517, Physician to the Emperors Maximilian II and Rudolph II, famous for the Histories he published of plants, flowers, etc.; Ulisse Aldrovandi, celebrated for having written a natural Dendrology, a Museum metallicum, a history of Monsters, of Serpents, and also of Dragons.

66 To these must be added Bacon’s Sylva sylvarum, or Ten Centuries of natural History, and the Works on Natural History of M. de Buffon (Description du Cabinet du Roy). What Physics in particular owes to these aids too, there is no leisure to relate one by one. For how many heads of this science have been called into examination? How many phenomena of nature discovered? How many errors wiped from minds, doubts uprooted, opinions emended? These things are treated at greater length by Regnault, who shows diffusely that Physics has in these last centuries been rendered more perfect in every part: I. By bringing the conjectures of the ancients to examination. II. By scrutinizing nature itself. III. By treating the discipline according to the laws of method. IV. By requiring observations, repeating experiments, inventing useful instruments. V. By establishing Academies. VI. By instituting Journals.

67 And with this it has pleased us to conclude the History of Philosophy: which indeed, if you compare it with the lengthy works of Laertius, Gassendi, Horn, Stanley, Jonsius, Vossius and Brucker, you will understand to be nothing other than an Epitome; you will find it, however, arranged on this principle, that the chief heads of this subject have been treated thoroughly, the rest touched upon, and, finally, nothing omitted of those things which pertain to, and suffice for, the first instruction of Philosophers.

PA RT I . ELEMENTS OF LOGIC
