ELEMENTS

O F T H E N E W E R P H I L O S O P H Y.

P RO L E G O M E N A .

hilosophy, whose principal parts we shall set forth as it were in a nut1

P shell, is the knowledge of the true, the good and the honorable, acquired by

the light of nature alone and by reasoning drawn from it. Reasoning, or

right reason, is the ready faculty of eliciting truths from other truths with

which they are connected. From this it is easily seen that Sceptical philosophy,

since it professes that nothing can be known with certainty, does not deserve

the name of Philosophy, whereas Dogmatic philosophy does.

2 Nor is it obscure that this name is not to be attributed to a knowledge of

the true and the good which we have either received from our elders, handed

down from hand to hand, or draw from the precepts of some learned man.

Hence Traditionary and Sectarian Philosophy are banished, since neither of them

is derived from right reason. For the first rests wholly on the authority of the

elders, the second on the authority of one man, who is an oracle to his sec‐

taries. Hence the divisions of Philosophy that are commonly offered are less

than accurate; for you would no more accurately call Sceptical and Sectarian phi‐

losophy Philosophy than call a statue a man.

3 As for that Eclectic Philosophy, in Latin Elective, it is the one in which we

seek wisdom by reason alone, and govern reason by the experiments of the senses

and by observations, by inner consciousness, by reasoning, and by authority in those

things that cannot be known by any other way. In this manner of philosophiz‐

ing one does not ask who said a thing, but how rightly, that is, how con‐

formably to reason. That one must philosophize in this way is splendidly

demonstrated by Lactantius, whose passage I shall give whole; for it is most

worthy of being read.

4 “Wherefore,” he says, “in that matter above all in which the conduct of

life is at stake, each man ought to trust himself and rely on his own judgment

and his own senses for investigating and weighing the truth, rather than, by be‐

lieving, be deceived by the errors of others, as if he himself

A were

p. 2

were devoid of reason. God has given wisdom to all according to each one’s share, so that they might both search out things unheard and weigh things heard. Nor, because our elders went before us in time, did they also go before us in wisdom; for if wisdom is given to all equally, it cannot be seized beforehand by those who came first. It cannot be diminished, like the light and brightness of the sun: for as the sun is the light of the eyes, so wisdom is the light of the human heart. Wherefore, since to be wise, that is, to seek the truth, is innate in all men, those deprive themselves of wisdom who without any judgment approve the discoveries of their elders and are led by others in the manner of cattle. But what deceives them is this: once the name of elders is set before them, they do not think it can happen either that they themselves are wiser, because they are called younger, or that those others were foolish, because they are named elders.”

5 All these things are to be understood of the natural sciences, such as, for example, Philosophy is. For of him who most arrogantly, with his brief human reason, insults the authority of God, that is, the highest reason, what else am I to say than that he casts off all reason? He who does this is not a Philosopher; he is not even rational. In natural science, therefore, we commend that freedom which approves no estrangement from the Church, none from her dogmas. This is the Eclectic Philosophy, to which I judge you must apply yourselves with all care and all zeal. For it is that philosophy, to speak with Tully, whose study, if anyone disparages it, I truly do not understand what it is that he thinks worthy of praise.

6 Since, further, Philosophy is designed for the true utility of man, and the end is of the same kind as the means: it follows that the subtler speculations of the Peripatetics about things that either cannot be searched out by human reason, or at least can bring no profit to the human race, will belong to the study of wisdom the less, the less they are joined with the true happiness of man, which, with the Theologians of better note, we judge to consist in knowing God, the founder of nature, and the beginning and end of everything true, good and honorable.

7 Since, finally, Philosophy consists in the knowledge of the true and the good: that part of Philosophy which prepares the mind for the knowledge of the true is usually called Instrumental, or Logic; that which imbues it with that knowledge, Theoretical; and that which finally leads it to the true good, Practical. The Theoretical, since it imbues the mind with the knowledge of the true, either inquires into truths about God, spirits and being, or investigates what is true concerning the causes of natural things. In the former case it is called Metaphysics, in the latter Physics. Finally, since the Practical shows the way to the good: it is either what is good in general, or in particular what is just, becoming, or useful, that it

teaches

p. 3

teaches. Of the good in general Ethics treats; of the just, the honorable and the becoming, Natural Law; of the useful, Politics and Economics. But since the narrowness of time does not allow me to linger too long in explaining all the parts of Philosophy, I shall explain Logic, Metaphysics and Ethics somewhat more briefly, perhaps, than was fitting; Physics much more fully.

8 But before I begin the work, I humbly invoke God, the Creator and Governor of all things, and I beg him not to fail me as I write, but to flood my mind with his light, lest I go astray in these lucubrations; rather, that I may hand down such precepts as will lead the minds of boys not only to a thorough understanding of these things contained in the visible world, but also (what we ought most of all to care for) in some manner to those heavenly things and to the blessed vision of the Maker; and that he not permit anything alien to the Roman Church or to the sanctioned Laws to slip from us unawares.

9 But if through human infirmity we shall have erred, whatever we have said we condemn: and we most willingly submit ourselves and all that is ours to the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff. And if at times we shall praise some heretical author, we praise the man’s learning and detest his wickedness, nor do we propose him for reading except to those to whom the most grave judges whose office it is have granted leave to read.

10 But you, most excellent Young Men, I both admonish and exhort humbly to call upon God, that he may grant you a good mind, and earnestly to pray to the Angelic Master St. Thomas Aquinas, that he may obtain for you from God, Best and Greatest, sharpness of understanding. For unless you first imbue your mind with the precepts of God, never (believe me) will you attain the true Philosophy. God grant that, just as I undertake a labor of this kind for your sake and to lead you to the best studies, you in turn may answer to me and to my efforts.

ELEMENTS OF LOGIC

CHAPTER I

PA RT I . B O O K I .

On the nature and constitution of Logic. 1

S ince Philosophy is the knowledge of the true, and Logic prepares the intellect

for that knowledge, it can very well be defined as the Discipline that refines the

mind so that it may attain the truth in every place and time, or more briefly: the

Science of finding and setting forth the truth. And since the truth is established ei‐

ther with certainty or only probably, the Logician must be concerned with

both.

2 And although all men, unless hindered by disease, are strong in right rea‐

son, that is, in the faculty of reasoning, so that it cannot be denied that there is

a natural Logic, it does not follow from this that the Artificial is to be neglected;

for art perfects nature, and the intellect must be furnished not only with the

faculty but also with readiness in reasoning, and indeed with method in arranging

thoughts and reasonings. For man enjoys, for example, the faculty of counting

under the guidance of nature alone, and the power of dancing, of speaking, of per‐

suading; and yet no one doubts that Arithmetic, the Art of Dancing, Grammar and

Rhetoric are most useful. The utility of Logic in every kind of learning is there‐

fore altogether to be admired. For what other end of all our studies do we set

before ourselves than to find the truth and, having found it, to communicate it

to others?

3 Zeno of Elea, to whom the origin of this science is commonly credited,

once cultivated Logic with great care. The Megarians, Stoics and Epicureans also

cultivated it. We shall apply ourselves to it with keen zeal,

so

p. 5

CHAPTER II. On the Nature of the human intellect, and on the operations of

so that we may set forth all the best precepts that we have received as handed down by the Moderns, in the order that seems to us most suited to the nature of this discipline; and it seems most convenient to consider first the nature of the human intellect, then the nature of truth, and finally to inquire how truth is to be found and set forth.

the mind.

T he intellect is occupied rather with the True, the will with the Good. Since,

therefore, Logic teaches the method of finding and setting forth the truth, it is easily seen that it cannot be taught unless we have thoroughly examined the powers of the mind, or human intellect, and its operations.

5 This living being which we call Man consists of Body and Spirit. In the body all these are found: extension, divisibility, solidity, figurability, mobility of parts, etc. Spirit, on the other hand, is that which is in man and is not body, nor is seen by anyone: we infer, however, that some incorporeal directing principle is present from the things, conspicuous enough, that take place in the bodily machine; while as for the internal operations of the mind, these are established, in the end, by the innermost conviction of man himself. For we experience that there is in us something that knows and wills. For we both know our friends and wish them well, and we turn our limbs at our pleasure. For I know for certain that I move my arm if I will to, and do not move it if I do not will to. Accordingly, there is something in me that presides over this machinery and rules and governs it.

6 In turn, if our body is affected by the impact of an external body, the mind feels it by means of those organs of our machinery which are called senses: for if you bring fire near the skin, this affection of the body is felt by the mind. Likewise I feel pain when a thorn pricks my finger. The body, therefore, obeys the mind and carries out what the mind commands, and in turn the mind itself feels whatever is perceived by means of the senses. But that the one

is

p. 6

is moved by the other and depends on it, this is the very thing that is called the complexion, or commerce, of the mind and the body.

7 Whatever, then, that may be which understands and wills (of which we shall have to speak in another place), this much is certain: that there is in man something which knows and wills, which we call the soul, the mind, the rational soul, the spirit, etc. Finally, it is certain that body and mind are two altogether distinct substances. The mind perceives the forms of things, discerns, judges, reasons, feels, is stirred by passions, etc., things which no one would attribute to the body except foolishly: the soul, therefore, is not body.

8 We have also found that our mind has this peculiar to it, that it understands, so that in understanding it elicits one cognition after another rightly and in order, and also that it acts freely. That is to say, when the mind makes an object present to itself, it perceives it. But what an idea is, and what a perception, is a matter of great disagreement. (a) In order, however, that all equivocation be removed, we lay down first that by the name of idea we mean any perception whatever of any thing whatever. Every notion, therefore, or comprehension, or perception, whatever it may be, is called by us an idea. Hence, e.g., the notion or perception of a figure, a plant, an animal, a pleasure, etc., is an idea.

9 We perceive the external things that affect our sense organs. Now this is the law of sensations, that whenever some change is produced by a sensible object in a duly

constituted

(a) There are those who hold that ideas and perceptions are the same thing, and say that they consist in motions of the senses and of the brain. So Hobbes, Leviathan, pt. 1, ch. 3, 4, and in Elem. Philosoph. ch. 25, art. 2. There are those who say that ideas and perceptions are the same cognition of the mind, yet in such a way that the same cognition, inasmuch as it is referred to the mind which perceives, is called perception; inasmuch as it is referred to the object of which it is the image, and which is perceived, idea. So Arnauld and Locke, Essai sur l’Entendement Humain, in the Preface, and bk. 2, ch. 8, §. 7, 8. Others altogether separate perceptions from ideas, and think that God impresses the ideas of things on the human mind. So Malebranche, Recherche de la Verité, bk. 3. Lastly, others say that material ideas are affections of the senses and of the brain, while intellectual ones, which correspond to the material, are perceptions of material things. So Wolff, from whom the Scholastics do not dissent, though they call the material idea an intellection. Amid so great a disagreement among the most learned men, it would be arrogant to wish to put forward anything as certain.

constituted sense organ, so often there arises in the soul a certain particular sensation corresponding to this change. Thus the motions of the senses affect the brain and impress something on it, from which the mind perceives the things that strike the sense, (b) as Haller (c) confirms with very many examples in his notes to Boerhaave. This perception of the mind is called an idea.

10 When the intellect acquires simple ideas, that is, when it makes an object present to itself and perceives it without referring it to another, e.g. when it knows the sun, or a horse, this cognition is called simply perception, or, as the Scholastics put it, Simple apprehension, that is, a cognition affirming or denying nothing; but when the intellect compares two ideas with each other, refers one to the other, and perceives that it agrees with the other, or not, e.g. when it says The sun is bright, The sun is not a horse, this cognition is judgment, or the act of the intellect by which we affirm or deny something of an object. When the intellect compares three ideas with one another, it is said to Reason. Reasoning, or discourse, is the action of the mind by which we put together several ideas, of which one depends on another, so as to uncover what lay hidden. The question is asked: is air heavy? This is not at once clearly apparent; I therefore use reasoning in this way: whatever, placed on a scale-pan, presses it down is heavy; air placed on a scale-pan presses it down: therefore air is heavy.

11 Further, our mind puts together several ideas of things very different from one another, as when it joins a lion’s body and wings to a human head and feigns a new animal. Sometimes, on the contrary, the mind as it were disjoins one idea from another: as when we think of the whiteness of a wall without thinking of the wall. Sometimes it arranges its thoughts and reasonings in order, the more easily to see whether one ought to proceed from some to others. This operation of the mind is called Method. Sometimes, after the matter has been argued and disputed on both sides, and it is not clearly understood

CHAPTER III

on which side the truth stands, the mind doubts, or suspends judgment. Finally,

to pass over other things, when the mind perceives a thing again and is more‐

over conscious that it had known that same thing long before, this operation is

called Memory.

12 From this it becomes manifest that there are more operations of the

mind than the common Aristotelian Logicians suppose; and by them the intel‐

lect is rightly defined: the faculty of the mind which perceives, judges, reasons, disposes,

etc. One must, however, keep well in mind the force and the variety of the

names that signify faculties of the mind and occur here and there. Phantasy, or

Imagination, is that power of the mind by which we represent to ourselves all

things expressed by a bodily image. Ingenuity is the mind’s skill in discovering

and devising. Judgment is the faculty of selecting the things that are right and of

using them according to the worth of the matter. And indeed the things that

ingenuity composes do not always exist in reality. For I can easily join in my

mind the ideas of gold and of a mountain, and form for myself the image of a

golden mountain, which nevertheless does not exist outside thought. Ideas of

this kind are called chimerical, or beings of reason.

13 From this, moreover, it is plain that these beings of reason are not to be

confused with non-beings, which are not objects of the mind at all, since nothing

can be thought about them. Thus a square circle is a non-being, because nothing

whatever can even be thought about it. Since, therefore, the things that inge‐

nuity composes do not always exist in reality, there is need of judgment to dis‐

tinguish accurately the thing from the shadow, the chimera from the reality it‐

self. Hence the more correct a man’s judgment is, the fitter he will be for find‐

ing and setting forth the truth. Hence it is also clear why those who are very

strong in ingenuity are generally not so in judgment: for ingenuity is occupied

in devising and composing anything whatever, whereas judgment is occupied in

separating the right from the not right, which differ widely from each other.

How are the senses related to the acquiring of ideas?

14

A lthough not all ideas whatsoever proceed from sense, as Locke holds (d), it

is nevertheless true, if we speak of the greater part of them, that the sens‐

es are the windows of the mind,

through

(d) Essai concernant l’Entendement Humain, bk. 1.

p. 9

through which the first notions enter into it, and by which it understands the other things that are outside it. But since how easily this comes about cannot be known unless we have some rough idea of the construction of the senses, we shall set down beforehand a very few things to pave the way for what follows.

15 There are five senses of the human machine, by which the ideas of things are communicated to the brain and to the mind: Sight, Hearing, Smell, Taste, Touch, by which names we designate five different organs. And to begin with sight: the eyes, by which it is perceived, have a peculiar and wonderful structure, which it is not the place here to elucidate minutely; let us say only that the eye is a globe composed of three principal membranes, namely the cornea, the uvea and the retina, each of which encloses its own humor. The humor that is in the middle, which is called the crystalline, is convex on both sides and has the shape of a lens. The rays of light reflected from the object body are refracted while they pass through this lens, and paint an inverted image (e) of the object on the back of the inner membrane, which they call the retina. The retina is an expansion of the innermost medullary part of the optic nerve, which reaches as far as the common sensorium, as Winslow (f) explains very well in his anatomical exposition of the human body.

16 When, therefore, the eye has been struck by light, and this impulse has been impressed on the brain by means of that nerve, there is at once an idea and perception, e.g. of a triangular figure, or of a square one, etc. These perceptions are followed by the judgment by which I declare that there exists a body of triangular figure, or of square, etc.; and this judgment follows upon the other perceptions of the senses as well.

17 The organ of Hearing is like a snail’s shell, at the bottom of which is a certain stretched membrane, which they call the Tympanum. Behind the tympanum are four movable little bones, and air within a certain twisted case which has two openings leading to the labyrinth, that is, to a tortuous passage hollowed out in the very substance of the bone; in the far part of this labyrinth the fibers of the auditory nerve spread out, and this nerve extends to the brain. Suppose you strike some piece of bronze: the motion and vibration of the bronze strike the outer air.

B The

(e) That this little image contributes nothing to vision insofar as it is an image, the Modern Philosophers had, already in the age of Descartes, not only suspected but all but proved. For René Descartes himself asks: by what other little eye, then, is the aforesaid little image to be seen?

(f) Cours d’Anatomie, vol. V.

p. 10

The air, thus struck and compressed in the cochlea, is carried to the tympanum of the ear and sets it in motion. The tympanum in turn strikes the little bones and the air, which, entering the labyrinth, communicates that very tremor to the fibers of the auditory nerve; and this nerve makes the same impression in the brain. Here you have the idea of sound, which varies according to the different tremor of bodies. The celebrated Bernard Nieuwentyt (g), from whom we have taken these things, reports innumerable others about the ear.

18 Willis, who treats of flavors at length (h), thinks that Taste is situated chiefly in the upper surface of the tongue. Now the tongue is wrapped in certain membranes: an outer one, which is called the Epidermis; a second, which is pierced with many holes; a third, which is sprinkled with very many papillae, which pass through the second and end in the epidermis. These prominences are certain expansions of very fine nerves; and it is in these papillae of the tongue that flavor is perceived, which is explained by most Anatomists in roughly this way, and so it comes about. Saline particles, and likewise a certain very thin spirit, with which all flavorful bodies abound, strike with their sharpness the sensitive nerves of which those papillae consist. This motion is communicated to the brain. Hence the mind feels this motion, that is, has the perception of flavor.

19 In like manner Smell: that villous membrane which lines the inner part of the nostrils is woven of very many nerves stripped of epidermis, which is the reason why it is of so exquisite a sense that, when barely touched, it produces a great commotion. And this is the organ of Smell: for the very fine particles, both of oil and of volatile salt, as they call it, which are exhaled from bodies, running into that membrane, twitch the nervous papillae in one way and another; and this titillation is impressed on the brain through the nerves, and so is felt.

20 Finally, this is proper to Touch, that it does not have a definite place, as the other senses do, but is in the whole body: so that whatever part of the body we scratch, the contact of a body is felt. Nevertheless, touch resides in a peculiar manner in the tips of the fingers of the hand, for distinguishing very many things. Further, under the cuticle or epidermis, that is, under the outer membrane of the flesh, there extend the reticular membrane and the skin, which is sprinkled with innumerable nervous papillae; and these papillae, rising out of the skin like very fine little brushes, touch the epidermis itself. Hence when you touch flesh you touch a nerve, and since all the nerves

are

(g) L’Existence de Dieu demontreè par les merveilles de la Nature, Contempl. XIV.

(h) De Anima Brutorum, ch. 12.

p. 11

are led from the brain, or from the cerebellum and the spinal marrow, they very easily excite the same motion in the brain, from which the mind perceives the contact, that is, acquires the idea of touch, as Haller, Faye and Verdier (i) explain very well.

21 Hence it becomes manifest that the office of the organs is to receive the impression of bodies and to transmit it to the brain, and to do so by means of the nerves, which are most apt for accomplishing this; but that it is the mind which elicits the ideas of things according to the variety of the senses. We say, however, that the eye sees, the ear hears, etc., which is not so. For the eye only receives, together with the image, a certain motion, so to speak, which it communicates to the brain; while the mind, prompted on the occasion of such a motion, forms for itself the idea of the thing seen. But since the perception of the mind follows that motion of the organ, we therefore confuse the two, and think that the eye sees, etc.; although it is altogether hidden from us how the affections of the senses reach the brain, and how our mind perceives those motions that are impressed in the brain. Thus in almost all sensations, as Malebranche (j) very well notes, four things, though different, are confused, namely because they take place together, and as it were in one point of time.

22 The first thing that is confused is the action of the external body, that is, in heat, for example, the impulse and motion of the particles of the wood against the fibers of the hand. The second is the passion of the sense organ, that is, the agitation of the fibers of the hand arising from the impulse of the particles of fire, which agitation reaches all the way to the brain. The third is the sensation, or perception of the mind, that is, what anyone feels when he approaches the fire. The fourth is the judgment by which the mind judges that what it feels is in its hand and in the fire.

23 These four, as may be seen, are very different, and yet they are not commonly distinguished; yet there is no one who, attending to the matter, does not see that of these four, which take place in us when we are affected by some external body, the first two pertain to the body, the last two to the mind alone. These things having been said in passing, we shall have to consider somewhat more accurately how our mind forms for itself clear, distinct and adequate ideas.

The Division of Ideas. 24

C H A P T E R I V.

A n idea, as we have already said, is the genuine image of any object whatev‐

er, which the mind contemplates immediately, or any thought whatever

about any thing. Sometimes we perceive a thing in such a way that, when it

presents itself again, we easily distinguish it from others; this is called a clear

idea: if I cannot so distinguish a thing from another, the idea is confused. Thus,

e.g., everyone, even among the common people, has a clear idea of the Moon,

but not likewise of Jupiter, Mars and Saturn, stars which a man of the people

will easily confuse with the fixed stars.

25 But even if I easily distinguish some thing from others, it sometimes

happens that I am able to enumerate one by one all the marks that separate the

thing from the rest, and sometimes not; in the first case the clear idea is distinct,

in the second indistinct. E.g., when I know that a triangle can be distinguished

from other figures by the number of the lines by which it is enclosed, I am said

to have not only a clear but also a distinct idea of it. On the other hand, if, seeing

that a magnet draws iron to itself, I separate the magnet from other stones by

this mark, but cannot enumerate one by one all the other marks that set the

magnet apart from other stones, I have a clear but confused idea of the magnet.

A distinct idea therefore expresses more than a clear one, and a clear idea is

rightly divided into distinct and confused.

26 But if I not only have the thing and its marks enumerated, but also have

a distinct idea of those very marks which enter into that distinct notion, this

idea will be adequate; where it is otherwise, the idea will indeed be distinct, but

inadequate. Thus, e.g., the marks by which I discern fire from other materials

are light, heat, the power of setting on fire, etc. If anyone has a distinct idea of

all these things, he will have an adequate notion of fire; if not, an inadequate one.

An adequate idea therefore expresses more than a distinct one; nor can we ac‐

quire adequate ideas of all things, for we do not have a distinct idea of all the

adjuncts of which each thing consists; indeed, very few adequate ideas can be

obtained in this life, as Wolff rightly warns on this point.

Moreover

p. 13

27 Further, ideas are either of Substances, or of Modes, or of Relations. For all the things we know either can exist apart from each single mode, and this we call substance; or they are modes of some thing, and these we call accidents, or modes; and among modes, again, there is something that is conceived as referred to another, and this we call relation. This division is adequate; for it is plainly impossible that there be any perception which is neither a perception of substance, nor a perception of a mode, nor a perception of some relation.

28 The whole is made clear by an example: a square piece of wood is a thing that can exist apart from the square figure, for it can be made round; and this we call substance. On the other hand, you will nowhere find squareness and roundness separately in natural bodies, and this we call an accident, or mode of substance; and if I conceive squareness as a mode proper to a body, it necessarily leads me to the knowledge of the body, and this we call relation.

29 From what has been said it becomes manifest that we do not have a clear and distinct idea of substance, but a very obscure one. For the ideas we have of particular substances are acquired by sense; but the senses reach only the modes that adorn the substance, not likewise the nature of the substance: hence substance cannot be clearly separated from other things. E.g., iron offers us the idea of a heavy, hard body, which is melted only by a great fire, which is consumed by rust, and which is altogether suited to cutting bodies, etc.; and however much we try to know the nature of iron thoroughly, we shall achieve nothing. For this idea represents nothing other than the modes of iron. Who indeed would dare to say that he finds anything else in iron besides these? Therefore the idea of iron that we have is composed of the ideas of all its modes. Since, however, we know for certain that those adjuncts can be changed, e.g. the square figure into a round one, etc., and that iron can become harder and better suited to splitting wood, without the very nature of iron being changed, we conclude that there is something in iron besides its adjuncts and properties, which we call substance and subject. But what that is, and in what it is distinguished from other things, we do not know.

30 Thus the notion of substance, as Locke rightly warns, is the idea of a thing altogether unknown to us, or the idea of a most obscure thing, which we feign to be the subject of accidents. But the idea of particular substances, as of iron and of wood, is an idea composed of the ideas of all their properties. Those, therefore, philosophize badly who hold that the nature of a thing is fully known from the properties we know. For even if we know some properties, we cannot affirm with certainty that no properties remain which are not known to us. Wherefore from the properties which we know

we

p. 14

we can separate things from one another, and the more properties we discern,

the more nearly we approach the knowledge of the nature; yet this is far re‐

moved from a clear and distinct perception of the essence, or nature, and much

farther still from an adequate one.

31 Relations, as we have said, are ideas of which one refers to the other in

such a way that one cannot be understood without the other, or that the con‐

sideration of the one involves the consideration of the other. From this we in‐

fer that those err not a little who affirm or deny something absolutely of a rela‐

tive idea, and do not duly weigh the foundation of the relation. How useful this

observation is for avoiding logomachies, and indeed for calming the sadder pas‐

sions, cannot be told. Thus many grieve that they are poor, though they lack

nothing necessary. And why so, unless because they take very rich men as the

foundation of the relation, compared with whom they seem to themselves very

poor? Elegantly says Seneca, (k)

To bear the lot that all men suffer

No one refuses.

No one believes himself wretched, though he be.

Take away the fortunate, take far away

The rich in gold, take away those who

Cleave rich fields with a hundred oxen;

The poor man’s downcast spirits will rise.

No one is wretched, except by Comparison.

C H A P T E R V.

On singular, particular and universal ideas, where also of the

five predicables. 32

S ome ideas represent to us the thing itself in the individual, e.g. Alexander;

others what the thing has in common with certain others, e.g. his royal dignity;

others what the thing has in common with all things of the same nature, e.g. hu‐

manity. Ideas of the first kind are called singular, of the second

particular

(k) In Troad. V. 1016.

p. 15

CHAPTER VI

particular, of the third universal. Universals, therefore, are not outside the mind,

or, as the Scholastics put it, a parte rei [on the side of the thing]. Universal man is

nothing but an idea; for the men who exist are singular.

33 The Peripatetics, following Porphyry, made five classes of universals:

Genus, Species, Specific Difference, Property and Accident. Genus is defined by

Porphyry as a universal notion which is predicated of many things differing in species,

when it is asked what a thing is: e.g. animal is the genus of man and of horse, be‐

cause it designates the notion common to both, and it is what is usually offered

by one who answers someone asking what a man, what a horse is. Species is a uni‐

versal notion which is said of many things differing in number, as their whole essence, as

man, which is predicated of Peter, and Paul, and the other individuals of human

nature. An Individual, moreover, is that which cannot be divided into several things

such as it is itself: e.g. Peter. Specific Difference is a universal notion which is said of

many things differing in number, as a metaphysical form, determining the genus to such a

species, e.g. rationality.

34 Property is said in four ways: first, what belongs to one species alone, but not

to the whole of it, as to be a Physician. Second, conversely, what belongs to the

whole species, but not to it alone, as to be two-footed. Third, what belongs to one

species alone and to the whole of it, but not always, as in man to be conversing. Fourth,

what belongs to the whole species, and always: such in man is the faculty of discourse,

or of conversing; for, as Cicero excellently says: for in this one thing above all we ex‐

cel the beasts, that we converse with one another, and that we can express our thoughts by

speaking. Accident is a universal notion which can be present to or absent from many

things while their nature remains intact, or, as the Scholastics put it: that which can

be present or absent without the corruption of the subject; such in Peter is whiteness. It

will be enough to have indicated these things for the present.

On the Antepredicaments and the Categories of the

Peripatetics. 35

T he Peripatetics call the categories, or Predicaments, a philosophical Dogma,

which cannot be called into doubt in Philosophy. Nonsense! For the

predicaments are nothing other

than

p. 16

than a nomenclature, which shows by what name Aristotle named certain beings: in actual fact it is an inept division, as we shall show below; but first we shall explain a few things about the antepredicaments.

36 Aristotle counted four Antepredicaments: Univocals, Equivocals, Analogues and Denominatives. Univocals are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether the same in all. Those words altogether the same signify not identity, but likeness. Equivocals are those whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is altogether different. A common example is Dog, which is taken for the domestic animal and for a star. Analogues are things whose name is common, while the meaning signified by the name is partly the same, partly different, or belongs properly to one, improperly to another; thus laughter is analogous with respect to a man and to a meadow. Denominatives are those which are derived from some name, as brave from bravery, etc. And these are the antepredicaments. But if we consider the things themselves, we shall understand without effort that all ideas can be reduced to three classes, as it were: Substance, Adjuncts, Relations, as we also said above.

37 Aristotle, however, refers all things that exist to ten classes, which he calls categories, and others Predicaments. One is that of substance, or of a thing that can exist by itself; the others are those of accidents, or of those things that cannot exist by themselves. In the first class he counts two substances. The second is Quantity, either discrete, as numbers, or continuous; and this either permanent, as a body, or successive, as motion. The third is Quality, either of the mind, as virtues and sciences, or of the body, as heat, etc. The fourth is Relation, by which one thing leads to the knowledge of another. The fifth is Action, either that which is in the agent, as love, or that which is received in another, as heating. The sixth is Passion, the contrary of action, as being heated. The seventh is Where, or place, as to be at Rome, to be at home, to be in the country, etc. The eighth is Time, as when, to words signifying time, we answer tomorrow, etc. The ninth is Position, which is expressed by these words: stands, lies, etc. The tenth is Habit, that is, the things that clothe the body, as a cloak, etc. Behold the predicaments. Behold the Philosophical dogma which the Peripatetics judge it rash to call into doubt.

38 Otherwise, however, have the most learned Moderns judged, to whom that division, or distribution, seems to have been devised somewhat too freely; for, as the celebrated Author of the Art of Thinking observes, it came forth from the imagination of some man who had no right to write laws for others, who could, no less than he, use their own right to arrange the objects of their thoughts by whatever method is most in keeping with their own way of philosophizing.

And

39 And in fact such a distribution seems altogether inept, since it certainly contains a great many things that ought to be called not true genera of beings but only extrinsic denominations, as Relation, Where, Time; for if all denominations and extrinsic modes were to be admitted, then not ten but almost infinite genera of beings would have to be admitted. Many things are also missing, e.g. several species of accidents, both of body, as rest, and of spirits, as cognition, etc. It is further faulted in this, that it places man under body as under a genus, although he could equally be contained under mind, and could with no less right be called Mind than Body. It contains things false and conflicting: for it refers length, breadth and weight to quantity, and then the objects of the senses to qualities, although extension and motion also fall under sight, and weight and motion under touch; and so Quantity would be at the same time Quality. To pass over other enormities of this kind.

40 More accurately, therefore, the Modern Philosophers count seven genera, or categories, of beings, so that under the common and supreme genus of being there are contained, in a neat and perfect series, two species of substance, namely body and spirit, or mind, and in addition five species of modes. Hence, in their view,

Mind, Measure, Rest, Motion, Position, Figure

Are, with Matter, the beginnings of all things.

41 For the followers of this Philosophy are persuaded that the whole of nature is exhausted by these seven things. By the name of Mind is understood spiritual substance, as God, the Angels and the rational Soul. Measure signifies quantity. Rest, the permanence of a body in the place in which it is found. Motion is the translation or migration of a body from one place to another. Position signifies the disposition of the parts, above all that which is innermost and which cannot be varied without the substance itself being varied. Figure is that disposition of the parts which appears outwardly, and which can be varied while the substance of the thing remains intact. Matter, finally, signifies body or corporeal substance, whatever in the end may be understood by the name of body or matter. And these seven genera of beings are called the beginnings of all things because nothing can be conceived that is not included in these genera of things; or, finally, no singular substance is found in which several, or even all, of these modes cannot be distinguished or found. But so that everything may appear more clearly, I offer you the following table, as it has been drawn by some of the Moderns.

CHAPTER VII

On Definitions and Divisions.

hoever has acquired for himself distinct and adequate ideas of 42

W things will now find it easy not only to describe things, but also

to define and divide them. And indeed one who is bound to the

study of investigating the truth cannot do without these instruments. For if we

have a distinct idea, we can define the thing; if an adequate one, nothing will be

easier than to divide it.

43 Definition, then, is a statement so determining a thing that it can always be dis‐

tinguished from all others. Description differs from definition in this, that although

both are true, the former applies to the thing only under certain circumstances,

the latter always. E.g. if I say: a clock is a little machine made in this or that way,

which, either by a hand or by striking, shows what hour of the day it is, this is the defi‐

nition of a clock; if I say: it is a round case that hangs from a chain near the bed, this

proposition, though clear, is a description of a clock.

44 Since, then, a definition must always apply to the thing, it follows that it

must comprehend first that in which the thing agrees with other things of the

same nature, and then the idea which belongs primarily to the essence of the

thing and by which it is distinguished from all the rest; and so it must consist

of genus and specific difference. E.g. a triangle is a figure bounded by three lines. But

if I take that specific difference from some mark by which I can always tell the

thing I meet apart from all others, that definition will be called nominal: e.g. a

circle is a figure whose periphery is everywhere equally distant from the center. If I place

the difference in showing the manner in which the thing arises, or how it is

possible, a real definition will result; e.g. a circle is a figure described by a radius

turned about a point.

45 If, however, the definition of the name is altogether accurate, so that it

distinguishes the very thing signified by the name from any other thing whatev‐

er, it makes no difference whether such definitions are called definitions of the

thing or of the name, as the celebrated Jacquier very well observes. From this it

readily appears, first, that a definition ought not to be negative, since in that

way a thing is not distinguished from a thing by what belongs to its essence.

Second, that it ought to be reciprocal with the thing defined, or, as the Schools

say, that the thing defined and the definition be mutually

convertible

p. 19

convertible. Third, that it ought to consist of proper and perspicuous words, or at least of words already defined beforehand. Fourth, that the thing defined should not enter into the definition, that is, that the same should not be explained by the same, e.g. a circle is a circle. Fifth, that the definition ought to apply to all of the thing defined and to it alone; hence that definition of man is faulty: a two-footed animal without feathers. From these rules flow four axioms received in the Schools: to whatever the definition belongs, the thing defined belongs also, and conversely; likewise: to whatever the definition is repugnant, the thing defined is repugnant also, and vice versa.

46 Two things, however, we must take care of here. First, that we define accurately the obscure names that come into controversy, lest we dispute from an ambiguity. Some Philosophers sin against this law, who, because they do not define their terms, wrangle with one another even to abuse and fisticuffs, even if both disputants are saying the same things in different words. Second: that when we define names, we should not think that we are defining the thing itself. Against this rule those very Philosophers also sin: for when they define certain words at their own discretion, they persuade themselves that they thoroughly know and define the natures of the things signified: e.g. ask them, what is a tree? They say it is a living insensitive thing. What is lightning? They answer that it is an exhalation kindled in a cloud, which tends downward. But these explanations declare only what things are signified by those names; they do not lay open the natures of the things, unless I first know distinctly what a living insensitive thing, an exhalation, a cloud, kindling and the rest are. But now let us say a few things about division.

47 Division is a statement that resolves a whole into its parts, so that what it contains may be more easily understood; or better: the resolution of a universal idea into several particular ones. That which is resolved is called the thing divided; the parts into which it is divided, the dividing members. One division is Physical, as when we divide wood into parts; another Logical, as when I divide substance in my mind into body and spirit. These parts are called inferiors.

48 The first law of division is that the dividing members be equal to the whole divided. Faultily, therefore, do the Aristotelians divide being into ten categories, since more can be established. The second, that one member not be contained in another; hence number is not rightly divided into even, odd and binary: for the binary is contained in the even. Let the Logician, therefore, in his wisdom so divide a thing that a clearer knowledge of the thing may be had from it, so that he may define it the more easily and accurately. And let him carefully beware of what we warned above concerning definition, lest, when he divides the signification of a name, he think he is dividing the thing itself: an enormity which Aristotle

C2 himself

p. 20

CHAPTER VIII

himself and some of the Ancients imprudently committed. What we have

warned concerning division must be understood of subdivisions as well, although

care must be taken that subdivisions are not multiplied beyond necessity. For

the more a great rock is ground into dust, the less do we grasp its size with the

mind.

On Judgments and Propositions, and on the matter, form,

quantity and quality of a proposition: on the opposition,

equipollence and conversion of propositions.

hen the mind compares two ideas, accurately perceived, with 49

W each other, and either connects them or pulls them apart, there

arises from this judgment, which is: the perception of the agreement

or disagreement that is found between two ideas. Judgment expressed in words is

called a Proposition, or enunciation. A proposition, moreover, is: a statement affirm‐

ing or denying something of something. For it corresponds to judgment, which ei‐

ther connects or disjoins two ideas.

50 Every proposition consists of a subject and a predicate, or attribute, terms

which the copula is joins together; although this, just like the subject, often lies

hidden in the predicate, and so the whole proposition consists of one or two

words, e.g. Peter loves, I die, in which these are understood: Peter is loving, I am

dying. The subject is that of which something is said. The predicate, what is said of

the subject. The copula is the link, or union of subject and predicate. By the copula,

or by the verb is, or is not, the force of judging is signified, that is, it is shown

that the predicate is included, or not included, in the subject. For this proposi‐

tion, God is just, means this: in the idea of God the idea of justice is included. This

other, a man is not a horse, means: in the idea of man the idea of horse is not included.

For no affirmative proposition is true except because the whole predicate is in‐

cluded in the subject; no negative

one

p. 21

one, except because the whole is not included. E.g. when I say I am living, by the pronoun I I designate the complex idea of my individual self, and I mean my individual self is living; which amounts to: in the complex idea of my individual self the idea of living is included.

51 The Matter of a proposition is those words of which the same proposition is composed, as it were of parts. By reason of its matter a proposition is called necessary when the predicate agrees necessarily with the subject, as man is an animal; contingent when it agrees contingently, as John is white; impossible when it is repugnant to it, as Sempronius is a stone. But this too is referred to the necessary: for the former is called necessarily true, the latter necessarily false.

52 The Form of a proposition is the copula itself, which joins the predicate with the subject. By reason of its form a proposition is divided into affirmative, which attributes one thing to another, and negative, which denies one thing of another. Note here in passing that a proposition is negative when the particle not falls upon the verb. It is divided also into Categorematic, which affirms or denies without condition, and hypothetical, which affirms under a condition, as if the Sun shines, it is day. A complex proposition is one that consists of several propositions, as the Master teaches, and the disciple learns.

53 The Quantity of a proposition is the extension of the formal subject to signify more or fewer things. Hence a proposition is universal if the subject is universal, as every man is an animal; particular if the subject is particular, as some man runs; singular if the subject is singular, as Peter runs. To these is added the indefinite proposition, whose subject is common and is not restricted, as man reads; for one does not say every, or some, or this, but indefinitely man reads.

54 The Quality of a proposition is said to be its truth or falsity, because a proposition in general abstracts from being true or false; but if it is taken reduplicatively as true or false, then truth or falsity, being a form that denominates the proposition, belongs to it essentially; whereas to a proposition taken specificatively it belongs only contingently. Those propositions are called modal in which the mode is expressed in which the predicate is affirmed or denied of the subject, as when one says: it is necessary that man be an animal.

55 Hence all propositions are referred to four classes, which the Scholastics express by four letters, A. E. I. O. A, the universal affirmative, as every man is just; E, the universal negative, as no vicious man is happy; I, the particular affirmative, as some vicious man is rich; O, the particular negative, as some vicious man is not rich; but so that these may stick more easily in the memory, they have been comprised in these little verses.

A

p. 22

A affirms, E denies, but both universally.

I affirms, O denies, but both particularly.

56 Opposition is the incompatibility of two propositions that consist of the same subject and predicate. Opposition of propositions is commonly held to be fourfold: contradictory, contrary, subcontrary and subalternate. Contradictory opposition is between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, one affirmative, the other negative, e.g. every man is white, some man is not white. Singular propositions are also called contradictory when one denies what the other affirms: e.g. Aristotle is the prince of Philosophers, Aristotle is not the prince of Philosophers. For contradiction is the affirmation and negation of the same predicate of the same subject, and at the same time.

57 Of contradictory propositions, one is always true, the other false. Contrary opposition is between two universal propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as every man is white, no man is white. Subcontrary opposition is between two particular propositions, of which one is affirmative, the other negative, as some man is white, some man is not white. Subalternate opposition (which is not opposition in the strict sense) is found between two propositions of which one is universal, the other particular, but both either affirmative or negative, as every man is white, some man is white; no man is white, some man is not white; and to understand these more clearly, cast your eyes on the diagram below.

A: Every man is white. — E: No man is white. — I: Some man is white. — O: Some man is not white. Above: Contraries. Below: Subcontraries. At the sides: Subalterns. Across: Contradictories.

p. 23

58 Take, finally, these most certain rules for recognizing opposition: those

CHAPTER IX

which can be neither true together nor false together are contradictories; those

which cannot be true together, but can nevertheless be false together, are con‐

traries; those which cannot be false together, and can be true together, are sub‐

contraries. Of subalternate propositions, sometimes one is true and the other

false, sometimes both are false, sometimes both true: e.g. every man is an animal,

some man is an animal.

59 Equipollence, or equivalence, of propositions is the reduction of opposite

propositions to the same sense by means of the particle not, which in contra‐

dictories is placed before the subject, in contraries is placed after it, and in sub‐

alterns is placed both before and after, as is shown by this little verse:

Before for contradic., after for contra., before and after for subalter.

60 Conversion of propositions is the reciprocal change of the subject into

the predicate and of the predicate into the subject, namely when the predicate

is put in the place of the subject, and the subject itself in the place of the predi‐

cate, the truth of that proposition nevertheless remaining, although sometimes

the extension, or quantity, of the proposition is varied. The conversion of

propositions, however, is to be gathered from Grammar rather than from Logic.

Here are the mysteries of the old Logicians, explained more accurately than

they themselves explain them. We did not wish, however, to omit them, lest

the Ancients should perhaps suspect that something useful or fruitful had been

snatched away from the youth.

On Reasoning, or the Syllogism, and the various kinds of

argumentation.

easoning, or Syllogism, is the operation of the intellect by which, having set 61

R up a comparison of two ideas with a third, it learns whether they are to be

joined or to be separated; or, as the Scholastics put it, Reasoning is the

cognition that infers another proposition from one or from two propositions. If it infers

another from one proposition only, e.g. I think: therefore I exist, it is called an

Enthymeme; but if another is inferred from two propositions, e.g. everything that

thinks exists; but I think: therefore I exist, it is called a Syllogism.

Since

p. 24

62 Since, then, as we have said, there are three ideas to be compared in a Syllogism, it follows that as soon as we cram four ideas into one Syllogism, a faulty reasoning results; which mostly happens when some word suffers from equivocation. Hence one would reason badly thus: Spirit is a thinking substance; but spirit of wine is spirit: therefore spirit of wine is a thinking substance; for four ideas are crammed into one Syllogism. Those three ideas, if they are expressed in words, are called terms; and the one about which something is asked is usually called the minor term, that which is asked about it the major, and that with which these two terms are compared the middle. E.g. if I wished to know whether air is heavy, and therefore compared these ideas with the pressure of bodies: air will be the minor term, because something is asked about it; heavy the major term, because this is the very thing that is asked about air; the pressure of bodies will be the middle term, because the other two are compared with this idea.

63 A Syllogism consists of three propositions, of which the first, which is composed of the major and the middle term, is called the major; the second, composed of the minor and the middle, the minor; the third, finally, composed of the minor and the major, is called the conclusion. Thus if I construct a Syllogism from the terms proposed a little earlier: what presses on lower bodies is heavy; air presses on lower bodies: therefore air is heavy, the first proposition will be the major, the second the minor, and the last is called the conclusion or consequent. In an Enthymeme the first is called the antecedent, the second the consequent.

64 A Dilemma is an argumentation from two questions, by either of which the respondent is caught, e.g. does he who sins remember hell, or not? If you grant it: then he is a fool; if you deny it: then he is a fool too, because he does not remember so great a punishment.

65 Induction is argumentation from singulars sufficiently enumerated to the universal, as if you say: gold can be melted; tin, lead and iron can be melted: therefore every metal can be melted. This argumentation will be bad and devoid of strength if it fails to examine even one part of those that are to be enumerated. Example, or parity, is argumentation from one thing to another similar thing in the same line. Demonstration is argumentation that consists of evident premises. Hence through demonstration a thing manifestly appears true to us. For that is truly and evidently known which is drawn out from clear and perspicuous principles. For the rest, we demonstrate either the effect from its cause, or the cause from its effect. The former demonstration is called a priori, the latter a posteriori.

66 Thus, e.g., if I demonstrate the roundness of the earth from its shadow in Lunar Eclipses, I demonstrate the cause from the effect, so

that

p. 25

CHAPTER X

that this demonstration will be a posteriori. On the other hand, when I demon‐

strate the immortality of the mind from its spirituality, and this from thought,

the demonstration will be a priori. The cognition that is acquired by means of

demonstration is called science. Science, moreover, is defined: certain and evident

cognition of a necessary thing, proceeding from demonstration.

67 It is called certain cognition, that is, firm and stable and altogether un‐

shaken, and by this science differs from opinion, which is nothing but probable

cognition of a thing. It is called evident cognition, namely clear and plainly per‐

spicuous, and hence it is distinguished from faith, which is wholly concerned

with obscure things. It is said to be of a necessary thing, so that it may thence be

plain that, properly speaking, no science can be had of those things which can

be otherwise than as they are known. It is said, lastly, to be proceeding from

demonstration, so that it may be distinguished from understanding, namely from

the cognition of first principles. For the notion of these does not depend on

demonstration, since they are most evident from their own terms, e.g. the whole

is greater than its part, etc. Just as one demonstration is a priori and another a pos‐

teriori, so a twofold science is distinguished: namely most perfect and less perfect.

The former is acquired through demonstration a priori, the latter through

demonstration a posteriori.

On the Form and Figure of the Syllogism.

he Form of a Syllogism is the disposition of the terms with a view to cor68

T rectly inferring the conclusion: this form is twofold, namely mode and

figure. Mode is the disposition of the propositions with respect to

affirmation or negation, universality or particularity; and since the middle can

be disposed in the propositions in three ways, from this there results the three‐

fold figure of the Syllogism, as is shown by these little verses:

The first first subjects the middle, then predicates it;

The second twice predicates, the third twice subjects it.

69 The first figure puts the middle in the major as subject, and the middle itself

as predicate in the minor. The second figure puts the middle as predicate both in the

major and in the minor. The third, finally, both in the major and in the minor,

puts the middle

D as

p. 26

CHAPTER XI

as subject. Here are examples. First fig.: what thinks is spirit; the mind thinks: there‐

fore the mind is spirit. Second fig.: body does not think; the mind thinks: therefore the

mind is not body. Third fig.: whatever thinks is spirit; something that thinks is in man:

therefore some spirit is in man. All the modes, moreover, nineteen in number, are

contained in these barbarous words:

Barbara, Celarem, Darii, Ferio, Baralipton,

Celantes, Dabitis, Fopesmo, Frisesomorum,

Cesare, Camestres, Festino, Baroco, Darapti,

Felapton, Disamis, Datisi, Bocardo, Ferison.

70 Here the Peripatetics would have it observed that all the words consist

of three syllables, if you except Baralipton and Frisesomorum, to which, for the

sake of the meter, as they themselves say, one or two syllables are added that do

not pertain to the figure. Recall to memory that A denotes the universal affir‐

mative, etc. Hence a syllogism in Barbara, e.g., consists of three universal affir‐

mative propositions; in Celarem, of a negative major, an affirmative minor and a

negative consequent, all universal. The first nine modes, contained in the first

two verses, belong to the first figure, the next four to the second, and the rest

to the third. Now we ought to treat of the reduction of the syllogism; but we,

following the more circumspect Peripatetics, deliberately leave aside a treat‐

ment of this kind: for generally, as St. Augustine says, a man of wit sees sooner that

a conclusion is not right than he grasps its precepts; a slow man does not see it, and much

less what is prescribed concerning it.

A universal principle is handed down for recognizing

whether a syllogism is legitimate or faulty, without any ac‐

count at all being taken of the common rules.

his is that celebrated rule devised by the most illustrious Author of 71

T the Art of Thinking: namely that, for the conclusion to be rightly in‐

ferred, it must be contained in one of the premises, and this very

thing must be shown, or indicated, by the other, which is called the

applicative, or indicative, just as the first is called the containing one.

In

p. 27

In affirmative syllogisms it makes no difference at all whether we call the major or the minor the containing or the applicative, since each in some way contains the conclusion, and each also mutually shows it to be contained in the other. For e.g. if I doubt whether an impious man is wretched, I shall argue thus: Whoever is a slave to his desires is wretched; but the impious man is a slave to his desires: therefore the impious man is wretched. Whichever of the premises you designate, it can be said to contain the conclusion, and this to be shown by the other. For the conclusion is contained in the major, because one who is a slave to his desires contains the impious man under itself; and it is shown by the minor, because one who is a slave to his desires comprehends in its idea the idea of the wretched.

72 Nevertheless, in affirmative syllogisms, since the major is almost always the more universal, it can for the most part be taken as the containing premise, and the minor as the applicative. In negative syllogisms, however, the negative premise is always the containing proposition, and the affirmative is the applicative proposition, because, since the consequent is negative, it is more reasonable that it be contained in the negative premise than in the affirmative, since a negation is included only in a negation. But let us apply the principle.

73 I doubt, e.g., whether this syllogism concludes rightly: The Gospel promises salvation to Christians; some impious men are Christians: therefore the Gospel promises salvation to some impious men. Having considered the premises, then, it is evident that the conclusion is by no means contained in the major proposition, although at first sight it seems to be comprehended in the minor. For the Gospel does not promise salvation to all Christians, but only to those who observe the commandments of Christ the Lord, which the impious do not do. Therefore the syllogism is illegitimate. By the same reasoning this one is null: every man is an animal; a horse is not a man: therefore a horse is not an animal. For the conclusion is not comprehended in the negative premise. On the contrary, these are excellent: They are wretched who are slaves to their desires; the avaricious are slaves to their desires: therefore the avaricious are wretched. No substance lacking parts can be destroyed by a created agent; the rational soul is a substance lacking parts: therefore the rational soul can be destroyed by no created agent. For the conclusion of each is contained in the major, as the minor proposition itself makes plain.

74 By the help of this principle, too, the fallacy of this syllogism can be detected with little trouble: he who says you are an animal says what is true; but he who says you are a goose says you are an animal: therefore he who says you are a goose says what is true. For it suffices to answer that neither of the premises contains the conclusion. For animal in the major is taken particularly, since it is the predicate of this proposition: you are an animal. Hence, too, may be sought the solution of the sophism that St. Augustine reports: you are not what I am; I am a man: therefore you are not a man: for each

D2 premise

p. 28

CHAPTER XII

premise speaks of a thing singularly proper to me, and so it cannot contain the

conclusion, which proceeds about a thing proper to you.

75 To this norm and easy rule submit every reasoning, and you will have no

need of the laborious and altogether useless reduction of syllogisms, if you fol‐

low this law of arguing, which is common to all and placed almost before one’s

eyes. For by the light of this principle the goodness of any argumentation what‐

ever can easily be detected, so that the other laws can accordingly be deemed

either more obscure, or less universal, or even useless; nay rather, they must be.

On the Fallacies of the Syllogism.

allacy of a Syllogism, which comes from many sources, is a fault both 76

F to be recognized and to be avoided. First, then, a Syllogism deceives

by the equivocation of some name, e.g. a gallus [cock] is a bird; but a

Frenchman is a Gallus [Gaul]: therefore a Frenchman is a bird. Second,

when there is a passage from genus to species, as Sempronius is an animal, but an ass

is an animal: therefore Sempronius is an ass. The third fallacy is called ignoratio

elenchi, namely when something other is attacked than what is in question, be‐

cause either something is attributed to the adversary which he himself does not

assert, or the state of the question is ignored. Here belongs the change of the

middle, when, intending to prove, e.g., that God is to be loved because He is

Good, you abandon the middle of Goodness and take up Wisdom or Omnipotence.

The fourth is petitio principii, when that is supposed which ought to have been

proved. To this sophism can be brought back those reasons by which the un‐

known is proved by the equally unknown, the uncertain by the equally uncer‐

tain, or by the more uncertain.

77 The sophism of petitio principii extends widely: for whoever, without any

proof, sets down as if perspicuous what altogether needs proof asks that some

principle be granted him which was to be proved. This happens either proximately or

remotely. Proximately, as when one puts forward as a reason the conclusion to

be proved, either in the same words or in synonymous ones, or by a circle.

Remotely, as when one brings forward a thing openly false, or mere words, or

something of this kind

to

p. 29

to prove the thesis: for in such a case too he asks that the principle be granted him which he had to prove in order to accomplish what was proposed. When one of the premises, either plainly doubtful or plainly false, is adduced as a reason, this sophism too is called petitio principii. This can happen in very many ways, as we said above. Aristotle proves that the fixed stars twinkle because they are very far distant from us (l), and that they are very far distant because they twinkle (m). Behold a circle.

78 When they assign as a physical cause mere words that in reality signify nothing, we have said above that there is a petitio principii. Here is an example. Very many Philosophers, while they try to explain things wrapped up by nature herself, since they cannot accomplish this with firm and perspicuous arguments and are unwilling to confess their ignorance, have recourse to empty words and applaud themselves as though they had unlocked some such mystery. Hence horror of the vacuum, soporific virtue, and words of that kind, sonorous indeed and bombastic, but which have no meaning and do not make us more learned.

79 The fifth fallacy is non-cause as cause, e.g. Peter squandered his fortune on studies, and they did him no good: therefore time ought not to be spent on studies. To this sophism must be brought back that common fallacy of the human mind: after this: therefore because of this. The sixth is imperfect enumeration of the parts. Thus he reasons very badly who attributes to a whole College the sin of some of its members. The seventh is the fallacy of the accident, when one judges of the nature of a thing from what belongs to it by accident; thus all the evils that come from the errors of quacks are attributed to Medicine. The eighth is when one argues from what holds in some respect to what holds simply, e.g. an Ethiopian is white as to his teeth: therefore he is white.

80 The ninth is inept parity: namely when, because two things are similar in one or another predicate, we conclude that the one is very like the other. Authors of the same sophism are those who, in order to persuade someone that something is to be done, cunningly pass over its faults and extol its advantages to the skies; e.g. the Scholastic Philosophers, in order to persuade us that their Logic is to be preferred to the others, boastfully state that they dispute out of Aristotle’s Dialectic; that it is useful for learning Scholastic Theology; and finally that no one can dispute in the more abstruse disciplines without it. But they are silent about this: that such Dialectic is the art of caviling and of contending without any end; that it does not hand down the ways of searching out the true, whether the certain or the probable; that it contains nothing on the art

of

(l) On the Heavens, 2, ch. 8.

(m) Prior Analytics, 1, ch. 13.

p. 30

BOOK II

of criticism; and finally that it brings the human race no utility toward reason‐

ing rightly in the other disciplines: which ought not to have been passed over

in silence.

81 The tenth fallacy is: when we weaken a true proposition by no other ar‐

gument than by ridiculing its author. The Scholastics often sin in this when dis‐

puting with the Modern Philosophers. But this way of refuting is altogether

weak. They must therefore be compelled to refute theses not with guffaws and

witticisms, but with firm and perspicuous arguments. In the same way shall we

deal with those who try to persuade us of something false by complaints, wail‐

ing and oaths, because they are guilty of the same sophism. Let what has been

said suffice.

On Truth.

f anyone uses the operations of the intellect rightly, he certainly uses 82

I reason well, and it follows that, proceeding in this manner, he will find

the truth, of which we must now treat a little more accurately. Truth is

either Metaphysical, or Moral, or Logical. Whatever has the essence befitting it is

called metaphysically true. Every being, too, whether existing or possible, is

called metaphysically true when it is in conformity with the idea that God has

of it. Hence in this sense Peter is a true Peter, because he corresponds to the

idea of God. This metaphysical truth is also called real. Moral truth is the agree‐

ment of words and of external signs with the thoughts of the mind. Hence one

who speaks out what he thinks is said to speak the True; one who thinks one

thing and says another, the False. We, however, are dealing with Logical truth,

which is the agreement of our ideas with the object. Hence if, e.g., I conceive a

tower, or something round, and these things truly are such, I am said to have at‐

tained the truth. For the ideas agree with the object. Conversely, the false is the

disagreement of ideas with the object. Further, one truth is certain, another

probable. Certain, when I am thoroughly persuaded that the thing is so.

Probable, when I am so persuaded that I fear lest it be false.

Chapter

p. 31

CHAPTER I

On the Criterion of the True and the False.

here are, moreover, certain characters, or definite marks of assent, 83

T which are likewise called Criteria of truth, by which the true is dis‐

tinguished from the false, and by looking upon which we find the

truth we seek. It is asked, then, by what argument, in the end, we

can be safe that the things we judge affirmatively are as we judge them to be,

and that we are in no way deceived in them: in establishing which the Moderns

disagree not a little.

84 Pierre Daniel Huet holds that the speech of God alone is what makes us

certain that we do not err (n). This opinion is false; for if we can determine

nothing with certainty by reason, how shall we become certain that God has

said this to us? Not all are breathed upon by the Divine Spirit; and then men

are very often deceived in judging. Therefore they cannot plainly establish

whether they are made certain by God, or otherwise. I do not deny that the

Prophets, while they were inspired by the divine power, often needed no other

argument by which to be convinced that God was speaking to them: but not all

were Prophets; the greatest part of men, therefore, knew nothing at that time;

so that today, since there are no Prophets, at least none whom the Church

holds as such, all must necessarily be sunk in ignorance of all things. Whoever,

then, defends this opinion casts us into the foulest Pyrrhonism.

85 Benedict Spinoza, a Jew by origin, whom the Pantheists and the more re‐

cent Fanatics follow, holds (o) that human reason is the criterion of the true for

no other reason than that it is the very reason of God itself, because our mind

is a particle of the Divine mind. These things are so monstrous that whoever

would refute them would himself be going mad by reason. For the reason of

God is simple and infinite: therefore it cannot be divided: therefore wherever it

is present, it is the same.

Now

(n) Traité de la foiblesse de l’Esprit Humain.

(o) Theological-Political Treatise, ch. 1.

p. 32

Now if our reason is itself the reason of God, we shall be ignorant of nothing; for to infinite reason all things are open. Is anyone so mad as to flatter himself in this way, and to persuade himself that there is nothing he does not know? Spinozism (p), therefore, teems with the most inept ravings.

86 Nicolas Malebranche, Priest of the French Congregation of the Oratory, holds that our mind is essentially joined to God, and that we perceive all things in God’s idea and light, or that the light of God is the criterion of the true, because our mind sees all things in God (q). But if these things are true, I do not see what difference there is between the state of the blessed and that of wayfarers, in which the human mind, subject to so many errors, very often strays from the truth. I pass over other things, lest I be longer than the limits of Elements allow. But this I shall certainly not omit, that this substantial union of the mind with God cannot be understood except in the Spinozist system. For indeed, if God is the place of minds, as space is of bodies, they will be either parts of God, or modes, or God himself. More on this subject in the celebrated Genovesi (r).

Chapter

(p) Spinozism is the error of those who admit only a single substance endowed with infinite attributes, among which are numbered infinite thought and infinite extension: each of these has an eternal and infinite essence, while finite beings are imagined to arise from the necessary modification of the attributes of this substance, namely souls from the modification of infinite thought, and bodies from the modification of infinite extension. Spinoza does not distinguish God from the world; he makes God mutable, extended, and yet intelligent. As the basis and foundation of his impious hypothesis Spinoza assumes that there cannot be two substances of the same essence, because if they have the same essence, he says, they are one and the same substance. But there is no one who does not see at once that two substances cannot have the same essence by numerical identity (as they say), but can by identity either generic or specific. Nor is there any man endowed with common sense who, from the fact that Peter and Paul are men, and therefore have the same essence, or are alike by reason of humanity, would conclude that Peter and Paul are numerically one and the same man, or are a single individual. But of these things more opportunely in the Ethics.
