CHAPTER II

On the Probable True, where also on Hermeneutic, Moral and

Physical Probability.

hat leaves some doubt in the mind is true only probably. The sole 87

W foundation of probability is a hypothesis, that is, a proposition that we

assume as true for this reason, that the properties and effects of a

thing are conveniently explained from it. E.g. if I assume as true that a subterranean

inflammable matter, chiefly nitrous and sulphurous, is the cause of earthquakes, this

hypothesis, until something more certain appears, cannot be held to be false: for from

it all the phenomena can be explained both easily and plausibly. Or else I assume as a

hypothesis the signification of the words, their position, and a connection in agree‐

ment with the aim of the author, or the authority of some witness. If the first, that

probability is called Hermeneutic, or probable interpretation; if the second, Historical,

which is specifically named faith.

88 The foundation, therefore, of Hermeneutic probability is of this kind: What

agrees with the signification, position and connection of the words, and likewise with the

Author’s aim, is to be held probably as the Author’s meaning. The foundation of Historical

probability is of this kind: What a trustworthy man testifies to be true is probably true.

89 What is handed down to us by men is, first, handed down either by those

present, or contemporaries, or by those absent and later. 2. The witnesses are either sever‐

al or one; and likewise 3. they either perceived the thing with their eyes, or heard it narrated

by others; nay, and 4. they either give a reason for their knowledge, or not; and 5. they

report a thing either possible in itself, or marvelous, or plainly impossible. Further, 6. they

are either known or unknown; 7. they follow the zeal either of neither party or of one

party only; 8. they are either prudent or foolish, honest or dishonest, and liars. From these

divisions are easily understood the rules by which one can judge of the degrees of hu‐

man faith. I. is: The more certain I am that the author did not wish to deceive me, the greater

the faith I am bound to have in him. II. Whether anyone has wished to deceive me must often be

judged from the very circumstances of the narration.

E It

p. 34

90 It is therefore most certain, 1. that little faith is to be had in a single witness narrating a marvelous thing, even if he is otherwise not much suspected, especially when the matter is such that the witness could easily have been deceived by his imagination; 2. that the degree of probability is greater if several witnesses report a thing that, however marvelous, is yet not impossible, even if not in every respect in the same manner and with the same circumstances; 3. that what several trustworthy men report with the same circumstances is much more probable, and that this probability is increased not a little if the witnesses are eyewitnesses, if they are public persons, if they are sworn. Very many other rules of this probability can be seen in the celebrated Antonio Genovesi (s).

91 Moral probability is had when, from certain signs that men display, we either declare something hidden or predict something future. According to the things it predicts, this is called either Practical or Political. E.g. I see Titius with a sad face spurning lawful pleasures, given over to gain, in a worn and sordid garment, perpetually crying out that he is poor. Hence I probably infer that Titius is avaricious. This way of divining, then, which by reasoning from external signs investigates the propensities of the mind, is called moral Probability, or Practical. Sometimes, however, we foresee some future event from the counsels of men, and this divination is named by a word of its own, Political Probability. But these consequences are more or less probable, just as the force of judging and the experience of things are greater or less in those who conjecture; those who see far ahead judge much more truly and more probably.

92 Physical Probability is given when, from the observation of phenomena and of sensations, we think out some hypothesis that explains all the phenomena lucidly and skillfully. But if the hypothesis that I posit is such that from it I cannot prove that the thing is so, it is not a hypothesis but a fiction. E.g. when the Peripatetics say that the horror of the vacuum is the cause why a pump draws water, it is a mere fiction, because such words do not explain why water rises 32 feet and rises no further in a pump a thousand feet long.

(s) In the Elem. Art. Logico-Critic.

CHAPTER III

Rules directing the human mind in believing doctrines that rest on

Divine as well as on human authority.

93

W e are led by authority when, in passing judgment on things, we abide by the

sayings of others. That authority which moves us to assent is either Divine or

Human. That we should be deceived by Divine authority is utterly impossible, as we

shall say. But that we can be deceived by human authority escapes no one. It matters

very greatly, therefore, that we instruct ourselves rightly in this respect. Here, then,

are the rules that can be of use to us in believing doctrines.

94 Rule I. All those things are to be admitted with the firmest assent which rest on Divine

authority. For it is more repugnant that God should be deceived, or deceive, than that

those things should not be true which reason shows most evidently. In those things,

therefore, which belong to Divine Faith it is most just, as the Apostle says, to bring into

captivity the understanding unto the obedience of Christ, namely, so that we do not doubt

even in the slightest of the truth of those things which are handed down to us to be

believed on divine authority. Rule II. Those things are to be admitted with a firm and con‐

stant mind which are proposed to us by the Church to be believed with divine faith. For it can‐

not happen that the Church should be deceived in defining those things which per‐

tain to faith, and lead us into error, since Christ our Lord said openly that it would

never come about that the faith of Peter should fail, nor that the gates of hell should prevail

against the Church.

95 Rule III. Great care must be taken that we hold that which has been believed every‐

where, always, and by all. For that is of such a kind that it was handed down by word of

mouth by Christ our Lord himself to the Apostles, and derived through them to us

by constant tradition (t).

E2 Rule

(t) Divine Tradition is the doctrine of God, not written, but revealed by God to our forefathers

and communicated to their successors from ear to ear. This tradition is usually called Dominical, be‐

cause it has been derived from Christ our Lord to the Apostles, and by them through their successors

down to us: of this kind is the tradition concerning the number of the Sacraments, and concerning

the perpetual Virginity of the Blessed Mary. Another is Apostolic, which the Apostles received at

the dictation of the Holy Spirit and communicated to the Church without writing, as the Council of

Trent teaches, Sess. 4.

p. 36

Rule IV. Not every opinion is to be deemed safe precisely because the Church has by no means

proscribed it. For the Church does not openly condemn all errors, but only those

that make a stir. For so long (says St. Augustine) is the sin or the error of anyone whatev‐

er tolerated, until it either finds an accuser or defends a depraved opinion with stubborn ani‐

mosity. Rule V. That is to be held firmly as certain which, in matters of faith and morals, all

the Holy Fathers teach. For since the Holy Fathers were sent by God to instruct the

Church, it could by no means happen that in those things which concern Religion

all should have erred. I said all; for not every one of them was endowed with such

infallibility that he could err in absolutely nothing, as St. Augustine expressly

teaches.

96 Rule VI. In the natural disciplines and the human arts (such as, for example,

Philosophy) the authority of the Holy Fathers is of no greater weight than is the authority

of those Philosophers whom the Holy Fathers themselves followed. Hence the sayings of

the Holy Fathers are to be valued by us in this matter precisely as much as the

reasons by which they are shown are worth. For, as the most illustrious Melchior

Cano excellently observes, the holy Authors were not so solicitous in scrutinizing the dog‐

mas of Philosophy that they did not either bid farewell to the books of the Philosophers, so as

to give themselves wholly to Divine Wisdom, or at times even greet them only from the

threshold.

C H A P T E R I V.

On the chief causes or occasions of errors, and first, on the fallac‐

ies of the senses.

ome things, however, and that frequently, prevent us from attaining 97

S truth, which the Logician must have clearly understood, so that he may

avoid them as far as he can, or, if he has not avoided them, may at least

in some measure amend his errors. These are conveniently referred to

three classes, those of the Senses, of the Will, and of the Mind, about which we

shall explain a few things in order.

98 In the first place, our senses very often deceive us. Not that they them‐

selves deceive, for they always present something that really exists, but because

they furnish the occasion of our being deceived, by judging that the objects really

are

p. 37

are just as they appear to us. Thus, while we see light, colors and other objects, it is indeed true that we see them, even if we were suffering from frenzy. For all the delirious without doubt see what they see, and their error consists solely in the judgments by which they judge that what they see really exists outside themselves, by the very fact that they see it placed externally. But as we are about to treat of the fallacies of the senses, let us begin with sight.

99 We can scarcely ever judge with certainty that we grasp the true magnitude of things. For just as glass lenses, if they are segments of a larger or a smaller sphere, and hence more or less convex, then represent objects larger or smaller, so our eyes, if they are more or less convex, will do the same. If, therefore, the eyes of two men differ from each other (as they really do differ) either in the density of the humors, or in their figure, or in their position and situation, they will exhibit a different extension of a body, as glass lenses do: hence we cannot say for certain how large the object is that we behold.

100 Experience confirms this very thing: for spectacles, and likewise optical tubes arranged in one and the same way, do not suit the eyes of all men equally. We are also sometimes deceived when we determine bodies to be equal or unequal; for example, if on some given horizontal straight line another straight line, perpendicular and equal to it, is erected at its extremity, both appear equal to each other to the eyes; but if this perpendicular is drawn not at the extremity of the other but toward the middle, the more it approaches its midpoint, the greater it appears than the other, horizontal, line, as is plain in the adjoined figure.

101 Nor shall we determine with any certainty the figure of large bodies if they are a long distance away. For a square tower that is viewed from afar appears without angles. Also, the very smallest bodies that appear round, like a grain of sand, if we contemplate them with a microscope applied, have a great many surfaces and diverse figures. And insensible things that do not appear to the naked eye, if we explore them with a microscope, present themselves as very many and endowed with many figures: e.g., in water, in vinegar we behold almost infinite animalcules, which cannot be seen without the glass; of which the most sagacious investigators of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, Hartsoeker, Hooke, Joblot and others, supply further examples.

Men

p. 38

102 Men are also deceived when they think that colors are in the object body, which happens not only to the unlearned but also to the Peripatetics. For, to pass over Descartes and his followers Malebranche, Arnauld, Rohault, and other most illustrious men who philosophized in France after the middle of the past century, the great Isaac Newton, the light and ornament of England, seems to have hit the mark exactly when by the most certain experiments he proved that all colors are contained in light itself, whose rays, it is established, are endowed by their very nature with this or that color. Accordingly, assent is given neither to the Cartesians, who contend that colors are located in the varied texture and disposition of the surface of bodies, nor indeed to the Idealists, who hold that they are wholly in the organ of sight, as though they were mere illusions, and that nothing exists outside the mind. Although, therefore, we do not wish (for there is no time) to bring in here the Newtonian opinion on light and colors, set out as it deserves, we nevertheless acknowledge no other as more probable.

103 For no slight argument for the Newtonians is this, that when the light is changed the color is changed: for if spirit of wine with a very little water is poured on tow sprinkled with much salt, and this is set alight, the human face itself appears with a horrible look. He who has fixed his eyes on the orb of the Sun, or suffers from ophthalmia, sees objects covered and surrounded with many colors, and as it were with a kind of rainbow; but the objects are by no means girt with those colors in reality; for if it were so, the said colors would be seen by all, which is altogether false.

104 By an easy experiment of the illustrious Newton (u) this very thing is shown. If in a dark room you catch with a crystal prism the rays of light that come through a hole made in the window, these, while they pass through the crystal and the room, are not seen colored; but when they fall on a white paper set opposite, or are carried onto the opposite wall, they are so refracted, and so affect the eyes, that they excite in us sensations of these seven colors, namely violet, purple, blue, green, yellow, orange and red, and the wall appears painted with them, arranged in the order in which we have enumerated them. But the wall and the paper have no faculty of producing colors, nor of changing the nature of rays that were not colored. From this follows what we should determine about colors, if we approached the matter as it deserves, and not as though we were busy with something else.

105 Hearing likewise is a frequent cause of errors. For, first, we think that sound is a thing that is outside us and comes from the body

that

(u) Opticks, p. 103 & 153.

p. 39

that sounds; which, however, is false. For the sonorous body does nothing other than tremble very swiftly and in a certain manner, and this tremor drives the air to the tympanum of the ear and so moves it as to excite in the mind the sensation of sound. For no sound arises unless the particles of the bodies that are called sonorous take on a tremulous motion, which can be very easily proved by one or two experiments.

106 For if water is poured into a glass vessel and a finger, brought to the lip of the vessel, is drawn round the mouth of the vessel for some time, continually pressing and rubbing, a tremor and quivering is in this way excited in the walls of the vessel, which is at once communicated to the water it contains, and that tremor plainly appears to the eye. And as soon as the particles begin to tremble, the sensation of sound immediately arises; and when that tremor is extinguished, whether this happens of itself or by our doing, all sensation of sound is immediately extinguished.

107 Further, if in the air pump, the air having been exhausted, a little bell is struck (which can certainly be done), although the particles of that metal, struck by the little hammer, take on a tremulous motion, yet since that tremor cannot be communicated to the air (for there is no longer any air present), and so cannot reach all the way to our ears, no sensation of sound arises from it; but when the air is restored to the machine, the sense of sound is immediately excited. What we perceive and call sound, therefore, does not exist in external bodies; there is only the undulatory motion of the particles of which they are composed, and when this is given, sensations of sound are excited in our minds, provided, however, that that motion is communicated to the air and reaches all the way to our ears.

108 Smell and Taste deceive us in the same way, because they are the cause of our thinking, imprudently, that Odor and Savor are in the body we touch; whereas they are nothing other than sensations of the mind, which are excited in us by the insensible particles of the bodies that touch these two organs. This will be plain with little trouble if we consider that no sensation, pleasant or unpleasant, can in any way exist outside the mind.

109 Moreover, if odors and savors were things existing outside us, the same odorous body and the same food would affect each man in the same way. But it is otherwise; for civet, for example, or the scent of the lily, is pleasant to some, to others utterly intolerable. Nor are all delighted by the same food. In the sick, more wonderful phenomena very often occur. Who does not know that women suffering from obstructions devour earth, coals, lime and other things of that kind, which those same women, when they are well and freed from the illness, cannot see without nausea, nay, cannot even name?

Those

p. 40

110 Those who suffer from fever find bitter the things that the healthy hold sweet and agreeable. The same happens with odors. These things, moreover, teach clearly that odors and savors are not in the object bodies, but only the occasion of our sensing them: for these bodies, according to the diverse constitution of the organs, whether of two men or of the same man when he suffers from illness or from age, move and prick the fibers of the senses in diverse ways, so that the nerves, affected in diverse ways, excite other perceptions in the mind, which are themselves either odors or savors.

111 Touch, finally, is a most abundant source of errors. This is established by the plainest experiments, of which we shall adduce only a few. We judge without any doubt that the things we distinguish by touch are in external bodies, which is false; for neither does what we call heat exist in fire, nor what we call cold in ice; and this, besides the reason brought forward in §. 108, is proved by almost innumerable others. For if you plunge one hand, well warmed, and the other, very cold, into the same lukewarm water, the one that is cold will feel it hot, and on the contrary the one that is hot will feel it cold. We would not say so if the water were hot of itself: for both hands would feel a moderate heat, just as both hands feel that it is a body, that it is fluid, etc., because it is so.

112 Further, if someone in wintertime enters a well-closed room and says that the air enclosed there is hot, or lukewarm, while one who has just risen from bed, placed in that same room, asserts that that air is cold rather than lukewarm or hot: since the same body cannot in reality be at once hot and cold, it manifestly follows that we cannot argue that what we call heat and cold inheres in reality in a given body from the fact that that given body excites heat or cold in us.

113 We are deceived by touch in many other ways. For if, e.g., you place the middle finger of the hand over the index finger and hold a small globule in the middle between both fingers, unless you employ your eyes as witnesses, you will swear that two globules are being touched by you. From all of which it follows that our senses give us very much occasion for being deceived. But since God gave us the senses not for ornament, but that we might use them and by their help acquire knowledge, there must therefore be some Criterion by which we may distinguish true and false notions. The criterion, then, is this.

114 Those images must be held most certain which, all the circumstances having been accurately weighed, are always found the same by the same sense, or by the other senses; and this by one man, and much more by diverse men who have examined them diligently. For if not even in this case could the images be held true, God would perpetually delude us:

which

p. 41

which is foreign to so great a Goodness. In this way, indeed, the fiction of the

Pyrrhonists is refuted by true Philosophers. For clarity’s sake we shall comprise

this doctrine in three canons. I. Do not pronounce that the things the senses represent

are true, or that things are not, because they do not fall under the senses, without first dili‐

gently weighing the matter and applying the opinion of experts. II. Beware of ever judg‐

ing, by the help of your senses, of things as they are in themselves. III. Do not make exper‐

iments as some of the Ancients did, but use most diligently the most exact instruments that

the Moderns have devised and perfected.

C H A P T E R V.

On the Affections of the Will that impede the attainment of

truth. 115

W e should have little to fear (says the illustrious Verney (u)) if the senses

alone led us into errors: for since errors of this kind are conspicuous,

the remedy would be at hand, namely, to pronounce cautiously about the things

that are perceived by the senses, and to call them to examination again and

again before we made a judgment. But there is another cause which, the more

hidden it is, the more strongly calls a man back from truth and drives him to

error. Of this kind are the affections of the mind. For when the mind perceives

sensible things according as they are good or bad, there arises a certain motion

of the mind, joined with a great commotion of the nervous fluid and of the

blood, which is called an affection; and this is followed either by pleasure of

mind or by pain.

116 It is wonderful to say how strongly and how swiftly these affections, if

they are vehement, lead a man astray, as has been ascertained by experience.

First, they hinder the mind from examining accurately the things about which

it ought to deliberate; from which it follows that it acquires obscure ideas and

is deceived in judging. Next, they bring it about that we love some things, and

shun others, as we ought not. For just like microscopes, they so enlarge and di‐

late the things that please and those that displease, that the mind, struck by

such brilliance,

F judges

(u) De Re Logica.

p. 42

judges to be good or bad what in reality is not. This can be proved by so many arguments that plenty makes me poor. I shall add a few, however; as for the rest, I advise each one to consult himself: for if he scrutinizes his own actions and weighs them as they deserve, he will find all too many examples.

117 The principal source of the affections, from which they all flow, is the immoderate love with which each one loves himself, which we call Philautia [self-love]: wherefore Philautia must be held to be the parent of the errors that arise from the Will. We love vehemently ourselves and everything that is ours, our sayings, deeds and thoughts. Nor do we think that anything so glorious can be declared of any man that we do not judge it ought to be said of ourselves with better right. This affection, like a kind of disease, sometimes pervades not only the half-learned but even the most learned.

118 Hence arises this too, that we pass judgment on things not as they are in reality, but according to the way in which they affect us. Thus what we think suits us we judge good, beautiful and just; what does not suit us, the contrary. Very many so extol their friends, kinsmen, teachers and countrymen that they think nothing holier, nothing more learned, nothing more heaped with every praise can even be conceived. But if they hear anyone noting their errors, they call down every evil upon him, and oppose him, as a man hateful to the gods above, pernicious to the commonwealth, and plotting new and nefarious crimes, so fiercely that nothing could go further.

119 This is seen more openly in those who have given their names to some sect. For who would tell such a Philosopher that his teacher has erred? Who would persuade him that he ought to bring his master’s opinions to the light of other doctors? Well known is that saying of Averroes, who, when he was interpreting Aristotle, did not hesitate to say this: The doctrine of Aristotle is the highest truth, since his intellect was the limit of the human intellect: wherefore it is well said of him that he was created and given to us by Divine providence, so that we might not be ignorant of what can be known. And in another place: None of those, he says, who have followed him up to this time, which is a period of one thousand five hundred years, has added anything; nor will you find in his words an error of any magnitude.

120 These things can be pardoned in a Heathen man, writing in so rude an age, and one who had not read good authors; but in Catholic men, and in this light of Letters, they are not to be borne. I have heard a Peripatetic say that the ancient Bishops, from the first century of the Church, held Aristotle as a kind of norm of disputing, even in matters of Faith, and did not depart a finger’s breadth from his opinions. Nor would I hesitate to affirm that very many even now persist in the same

heresy

p. 43

heresy, though more covertly.

121 Hence arises this too, that those who are held by such opinions think nothing right except what flows from those sources. These they defend constantly and stubbornly; the rest they reject as false and harmful. They fear, namely, lest they incur the mark of inconstancy or of error, and lose by an ingenuous confession of error the praise they acquired with so much sweat. This philautia prevents men from tracking down the truth; and this happens much more in the old than in the young.

122 Hence the writings of those who hold the contrary opinion they either do not read at all, or read yawning; and if they examine them a little more attentively, they do so with this design, to refute their opinions. For how few are there, even of those who with great disdain censure the opinions of the Moderns, who, when they have turned over Descartes, Gassendi, Malebranche, Leibniz, Wolff and the other most acute Philosophers, do not rather condemn them on another’s judgment than call them back to their own circumspect examination?

123 Hence that zeal for dissenting, and a certain inexplicable desire of wrangling, which so drives some men that nothing is held so firm and so evident that they do not try to weaken and obscure it with their disputations. For these men, as if they had been born for discord, call everything to the balance of disputation; and if perchance arguments fail them on the matter proposed, they immediately ask whether they are making a conjoined or a separated kind of syllogism. There are Philosophers who, when about to hand down to youths the rudiments of some science, first teach them to contend with words and to chatter rather impudently, instead of handing down some precepts that would lead the boys into the very inner recesses of the science. Books are full of examples, which it would be easy to bring forward, were the matter not exceedingly well known.

124 Hence is born that intolerable pride by which men so arrogate to themselves the first place in letters that they either diminish the learning of others in other studies or, if they spare these, nevertheless prefer themselves to all in the faculty they profess. It is the way of men (says Cicero) that they do not wish the same man to excel in many things. (x) This way, moreover, has come down even to our own age. A jurist, for example, if he hears a Theologian disputing about Law, whether Public or Private, generally laughs at him. Jurisprudence, forsooth, is open only to him who is adorned with the insignia of a Doctor; all others

F2 it

(x) Cic., Brutus, ch. 21.

p. 44

it repels from itself. The Theologian, on the other hand, even if he praises the Jurisconsult, nevertheless thinks it a heinous crime if the latter touches on anything of the Sacred Science. As though the laws of the Caesars were not illustrated by the Sacred Letters and by Ethical discipline; or as though the statutes of the Sacred Canons were not aided by the constitutions of Princes. And so much in particular on philautia; and since the remaining affections are reduced to it, we shall append a few things about them.

125 Hope, and much more Desire, what do they not disturb in the breast of mortals! How they distract the mind, so that it does not attend to the things that are! Those who desire and hope feign dreams for themselves: these they love, these they adore, they see nothing besides. Hence they readily think that they have what they hope for; they lend their ears to flatterers, believe them, and are wonderfully deceived. Let some mountebank tell a man suffering from paralysis or dropsy that he has an exquisite remedy by which he would free such men from the disease within the course of a single day: though a thousand most weighty men should show that this cannot be done, the sick will think it true.

126 But Ambition, how vehemently it torments men! How it drives them headlong, without any shame, into many unseemly things that diminish the dignity of man! This affection spreads more widely than is commonly thought; and men take studious care to obscure it under one name or another, lest they be exposed to reproach and laughter.

127 There are those who say they seek honors so as to be a protection to their kinsmen and connections. These conceal their ambition under the title of piety. Others, a little more cunning, perpetually cry out that they will never allow themselves to be raised to honors, because they are altogether unworthy of them. These, namely, hope that by this art they can easily be advanced to some eminence. Here is ambition wrapped in the name of contempt of honors. Most of those who live in the courts of Kings cover it with the specious name of compliance. They, namely, perpetually praise the deeds and sayings of those from whom they hope for fortune; and, mindful of Terence’s saying, compliance begets friends, truth hatred, they command themselves to assent to everything and to hold everything as true. This habit corrupts judgment and blunts the edge of judging.

128 Most like this is Avarice: how far it has blinded the minds of men, how many wars it has stirred up in every age of the world, how many kingdoms it has made solitary and deserted, History shows clearly. Truly, those who are driven by such an affection can scarcely, or not even scarcely, hear the truth, much less comprehend it by reason and consider it attentively.

129 Fear also generates wonderful phenomena in the minds of men. Those who are seized by excessive fear scarcely ever understand things

as

p. 45

as they are: they think they see what they do not see, and perpetually reason badly. Hence so many prodigies present themselves in the Histories of the Heathen, which flowed from this source, that peoples persuaded themselves that the immortal gods would exact the penalty for crime by a visible punishment. And once their minds had been stirred to religious awe, it was easy for them to think that whatever happened less ordinarily, whether an eclipse of the Moon or of the Sun, or an egg larger than usual, or a serpent in the house, and follies of that kind, that these, I say, were portents by which those Gods of theirs declared their anger and indignation.

130 But among our own people too, how many fables are born of fear! Those who fear assert that they themselves see apparitions of the night, specters of tombs, things horrible to tell. Whatever is heard by night is ghosts. If some old and ragged woman comes along, she, forsooth, displays a marvelous power of calling up demons at pleasure, of doing harm to whomever she will, and of killing a man with impunity: and six hundred most trifling things of this kind, which none but those seized with terror, or fools, will ever affirm.

131 How headlong Anger drives men, no one fails to perceive. It clouds the mind and blinds the very eyes, so that nothing so absurd can be said or thought that the angry man does not do in his very fury; so much so that, when master of himself, he is sometimes ashamed of having perpetrated such things. Hence the mind is so vehemently shaken that it can scarcely judge rightly of things: it thinks the things that stand in its way greater, and the rest much smaller, than they are; and therefore it always chooses the worse part. Wherefore, if we reckon up the account, we shall find that the greater calamities of mortals have proceeded from anger.

132 These things being briefly surveyed, it becomes manifest that those motions of the mind which disturb reason (for all of them disturb it) must be restrained, and that it is the Philosopher’s business to take care that we are not agitated by any affections, but have a serene mind, if we desire to judge rightly and wisely. For as a ship in mid-sea, driven by vehement and contrary winds, can neither hold its course nor make for port, so our mind, driven about by those affections as by a wind, will scarcely ever attain the truth toward which it tends; therefore commit this Canon to memory: Do not judge while you are occupied by some affection: and if you have judged, call the matter back again to examination; then at last pronounce, freely, and after the matter has been accurately weighed.

Chapter

p. 46

CHAPTER VI

On the fallacies of the Mind, which prevent us from finding

the truth.

ut the weakness of our mind too (continues the cited Verney) will 133

B more often be the cause of many errors, into which we very fre‐

quently slip, and which wonderfully retard the attainment of truth.

To avoid them it is necessary to know their causes thoroughly and to fix them

deep in the mind, so that we may more easily avoid them when they occur. We

refer them, not inconveniently, to three classes, our slowness, perverse method, and

prejudices, which we shall explain in the same order.

134 The first and chief cause on account of which we are deceived in judg‐

ing is the very nature of our mind, which both has its faculty of understanding

confined within narrow limits, and understands the very things it understands

so obscurely that it can scarcely be believed. We shall perceive this most plainly

if we examine our cognitions more diligently.

135 For our mind, even though it dwells in the body, is nevertheless igno‐

rant of the wholly wonderful fabric of the body, of the brain especially. Not that

it is not at all suited to knowing it; for if another’s brain is set before it and its

parts are visible, it knows them perfectly: but on this account only, because

God did not will that the soul should know corporeal things thoroughly except

through the senses.

136 Next, it does not attain the nature of things, however common: for ex‐

ample, it cannot determine whether a body has infinite parts or not; what the

nature is of the Sun, of the Moon, of the Stars, both of those that are called

wandering and of those that are called fixed; finally, whether there are living

creatures in the stars; and six hundred things of that kind. To pass over for the

present the things that can be done by God, about which the School tells many

most trifling tales, and which can by no means be understood, much less

defined.

137 But this slowness and weakness cannot be wholly amended: we can ap‐

ply one remedy, to beware studiously of defining those things for the investiga‐

tion of which we are altogether unfit. Of these, moreover, there are two classes:

the one, of those things that surpass our intelligence, such as the nature of the

divine properties;

likewise

p. 47

likewise all possible things, which can be neither determined nor explained by the reasonings of nature or by divine utterance. The other is of things that can indeed be understood, but we lack the necessary aids by which we might arrive at the knowledge of them: such are those we named a little before, and also the most ancient histories, and infinite things of this kind. And so much on the first cause.

138 The second cause is perverse method. This extends very widely, and from it arise very many errors and infinite evils. For in the first place there are those who, having entered upon a winding road set in darkness, do not arrive at the end they proposed to themselves, but frequently slip: nay, the further they advance along it, the more they swerve from the truth. Certain men of letters very often strike upon this rock.

139 There are men who, even if they are not versed in the Mathematical disciplines, nevertheless pass judgment quite confidently on the writings of the Modern Philosophers, and dare to work out a great many things in Physics. There are those who interpret the Sacred Bible without knowing Greek and Hebrew, without having any knowledge of Jewish and Profane history, who are plain strangers to the Critical art. There are those who expound the Roman laws who are tinged with no knowledge of Roman history, and have not tasted even with the tips of their lips the rudiments of Ethics and Politics. There are those who teach Pontifical law, who teach Sacred science, without ever having turned over the writings of the Fathers and examined the ancient discipline of the Church. Finally, to omit the rest, there are Physicians who persuade themselves that they will cure the infinite variety of diseases that afflict the human body without ever having seen a dissection of the human body. All these, because they are ignorant of what is necessary, will never be able to bring forth anything good.

140 Others, again, although they proceed rightly, nevertheless fall into the contrary vice. Namely, since they long to know everything and to be praised above the rest, they read quite different things at the same time; and though they desire to seem anything but unlearned, they are the most unlearned of all. For our mind, which scarcely grasps any one discipline perfectly, knows nothing thoroughly and deeply while it reads many things at once, and so acquires nothing but confused ideas, and for that reason is deceived in judging.

141 The third cause of errors is prejudices, or anticipated judgments that our mind makes about certain things: from which it comes about that we form our other judgments quite similar to them, and do not judge freely and deservedly about anything. For since men from their earliest age are accustomed to listen to others, who imprint on their minds the images of certain things,

they

p. 48

they easily persuade themselves that what they hear is true, and attach such faith to such things that they can only with difficulty be turned to the contrary side. From this an infinite crop of errors springs up. And so the incredible multitude of prejudices that holds men is reduced to the prejudice of authority, if you take away a few that arise in adult men either from hatred or from love.

142 And first, the authority of parents is to children the norm of judging, and the cause of many errors. For parents imbue their children from the earliest age with foolish prejudices, which the nurses unceasingly confirm; and since tender minds are not strong in the use of reason and are not at all practiced in judging, they cannot persuade themselves that they have been deceived by their parents: and therefore they are deceived to a wonderful degree. Hence specters, and goblins, and ghosts, and the virtues of herbs and of medicines, and the miracles of mountebanks, and the other most trifling things that beat upon the ears of unhappy boys: so much so that, when they have become men, and are admonished by most learned men, they can scarcely at any time free themselves from those prejudices.

143 Next, nearly all parents treat their children softly and let them indulge their inclination, because they persuade themselves that if they did otherwise it would be to the harm and injury of their little ones. Hence boys are very often immersed in bodily pleasures, especially those of food and of venery, which both blunt the edge of the mind and weaken the memory, and so lead a man astray that he can scarcely ever think about and examine anything seriously and with meditation. For hold this for certain, young men: no more deadly plague befalls either body or mind than the pleasures of the body, which not only gradually undermine the fabric of man, but extinguish all the light of the mind. For laden tables carry off more men from our midst, frequent cups more, venery itself more, than plague, than war.

144 Parents are succeeded by Teachers, who frequently imbue little boys with marvelous opinions, and by their authority restrain them from learning other disciplines than those in which they themselves are versed.

145 The Peripatetic Doctor cries out that the disciplines of the Moderns are futile and weak; the Critical Art, Natural History, Geometry, Arithmetic, Mechanics and things like these he thinks to be boys’ trifles; and he hisses off men illustrious in these disciplines just as if they were madmen. On the other hand, he everywhere sounds forth Universals and Signs, and Syllogistics, and Topics, and the huge throng of despicable little questions that he entitles Physics and Metaphysics; and he contends that the limits of philosophical science are wholly defined by these. Nay, at times he strikes, as it were, terror into the minds of the boys,

lest

p. 49

lest they learn Mathematics or the Philosophy of the Moderns, or ever call back to a severe examination the things that he himself holds as settled and fixed.

146 The little boy, nourished on these admonitions, reverently kisses the pronouncements of his Teacher, and thinks that nothing more excellent can be conceived; he turns away from the splendid discoveries of others as though they were mere trifles, and shudders at the mere hearing of the name of the Systems of the Moderns: therefore he is ignorant of the sources of the disciplines, and can neither think nor utter anything worthy of learned ears. And so, when he has grown older, he too nourishes others with the same milk, and propagates ignorance with as much labor as would have been needed for him to be held most illustrious in the best disciplines.

147 This was the reason why the weightier disciplines lay in squalor for so many centuries: namely, because the teachers who were thought most learned strove with all their might to keep the boys from deserting the old Masters, or from thinking anything new that was not in them. For men of this kind grieved to be surpassed in learning by younger men, and ambitiously took care that this new doctrine and new way of teaching should not undermine the glory they themselves had won by so many labors. And so they confidently objected that very many heresies are stirred up in Theology even by the help of a better Philosophy; and by this argument, drawn from envy, false indeed but received with applause, they ruined the discoveries of others, nay, even their talent.

148 From this education, moreover, there arise all too many prejudices, which are usually taken from the circumstances of persons and of books. For who, they say, would not do, or think true, the things that are done by a man advanced in age? by one who has piety toward God? who displays wisdom and moderation of mind? who surpasses the rest in nobility, in riches, in dignity, in honors? who is distinguished from others by his kind of life, by his name, by his talent? who would think that such a man can err? On the other hand, who would persuade himself that anything excellent can be thought by a young man, or by a poor man, and a ragged one at that, known above others by no ornaments, by no insignia of dignity? by one who tells no stories readily at a banquet and a drinking-party? who shows something unsightly in his manner of life, his face, his gesture, and is therefore hissed off both by silly women and by effeminate busybodies?

149 These are the common prejudices of authority by which men are led in every part of life. Not that they say expressly: he is rich, or noble, or old: therefore he cannot err: for the fault of this consequence is at once placed before the eyes. But tacitly they feel and settle it so; and without thinking distinctly about

G these

p. 50

these things, yet from a long habit of listening and of thinking imprudently, as if by a certain impulse of nature, they conform their actions to this rule.

150 Add to these those who measure the learning either of the author or of the possessor by the multitude, size, titles, rarity and price of books. Truly nothing occurs more frequently, not only among the unlearned but even among most of those who apply themselves to letters, than this prejudice.

151 For who would persuade some people that those copious volumes of Tostado, Bishop of Ávila, which expound Sacred Scripture, are in many respects to be ranked below, I do not say Calmet and other more copious writers, but even Tirinus and Menochius and the others who have written briefly? Who unskilled in History and Criticism would think that Salian’s Annals of the Old Testament, in six great volumes in folio (as they call it), are to be valued much less than Petau’s Rationarium or the brief commentaries of Sigonio and others on the Republic of the Hebrews? Which of the Casuists would persuade himself that the huge volumes of Leandro, Torrecilla and other Casuists that hand down Moral discipline ought to give place even to the single little book of Antoine On Moral Matters, to say nothing of others? Moreover, who that is ignorant of the newer Physics would think that Newton’s Principles of Natural Philosophy alone surpasses all the Libraries of the Scholastics in firmness, solidity and utility, if one weighs the sources and order of things? Let the same judgment hold for the rest, which very often lead men into errors.

152 Weigh the other circumstances of books, and with free judgment: you will plainly discover that not the pomp of a title that seems to promise something great, such as Theatre of Human Life, Thesaurus, Polyanthea, Encyclopedia, Library of Canon or Civil Law; not the rarity or price of books; not the other things of this sort, can give books either name or esteem. Yet from these prejudices nearly all the errors of the half-learned proceed. From these they would free themselves admirably, if they judged things by their own merit, not by the opinions of others.

153 Now when a man leaves the discipline of his teachers, he runs into the manners of those who live in popular fashion, who are so far from polishing his judgment that they rather generally confirm him in error. For since the errors we drank in with our first milk are cured only by the most accurate meditation, and there are few who weigh with free judgment their first ideas and the force of words, it so happens that the greater part of men persevere in the errors of childhood, and by their error and obstinacy confirm their fellow-countrymen in them. Hence fellow-countrymen generally have the same manners, gladly live on the same foods, and cherish the same opinions. And this not

only

p. 51

only in a light matter, but also in the gravest affairs; and, what is more, in that affair of the greatest moment which concerns religion.

154 Ask the people what an Angel is: they will answer that it is a winged boy; ask what the Devil is: you will hear that it is a most hideous man, who bears the appearance of a satyr. Ask also what the Moon is, what the Sun: you will hear that it is an animal that resembles a man in its face, and things like these. Ask what God is: you will be sent off to the Theologians.

155 What? Even of those who are engaged in letters, very many embrace wonderfully absurd opinions. There are those who persuade themselves that, provided they confess their sins against God to the Priest and hear the words of absolution, they are truly freed from all guilt, giving no thought meanwhile to whether they grieve for the crimes they have committed and firmly resolve to live holily in the future. How frequent the number of these is, would that we had not ourselves experienced! Others defend other things no less harmful. So that I seem to myself to speak truly in saying that, of those who do not of set purpose devote themselves to the more solid Theology, there are few who have a true idea of religion and of the manner of worshipping God, and that everywhere there are very many who hold doggedly to one that is generally confused and erroneous.

156 Therefore, to meet these fallacies, the following Canons are to be established, according to the order of the errors, and what they prescribe is to be observed.

157 Canon I. Do not investigate the things that exceed the powers of the human mind: for you will lose your oil and your labor. Avoid the things that plainly cannot be understood. Do not investigate possible things. Canon II. Study with method and order: learn first the clearer and easier things, by which the things that follow may be elucidated. Do not learn many things at once, but meditate on each one separately and most keenly. Cut away useless and empty things; give your time to the more useful. Canon III. Beware of prejudged opinions, which you have acquired by the usage of the home, or of the School, or of the people. Call back each idea and each word to examination, and do not assent to them before you understand that the matter is so. Do not pronounce rashly on the opinions of others; and estimate things not by the sense of the crowd, but by that of the best.

G2 Book

p. 52

BOOK III

CHAPTER I

On the means of finding the truth, and of communicating it to

others.

ince enough has now been said, as the plan of Elements allows, about 158

S the operations of the human intellect and the very nature of truth,

and about the fallacies of the senses, of the will and of the mind which

impede the attainment of truth, the next thing is that we should say a little

more accurately how these operations of the intellect are to be used for investi‐

gating and communicating truth. We shall treat, therefore, first of the Method

by which the truth is to be found, then of that by which a truth known to us is

to be explained to others; to which we shall then append a few things on the

method of Studying and of Disputing, and some on routing philosophical Pedantry.

On the Logico-analytic Method, or method of invention.

hat manner and method of investigating hidden and desired truth 159

T is called the Analytic Method, or method of invention, which can be de‐

fined: the art of disposing our thoughts so that, as far as the human condition

allows, we may uncover the truth that is hidden from us. It is called Analytic,

that is, of resolution, because, in order that what lies concealed in hiding may

become open to us, every whole must be divided into its parts, every composite

must be resolved into its principles, and every effect must be referred back to

its cause.

160 The Peripatetic Philosophers scarcely, or not even scarcely, touched

this most excellent, nay truly the most important, part of Philosophy,

although

p. 53

although it is the chief aim of this most excellent discipline, which takes upon itself the arduous charge of correcting and ruling the mind. We shall select whatever the Moderns have committed to writing on this subject, and shall explain it as briefly and as neatly as can be done.

161 Before we approach the work, however, it must be noted that the nature of this mind of ours is such that it cannot attain everything that is unknown to it. It must therefore be kept before our eyes that we are ignorant of the essences of things, and so ignorant of the essence of matter; and this being posited, there are insoluble questions which we cannot answer, such as those which depend on knowledge of essence, of which we are not speaking. Lest anyone, then, should perhaps incautiously waste his time in inquiring by the Analytic method into those things which, wrapped always in thick darkness, will lie hidden from men, we have thought it fitting to forewarn you to abstain from inquiring into them.

162 There are also useless questions, such as are nearly all those that are handled by the Peripatetics in endless quarrels, e.g. whether the copula is a term? Whether privation is a principle of the composite as already made? Whether matter desires corrupted forms? and others emptier still by far, which I should be ashamed to say I do not understand, if those who treat them understood them themselves: questions which either can never be settled, just as they are certainly still disputed on both sides by the Scholastics, or, if perhaps they could be settled perfectly, would nevertheless make us not a whit more learned; so that it is accordingly absurd to apply the laws of the Analytic method, or the force of the mind, or any part of precious time, to settling them.

163 We have, besides, questions that are soluble and not useless, which are conveniently divided into three classes; for in any question whatever, either, an attribute being given, it is asked to what subject it belongs? or, a subject being posited, it is inquired what determinate predicate belongs to it? or finally, a predicate and a subject being posited, it is asked whether the one belongs to the other. There are, therefore, three highest genera of all questions, nor can there be more. Of the first kind is, e.g., this question: what is the cause of earthquakes? For in this question, an attribute being given, namely the cause of the earthquake, it is asked what the subject is to which that attribute belongs? that is, what is that thing to which this attribute belongs, that it produces the earthquake? and so of the rest. Here, then, are the rules by which we must proceed in the investigation of the truth.

164 Rule I. Weigh whether you are so prepared in mind as to be fit for discovering that truth or for solving the question, lest you either wander about to no purpose, or blurt out inept and ridiculous things. Suppose, e.g., the matter in hand is Theological, Medical, Astronomical, things of which you are ignorant. Will you not be utterly ridiculous

who,

p. 54

who, ignorant of such faculties, come forth upon the stage to play the Theologian, the Physician, the Astronomer? To this may be applied that saying of Horace:

Take, you who write, a matter equal to your strength,

and turn over long what your shoulders refuse to bear,

what they can carry.

165 But if we have ideas of the thing in question, and are fit to solve the question, then follows Rule II. Weigh whether the question is simple or compound: and if it is compound, divide it accurately into all its simple questions, examined minutely, and inquire first into that one which can carry light before the others. E.g. It is asked, what is the use and the structure of the parts of the eye? Two questions are proposed: of these the second will be examined first of all; for unless it is known what the parts of the eye are, it cannot be explained what their uses are. Rule III. Explain the knot of the proposed question in the clearest words. For unless it is plainly established what is to be sought, the whole disputation will wander in uncertainty. Rule IV. Understand the question, and express it exactly and as simply as possible, that is, cutting away from it whatever does not at all bear upon it. Concerning which, if there are things in the proposed question that can be removed while the question remains intact, it belongs to prudence to cut them away.

166 Rule V. Let every genus be divided, as far as can be done, into its species, and let them all be separated and distributed into definite classes. Rule VI. Having established what is to be investigated, we must attentively observe what, in that very thing, becomes known to us. For our mind is equal to grasping unknown things only insofar as they participate in diverse ways in the nature of those things which were previously known to us. Rule VII. It is of the greatest importance (as Descartes excellently advises) to advance our thoughts in a fixed order, beginning, namely, with those things which are easier for us to know, and from these proceeding little by little, and as it were by steps, to the more difficult investigation. Rule VIII, and last. If you have searched long and have not found the truth, renew the examination. If you have tried again in vain, do not pronounce the thing either false or less than possible merely because you do not understand it, unless you are so utterly ridiculous as to think your own mind the measure of the true and the false.

Chapter

p. 55

CHAPTER II

CHAPTER III

On the Logico-Synthetic Method, or the Method of Imparting

Doctrine.

ruth sought by the analytic method and found is demonstrated to 167

T others by the synthetic method. Synthesis, therefore, is the method

of imparting doctrine, or of demonstrating the truth as conveniently

as can be done. To demonstrate, moreover, is to reason so aptly for persuading

that the person with whom we are disputing can in no way seriously and sin‐

cerely refuse his assent. But in order that the persuasion of others may be ob‐

tained beyond escape, these four laws must be observed.

168 Rule I. Use no word or expression that is, or can be, ambiguous or obscure, left

undefined; but explain most lucidly the determinate sense and the precise signification in

which you wish such words or expressions to be taken. Rule II. Do not, through careless‐

ness, twist words or expressions once defined into another sense in the course of arguing.

Rule III. Draw no inference that is not connected by a necessary and immediate bond

with the propositions from which you gather it. Rule IV, and last. Every proposition

from which something is to be gathered or inferred by you must either be self-evident by

simple intuition, or be deduced from other premises as a necessary consequence. These

laws are not only necessary for constructing a demonstration, but they alone

suffice, as the celebrated Soria excellently proves. (y)

On the Method of Studying.

ethod of studying I call that by which our studies are to be directed, 169

M so that from the reading of books we may thoroughly learn the

discipline we desire by our own efforts as well. Truly, I judge that

it has come about only through lack of a right method

(y) Elem. of Logic.

p. 58

until one occurs both of whose premises are granted by the respondent. It is

characteristic of Pedagogues, whom in Spanish we call Pedantes, when they take

it upon themselves to refute a thesis, not to prove the antithesis and to act in

good faith, but to resort to stratagems: either to weaken things that are said in

passing, and not deliberately and as one’s real opinion; or to drive the respon‐

dent off course with inept little questions, to mock him, or to weary the begin‐

ner with arguments utterly foreign to the matter in hand; or finally to thrust

forward the same arguments again and again, as though the adversary had made

no reply to them.

T H I N G S P RO P E R T O T H E R E S P O N D E N T.

176 The respondent should take up the syllogism proposed by the oppo‐

nent, that is, repeat it, so that it may appear that he has grasped the opponent’s

meaning. Let him repeat the premises a second time, noting at each one

whether he grants it, or desires a further proof, or allows it to pass for the

meantime until the other has been sufficiently proved, using, e.g., these formu‐

las: I grant the major, I deny the minor, I deny the antecedent, let the major pass, etc. If

he grants the premises in one respect and denies them in another, let him use a

distinction and apply it to the argument; in which case it is the opponent’s part

either to prove the premise under the limitation under which it is denied, or to

attack the limitation as inept. When the President takes upon himself the part

of the respondent, the same duties are his as are the respondent’s.

C H A P T E R V.

On Banishing Philosophical Pedantry.

his word Pedantry takes its origin from Pedagogues, who, because 177

T they follow noble boys on foot, are called Pedanti in the Italian

tongue. These men, from long habit of commanding boys, affect

such authority that even when speaking with other men and about

other matters they display authority in their voice, their look, and their very

gestures. And since they are educated in humane letters or in Philosophy only

lightly, or not even lightly, they so imbue their minds with most inept opinions

as utterly to deprave their judgment,

and

p. 59

and blunt the edge of their judging: nay (what is most to be lamented), they frequently instill the same vices even in those to whose education they devote their labor. From this is born that most rotten Pedantry, that is, a general ineptitude of judgment: which, like a plague of the liberal arts, creeps far and wide to the ruin of young men, and contaminates both humane letters and the weightier disciplines.

178 And hence it becomes manifest that a pedant is to the Moderns the same as an ineptus [inept man] was to the Latins. They called ineptus the man who was not apt for judging well about things. This ineptitude of judgment, however, is not confined within narrow regions, but extends far and wide. We nevertheless designate it by the single name of Philosophical Pedantry, because it flows from imprudence in judging, which is most directly opposed to the prudence of thinking rightly, that is, to Logic, whose chief use is in all the disciplines.

179 Hence those are deservedly condemned who swear by the words of a master, and make it a matter of conscience to depart even in the least from his opinions. This Pedantry darkened the old Pythagoreans, who attributed so much to their teacher that they always had in their mouths he himself said it; which for them stood in place of a Geometrical demonstration. The Arabs did this very thing with their Aristotle, and with Galen. Those who had received their doctrine from the Arabs practiced it from the twelfth century on with such zeal that they anxiously explored, not what was true, but what Aristotle had said; nay, they investigated not what Aristotle, a man not inept, had said, but what the Arabs, who had wrongly interpreted the Philosopher’s opinions, had foisted upon him. From this came those disputations which prevailed for so many centuries, and stood in men’s way, so that they attempted nothing distinguished in good studies. And unless, as the last century was drawing to its close, the Philosophers had thoroughly shaken off such a yoke, all the disciplines would still be lying in that barbarism and squalor.

180 Hence those labor under the same Pedantry who, when they apply their mind to some discipline, do not notice to what end the matter disputed pertains, and what fruit the human mind ought to gather from such disciplines. Of this kind are those who give themselves to the disciplines without any method, and take no thought for polishing the mind and forming the judgment. Of these the number is truly infinite. To the same class are referred those who apply themselves to one discipline with their whole heart without so much as touching those things from which it receives its light. Who would bear men who devote themselves to Natural philosophy without rightly grasping Geometry in their minds?

181 In the same number are placed those who dispute, with loud voice and straining of lungs, about things which they themselves, to say nothing of others, do not understand. This is frequently done by those who wrangle among themselves about quiddities,

H2 haecceities,

p. 60

haecceities, formalities, the appetite of prime matter, and six hundred things of this kind. They understand, to be sure, the words, and sometimes the abstract ideas which they join to the words. But since no such things correspond to such ideas, they are disputing about nothing. Accordingly, though they pour out many words, they say nothing in truth, and therefore do not understand themselves, both because they say nothing and because they very often put different ideas under the same words.

182 Among the pedants are also reckoned those who confidently pass judgment on the writings of others without having the things that are necessary in order to judge aptly. For how rash it is to judge of the opinions of the Modern philosophers before having so much as greeted their tenets and the History of Letters from the threshold! Who would bear those who, imbued with no learning in true Theology, tinged with no knowledge of the Critical Art, repudiate with great haughtiness the opinions of certain authors as though they were repugnant to the Catholic faith, opinions which they, I will not say do not weigh, but do not even understand?

183 Deservedly, too, you would count among the Archpedants men of that stamp (to speak more merrily) whose heart’s concern it is to pronounce, before the benches of the women, on the right method of philosophizing and on the Newer Philosophy: forsooth, a great weight of authority must accrue day by day to the Peripatetic School from that very Decree of the Women’s Senate: as if it were not unbecoming for men, where there was need of counsel, labor, alacrity, and training in the best arts, to take refuge with chattering women and the ruder rabble. But enough of this.

184 To the Pedants are also added the Consequence-mongers: those, namely, who, while they refute the opinions of others, without overturning the foundations of the contrary opinion, take refuge in consequences, by which to bring the honor and good name of their adversaries into jeopardy; thinking that, if not by reasons, at least by threats and abuse, they will dislodge their adversaries from their ground and their cause. E.g. someone praises the philosophical investigation of Boyle, Leibniz, Newton, Leeuwenhoek, Clarke, Derham, and the other heretics who have set Philosophy in a good light. The consequence-monger infers: that he is a Heretic, or suspect of heresy; that he is not to be listened to; and that whatever learning flows from that source is to be hissed off the stage as pernicious.

185 Now this reasoning: He praises the philosophical investigation of Heretics: therefore he is a Heretic, is false. And so the other things that are drawn from it labor under the same vice. For not everything the Heretics have said is false, nor is everything Catholics have written true. Both have written things good and bad, which are to be weighed by the oracle of the Vatican: and if by Pontifical

laws

p. 61

laws they may exist and be read, they are surely censured rashly with arguments drawn from envy. By the same right we might argue in this way: he stubbornly defends the dogmas of Aristotle, adheres to the tenets of Galen, Avicenna, Averroes: therefore he is a Heathen, or a Mohammedan. Which, however, is a most inept kind of arguing.

186 Joined with the pedants, too, are those who think they will win the praise of the most polished Moderns in no other way than if, when about to write a Philosophy, they stitch together a patchwork of conflicting opinions: as if someone, e.g., about to write a Physics, after stubbornly defending the system of the Scholastics on substantial and accidental forms, nevertheless, in explaining certain phenomena, embraces the opinions of Gassendi, Descartes, Newton. He indeed is a pedant, and writes without any judgment.

187 Lastly, those are counted among the pedants who overwhelm the minds of boys with a multitude of precepts, and are wholly bent on weaving long disputations, without first examining whether they conduce to the end they set themselves. From this it comes about that the beginner, however well trained in those trifles and quibbles, if he is brought to some controversy that is not disputed in the school, does not know what he ought to decide.

188 Lest you should think, young men, that this has been said by me out of ill-will or for any other cause, I affirm to you for certain that in disputing and writing these things I am moved by no partisanship. I should certainly sin, and deservedly be laughed at, if I, who counsel beginners not to judge from prejudiced opinions, should myself pronounce on the opinions of others with a prejudice to be repented of. I do not wish to be judge in this cause: let those most learned men judge who have long and greatly tormented themselves in the Peripatetic philosophy; who, if they are honest men, must confess that this common Logic in which they are versed, and which they extol to the skies with praises and call a divine invention, that very Logic helps them not at all to dispute about matters that are not taught in the Schools.

189 And these are the chief kinds of pedantry, to which the rest are easily reduced. We pass over the others, lest our discourse run on without end. From what we have said it is sufficiently manifest that a preposterous, absurd, and inept manner of reasoning, and the want of true Philosophy, have been the cause of our falling into pedantry: that is, of our failing, in any discipline, properly to recognize its end and its aids, and to keep due measure. If we rightly recognized these, we should surely beware of the inepties that expose us to the mockery of the learned and the prudent; and this is the very thing that being a Philosopher in each matter means. The celebrated Verney, from whom we have excerpted these things, discourses of many others concerning pedantry. Consult him.

Scholastic

p. 62

SCHOLASTIC EXERCISES

ON LOGIC

E X E RC I S E I .

Whether an idea, or the simple perception of a thing, can be

false?

ogical truth, as was said above, is the agreement of our ideas with the 190

L object, and this is also called the truth of cognition; whence, whatever

the idea may be, whether simple or complex, its truth consists solely

in agreement with the thing perceived, apart from affirmation or negation. But

the truth of judgment, which is called the truth of composition, lies in affirmation

or negation. And so a judgment is deemed true when it says that that is which

really is, or denies that that is which is not; but false if it affirms that that is

which is not, or denies that that is which is. These things being posited,

191 I say I. A perception or idea, whether simple or complex, can be true.

Proof: a perception is called true when it agrees with its object; but a percep‐

tion, whether simple or complex, can agree with its object: therefore. Proof of

the minor: the perception of a mountain, which is simple, and the perception of

a steep mountain, which is complex, can agree with their objects, or the things

perceived, as all understand: therefore.

192 I say 2: a perception, whether simple or complex, can never, properly

speaking, be called false. Proof: that perception would, properly speaking, have

to be called false which disagreed with the object perceived; but a perception,

whether simple or complex, cannot be said to disagree with its object; for if it

represents a present thing as it is, e.g. gold when gold is present, then it agrees

with its object, as no one denies. But if it does not represent the present ob‐

ject, but something else, e.g. if, when brass is present,

it

p. 63

it presents gold, it is indeed a true perception of gold, but by no means of brass, and so it is not a false perception of brass, but none, or rather it is no perception of brass at all: therefore a perception, whether simple or complex, cannot, properly speaking, be called false.

193 I say 3: a perception, whether simple or complex, can be called false materially, as they say, and by occasion of the subsequent judgment. Proof: for a perception or idea to be capable of being called false in this way, it is enough that it can be the matter and the occasion of a false judgment; but a perception, especially a complex one, can be the matter and the occasion of a subsequent false judgment: therefore. Proof of the minor: the perception of gold when brass is present can be the occasion for someone’s judging that to be gold which is only brass: therefore.

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

194 Obj. 1, against I. A perception, whether simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing: therefore it cannot be true. Dist. the consequent: it cannot be true with the truth of composition, which belongs to judgment, I grant; with simple or complex truth, which is the truth of a cognition agreeing with the object perceived, I deny. Secondly: the same reason holds for a simple perception’s being unable to be false as for its being able to be true; but on our view it can be true: therefore also false. I deny the major of the argument: for a perception would be false only when it did not agree with the object represented and perceived, which certainly can never be said; nay, it is true precisely because it always agrees with the object represented; and if an idea does not agree with the object that was to be represented, it will not be false, but none, as we have said.

195 Obj. 2: an idea which does not represent the object as it is, is false in itself; but the idea of gold when brass is present does not represent the object as it is: therefore. Dist. the minor: it does not represent as it is the object which is present and which ought to have been represented, I grant; it does not represent the perceived object as it is, I deny; and I deny the consequent. You will say: a complex perception is a true judgment, for it is equivalent to a judgment; but a judgment can be false: therefore a complex perception can be too. I deny the major: for a perception, whether it be simple or complex, affirms or denies nothing, whence it cannot itself be a judgment, although it is said to be equivalent to a judgment. You will insist: a complex perception, e.g. of a golden mountain, or of a broken stick, attributes something to the mountain, namely that it is golden, and takes away from the stick its integrity; but a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or takes something away from it, is equivalent to a judgment, or is a true judgment: therefore.

Dist.

p. 64

196 Dist. the minor: a cognition which attributes something to some subject, or

takes something away from it, by affirmation or negation, is a true judgment, I grant;

by a mere conception of the subject together with the attribute, without affirmation

or negation, I deny. You will say: the perception of an unjust God is false: therefore

some false perception can be given. I reply by denying the hypothesis, namely that

there can be a notion of an unjust God; for either by the name of God is understood

what must necessarily be understood, namely a supremely perfect being, or not? If

the first, there is not, nor can there be, any perception of an unjust God, because

there would be an evident contradiction; if the second, it is nothing to the purpose,

since that idea is not false which attributes injustice to an imperfect being. We say

the very same of those perceptions which are called chimerical: for either they are

none, if they involve contradictories, or they are true, if no contradiction is found in

them, because they agree with the things that are perceived, even though those

things do not exist in the nature of things.

197 Obj., finally: an idea must express that by which it is excited; but the idea of

gold which is excited in us when brass is present does not express brass: therefore it

does not express what it ought to express: therefore it is false. Dist. the major: every

idea, I deny; the greater part of them, I grant. For there are very many bodies differ‐

ent in nature, but quite similar as to certain sensible qualities. It is certain, moreover,

that from similar motions made in the organs of the senses the same ideas are neces‐

sarily excited in the mind: therefore we cannot prevent dissimilar bodies from some‐

times exciting similar ideas in us, nor, accordingly, some idea from sometimes pre‐

senting to the mind a thing altogether different from that by which it is excited.

E X E RC I S E I I .

Whether all ideas take their origin from the senses?

The opinions of the Philosophers are set forth and refuted, and our

own view is established.

wo species of perceptions are distinguished. The first is pure intellection, by 198

T which the mind knows something without the aid of a phantasm or of a

corporeal species, e.g. when it perceives itself, its thoughts and affections,

say joy, sadness, etc. Where it must be observed that this

perception

p. 65

perception is called consciousness, because it is conscious to itself of its own thoughts or affections, and in a certain way knows within itself that it is thinking. The other species of perception is called imagination, of which we have already spoken (§. 12.)

199 That all ideas are acquired by the mind is most certain; but how it acquires them is not sufficiently agreed among the Philosophers. Lucretius (z) thinks that from the objects themselves certain images fly off, which enter the senses and make similar motions in the brain, and that in this way the mind acquires its ideas. Which is altogether false: for according to him these idols are bodies, and since they would be continually flying off from the surfaces, these would at length be worn away and perish utterly. Moreover, abstract things, such as reasonings and volitions, etc., could not be understood, because no images come from them to the senses; but these things are repugnant to experience.

200 The Aristotelians admit no purely intellectual ideas, but believe that the mind acquires all the images of things from the bodily senses. Hence that most celebrated maxim among them (a): nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense. Gassendi defends the same opinion. Malebranche (b) thinks that the mind sees all things in God, to whom it is essentially joined, as in a mirror; which is false, for the mind does not see in God as in a mirror. For a mirror offers the same thing to all who look into it: yet not all men see all things. The unlearned do not see what the learned understand. (See what was said in §. 86.)

201 The Cartesians hold that our intellect is a merely passive power, which does not itself produce its ideas, but receives them from God. And they distinguish ideas of a threefold kind: innate, adventitious, and factitious. They call innate the ideas which were divinely impressed on our mind immediately from its birth, and which have their origin from the first cause alone, without the aid of the body or of any second cause whatsoever. They call adventitious those which are produced on the occasion of motions in the bodily organs. Such are the sensations of heat, sound, smell, etc. Factitious, finally, they call the ideas which are composed from those with which our mind has already been informed, as when someone, from the idea of a mountain and the idea of gold, makes up for himself a golden mountain.

202 About adventitious and factitious ideas there can be no doubt. But as regards innate ideas, the state of the question is not
