REPLIES TO THE OB JECTIONS

usually set out clearly enough, as the celebrated Jacquier excellently observes. For if by this name they understand ideas perpetually present to the mind, there can be no controversy. For who would say that there is some idea in us which we contemplate unceasingly? But if they mean ideas which are always at hand before all experience and all reasoning, no one surely remembers any idea of this kind which the mind thought of before all experience and all reasoning.

203 But if by innate ideas we understand those notions which are sometimes acquired without the occasion of external objects, and by an easy and ready use of reason, we say that ideas are to be admitted as innate in this sense only. And in truth nothing else can be signified by the term innate ideas, as he will confess who weighs this most weighty question, not from the heat of disputation or the ambiguity of a definition, but from the proper testimony of his own consciousness. These things explained, let the conclusion be against the Peripatetics, Gassendi, and Locke.

204 We have many purely intellectual ideas, some of which we acquire by an easy use of reason. Proof: in those things which pertain to the mind, no safer rule ought to be applied than the inmost testimony of consciousness: but by the testimony of consciousness we experience that we perceive many things by pure intellection without any bodily image: therefore we have many purely intellectual ideas. Proof of the minor: many ideas of things present themselves to our mind which are entirely separated from all matter and sensible quality, such as are the ideas of assent and dissent, of justice, of intelligence, of God: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: assent and dissent, justice, etc., and other objects of our ideas have no likeness to sensible things, are endowed with no sensible quality, and accordingly can be represented by no sensation or imagination.

205 The conclusion is confirmed: those ideas are purely intellectual whose objects are neither colored, nor savory, nor sonorous, nor affected by any sensible quality, as St. Augustine says (c): but there are many ideas whose objects are neither colored, etc., such as are the idea of being in general, the idea of God, etc.: therefore purely intellectual ideas are given.

206 Obj. 1: if there is any purely intellectual idea which does not have its origin from the senses, it is above all the idea of being in general, the idea of God,

etc.:

(c) Bk. 10 of the Confessions, no. 17, otherwise ch. 10.

p. 67

etc.: but these ideas take their origin from the senses: therefore. I deny the minor: because being in general is neither colored, nor savory, nor endowed with any sensible quality. But you will prove the minor: the idea of being in general is formed by abstraction from singular and individual bodies; but singular bodies are perceived by the senses: therefore such an idea takes its origin from the senses. To the proof, I distinguish the major: it is formed by abstraction from corporeal and spiritual things, I grant; from corporeal things only, I deny the major and the consequent.

207 We call being in general that which can exist; and so, even if it were supposed that there are no bodies, we could form this idea of being from the inmost consciousness of the operations of our mind, and without any relation to body. Moreover, if this idea took its origin only from the senses, it would not comprehend in its extension absolutely all the genera of being, but only corporeal beings; which, however, is false. You will insist 1: Nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the sense; therefore all ideas, and accordingly the idea of being in general, depend on the senses. Dist. the antecedent: which was not first in the external or the internal sense, I grant; in the external sense only, I deny the antecedent, and the consequent.

208 We confess that there is a twofold origin of ideas: the external sense, by which we acquire the ideas of corporeal things, and the internal sense, by which, through the mind’s attention and reflection upon its own operations, we procure the ideas of spiritual things. You will insist 2: but nothing is in the intellect which was not first in the external sense only: therefore the distinction is false. Proof of the subsumption: that was first in the external sense which is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things; but we do not know spiritual things except by comparison with corporeal things: therefore. Proof of the minor: God is a spiritual substance; but we have no idea of God except insofar as we represent Him to ourselves under the image of a Venerable Old Man: therefore.

209 I reply by denying the minor. It is true indeed that our mind cannot, without the utmost care and attention, entirely purge its ideas of every bodily taint, and that for this reason the ruder sort of men perceive nothing except with an image. But those images, e.g. of an Old Man and of a winged youth, are not themselves the ideas of God and of the Angels, but mere phantasms which accompany those ideas. For if we had no other idea of God than the idea of a Venerable Old Man, all the judgments that we form about God would have to appear to us entirely false, as being contrary to this idea; for we believe those judgments to be false which are contrary to the ideas of things that we have in our mind; and therefore we could not judge God to be incorporeal, invisible, since none of these can in any way agree with the idea of a Venerable Old Man.

I2 You

p. 68

210 You will insist 3: The Apostle writes in Rom. ch. 1: the invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made: therefore God is not known by us except by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: insofar as from the consideration of corporeal and spiritual things we rightly conclude that the supreme Maker of all things exists, I grant; insofar as the idea of God is some phantasm formed by comparison with corporeal things, I deny. We must beware, therefore, lest, as St. Paul says in the same place, the glory of the incorruptible God be changed into the likeness of the image of a corruptible man.

211 You will insist 4: the idea of God is formed from the ideas of the perfections of all creatures, even corporeal ones: therefore the idea of God is formed by comparison with corporeal things. Dist. the antecedent: it is formed from the ideas of the perfections of creatures, even corporeal ones, taken eminently, I grant; taken formally, I deny, and the consequent. We do not include corporeal attributes in the idea of God formally, that is, as they are in bodies, but only eminently, that is, in a certain nobler and more sublime manner, without any imperfection, removing from God all the ideas of matter, of division, of color, and the rest, which, taken formally, necessarily include certain imperfections, and cannot belong to the supreme Being except eminently.

212 Obj. 2: if someone were born deprived of every sense, so that he neither saw nor heard, etc., he would surely have no ideas: therefore there are no purely intellectual ideas. I deny the antecedent: for in that hypothesis the mind would live; but the life of the mind consists in thinking, that is, in the perception of the intellect and the inclination of the will: therefore the mind would think. It would not, however, think of things remote from it, but of those which were present to it and by which it was moved. But nothing is more present to the mind than itself, as St. Augustine teaches: therefore it would know itself by a certain consciousness.

213 Obj. 3, against the second part of the conclusion: if there were any ideas acquired by an easy use of reason, such would be the ideas of God and of the morality of actions; but these are not: therefore. Proof of the minor: experience testifies that men have no idea of God and of the morality of actions unless they receive it from other men with whom they live: therefore the ideas of God and of the morality of actions are not such as to be acquired by an easy use of reason. Proof of the antecedent: from two examples which are reported by the Royal Academy of Paris,

it

(d) Bk. 14 of On the Trinity.

p. 69

it is plain that a man brought up among bears, and another who had been deaf

and dumb up to the twenty-fourth year of his age, had no idea of God and of

the morality of actions before they conversed with other men and received that

idea from them: therefore.

214 To the argument I reply by denying the minor, whose proof we shall ex‐

plain. The examples adduced hold good only against those who think that

those ideas are present to our minds before all attention. But since, according

to our definition, innate ideas are not perceived without some use of reason,

the cause to be assigned for so gross and almost incredible an ignorance is this:

that those men neglected the faculties of their mind and did not apply them to

the investigation of the first truths.

E X E RC I S E I I I .

On the principal laws of sensations.

et the conclusion be: it is a law of sensations that as often as some 215

L change is produced by a sensible object in a duly constituted sense

organ, so often there arises in the soul some particular sensation cor‐

responding to this change. Proof: that sensation corresponds to the change

which cannot be varied at our will; but the change made in a duly constituted

sense organ cannot be varied at our will: therefore. Proof of the minor, from

daily experience: if, e.g., the crash of a cannon strikes the ear, we necessarily

perceive it, nor can we change that sensation into a gentler sound; if a stench

fills the nostrils, we can in no way bring it about that in its place we perceive ei‐

ther a sweet odor or a less offensive stench: therefore.

216 From this general law of sensations four rules are gathered. I. If the

change in the same organ is the same, the sensation in the soul must also be the same. II. If

it happens that the same change is produced in the same sense organ by different sensible

objects, the objects must appear the same. III. If the change in the sense organ is different,

the sensation in the soul must also be different. IV. Hence if it happens that the same ob‐

ject produces a different change in the same organ, the object too must appear different.

From these flow the general principles for explaining vision, and the founda‐

tions of optical illusions.

The

p. 70

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

217 Obj. 1: many changes are produced in a duly constituted sense organ without any sensation of the soul: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: when by day we gaze at the sky, the single stars send rays of light into the duly constituted eye, by which the image of the stars is delineated in the eye, and accordingly they produce changes in the sense organ; and yet the soul does not perceive the stars: therefore. Dist. the antecedent: many changes are produced without sensation that are insufficient, I grant; sufficient ones, I deny. To the proof, I grant the major and distinguish the minor: the soul does not perceive the stars by day, that is, the soul does not distinguish the weaker perceptions of the stars from the other, stronger ones, I grant; it has no obscure perceptions of the stars, I deny; and I deny the consequent.

218 Not every change made in the sense organ suffices for the soul to feel; but it is required that the change be transmitted all the way to the brain; and for this reason we said that the change must necessarily be made by a sensible object, that is, by an object which can produce a sufficient change in a duly constituted sense organ. But you will insist: the same sensation in the soul does not correspond to the same change made in the same sense organ: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: the Sun and the Moon, when they hang over our zenith, appear smaller than when placed near the horizon; and yet in both places they produce the same change in the same eye: therefore.

219 I deny the antecedent, and to the proof I distinguish the minor: they produce the same change in the eye, joined with different other changes in each place, I grant; otherwise, I deny, and the consequent. We explain the phenomenon thus. The Moon and the Sun are usually seen larger on the horizon than at the meridian because on the horizon, together with their images, the intervening terrestrial bodies and the oblong vault of the sky are painted in the eye. This series of objects does not affect the eye when the Sun and Moon are seen at the top of the sky; and hence it is that if you look at the Sun and the Moon on the horizon through a narrow tube, they do not appear larger than at the top of the sky. When, therefore, we say that the same sensation in the soul corresponds to the same change made in the same organ, the proposition is to be understood of the changes each considered separately.

E X E RC I S E I V.

On the criterion of the true and the false.

e often observe that in many cases the agreement of the predi220

W cate with the subject is known to us so clearly and plainly that it

is at once manifest and wrests our assent. By this supreme evi‐

dence we are persuaded that there has never been any sect of men that serious‐

ly doubted of all things. This being so, those seem not to understand sufficient‐

ly the state of the question who, in investigating the criterion of truth, place it

in evidence, and demonstrate at length against the Sceptics that evidence ex‐

ists. These, indeed, invent for themselves enemies to strike. We, however, shall

explain this question by the following conclusion.

221 Conclusion: to distinguish the true from the false the rules of Logic

suffice, and no other criterion of truth is needed. Proof of the 1st part: he dis‐

cerns the true from the false who demonstrates that the predicate agrees with

the subject; but the rules of Logic suffice for demonstrating this: therefore.

Proof of the minor: a demonstration consists of a chain of syllogisms whose

premises are definitions, axioms, and propositions already demonstrated; but

Logic hands down the rules of definitions, establishes the distinction between

axioms and demonstrable propositions, delineates the form of syllogisms, and

shows, finally, the modes of joining syllogisms together, etc.: therefore. Proof of

the 2nd part: if some other criterion of truth were needed besides the rules of

Logic, those rules would not suffice for discerning the true from the false; but

we have demonstrated that they suffice: therefore.

222 Some place the criterion of truth in evidence itself. But that criterion

of truth is not sufficiently determined: for clear perception, or evidence, must

in any given case be applied through the rules of Logic. One must, namely, ar‐

gue thus: whatever can be clearly and distinctly perceived is true; but this can be clearly

and distinctly perceived: therefore this is true; and this is done through the rules of

Logic. Rules must therefore be handed down by whose help it may be judged

that evidence, or truth, is present; and these are the rules of Logic. When it is

said, therefore, that evidence is the criterion of the true, the matter stands just

as if it were said that truth is the criterion of truth, which is to trifle.

Contrary

p. 72

C O N T R A R Y V I E W S A R E R E F U T E D.

223 Obj. 1: that is the criterion of truth which so separates the true from the false that we cannot refuse assent to the truth; but evidence does this, or, what is the same, the proposition whatever is clearly and distinctly perceived is true: therefore. I distinguish the minor: and that criterion is not sufficiently determined by itself, but through the rules of Logic, I grant; and it is so determined that there is no need of the rules of Logic, I deny; and the consequence. The solution remains explained. You will insist: that is not the criterion of truth which needs another criterion; but the rules of Logic need another criterion of truth, for evidence is needed to demonstrate the rules of Logic: therefore.

224 I distinguish the minor: evidence is needed, which must then be applied through the rules of Logic, I grant; evidence that does not need them, I deny. The whole difficulty vanishes if the state of the question is rightly understood. You will insist 2: the criterion of truth can be the principle it is impossible for the same thing at once to be and not to be: therefore, besides the rules of Logic, at least something else could be the criterion of truth. I distinguish the antecedent: and the proposition to be demonstrated must be reduced to that principle through the rules of Logic, I grant; otherwise, I deny. To this objection the reply is the same as to the preceding one.

225 You now have, excellent young men, the precepts and questions of Logic, which we put before you as the most useful; if you lay hold of them as befits your talent and your eagerness to learn, we are confident that you will have done work not to be regretted. These things are few, but for the character of your age many enough. If you want more, you will easily acquire it by reading the authors whom we have commended thus far.

E L E M E N T S O F M E TA P H Y S I C S.

fter Logic, not Physics, as the Peripatetics do, but Metaphysics 1

A is what the Moderns teach, and rightly so; for since this discipline is

called first Philosophy, and in its first part is occupied with weighing

the meaning of words and with unfolding the most generic principles, it must

therefore enter into partnership and alliance with the faculty of discoursing. The

name of Metaphysics, moreover, altogether unknown to the ancient

Philosophers, is said to have been first used by Alexander of Aphrodisias and

John Philoponus, interpreters of Aristotle. By this name, however, were enti‐

tled those writings of Aristotle which, once the Logical, Ethical and Physical

works had first been put in order by Tyrannio the Grammarian and a certain

Andronicus of Rhodes,

L seemed

p. 2

seemed unable to be referred to any definite class (a).

2 Now, however, by the name of Metaphysics there comes to the mind of Philosophers that discipline which pursues things placed on high, that is, things established above the nature of bodies, or spiritual things freed from all commerce with matter. Hence it is commonly and very well defined by all Philosophers: The faculty which considers all the general affections of being that are common to corporeal and incorporeal beings alike, and which also contemplates incorporeal substances and their affections, as they are perceptible to us by the light of reason alone. There are three principal parts of Metaphysics. The first of them is called Ontology, or Ontosophy, that is, the science of being, and so it treats of being taken in general, and weighs its affections as abstracted by the mind. The second so scrutinizes spiritual substances as to set before us their nature, existence and operations by the light of reason alone. And since there are chiefly two spiritual substances that can be known by us through the light of nature, namely God and the human mind, Pneumatology, or the Science of Spirits, has customarily been divided, quite fittingly, into two parts: that which treats of the human mind is called Psychology, or Pneumatology; that which discourses of God, with reason alone as guide, Natural Theology.

3 Accordingly we shall have three parts of Metaphysics, of which the first will comprise Ontology, the second Psychology, the last Natural Theology. The Peripatetic Philosophers handed down Metaphysics in so confused a manner that nothing more obscure can be conceived. We, however, excellent young men, shall give you a Metaphysics, not that old, long and intricate one, but a brief and very expeditious one, such as may sharpen the mind and pave the way for grasping the remaining disciplines.

Metaphysics

(a) The writings of Aristotle, which were left first to Theophrastus, then to Neleus, were hidden and buried under the earth by his heirs for some centuries. Then, when they were drawn out thoroughly corrupted by damp, they were sold to Apellicon of Teos, who unskillfully filled in the corrupted passages. When Athens had been subdued by L. Sulla, Apellicon’s library was carried to Rome by his order, where first Tyrannio, then Andronicus of Rhodes revised the works of Aristotle and put them in order. See what was said in the Hist. of Philos.

CHAPTER I

PA RT I .

On Being, its species, and its properties.

he science which knows being in general, or in common, that is, 4

T separated from all circumstances and accidents, so that from the

contemplation of it as universal a clearer knowledge of any particu‐

lar being may afterwards arise, is called Ontology, or the science of being. We shall

embrace this science in the clearest and most accurate order possible; and since

its greatest obscurity arises from the countless and altogether useless questions

with which the Arabs and the common Peripatetics have most wretchedly dis‐

figured it, we shall omit those questions as useless, and shall contemplate being

itself, its species, and all its properties.

On Being in common, and its division. 5

B eing is that which is, or can be; hence whatever is conceived by our intellect is

called Being, and nothing can be understood, imagined, affirmed or denied

to which this general and most universal idea, concept or name of Being does

not apply. Being taken universally is divided into substance and

L2 accident

p. 4

accident, or into being properly and strictly taken, and a mode of being. Substance, or thing, is the name given to that being which exists by itself, or can exist or be perfectly conceived independently of another being, as a stone, a man, etc.: an accident, on the other hand, or mode of being, is that being which must exist in another, and can neither be nor be conceived except as inhering in and joined to another, as whiteness, roundness, motion, etc.

6 Substance, or thing, is divided into created and uncreated: that is called uncreated which receives from no one the being that it has, as God alone is; created, that which has been produced freely, contingently, by another, that is, by God, as men, stars, etc. Created substances are divided into corporeal and incorporeal. Accidents are divided chiefly into extrinsic and intrinsic. Those are called intrinsic which affect intrinsically and really the thing, the substance or subject itself in which they are found, as motion and figure in a body; extrinsic, those which posit nothing intrinsically, truly and really in the thing, but are only conceived in it by our intellect, and yet are considered by us as beings, of which kind are all relations, privations, and extrinsic denominations.

7 Substance, therefore, can be defined: an essence separated from its modes. A mode, moreover, is that by which a substance is in this or that way, and which in a manner clothes it and makes it perceived by the senses. Hence it becomes manifest that substance is an idea related to the modes from which it is imagined as separated, and therefore that it is an abstract idea: for no substance exists lacking all modes. Therefore those who dispute about substance taken without modes are disputing not about some thing that is outside the mind, but about an abstract idea that exists only in their mind. For we have no other idea of substance than by conceiving a cluster of modes and properties, and adding to them the obscure idea of a nature unknown to us, that is, of a combination, e.g., of parts of matter not known to us, which we think such things contain. (§§. 29, 30, Log.)

8 Accidents, or internal modes, so inhere intrinsically in substance that they can neither be, nor be understood to exist, separated from it: as figure and motion: for where is there figure without a body? motion without a movable thing? External modes, however, do not really exist in the substance, but are conceived by our mind as something that affects it, of which kind are, as we have already said, all relations.

9 Therefore substance taken physically and really must have some internal modes. Hence it is inept to ask whether it can be without modes: because even if a substance is at times without this or that mode, yet in this order of things it cannot be stripped of all modes. Taken metaphysically, however, it is plain that it can be without modes. Therefore it is also inept to ask whether it can be without modes; because substance taken metaphysically signifies precisely this, namely a nature separated from modes. Yet since the abstract idea of substance, as of essence, is not the same in all things, but according to the variety

of

p. 5

of things is itself also various, it is at times such as to comprise some modes: which for that reason are no longer to be called modes, but the essence and substance of the thing. But we shall conveniently explain these things by an example.

10 E.g., the pen that I am at present moving with my hand in order to write these things can be not moved, if I stop: therefore it can be deprived of motion, and be at rest, without ceasing to be a pen. It cannot, however, be deprived at once of motion and of rest, but must necessarily have one or the other. Likewise it cannot be deprived of all magnitude, figure, and the rest: but it necessarily has one or another. A clock, on the contrary, e.g., comprises, besides the artful construction of its parts, their motion. And therefore, although motion taken in general is a mode of body, it is nevertheless the essence or substance of the clock. Likewise a thunderbolt, besides the inflamed matter, includes a most violent motion. For this reason this motion is no longer a mode, but the essence of the thunderbolt. Therefore, that we may judge rightly of modes, we must first establish in what the nature of the thing consists, lest we unwittingly call a mode that which constitutes its nature.

11 Hence internal modes are in reality nothing other than the substance, which is in this or that way: therefore they cannot be separated from it. But it is incredible to say how many logomachies about the nature of modes or accidents are heard in the Schools of certain Philosophers, who, deceived by abstract ideas, to which they are wont to attribute a nature and existence of their own, sharply contend that modes are certain beings which can exist apart from substance. But if they considered the matter with a free judgment, they would plainly recognize that there are no such beings, and that the roundness or magnitude of a golden globe, e.g., is nothing other than gold shaped in this way and having this magnitude. I can indeed consider roundness abstractly, but I cannot understand it as existing without the matter in which it is. If the Peripatetics deny this, let them show us roundness and motion without a subject, and we shall be grateful to them for so wonderful an explanation of the phenomenon. But of these things more fittingly in the Physics.

12 Privation is the lack of a perfection in a subject that is apt and capable of receiving that form or perfection, as darkness in the air, blindness in a man, etc.; and so it is distinguished from negation, which is the privation or lack of a form in a subject that is otherwise incapable of that form, as darkness in an opaque body, blindness in a stone, etc. And so blindness and darkness are conceived by our intellect as if they were some mode, although they are pure nothing.

13 Relation, on the other hand, is a certain order, habitude, or respect of one thing to another, which is conceived in some thing because that thing is ordered or referred to another, as, e.g., if Alexander is referred to Philip, he is called son, although this being a son is found only in the intellect. An extrinsic denomination, finally, is a pure name that is attributed to some thing, although it is conceived by the intellect as some being, perfection or mode inhering in another, as when one is made a judge,

a

p. 6

a knight, a nobleman, or is praised or blamed: he receives indeed only this outward word, or denomination, yet something is conceived by us that inheres, as it were intrinsically, in the judge, the knight, the nobleman, the man praised or blamed.

14 Hence another division of being is drawn, into real being and being of reason. Real being is said to be that which truly and really is, independently of the intellect, or which must be even if the intellect considers nothing, as a rose, a man, a stone: a being of reason is that which is only conceived, is made by and depends on the thinking intellect, and therefore, if the intellect considers nothing, a being of reason cannot be. Here the Peripatetics raise the question whether being itself taken generally, or the concept of being, is univocal with respect to God and creatures; as also with respect to substance and accident, and finally with respect to real being and being of reason: whether, namely, the concept of being applies to them in the same way, and all things are equally being, although they are afterwards distinguished by various properties and differences?

15 But you see already, from the mere exposition of the question itself, that it is altogether useless and can make us none the more learned. But truly, lest you be altogether ignorant of the more celebrated questions of the Peripatetics, I have decided to say something about them with Corsini. Accordingly, if God himself is compared with creatures, or substance with accident, the more probable opinion seems to me to be that which holds that the concept of being applies to them equally and univocally. For since the common and most general concept of being signifies nothing at all, as we said before, but that which is, or that which has being, and God and creatures have being, they will be contained equally under this common genus of being, as the Scotists maintain.

16 But if it be said that God exists in a far different manner from creatures, God namely in an infinite and most perfect manner, essentially, necessarily, independently of another, so that he accordingly said of himself (b) I am who am; but creatures in a finite manner, contingently and dependently, on the free will of God, so that all, as Isaiah says (c), all nations are before him as if they had no being at all, and are counted to him as nothing, and vanity, it can easily be answered: such an infinite interval, by which God, the Best and Greatest, is distinguished from creatures, arises not from the idea of being itself, but from those infinite perfections which are found in God; just as the common idea of soul is attributed univocally to the rational and to the vegetative soul, although these are distinguished by a wonderful difference.

17 And indeed, if the concept or idea of being is conceived most accurately, it will be seen to be most simple and altogether indivisible, which could not be verified if one idea of being applied to creatures and another to God. Then, the ideas of God and of the creature must be distinguished by means of some character, or difference, which is joined to either concept, or to being;

and

(b) Exodus, ch. 3, v. 14.

(c) Ch. 40, v. 17.

p. 7

CHAPTER II

and therefore that universal and common concept of being, to which those charac‐

ters or differences are superadded, must always be admitted. Again, then, it can be

asked whether that common concept, to which the differences are not superadded,

is one and the same and univocal, or is rather distinguished by those differences? If

the first, it will be univocal with respect to its inferiors. If the second, it can be ab‐

stracted from the differences, and so be rendered one, simple, undistinguished and

indivisible, and therefore univocal as well. What has been said must also be under‐

stood of substance with respect to accident.

On essence, existence, and subsistence.

lthough the concept of being seems altogether simple and uncom18

A pounded, several attributes, and as it were parts, must nevertheless be

distinguished in it, which are commonly held and called, as it were, prop‐

erties of being. Such are essence, existence, subsistence, from which are then

derived the distinction of things and the names of hypostasis and of persons, and very

many other things of the kind which are treated at length among the Theologians

and the Peripatetic Philosophers. We, however, shall set forth all these things as

briefly as possible, because, by the now accepted custom of the Schools, to be igno‐

rant of these very distinctions of things, or of words, would seem almost a crime.

19 Accordingly essence, to begin with it, is nothing other than the first attribute

that is conceived in a thing, and from which all the rest proceed as from a root. In

the Schools it is commonly defined: that through which a being is, or is conceived to

be; or that which intrinsically composes a thing; or that which intrinsically gives be‐

ing to a thing. Such a principle, which gives being to a thing, is called the essence, the

nature, the constitutive of that same thing, with this one difference, that where it is

conceived as the source and origin of properties it is called essence, but where it is

conceived as the source and origin of the operations which are produced by such a

thing it is called nature; most often, however, nature and essence are used

indiscriminately.

20 Hence those most celebrated questions which are wont to be agitated in the

Schools with so much apparatus can be briefly settled: namely, whether the essences

of things are eternal and invariable, and whether God can bring about contradicto‐

ries? For although very many think that the essences of things can be varied by God,

even against the resistance of our intellect, in such a way that a circle could be

turned into a figure endowed with angles, or into a square one, and that God could

bring it about that twice two is not four, etc., yet it seems far more probable that

the essences of things are so certain and invariable that they cannot be varied even

by God.

For

p. 8

21 For since by the name of essence nothing else is understood but that attribute, or that perfection, which gives being to a thing, it is certainly impossible for that principle to be varied without the thing itself, which receives its being, having to be varied as well; as, e.g., if the equality of the radii and the privation of angles are taken away, the circle too will have to be taken away, or a circle can no longer be conceived or had. And certainly such essences of things are nothing other than the archetypal ideas of things, or those images which God had in his mind from eternity, and in whose likeness he created things in time; and therefore, just as those images, or divine ideas, are immutable, so the essences of things themselves must also be deemed invariable.

22 Existence is commonly defined: the placing of a being or essence outside nothing and all causes; and therefore between essence and existence there is found this difference, that essence applies also to possible things, which are contained in the power of the first or of a second cause, whereas existence applies only to those things which have been placed outside the first or second cause. Since, however, essence and existence apply equally to all substances and to accidents, so that accidents no less than substances, if they are possible, have being, and, if they have been produced, have existing, and since accidents or modes are nonetheless very greatly distinguished from substances, in substances themselves, besides essence and existence, which are common to accidents as well, another perfection must be conceived or admitted which cannot apply to accidents, so that those substances may accordingly be distinguished from accidents as by a constant and most clear difference.

23 This new perfection, which applies to substances alone, is called hypostasis, or subsistence: namely the ultimate perfection, form or act by which a thing, or nature, or essence, is so perfected, terminated, completed, or made its own master, not only so that it does not need another for being and operating, but also so that its operations are attributed to it, or so that it is and operates independently of another; which can belong only to a certain substance, which subsists by itself, and stands under, or is subjected to, accidents. The subject, moreover, the substance or composite, that is endowed with this ultimate perfection, or that subsists and operates by itself, is called a suppositum; and if it is spiritual and capable of incorporeal knowledge, as in God, the Angels and men, it is called a person, which is accordingly defined by Boethius: an individual substance of a rational nature.

24 Hence in divine things three hypostases, or subsistences, are found, and therefore also three persons: and since the subsistence of the Divine Word took the place of the created, or human, subsistence in Christ the Lord, or terminated the human nature, which ought to have been terminated by its own created or human subsistence, it appears most clearly that in Christ the Lord there is found a twofold nature, divine, namely, and human, and therefore a twofold will, as the Sixth Synod against the Monothelites

defined

p. 9

25 And since it is not the nature but the person that is said to operate or to

defined; but only one hypostasis, or divine subsistence, and therefore only one di‐

vine person, was found in him.

suffer something, according to that common principle, operations belong to supposi‐

ta, the operations or merits of Christ the Lord had to be of infinite value and dig‐

nity, and therefore equal to redeeming infinite men from the guilt or the punish‐

ment of their crimes: since they were produced by an infinite person, or divine

Suppositum. But these things we leave to the Theologians, to be explained ac‐

On the other properties or attributes of Being, or on Unity,

Truth, and Goodness.

he properties or attributes of being which were explained in the chap26

T ter above can apply not to every being, but to the individual genera of

being: essence, indeed, is found in all beings, even possible ones, exis‐

tence in those things which have been placed outside every cause, and subsis‐

tence, finally, in substances only. There are, however, other attributes which apply

to being so universally that they transcend, or exceed, all the bounds or limits of

beings, whence they are called transcendentals; and therefore they embrace not

some only, but absolutely all the genera of beings; and three in particular are com‐

monly enumerated by the Philosophers: namely Unity, Truth and Goodness.

27 Unity is nothing other than the lack or privation of division, and for no

other reason is the concept of being one and simple except that it cannot be di‐

vided into various parts. Since, therefore, unity is opposed to division, as many

kinds of unity can be distinguished as there are divisions themselves, or distinc‐

tions, found among beings. Distinction or division is reckoned threefold by the

Philosophers: namely generic, specific and numerical. Generic distinction is said to be

that which is found between beings that are contained under a different genus or

category, as between a circle and a straight line; for the circle is contained under the

genus of curvilinear figure, whereas the straight line belongs neither to the curvilin‐

ear genus nor to any other genus of figure.

28 Specific distinction is found between beings which, though they are con‐

tained under the same genus, are yet of a different species, as between a circle and

a triangle, which, though placed under the same genus of figure, yet belong to dif‐

ferent species of figure. Numerical distinction, finally, is that which is found

M between

p. 10

between individuals of the same species, or between those that are contained under the same species and are distinguished only by individuating circumstances and conditions, as circle A, circle B. Generic and specific distinction is conceived to be drawn from the form, nature, or essence of things; whence those things that differ specifically or generically must have a different essence.

29 Numerical distinction, on the other hand, which is also commonly called material, must, as very many think, be drawn from matter alone, which is accordingly called the principle of individuation, or from material circumstances; whence the Thomists hold that in Angels, because they lack matter, this numerical distinction is not admitted, or that several Angels cannot be found in a single species, but rather that individual Angels differ specifically from one another. Yet just as rational souls, though they are incorporeal, are numerically distinguished from one another by the order or habitude by which each is directed to its own body, so too Angels can be numerically distinguished by the spiritual accidents or circumstances with which they are affected, or at any rate by the varied action of God by which they were created or are conserved.

30 Real distinction is that which is found in the thing independently of the intellect. Distinction of reason is that which depends on the intellect. Real distinction is divided into entitative, modal and virtual. Real entitative distinction, which is also commonly called major, is said to be that which is found between various things whose entities are so distinct that one can be separated from the other, or at least one can be perfectly conceived without the other, as between the Moon and the Sun, gold and silver, etc. Real minor, or modal, distinction is said to be that which obtains between a thing and a mode of the thing, which mode cannot be separated from the thing itself, or perfectly conceived without it, as between figure and the figured body. Virtual distinction, finally, which you might rather call the foundation of a distinction than a distinction, is that which is found in a thing which, although it is one and simple, is yet equivalent to several, and therefore gives the intellect occasion to conceive several parts in it; as in God and in his attributes and perfections we conceive the attributes themselves as distinct, e.g., Justice from Mercy.

31 Besides these kinds of distinction Scotus admits another distinction, which he says is formal, actual, and from the nature of the thing: formal, because it is found not between thing and thing, or between a thing and a mode of being, but between various formalities or perfections of the same thing, as between the attributes of God, between the animality and rationality of man, etc.; actual, and from the nature of the thing, because it is found in things actually and in fact, independently of the intellect. Hence arose a most weighty question between the Thomists and the Scotists: by what kind of distinction, namely, the metaphysical grades of the same thing are distinguished, as, e.g., the animality and rationality that are found in man, the grade of vegetating and of sensing that is found in brutes, and universally the genus and difference that are contained in individual things or species.

The

p. 11

32 The Thomists think that among all these only a virtual distinction suffices. The Scotists, besides this virtual one, admit also a formal one, by which the grades themselves are conceived not as two things or modes (otherwise the distinction would be real) but as two formalities; and therefore that formal distinction is less than the real, but greater than the virtual, or midway between the two. But let the Scholastics see to these things. Distinction of reason is commonly divided into major, minor and minimal. The first is the name given to that by which, in one and the same thing, various concepts are distinguished, of which one is not contained in the other, as justice and mercy, which are distinguished in God. Distinction of reason is minor when the concepts themselves mutually include each other implicitly, as one, good, true, which are conceived in being.

33 Minimal distinction of reason, finally, is the name given to that which, without any foundation, and by the mere choice of the intellect, or rather by its weakness or by a bad habit, distinguishes one thing from another, as, e.g., God from the Divinity, man from humanity, etc. Hence this distinction is called a distinction of reasoning reason, because, namely, it depends on reason alone, whereas the major or minor distinction of reason is commonly called by the name of reasoned reason, as if, namely, some ground or foundation of the distinction were found in the thing itself. But these and other things of the kind, which are explained at length by the Peripatetics, are certainly not of such worth that they should be set forth more fully. They had to be hinted at here, however, because the very frequent use of them has crept into Theology itself; and therefore many things cannot be understood unless this meaning of the words is explained.

34 The second property of being is Truth, namely the aptitude of being itself to be known by the intellect. It is divided into transcendental and formal. The first is the very entity of the thing, insofar as it is conceived by an intellect, especially the Divine one: for since the very entity and essences of things are contained, expressed, in God, or in his archetypal ideas and images, it can be known by God, and therefore conceived as the object or term of the Divine knowledge, which corresponds most perfectly to the thing itself, or to the idea known, and therefore derives its truth from it, and in turn communicates it to it, so that it is called a true idea, or true knowledge. Formal truth, however, is that same conformity of the knowing intellect with the thing known.

35 What we have said, finally, about truth can easily be understood also of the last affection of being, namely of Goodness, except that truth is referred to the intellect, and goodness to the will. Transcendental goodness, then, is being itself, insofar as it can be desired or loved by the will; formal goodness, which is also called moral, is the conformity of the object willed and loved with the laws of morals, namely with the precepts and with the archetypal image of the good, which are found in God. And let these things, which have been excerpted from the distinguished Corsini, suffice as said.

On the Rational Soul.

hat can the loftier sciences profit us, excellent young men, if we are 36

W ignorant of ourselves? If we do not know what our soul is, whether it

is spiritual and immortal, and what commerce intervenes between it

and the body? And all these cognitions, what do they profit us, if we lose the soul it‐

self, if we do not use its faculties to attain true immortality, namely eternal beatitude?

We shall therefore divide this second part of Metaphysics into two Dissertations.

The first will be on the origin, spirituality and immortality of the human mind; the

second on the admirable commerce that exists between the mind itself and the body.

On the Origin, spirituality, and immortality of the human mind.

On the origin of the Soul, and at what time it is infused into the

body. 37

T hat a true notion of creation may be had (says the celebrated Clarke (d)), one must not

picture it to oneself as the generation of some thing drawn out of nothing considered as mat‐

ter. To create is to give existence

(d) De l’Existence de Dieu, vol. 1, ch. 11.

p. 13

to a thing that did not have it before; that is, to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before. All Philosophers admit that no created agent can bring about any of those things which cannot be except through creation. For the power of creating belongs to God alone: For it is not lawful, says St. Augustine (e), to believe or to say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone but God. These things being laid down,

38 I say 1: the rational soul is created by God alone when it is infused into the little body. It is proved: to create is to bring it about that a thing exists which did not exist before; but God brings it about that the soul exists, which did not exist before: therefore. It is proved 2: to create is to make something when nothing that intrinsically pertains to it exists beforehand; but it is thus that God makes the soul: therefore. Proof of the minor: the human mind is a simple substance, lacking parts, devoid of composition and divisibility, as we shall see in what follows: therefore it is made without any succession of parts, and with nothing that intrinsically pertains to it existing beforehand: therefore it comes to be by creation alone; but creation belongs to God alone, as has already been said: therefore the rational soul is made by God the Creator.

39 It is proved 3: the rational soul is not generable; but what is not generable comes to be by creation: therefore. Proof of the major: what is generable is corruptible, as all admit; but the rational soul is incorruptible, because it is immortal, as will be shown later in Ch. III: therefore. It is proved 4: nature extends only to generating; but what is not is not generated, for there is nothing from which it might be generated, as Hippocrates says very well (f); therefore creation exceeds the power of nature: therefore it cannot be done except by God.

40 Christian Wolff (g), a celebrated philosopher of our age, admits indeed that the rational soul comes to be by creation from God alone; but, following Leibniz, he contends that the souls of all men were made by God together at the beginning, and each of them enclosed in its own little body. Souls, he says, pre-exist in pre-existing organic corpuscles, from which the fetus is formed in the womb.

41 I say 2, against Leibniz and Wolff: rational souls were not all created together by God at the beginning of time and enclosed in those organic corpuscles which, likewise made by God at that time, lie hidden in the mother’s womb. It is proved 1: from the Fifth Lateran Council (h), where it was expressly defined that the rational soul, according to the multitude of the bodies into which it is infused, is singly multipliable, multiplied, and to be multiplied: therefore the souls of all men who are to be born until the end of the world were not created by God at the beginning of time, because at that time, although they are multiplied, they are not, however, to be multiplied:

therefore

(e) Bk. 12, City of God, ch. 24.

(f) Bk. 1, On Regimen, no. 5.

(g) Psychologia Rationalis, §. 704 ff.

(h) Under Leo X, Sess. 8, vol. 19 of Labbe’s Collection of the Councils.

p. 14

therefore the pre-existence of souls is openly contrary to the Lateran Council, and consequently can by no means be defended.

42 It is proved 2. from absurdity: once this opinion is granted, Virginity could not be urged upon all women indiscriminately; for since it is not known which women are endowed with animated corpuscles, virginity cannot be urged upon individual women without its being true that it lies in our choice that as many souls should perish as those animated corpuscles contain. For the same reason, too, no woman would be permitted to bind herself by a perpetual vow of virginity unless it were first certainly established for her that no animated corpuscles are contained in her womb; and since all these things are no less false than absurd, it follows that the Wolffian opinion is to be utterly rejected by a Catholic man.

43 For the second part of the question, it should be known that all the ancient Philosophers agree in this, namely that the rational soul is not infused immediately upon conception, but after some time. The most common opinion holds that the rational soul informs the fetus after forty days, because then, and not before, the little body is perfectly organized. So Galen (i). Hippocrates (j), or whoever is the author of the book On the Nature of the Child, teaching a difference between male and female fetuses, said that the former are articulated in thirty days, the latter in forty-two, that is, perfectly organized. But the same Hippocrates, in the book On Flesh, no. 10, assigned a much shorter term for perfection of this kind, saying in seven days it has whatever the body ought to have; and in this way, if the body is complete in seven days, it seems consistent with the opinion of Hippocrates that it is animated on the seventh. Others assert that the human fetus is completed in three days, and receives the rational soul on the third day. Aristotle (k) asserts that man lives the life of a plant, the life of an animal, and that of a man, and hence that the rational soul comes to the fetus after some time, although he did not define that time. These things being laid down,

44 I say 3: with the distinguished Paolo Zacchia (l) and other authors of great name, whom the Most Illustrious Don Feijóo (m) praises and follows: the rational soul is infused into the fetus at the first moment of conception. It is proved by most effective reasons: it can in no way be denied that the fetus, as soon as it is conceived, lives, is nourished, and grows; but it cannot have all these things from any other soul than from the rational one: therefore. Proof of the minor: it is absurd to say, as Aristotle affirmed, that the fetus lives first by a vegetative soul, then by a sensitive one, and finally by a rational one; otherwise those three souls would be in man at once, which no one in his right mind would say: therefore the life, nutrition, and growth of the fetus cannot come except

from

(i) Bk. 15, De Usu, no. 5.

(j) On the Nature of the Child, no. 10.

(k) Bk. 2, On the Generation of Animals, ch. 7.

(l) Quaestiones Medico-Legales, bk. 9, tit. 1, last question.

(m) Teatro Crítico, vol. 8, Discourse 11.

from the rational soul alone; but from the first instant of conception it lives, is nour‐

ished, and grows, as all agree: therefore at that very instant it is endowed with the

rational soul. Proof 2: God and nature always act for an end, God indeed from his

own free will, nature from necessity; but the delay of the infusion of the rational

soul can have no end: therefore.

45 Proof of the minor: such an end would be either the perfection of the body,

or this, that it might be able to perform its operations rightly. Not the first; for then

the rational soul would have to be infused much later, since at the term of forty days

the body has not attained its perfection so as to be evident to the eyes; indeed, after

some months it has nothing more than a certain rough delineation of the parts,

scarcely perceptible even to the eyes of a Lynceus. Not the second: for as regards

the operations proper to the rational soul, neither after forty days, nor after the in‐

fant, the ninth month completed, has come forth into the light, is the soul fit to ex‐

ercise any of them: therefore the delay of the infusion of the rational soul can have

no end. We must therefore conclude from these things that, since the conceived fe‐

tus lives, is nourished, and grows immediately, and cannot have this from any other

soul than the rational one, which can vegetate, and nourish, and communicate life,

since it is furnished with all the faculties necessary for accomplishing these things, it

is created by God at the very instant of conception and infused into the fetus, and

by itself nourishes and increases the conceptus, and communicates life and sense to

it.

46 The conclusion is confirmed: either the rational soul can communicate life

and sense to the conceptus, or it cannot: if the first, nothing prevents it from being

able to do the same before forty days, for it does not acquire those faculties from

the body, but possesses them from its own nature. If the second: then the body, even

when the rational soul is present, receives life, growth, nutrition and sense from an‐

other soul; for it is not likely that all these things are supplied before the fortieth

day by another soul, and after forty by the rational one. It is further confirmed: if

man does not receive the rational soul before forty days, he will not be a man before

the said term; for how would he be a man, not having the form of a man? Will he

then be a plant, or a worm, or an insect, or some other animal, or some beast re‐

ducible to no genus, or to no definite species of living things, and will he constitute

of himself a new species of animal? What, then, will this species be? Let what has

been said about the animation of the human fetus suffice: these are the things that

seemed to me could be said with probability.

Arguments against the first conclusion. 47

O bj. 1. Creation is the production of a thing out of nothing; but out of nothing

nothing comes: therefore the rational soul is not created. I distinguish the mi‐

nor: out of nothing nothing comes, that is, something is not drawn out of nothing as

from

p. 16

from a material and pre-existing cause, I grant; that is, it cannot be brought about that what did not exist before should exist, I subdistinguish: if we speak of an agent whose powers are finite, I grant; if the discussion is of an agent whose power is infinite, such as God is, I deny; and I deny the consequence as well. You will say with Toland and Gildon: God communicated divisibility and figure to matter, although God does not have them in himself: therefore an intelligent substance too, namely the soul, can emanate from a non-intelligent substance, such as matter is: therefore it is not created by God. I deny the consequence, and there is a disparity, because God contains in himself most eminently whatever good and perfection there is in matter, and by his power produces all things in matter; but matter can contain neither formally, nor virtually, nor eminently the true and simple perfections of the soul; since in a corporeal and inert being, such as matter is, there cannot be the adequate ground of an intelligent and freely acting being, which is found only in a free, acting, intelligent being.

48 Obj. 2. with Antonio Rocco: the soul depends entirely on the body, or matter: therefore it is produced dependently on matter: therefore it is not created. The antecedent is proved 1. because this soul depends on the temperament of this body; otherwise any soul could enter any body. 2. because if the soul did not depend on the body, it would not depart unwillingly when the body perishes and is dissolved: therefore. To the argument I distinguish the antecedent: it depends on the body in order to be, I deny; in order to exercise the office of a form that vivifies and moves the body, I grant; and therefore the soul is not free to enter any body whatever, since it is destined by God its Creator to rule and vivify this one, and is produced under this law, that together with this body it should constitute an individual man. That the soul departs unwillingly when the body is dissolved, however, is a penalty of original sin. The distinguished Berti (n) explains most happily and aptly, by the example of a sailor, how the soul is both dependent on the body and independent of it, which it will not be unwelcome to you to hear.

49 A sailor is a man destined to steer a ship. Insofar as he is a man, he has no need of the vessel, than which he himself is far nobler, for he can at times lead his life otherwise than by sailing; but insofar as he is a sailor, whose business is to cross the seas by navigation, he certainly needs a ship. When this is broken up, he is forced to lead either a most wretched life on the shore, or a happier one in port. But when the ship has been repaired, he at length returns to his homeland. The soul likewise is a spiritual substance, but it is the form of the body and, as it were, its shipmaster, for it steers and moves it, and, having taken its bearings, tries to bring it into port. As a spiritual substance it is more excellent than the body, and gains no advantage from it: as the form of the body it depends on it, not indeed in order to be, but in order to travel the sea, namely the mortal life. By death the body is dissolved, like a ship by a storm, and the soul, according to its merits, leads a life either wretched or tranquil. The mortal body will rise again to everlasting life, and this resurrection itself is, as it were, the restoration of the wrecked ship.

50

(n) De Theologicis Disciplinis, vol. 1.

p. 17

50 Obj. 3. with the same: If the rational soul were created, it would not con‐

tract original sin from the seed of Adam; but it does contract it: therefore. I deny

the major: original stain is not contracted by the son because his soul fell away

from the infected soul of the father in his generation, like a part from a whole, as

Rocco and Pomponazzi stubbornly contend; rather, the rational soul is polluted

by original guilt from this, that it is joined to corrupted flesh, as water is corrupt‐

ed in a tainted vessel. How this comes about, indeed, the Theologians, to whom

it belongs, explain most clearly. But Rocco insists: accidents are not transmitted

without their subject; but the subject of original sin is the soul: therefore if the

soul is not propagated from the seed of Adam, neither is sin spread by propaga‐

tion. I deny the major: for, as Estius very well replies, heresies, vices, leprosy, and

other contagions of morals and of diseases pass from one subject into another

without the subject being transferred.

51 Obj. finally: man begets his like; but likeness consists not in matter, but in

species, nature and form: therefore the form too, which is the soul, is begotten

by man: therefore it is not created by God. To the argument I reply that man

begets his like insofar as he so disposes matter that God may put into it the soul

by which the human species and nature are perfected. For once the soul has been

put into the body, the son bears the image and likeness of the Father, even

though the soul is not propagated from him by generation. Nor does that text of

Genesis (o) support Rocco: All the souls that went with Jacob into Egypt, and that

came out of his thigh. For the sense of these words is: all the men who descended

from Jacob by generation, etc. For it suffices that the son descend from the thigh

of the father as regards the body alone for the whole son to be said to have de‐

scended; for although the body is not the principal part in man, it is nevertheless

what meets us immediately in ourselves and what is seen by us; just as a statue

too is called the work of the artist, although it depends on the sculptor only as

regards its form.

Arguments against the other conclusions. 52

O bj. against the second, with Wolff (p) and Sennert: that God rested on the sev‐

enth day from all his work which he had done, we read in Gen. 2, v. 2: therefore

today he creates nothing more: therefore the creation of souls was accomplished

by God in the first creation. This is Wolff’s chief argument. But with the great

Augustine (q) we reply that God rested from founding kinds of creatures,

N because

(o) Gen. ch. 46, v. 26.

(p) In Princip. Philos. § 705.

(q) Bk. IV, On the Literal Meaning of Genesis.

p. 18

because beyond that he no longer founded any new kinds. And so, when God is said to create a soul, he is not said to do something that he had not done before. For already on the sixth day he had made man to his own image, which is certainly understood according to the soul. And this he does now, not by instituting what was not, but by multiplying what was. Hence both that is true, that he rested from instituting things that were not; and this is true, that he works until now, not only by governing what he made, but also by creating in greater number, not what he had not yet created, but what he had already created.

53 Obj. against the third: The presence of the soul is detected more, and more certainly, from the motion of the embryo than from its other operations; but before the fortieth day the embryo does not move, and moreover the female moves later than the male: therefore before the fortieth the embryo does not receive the rational soul, and male and female do not receive it at the same moment of conception. I deny the major of the argument: because the other operations that precede motion cannot be attributed to any other agent than the rational soul, and it is all one to elicit the presence of the rational soul from motion and to deduce it from life, from nutrition, from growth; hence, since the fetus in the womb immediately lives, is nourished, grows, and feels, it must immediately have a rational soul. Besides: what dependence does motion have on the rational soul as rational? One ought therefore to have affirmed that the fetus receives the rational soul when it performs some operation pertaining to the rational soul as rational, not when it begins to move. The minor of the argument, moreover, is false, absolutely speaking. For who will dare to affirm that the embryo does not have some unobservable motion before the fortieth day? Nor, even if all motion were absent, ought one to infer from this that the rational soul is not present.

54 Much more reasonably, therefore, ought the presence of the soul in the embryo to be inferred from the operations of life and from the formation of the fetus itself; for none of these can depend on any cause other than an intrinsic one, nor can any other intrinsic cause be imagined in the fetus than the soul itself. The difference, moreover, between the male and the female as to the first motion excited in the mother’s womb (if what is reported is true) perhaps consists in this, that the matter from which the male is produced swells with a greater abundance of spirits and obtains a livelier heat. Besides, it has been observed that some males, because of their weakness, move later than females, and on the other hand that some females, because of their strength, move sooner than males; whence the included minor, absolutely speaking, is altogether false.

55 Obj. 1. The fetus ought not to receive the rational soul unless it is perfectly organized; but this organization is not completed at the same time in every individual, because of the variety of temperaments and powers: therefore the soul is not infused at the very moment of conception. The argument can be answered in several ways. First: by granting that organization is required for the soul to operate, but denying that it is necessary

for

p. 19

for it to inform. Second: by saying that God ought not to be subject to nature, so that before he infuses the soul he must wait for the organization of the fetus contrived by nature itself. But it is preferable to satisfy the argument in another way, according to the mind of the Moderns. The most common opinion among the Moderns is that of the perfect delineation of the embryo in the corpuscles lying hidden in the mother’s womb; and once this is granted, it can be denied that the fetus is not perfectly organized before the fortieth.

56 But if by perfect organization our adversaries understand an organization so complete in every respect that by it the fetus has whatever an embryo ought to have, so that, as the eye bears witness, it is furnished with all its members and necessary organs, we shall deny that this organization is necessary for receiving the soul; for if it were so, the reception of the soul would have to be delayed for several months; hence, when the Angelic Master says (r) that the rational soul is infused when the body is disposed, he is not to be understood of this final disposition; otherwise the holy Doctor himself would be asserting contradictory things, which it is wrong even to think.

57 For the most wise Master himself (s) asserts that, since the soul is the proper act and form of the body, it must necessarily be produced together with the body; but the body is produced immediately when it is conceived: therefore, according to the mind of the Angelic Doctor, the rational soul too is infused then; and once infused it operates immediately, and thus it is present at the first moment of the conception of the embryo itself; for otherwise it would always be true to say that the body is produced before the soul, contrary to what the Theologians teach with the Angelic Master (t).

58 But you will say: the soul was breathed into the face of Adam when his body was perfect: therefore it ought to be introduced into any man when the body is perfect in every way. I reply that the argument proves nothing: for however perfect our adversaries may wish the embryo to be on the fortieth day, it will never be as perfect as the body of Adam when God breathed the soul into it. Besides: there must be a great difference between a work emanating immediately from God himself and a work entrusted to nature in the generation of man.

59 Obj. 3. If the rational soul were present at the first instant of conception, then when an abortion occurred before the fortieth day the Canons would order that fetus to be baptized; but they do not so order: therefore it is because it is not informed by the rational soul before the fortieth. I reply that in these abortions it is impossible, because of their weakness, that the soul should not be separated from the body at once, and for that reason the Sacred Canons make no mention of baptism; and it was enough if, whenever they give some sign of life

N2 by

(r) Pt. 1, q. 100, art. 1, ad 2.

(s) Pt. 1, q. 90, art. 4.

(t) Pt. 1, q. 91, art. 4, ad 3.

p. 20

by motion, even if this happened before the fortieth, they should be cleansed in the laver of baptism, at least conditionally; but this in no way prevents us from affirming with the distinguished Feijóo that, at whatever time the abortion occurs, the fetus ought to be baptized conditionally; for according to everyone it ought to be washed in baptism when it is probable that the fetus is animated; but from what has been said it is highly probable, both by the intrinsic probability of the reasons and by the extrinsic probability of authors of great name, that the fetus is informed by the rational soul from the very instant of conception: therefore, at whatever time the abortion occurs, it ought to be baptized, at least conditionally.

60 Obj. finally: the Laws, Canon as well as Civil, distinguish the animated fetus from the inanimate, and declare it animated only after forty days, and for this reason impose a greater or a lesser penalty on offenders and on those who procure abortion; in confirmation of which the Constitution of Sixtus V, Supreme Pontiff, was finally issued, in which it is determined that those who procure the abortion of an animated fetus are subject to the same penalties as true homicides: therefore our conclusion is contrary to the authority of the Ecclesiastical and Secular Laws. To the argument I reply, with Zacchia, praised above, that both the Canons and the Laws speak in the texts cited not from their own scientific knowledge, but from the opinions of the wise men of that age, Philosophers and Physicians, as they have been accustomed to do elsewhere in matters that belong to other professions. Therefore, since the aforesaid wise men had been consulted on that matter, the Canons and Laws, wishing to follow their determination in this, imposed on offenders penalties now greater, now lesser, according to the difference that those men made between the fetus not animated by the rational soul and the animated one. But even with these things granted, we contend that the determinations of the Canons and Laws issued in accordance with justice, and must remain safe and intact, while our opinion on the animation of the fetus at the first moment of conception also remains firm.

61 For the Canons and Civil Laws always follow the milder opinion in imposing penalties; since, therefore, it was called into doubt whether one who procures abortion always, and at any time whatever, should be punished with the same penalty, and some, of the milder opinion, had judged that he should be punished with a lesser penalty when the fetus is more tender and before the fortieth, while others thought the contrary, the Canons adhered to the former opinion, and with the greatest reason they establish a greater penalty for one who procures abortion after forty days than before, because the former inflicts much greater violence both on the fetus and on the mother than the latter does. For the abortion of a more tender fetus, because of the weakness of the ligaments, takes place easily and with the least discomfort to the mother, whereas the abortion of a more advanced fetus does not take place without evident danger to the mother; whence from Hippocrates (u) and from daily experience we know that abortions are safer

in

CHAPTER II

in the first forty days, but difficult in the following ones, and much less safe. Let what

has been said in reply to the argument suffice. The most distinguished Feijóo, howev‐

er, contends further that one who has procured an abortion two or three days after

conception incurs the penalty of irregularity established by Gregory XIV against

those who procure the abortion of an animated fetus, as may be seen in his work (x).

It is examined whether the human mind is a spiritual substance,

or rather a corporeal one?

he human mind is that which thinks in each of us. By the Scholastics it is 62

T commonly defined: the first act of a physical organic body having life in potency.

They explain, namely, the unknown by the more unknown. We, however,

define it: the principle by which man thinks, or by which he understands the true

and wills the good, and is moreover conscious of his own perceptions and volitions. It is called

mens [mind], because the power of thinking is preeminent in the soul. It is called anima

rationalis [rational soul], or animus, because it is capable of incorporeal knowledge, or

reason.

63 That a principle of this kind, or a soul, exists in us is most evident; for nothing

can be more manifest than that we think while we think, that we will something

when we will, that we perceive, doubt, remember, when we perceive, doubt, remem‐

ber: therefore that principle exists in us by which each of these operations and acts is

carried out in us.

64 By body, or matter, we understand an extended, divisible, solid substance, wo‐

ven together from various parts of various figures. By a spiritual substance, on the

other hand, we understand a substance devoid of matter, or one that excludes exten‐

sion, divisibility, solidity. The question, therefore, is whether that which thinks in

each of us is a substance devoid of extension, divisibility, solidity, etc.?

65 The Materialists, namely unbelieving and most perverse men, maintain that

there is nothing in man besides physical sensibility, and hence that it is through this,

which is something material and depends on matter, that man understands, thinks,

reasons, and consequently that our mind is matter. This most pernicious error is

maintained by Spinoza,

Hobbes,

(x) Teatro Crítico, vol. 8, Discourse 11, no. 27.

p. 22

Hobbes, Toland (y), nor is Locke very far removed from him. Among the more recent Materialists are counted Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Voltaire and other French Philosophers, with most pernicious little books by which they corrupt Religion and morals; from reading these, as befits a Christian philosopher, you must always abstain. Against these unbelieving and lost men, then:

66 I say 1. The human mind is a spiritual substance, or one distinct and different from matter, or body. The first part is proved, namely that the human mind is a substance. We experience that our thoughts are continually changed in us, and that they succeed one another in a perpetual flux; but the changeable things that are in a being are called modes, and cannot be without a subject: therefore that which thinks in us, namely the soul, is the subject of thoughts. A subject, moreover, does not need another subject in order to exist; and therefore it is a substance: therefore the soul is a substance.

67 The second part is proved: the principle of operations that cannot belong to matter is a substance altogether distinct from matter, and consequently spiritual; but the soul is the principle of thoughts, which can in no way belong to matter: therefore it is a spiritual substance. Proof of the minor: if thought belonged to matter, it would be an intrinsic modification of matter; for since thought is an internal action of the thinking subject, it is an intrinsic modification of the thinking subject; but thought cannot be an intrinsic modification of matter: therefore it can in no way belong to matter. Proof of the minor:

if
