§. II.

Postulates.

I.

F rom any Point to any point a Straight Line can be drawn.

II. A straight Line can be continued in a straight line as far as you wish.

III. From any center at any interval a Circle can be described.

IV. Any line can be divided into Equal or Unequal parts.

V. To any Straight line another can be placed, Equal or Unequal, Perpendicular or

Parallel.

Axioms.

I.

T hings which are equal to the same thing are equal to each other.

And things which have a common measure are equal.

And what is greater or less than one of equals is also greater or less than the other

of the equals.

II. If to equals you add equals, or something common, or take them away from

them, the things that remain are equal.

III. If to equals you add unequals, or take them away from them, the things that

remain are unequal.

IV. Things which are double, triple, or half of the same thing, or of equals, are

equal to each other.

And whenever two things are equally exceeded by the same thing, or equally ex‐

ceed it, they are equal.

V. Things which mutually coincide with each other are equal.

VI. The Whole is greater than its Part.

And it is equal to all its parts taken together. And the Part which is equal to all the

other parts taken together is the Half of the whole.

p. 8

CHAPTER II

VII. Two straight Lines do not enclose a space.

That is, to enclose a space on all sides, at least three straight Lines are required.

VIII. Two straight Lines do not have a common segment, or Part.

That is, two straight lines which make an angle cannot be continued into one straight line unless they are bent.

Problems.

P roblems are Propositions which teach how to do some Work concerning Lines,

Angles, or Figures. The principal ones, pertaining to rectilinear Figures, are proposed here, and their demonstrations are only indicated, except for the first: both because these are easily deduced from the Principles laid down, or from the Theorems to be demonstrated; and because Problems are not Principles for showing the other truths, but can be supposed as Hypotheses. This Method seems better suited to Learners, so that they may not be thrown into confusion at the beginning, but, once the Theorems have been demonstrated, may exercise themselves in finding the demonstrations of the Problems.

Problem I. (Plate I. Fig. 1.)

To make an Equilateral Triangle.

L et the Compass be opened to the interval of the given line AB; then from each

end of the line, with the Compass unchanged, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C; finally from the Point C let the lines CA and CB be drawn, which will constitute the Equilateral Triangle ABC.

For the demonstration, let the circles ACF and BCE be completed.

Demonstration. The line AC is equal to the line AB, because they are drawn from the center to the circumference of the same Circle: from definition XV. But the line BC is also equal to the same line AB, by the same definition: therefore the lines CA and CB are equal to each other: from Axiom 1; and so the Triangle ABC, consisting of three equal lines, is Equilateral.

To make an Isosceles Triangle, let the compass be opened once to a greater or a lesser interval than the given line; and then let arcs be made, as above. But if, while the arcs are being made, the interval of the compass is changed each time, a Scalene Triangle will be made.

Problem

p. 9

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

To bisect a line.

F rom the ends A and B of the given line let two arcs be made with the same open‐

ing of the compass, cutting each other at C; and two others below the same line, cutting each other at D. The line CD will bisect the line AB. It is demonstrated from Theor. IV of this book, pt. 1, if from C and D lines are drawn to the ends A and B.

To bisect an angle.

F rom the vertex of the angle A, at any interval you please, let equal sides be cut off

on either side at B and C; then from the points of section B and C, with the same opening of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. The line DA will bisect the angle. Dem. from the same Theor. IV, with lines drawn from B and C to D.

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

To draw a parallel line.

L et a line parallel to FG be drawn, passing through the point D. First, let one foot

of the compass be placed at D, the other at any point of the line FG, as at A. Second, from A, with the opening of the compass unchanged, let the same line be cut at B. Third, from the points B and D, with the same spread of the compass, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at C. The line DC will be parallel to the line FG. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

Otherwise. From any point, such as the middle point E, let an arc DF be made, and another, GH, on the other side; then let the arc GH be cut equal to the arc DF. The line DH will be the parallel sought.

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

To draw a perpendicular line.

I f from a given point F outside a line a Perpendicular is to be drawn to the line BG:

placing one foot of the compass at F, let the line be cut on either side, extended further (if need be), at B and G; then from B and G let two Arcs be made, with the same opening of the compass, cutting

Z each

p. 10

each other at H. The line FH will be the Perpendicular sought. From Theor. IV, pt. 2.

It must be noted, however, that a Perpendicular cannot be drawn from any point whatever to any point whatever of a line; but it is sometimes necessary to produce the given line further, so that a Perpendicular can be drawn to it from the given point.

If a Perpendicular is to be drawn at a given point C within the line BG, whether that point is the end of the line or not: from the point C let an arc of nearly a semicircle be made, at any interval you please, and, with the compass unchanged, let there be cut off first the arc GE, then the arc ED; then also, with the compass unchanged, from the points D and E let two arcs be made, cutting each other at F. The line FC, when drawn, will be the Perpendicular sought. From the same Theor.

Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

To make a Square.

L et a perpendicular CA, equal to the line AB, be drawn at its end: then, with the

same interval of the given line, from C and B let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Square will be had. From Theor. VI, Cor. 2.

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

To make a Rhombus.

A t the end of the given line AB let another, CA, equal to it be drawn, at any

Angle that is not right: then from the extremities C and B, with the same interval of the given line, let two arcs be made, cutting each other at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhombus will be had. From the same Theor.

Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

To make an oblong Rectangle.

A t the end of AB let a perpendicular greater or less than it be drawn: then from

the end C let an arc be made with the interval of the line AB, and from the end B let an arc be made with the interval of the line CA, intersecting the former arc at D: finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and a Rectangle longer on one side will be had. From the same Theor.

Problem

p. 11

Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

Problem X. (Fig. 10.)

To make a Rhomboid.

A t the end of the line AB let an unequal line CA be drawn, at an angle that is

not right: then from the end C, with the interval of the line AB, let an arc be made; and from the end B, with the interval of the line CA, let another be made, intersecting the former at D. Finally from the point D let lines be drawn to B and C, and the Rhomboid will be had. From the same Theor.

To make a Triangle equal to another.

L et a line DE be taken equal to the line AB: then, with the interval of the line

AC, let an arc be made from the end D; similarly, with the interval of the line BC, let an arc be made from the end E, which intersects the former at F. The Triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC. It is evident from the construction itself.

In like manner a Triangle is made from three lines not joined, A, B, C; provided that the two taken together which constitute an angle are greater than the one Straight line: by def. VI.

Problem XI. (Fig. 11.)

To make an Angle equal to another.

F rom the given Angle A, at any interval, let an arc BC be made: then from the

end D of the line DE, where the equal Angle is to be placed, with the same interval of the compass, let an arc be made which cuts the given line at F: then let the arc FG be cut off equal to the arc BC. The line drawn from D through G will constitute at D an angle equal to the angle A. From the def. of an Angle, note 1.

Problem XII. (Fig. 12.)

To make a Rectangle, or another Parallelogram, equal to a given Triangle.

L et a Parallel CD be placed to the Base AK of the given Triangle: then let the

Base be divided in two at E, and upon a line equal to half the Base let a Rectangle, or any Parallelogram FDBG, be made, within the parallel CD: and the Parallelogram BD will be equal to the given triangle ACK. From Theor. VIII.

Z2 Hence

p. 12

CHAPTER III

Hence it is evident how a Parallelogram may be made equal to any Trapezium whatever. For let the Trapezium be divided into two Triangles by drawing a line to the opposite Angles HI, to which let Parallels be drawn through the vertices L and M: then, HI having been bisected at N, between the same Parallels, upon a base BG equal to the half HN, let the Parallelogram FBDG be made: which will be equal to the Trapezium LM, inasmuch as it is equal to the two Triangles HLI and HMI, which compose the Trapezium. From the same Theor.

Theorems.

A Theorem is a Proposition demonstrating some property of quantity. Its prin‐

cipal parts are three: the Proposition itself, which proposes the truth to be shown; the Preparation, which arranges the lines sometimes necessary for the demonstration; the Demonstration, which concludes the proposed truth from the Principles laid down, or from Theorems.

Twelve Theorems selected from the 1st and 2nd books of Euclid are proposed in this chapter, with Corollaries, or inferences, added, which follow easily from the Theorems: some of these are contained in the propositions of Euclid, others lie outside Euclid; the order of that Author has been varied somewhat, so as to keep, if it please Heaven, a clearer method. For, beginning from Angles and Lines, we come to the properties of Triangles, and from these to demonstrating Quadrilateral figures.

But lest the Number of the more notable Propositions of Euclid, as it is commonly used by Mathematicians, should lie hidden, we shall place it at the foot of the page. The Principles, however, from which the Demonstrations descend, we shall not always indicate, because they are so clear that they may be supposed present to the mind.

Theorem I. (Plate II. Fig. 1.) A straight line falling upon another straight line, as GA upon DE, makes the angles on both sides together equal to two Right angles. (a)

Preparation. A Circle having been made from the center A at any interval, let a Perpendicular BC be drawn to the line DE.

Demonstration.

(a) Euclid, bk. 1, prop. 13.

p. 13

Demonstration. The two Angles DAG and GAE together have the same Measure as the two Right angles DAB and BAE, namely two quadrants of a Circle, according to the def. of an Angle, note 1. Therefore the two Angles DAG and GAE together are equal to two Right angles: from Axiom 1.

Corollary I. If two lines are not placed in a straight line, as DA, AG, they comprehend on one side an arc less than a semicircle, on the other an arc greater, as is evident; whence only a straight line, as DE, upon which another straight line falls, comprehends Angles equal to two right angles. (a)

II. If two lines cut each other, the vertically opposite Angles, as DAF and EAI, are equal. For the arc DBE is a semicircle; likewise the arc FGI is a semicircle, inasmuch as they are cut off by diameters: therefore if the common arc FE is taken away from each, there remains the arc DF equal to the arc EI, and the Angle DAF equal to the Angle EAI. (b)

III. If several straight lines are united upon the same straight line at the same point, they make all the angles equal to two right angles. And if two straight lines, or more, cut each other, they make all the angles about the same point equal to four right angles: for they are all comprehended by two semicircles. (c)

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.) If a straight line cuts two Parallel straight lines, then I. the two Internal Angles L and N together will be equal to two right Angles. II. The Alternate Angles I and N will be equal to each other. III. The Exterior Angle H will also be equal to the Angle N, the Interior opposite toward the same side. (d)

Dem. I. The four Angles I and L, M and N together are equal to four right Angles: from the preceding Theor.; but the two internal Angles L and N together are equal to the two internal ones together on the other side, I and M: according to defin. 13, Parall. Therefore the two internal Angles L and N together on one side are equal to two Right angles, just as the two internal ones on the other side, I and M.

Dem. II. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two Right angles: from what has just been demonstrated; but the two Angles I and L together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle I equal to the alternate Angle N.

Dem. III. The two Angles L and N together are equal to two right angles: but the two Angles L and H together are also equal to two Right angles: from Theor. I; therefore, the common Angle L being taken away, there remains the Angle

the

(a) Prop. 14.

(b) Prop. 15.

(c) Cor. of prop. 15.

(d) Prop. 29.

p. 14

the exterior H, equal to the Angle N, interior and opposite toward the same side.

Cor. The Converse of this Theorem is easily demonstrated; namely, that if a Line cutting two other lines makes the two internal angles on the same side equal to two right angles, those two lines will be Parallel: For they will be equally inclined to the middle secant, and to each other. Likewise if it makes the alternate angles, or the internal and the external, equal (a).

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.) In any Triangle I. the three Angles together are equal to two Right angles. II. The exterior Angle G is equal to the two interior opposite ones together, A and B. (b)

Preparation. Let a Line DE be drawn Parallel to the Base BC through the vertex A.

Dem. I. The Angle B is equal to the alternate angle D, from the preceding Theor., and the Angle C is equal to the angle E, likewise alternate: but the Angles D, E and A together are equal to two right angles, from Theor. I; therefore if to the Angles B and C the Angle A is also added, the three angles B, C and A together are equal to two Right angles.

Dem. II. The Angles B and A together with C are equal to two Right angles: but the two Angles C and G, the exterior, together are also equal to two right angles; therefore, the common Angle C being taken away, there remains the exterior Angle G equal to the two interior opposite Angles A and B together.

Cor. I. When two Angles of any Triangle are known, the third at once becomes known, as the remainder up to two right angles.

II. If two Triangles have two Angles equal, they will also have the third, the remainder up to two right angles, equal.

III. From the same point to the same straight line only one Perpendicular can be drawn; because a Triangle cannot have two right Angles.

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.) Two Triangles are wholly equal, I. If they have two sides equal, each to each, and the angle comprehended by them equal. II. If they have three sides likewise equal. III. If they have two equal angles, and the side comprehended by them

equal.

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 28, 27.

(b) Prop. 32.

p. 15

equal. IV. If they have a side opposite one of the two equal angles equal (a).

Dem. I. If the side AB is equal to the side DE, and the side AC equal to the side DF, and the Angle A equal to the angle D: the Side DE, superposed on the side AB, will coincide with it, and the side DF with the side AC, and the points E, F with the points B, C: therefore both the Bases and the remaining Angles at the Base will coincide, and will be equal in each triangle: from definition VI of the straight line.

Dem. II. If the distance BC is equal to the distance EF, and the remaining sides containing the Angles A and D are equal, each to each, the angle A will be equal to the angle D: from the definit. of Angle, no. 3; therefore the whole triangle DEF will be equal to the triangle ABC: from pt. I of this.

Dem. III. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, then, superposed on it, it will coincide with it; and if the angle E is equal to the angle ABC, the side DE will also coincide with the side AB (for if the side DE fell inside, as at H, the angle E would be smaller; if outside, as at G, the angle E would be greater than the angle ABC, contrary to the hypothesis); and if the angle F is equal to the angle ACB, by the same reasoning the side DF will coincide with the side AC; therefore the triangles ABC, EDF will be wholly equal.

Dem. IV. If the line EF is equal to the line BC, and the angle E equal to the angle ABC, and the angle A equal to the angle D: the angle F will also be equal to the angle ACB: from Theor. III; therefore the triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equal: from the third part of this.

Cor. Hence it is plain that the nearer to the Base the lines produced from the extremities of the same Base are joined, the greater they make the Angle H than the Angle A, and the Angle A than the Angle G: because, since the angles at the Base HBC and HCB are smaller than the angles ABC and ACB, the third, H, above the Base, the remainder up to two right angles, must be greater than the Angle A. From Theor. III. (b)

Theorem V. (Fig. 5.) An Isosceles Triangle, as ABC, has the angles above the Base, B and C, equal to each other. (c)

Prep. Let the Base be understood to be bisected at L, and let AL be drawn.

Dem. In the Triangles ABL and ACL, the line BL is equal to the line LC: from the construction. The side AB is equal to the side AC: from the supposition. The side AL is common: therefore the Triangle ABL is wholly equal

to

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 4, 8, 26.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 21.

(c) Prop. 5.

p. 16

to the Triangle ACL, and the angles B and C, opposite the common side, are equal. From the preceding Theor.

Cor. I. The Angles D and E below the Base are also equal; for the two angles B and D together are equal to two right angles, and no less the angles C and E: from Theor. I; therefore, when the equal angles B and C are taken away, the angles D and E remain equal.

II. If the angles B and C are equal, the sides AB and AC will also be equal; for when CL is placed upon the equal LB, the angles and the extreme points B and C will coincide; the Point A is common to both sides AB and AC; therefore the lines AC, AB will be equal: from defin. VI of the straight line. (a)

III. If the Triangle AHI is equilateral, each of its three angles will be equal; and conversely, if the three angles are equal, the three sides opposite the equal angles will also be equal.

IV. If the line AL bisects the Base, it will also bisect the angle A: and if it bisects the angle A, it will also bisect the Base of the Isosceles triangle ABC, and perpendicularly: for two Triangles ABL and ACL come out wholly equal, from Theor. IV; and the angles at L, being equal on either side, are right.

Cor. V. In Triangles the greater angle is opposite the greater side, and conversely. For let the Triangle HAI be equilateral and equiangular: if, e.g., the Side HI grows to C, the angle A also grows, and the angle C diminishes (from Theorem III), which is opposite the smaller side AH: and if the angle A grows, the Side HI also grows to C, or B. (b)

VI. The Perpendicular AL is the shortest of all the lines that can be drawn from the same point A to the line BC: for the other lines, being opposite the Right angle L, which is greater, are greater; and the farther they recede from the perpendicular, the greater they are, because they are opposite more obtuse angles.

Hence the Perpendicular Line measures all distances; because of all the straight lines that can be drawn from one point to the same line it is the shortest, and therefore the one and certain Measure.

Theorem VI. (Fig. 6.)

The Diameter divides a Parallelogram into two equal Triangles. (c)

Dem. The Triangles ABC and BDC have the side BC common, and the Angle ABC equal to the alternate angle BCD, and also the angle

DBC

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 6.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 18, 19.

(c) Prop. 34.

p. 17

DBC equal to the angle ACB, likewise alternate: from Theor. II; therefore the sides opposite the equal angles, and the whole triangles, are equal to each other, from Theor. IV.

Cor. I. Hence it follows that in a Parallelogram the opposite angles are equal: for since the alternate angles about the diameter are equal, from what has just been demonstrated, the other two opposite angles will also be equal, from Theor. III.

II. In a Quadrilateral Figure, if the lines opposite each other on either side are equal, they will also be Parallel; and if two opposite lines are equal and Parallel, the other two will also be equal and Parallel; for when the Diameter is drawn, two equal Triangles will be formed, from Theor. IV. (a)

III. The complements AE, ED about the Diameter have an equal surface. For the Triangles ABC and BCD are equal, from the preceding Theor.; therefore if from them we subtract the Triangle HBE, equal to the Triangle EBI, and also the Triangle FEC, for the same reason equal to the Triangle ECG, the complements that remain, AE and ED, are equal. (b)

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

Parallelograms constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels are equal. (c)

Dem. Since AG and GF are Parallelograms constituted on the same Base CG, the sides opposite it, AE and FB, will be equal, from the preceding Theor.; adding the common line EF, the sides AF and EB will be equal; and the side CF is equal to the side GB, and the exterior angle AEC equal to the interior opposite angle ABC, from Theor. II; therefore the Triangles AFC and EBG are equal: therefore, taking away the common Triangle ELF, there remains the Trapezium AECL, equal to the trapezium LGFB: therefore, adding the common Triangle LCG, the Parallelogram AG becomes equal to the Parallelogram GF.

Cor. I. Parallelograms AG and ED constituted on equal Bases and between the same Parallels are also equal to each other; for both are equal to the same Parallelogram FG. (d)

II. But since the distance between the Parallels AB, CD is measured by the perpendicular AC, from Theor. V, last cor., the Surfaces of Parallelograms are generated by drawing the base into the perpendicular, according to Def. V; so that if the side AC is, e.g., 9 palms, and GC 4, the surface made by the motion of the line CG along the line AC, and the Parallelogram AG, or GF equal to it, will be 36 palms.

Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

III. Hence if Parallelograms on the same or an equal Base are equal, it is manifest that they also have the same perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels.

A Triangle constituted on the same Base and between the same Parallels is half of the

Parallelogram. (a)

Dem. The Triangle BCG is half of the Parallelogram FG, from Theor. VI; but the Parallelogram FG is equal to the Parallelogram AG, from the preceding; therefore the Triangle BCG is also half of the Parallelogram AG, constituted on the same Base CG and between the same Parallels.

Cor. I. It is plain that the Triangle BHD also, constituted on an equal base and between the same Parallels, is half of the Parallelogram AG, since it is half of the equal Parallelogram FD.

II. It is also manifest that Triangles which are on the same or equal bases and between the same Parallels are equal to each other, since they are halves of equal Parallelograms (b).

III. But since half of the Parallelogram AG is made by drawing half the base into the Perpendicular AC, the surface of the Triangle, which is equal to half the Parallelogram, from Theorem VI, is likewise known by drawing half the base into the same Perpendicular altitude; whence if the base of the Triangle BCG is 4 palms, and the Perpendicular altitude BD, or AC, 9 palms, the whole Surface of the Triangle BCG will be 18 palms.

IV. Equal triangles, therefore, on the same or an equal base, have an equal perpendicular altitude, or are between the same Parallels (c).

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.) In a right-angled Triangle the Square of the side AC, subtending the right angle B, is equal to

the two Squares together of the sides AB, BC, which contain the right angle (d).

Prep. Eight equal Triangles having been constructed, which are marked by the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, let there be understood the Square HO upon the line HI, equal to the line AB; the Square DM of the side BC; and the Square AE of the side AC.

Dem.

(a) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 41.

(b) Eucl. bk. I, prop. 37, 38.

(c) Prop. 39, 40.

Dem. The two Squares HO and MB together are composed of the Square LO and four equal Triangles 1, 8, 4, 5. Likewise the Square AE is composed of the same Square LO and four equal Triangles 5, 3, 7, 8; therefore the Square AE is equal to the two Squares HO and BM together, since they consist of equal parts.

Cor. In a Square, since the Diameter is opposite a right angle, the Square of the Diameter will be equal to the two squares of the equal sides, and consequently double one Square.

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.) If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, the whole Square of the line AB will be equal to the two Squares of the parts together, and the two Rectangles which are made from the same parts

(a).

Prep. Let the Perpendicular FI be drawn Parallel to the line AC; let AH be cut equal to AF, and let the Perpendicular HE be drawn Parallel to the line AB: from which all the lines in the square AD will be at right angles, and the opposite ones will be equal, from Theor. VI, cor. 1 & 2.

Dem. The Square AG upon the part AF, the Square GD upon GE, equal to the line FB, and the two Rectangles CG and GB from the parts of the line AB, are all the parts of the whole Square AD: therefore they are equal to it.

Cor. I. If the straight line AB is cut anyhow at F, with the same construction, the Rectangle AI, one side of which is equal to the whole line AB, the other to the part AF, and the Rectangle FD, one side of which is equal to the whole AB, the other to the other part FB, are together equal to the whole Square AD, of which they are the parts (b).

II. If the same line is cut anyhow at F, the Square AG from its part AF, and the Rectangle FE from the two parts FB and AF, or the equal FG, are likewise equal to the whole Rectangle EA from the whole line AB and its segment AF, since those two are all the parts of the Rectangle AE (c).

contains, besides the Squares of the two sides CB, BA, two rectangles which

which lies between the acute angle B and the Perpendicular AD (b).

Cor. Hence it becomes manifest that in Triangles, if the Squares of the sides are greater than the Square of the Base, the angle opposite it will be Acute; if they are less, Obtuse; if they are equal, Right.

The four Theorems just demonstrated are very well explained by numbers, which you have in Clavius and others. Of these, however, the last two, although very useful for practical Geometry, are nevertheless not necessary for the following Propositions, after which they can be gone over again, if they seem rather difficult to anyone. In the Demonstrations that follow, moreover, when the Book is not indicated, the one under discussion is understood.

On Curvilinear Figures.

A mong the figures that are contained by a curved line, the first place in

Geometry is held by the Circle, which alone is completed by one sure sweep of the Compass. Aristotle, in ch. 2 of the Mechanical Questions, considers three especially wonderful properties of it. The first is that the circle is made from a line that is moving and at rest: for while the whole line is carried round to make the circle, its end rests in the point of the center.

The second is that the single points of the line, although continuous, are moved with unequal velocity while the line is carried round: for the point that is farther removed from the center runs through a greater space.

The third is that the Periphery that surrounds the circle consists in a certain manner of contraries, and of extremes without a middle: namely of the concave and the convex; between which the Straight is a middle, just as the Equal is between the great and the small. For just as a line, in order to become small from great, must first become equal, so, in order to become convex from concave, it must first become straight. And this is the more wonderful in that these contraries are found in a line having no breadth, such as the Periphery of the Circle.

Of the Circle, then, Euclid treats in the third and fourth books of the Elements; and here we, having laid down the principles, shall deliver both the Problems that pertain to Circles and to Figures to be inscribed in the circle, and the more useful Theorems for investigating their properties.

Chapter

p. 22

CHAPTER I

Principles.

N o other Axioms and Postulates are employed in this Book than those which we

delivered in the first book. There remain only some Definitions to be explained, of which:

I. Circles are equal whose Diameters are equal.

II. A straight line is said to touch a circle which, when produced further, does not cut the circle.

III. The angle that is made by a tangent line and the circumference is called the Angle of contingence.

IV. In a Circle, lines are equally distant from the center when the Perpendiculars drawn from the center to them are equal.

V. Segments of a Circle are the parts of the Circle that are cut off by some straight line.

VI. An angle is said to be in the Segment of the circle by which the lines constituting the angle at the circumference are surrounded.

As in Figure I, Theorems, Pl. III: a Semicircle surrounds the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAG; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAE.

VII. An angle is said to stand upon the Segment that is opposite the angle and closes it.

As in the same Figure, a semicircle closes the Angle BAC; the greater part of the Circle the Angle BAE; the lesser part of the Circle the Angle BAG.

VIII. The angle of a Segment is that which is mixed of a straight line and a part of the Circumference within the circle. But if the straight line is a Diameter, it is called the angle of the semicircle.

As in the same Figure, the angle composed of the diameter CB and the circumference BA.

IX. A Sector of a Circle is the Portion of the Circle comprehended by two semidiameters.

X. A Figure is said to be inscribed in a circle when the vertices of all its Angles are in the circumference. As, in the same place, the Triangle BAC.

CHAPTER II

Problems.

Problem I. (Pl. III. Fig. 1.)

To find the Center of a given arc, and to complete the Circle.

L et ABC be the given portion of a circle, whose Center must be found and the

Circle completed. From two points taken at pleasure, A and B, with an equal radius, let two arcs be made outside and inside the circle, cutting each other at O and E. Likewise from the points B and C, taken at pleasure, let two arcs be made cutting each other at F and G. Then through the points of the sections let the lines OE and FG be drawn, which will bisect the arcs and will meet each other at H, where the Center of the circle to be completed is. Dem. from Theor. III, Cor. 1, with the lines AB, BC drawn.

In the same way a Circle is made that passes through three points A, B, C which are not placed in a straight line.

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

To draw a Tangent.

F irst, if a Tangent is to be drawn to a given Point in the Circumference, as A: let

the semidiameter AD be drawn, at whose extremity A let a perpendicular be raised in this way. With the interval of the Semidiameter AD let the circle be cut from A at B, and through B let the indefinite line DF be drawn, which from B, with the same interval of the semidiameter, is to be cut at F. When FA is joined, the perpendicular will be Tangent to the circle. From Theor. I & V.

Second, if from a Point F outside the circle a straight line Tangent to the circle is to be drawn: let the line FD be drawn to the center of the Circle, and let it be bisected, as at B; then from B, with the interval of the half, namely FB, let the Periphery be cut at A. (Having made, for the demonstration, the semicircle FAD.) The line FA will be Tangent to the circle. From the same.

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

To construct a Right-angled, Obtuse-angled, and Acute-angled Triangle in a Circle.

L et any Diameter AB whatever be drawn in the Circle: if upon the Diameter a

Triangle is made whose vertex C touches at any point

the

L et there be given any Triangle PHO, to which an Equiangular one is to be in‐

the Circumference, BCA will be Right-angled: if the vertex D falls outside the Circumference, BDA will be Acute-angled: if it falls inside the Circle, as at E, BEA will be an Obtuse-angled Triangle. From Theor. I of this book, & Cor. of Theor. IV, Bk. I.

To inscribe in a circle a Triangle Equiangular to another given one.

scribed in the circle DBE. Let any tangent AC be drawn: then let the Angle ABD be made equal to the angle O, and the angle CBE equal to the angle P: then let DE be drawn. The angle D will be equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, from Theor. VI of this book; and the Triangle BDE equiangular to the Triangle PHO.

But if a straight line DE is given, upon which a segment of a circle is to be described that contains the given angle H: let the angle D be made equal to the angle P, and the angle E equal to the angle O, and let DB, EB be produced until they intersect; then through the three points D, B, E let a Circle be drawn, according to Probl. I. The segment DBE will be the one that was sought, in which the angle B will be equal to the angle H, from Theor. III, bk. I.

Problem V. (Fig. 5.)

To inscribe a Square, a Hexagon, a Trigon in a Circle.

F irst. A Square is inscribed in a circle if two Diameters AB, CD are drawn at right

angles; for the lines drawn through their extreme points will constitute the Square ACBD, from Theor. I & IV, cor. 2.

An Octagon, moreover, is inscribed in a circle if each arc subtending a side of the Square is bisected: for the lines drawn through the eight points of the circumference will constitute a regular Octagon, that is, one all of whose sides and Angles are equal.

Second. A Hexagon is inscribed in a circle if the semidiameter is carried round six times in the circle; for the lines drawn through those points of the circumference will constitute the Hexagon AEMBNG, from Theor. III, cor. 2. A Dodecagon is inscribed in a circle if the arcs of the Hexagon, as AE, are bisected.

Third, if through three points of the Hexagon, omitting the intermediate one, lines are drawn, they will constitute an equilateral Trigon in the circle, as AMN, from Theor. V, cor. 2.

Half the side of the Trigon gives the side of the Heptagon in the same circle, not Geometrically and perfectly, but very nearly.

Problem

p. 25

Problem VI. (Fig. 6.)

To inscribe a Pentagon in a Circle.

A Pentagon is inscribed in a circle when two diameters AB, CD have been drawn

at right angles: then let the semidiameter EB be bisected at F: let the interval FC be transferred from F to G: and CG will be the side of the Pentagon, from Theor. XI, bk. III. The side of the Decagon, moreover, will be the line GE, from Theor. X, bk. III. But if the arcs of the Decagon are bisected, one will have the side of the Icosagon, or regular Figure of twenty sides.

If in a circle in which a Pentagon is inscribed a regular Trigon is also inscribed, in such a way that a vertex of the Trigon coincides with some vertex of the Pentagon, the least distance between an angle of the Pentagon and one of the Trigon will be the side of the Quindecagon.

All Figures, moreover, are circumscribed about Circles if the Figure sought is first inscribed in the Circle; and then through the vertices of the angles of that same Figure, inscribed in the Circle, Tangents are drawn, which will constitute a similar Figure about the circle.

These and all other Figures can also be inscribed in a Circle when a Quadrant of the Circle has been divided into 90 degrees. For let as many degrees be taken in the Quadrant as belong to the Figure sought; if the circle is divided according to them, there will be given the arcs which the sides of that Figure subtend and which its Angles at the Center comprehend.

But in order to know how many degrees belong to each Figure, let the 360 degrees of the circle be divided by the number of the sides of the Figure to be constructed; and the Quotient will give the degrees sought. E.g., 120 degrees of the circle belong to the Trigon, because 360 divided by 3 gives 120.

Similar Figures can also be constructed without a circle upon a given line, by finding the angle that two sides of the Figure to be constructed comprehend; which is usually called the Angle at the Circumference.

This, moreover, is found by subtracting the angle at the center from 180 degrees of the circle. E.g., if the angle of the Trigon at the circumference is sought: since its angle at the center has been found to be of 120 degrees, when these are subtracted from 180, there remain 60 degrees for the angle of the Trigon at the circumference, which, that is, the sides of that Figure comprehend: as may be seen in the adjoining Little Table.

Theorems.

H ere we shall consider first the lines and angles within the circle; then the lines

touching the circle; some having been put off to the third book, on Proportions, where they will be shown more clearly.

Theorem I. (Pl. III. Fig. I. Theor.)

The Angle in a Semicircle is Right. (a)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameter AD be drawn.

Dem. The angle CAD is equal to the angle ACD; and the angle ABD is equal to the angle DAB, since they are opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V of the first book. Therefore the whole angle BAC is equal to the two B and C together; therefore it is half of two right angles, or is Right, from Theor. III, bk. 1, & Axiom VI.

Cor. When the line AE is drawn, it is plain that the angle BAE, having for its base an arc greater than a semicircle, is Obtuse; and the angle GAB, standing upon an arc less than a semicircle, is Acute.

Theorem

Theorem II. (Fig. 2.) The Angle at the Center, as BDC, is Double the angle at the Circumference BAC, if they stand

upon the same arc. (a)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the Diameter AE be drawn.

Dem. The angles DAB and DBA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters, from Theor. V, bk. I; therefore the exterior angle BDE is double the angle DAB, from Theor. III, bk. I. Likewise the angles DAC and DCA are equal, as being opposite equal semidiameters too: therefore the exterior angle CDE is also double the angle CAD: therefore the whole angle BDC at the center is double the whole angle A at the circumference.

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference, as G, A, F, if they have for base the same portion of the circle, are equal to each other: for the angle BDC at the center, as exterior, is double each of them, from Theor. III, bk. I. (b)

II. The angle at the circumference has for its measure half the arc upon which it stands, since it is half the angle at the center, whose Measure is the whole arc upon which it stands. From the def. of angle, note 1, bk. 1.

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.) If a Diameter in a Circle bisects another straight line, it will be Perpendicular to it; and if it is

Perpendicular, it will bisect it. (c)

Prep. For the demonstration, let the semidiameters FB, FC be drawn.

Dem. The Triangle FBC is Isosceles: therefore if the line FA bisects the line BC, it is perpendicular to it: if it is perpendicular, it bisects it. From Theor. V, bk. 1, cor. 4.

Cor. I. If a perpendicular bisects some line in a circle, the center is in the middle of the perpendicular; for it is easily demonstrated that only from that point are all the lines to the circumference equal. (d)

II. If BC is the side of a Hexagon, it will be equal to the semidiameter; for since the arc BC in the Hexagon is the sixth part of the circle, the angle BFC will be of 60 degrees: and on account of the Isosceles Triangle, the two equal angles B and C will each also be of 60 degrees, half of the degrees

III. If the Chord BC is bisected by the diameter ED, the arc BC will also be bisected at D by the same diameter: for when the point C is laid upon B, the whole semicircle ECD will coincide with the semicircle EBD, and the arc CD with the arc BD; and so they will be equal.

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.)

In a Circle, equal lines are equally distant from the Center. (b)

Prep. From the center let the Perpendiculars AB and AC be drawn: then let AD, AE be joined.

Dem. Since the lines AD, AE are equal, their Squares will be equal. Again, the Square of the line DA, on account of the right angle at B, is equal to the two Squares together of the lines DB, BA, from Theor. IX, bk. I; and the Square of the line AE is equal to the squares of the lines EC, CA: but the lines DB and EC are equal, from the preceding; and so their squares are equal too; therefore, when the equals are taken away, the squares of the perpendicular lines AB, AC also remain equal; and so the perpendiculars themselves are equal: therefore DF and EG are equally distant from the center. From Def. IV of this book.

Cor. I. Lines that are equally distant from the center are equal to each other: which is plain from the same demonstration.

II. If chords, or lines DF, EG, subtending an arc, are equal, the arcs will also be equal; and conversely: because if they are laid upon each other, they coincide. (c)

III. Hence the greatest of the lines in a circle is the Diameter; and lines that recede farther from the Diameter are less, because they subtend a lesser arc. (d)

IV. Whatever has been demonstrated of the same Circle is true also of equal Circles, which, when laid upon each other, coincide entirely.

point. (e)

BOOK III

CHAPTER I

On Proportional Figures.

Principles.

U nder the Name of Principles we comprehend the Definitions which belong to

Euclid’s books 5 and 6; certain Axioms; and the Arguments about Proportions, which need explanation rather than demonstration.

§. I.

Definitions.

A I. part is a lesser magnitude that measures a greater.

Part is divided into Aliquot and Aliquant. An aliquot part is so called which, repeated a number of times, exactly equals its whole: as 4 is exactly contained in 8, 12, 16, etc. An aliquant part is so called which, repeated a number of times, does not exactly equal its whole, but either exceeds it or falls short of it: as 4 in 6, 7, 9, etc. Only the aliquot part, which measures and exactly equals the whole, is defined here; both because its chief use is in demonstrating proportions, and because an aliquant part is not properly called a part, but parts of the whole; for the number 4, e.g., is called two thirds of the number 6.

II. A multiple magnitude is one that a lesser measures.

That is, a magnitude is called multiple when compared with its aliquot part, which it contains exactly several times; as 6 contains 2.

III. Ratio, or (as others prefer) Proportion, is the Mode in which one quantity contains another of the same kind, or is contained by it.

Those things, moreover, are said to be of the same kind which, when multiplied, can exceed each other: hence between God and the Creature, the Finite and the Infinite, there is no proportion, because they cannot exceed each other: likewise between the angle of contingence and a rectilinear one; because the angle of contingence, however much increased, does not exceed a rectilinear angle.

Proportion

p. 31

Proportion is divided, 1, into rational and irrational. That is called rational which can be expressed by numbers: as double, triple proportion, etc. That is called irrational which cannot be expressed by numbers: such is the proportion of the diameter to the side of the square; for by no number can it be expressed by how many parts the Diameter exceeds the side of the square (whoever does not know this, says Plato, is to be counted not among men but among the brutes). And quantities that have a rational proportion to each other are called Commensurable; those that have an irrational one are called Incommensurable.

Proportion is divided, 2, into the Proportion of Equality, which obtains between equal things, and of inequality, which obtains between unequal things: of these, when the greater contains the lesser exactly, it is called multiple proportion, as in definition 2. When it contains the lesser and, besides, some aliquot part of it, it is called superparticular proportion, as 6 to 4. When it is greater by some aliquant part, it is called superpartient proportion: as 8 to 5. But if the lesser is referred to the greater, the particle sub is prefixed: as 2 to 4 is subduple proportion.

IV. Proportionality, which is also usually called Proportion and Analogy, is the Comparison and Similitude of Ratios, or Proportions.

It is divided first into Arithmetical and Geometrical. Arithmetical proportion is the Equality of the excesses among several quantities: as 1, 2, 3, 4, which numbers all exceed one another by unity; or 1, 3, 5, etc., which exceed one another equally by two.

Geometrical proportion is the similitude of the excesses among several terms that contain one another in the same way: as 1, 2, 4, 8, etc., which likewise exceed one another in double ratio; or 1, 3, 9, 27, etc., which are in triple ratio.

There is, besides, Harmonic Proportion, which does not pertain to the present matter.

Proportion, or proportionality, is divided secondly into discrete and continuous. It is discrete when there is some interruption between the terms: as if you say, 8 is to 4 as 6 to 3; there is an interruption in the middle terms, because 4 is not to 6 as 8 to 4.

Proportion is called continuous when there is no interruption: as if you say, 1 to 2, as 2 to 4, as 4 to 8, as 8 to 16, etc.; for in these terms the earlier are referred to the later in the same way, with no interruption made. This continuous proportion is also usually called a progression: and if it goes from the lesser to the greater, it is called an increasing progression; but if from the greater to the less, a decreasing progression.

V. Four terms are said to be in the same Proportion when the first contains the second, or is contained by the second, as many times as the third contains the fourth, or is contained by the fourth; and terms of this kind are called Proportionals.

Of these, moreover, the first, which is referred to another, is called the antecedent; the later, to which the first is referred, is called the consequent: and the two antecedents

and

p. 32

are called homologous to each other, just as the two consequents are to each other: e.g., if it is said, as 4 to 2, so 6 to 3: 4 and 6 are called antecedents and homologous to each other; 2 and 3 are also called consequents homologous to each other.

VI. Proportion, moreover, or Proportionality, consists in at least three terms;

Because proportionality is the comparison of two relations, each of which requires two terms. For if the Proportion is continuous, three terms suffice, because the second is repeated: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 4 to 2. But if the Proportion is discrete, four terms are required: e.g., as 8 is to 4, so 6 to 3.

VII. Compound Proportion is that which is produced by the multiplication of proportions.

As duodecuple Proportion is that which is produced from sextuple and duple proportion, because twice six make 12.

Hence the Proportion of the extremes is said to be compounded of the proportion of the Means: as if there are 20, 10, 2, the Proportion of 20 to 2 is decuple, compounded of the duple proportion of 20 to 10 and the quintuple of 10 to 2.

VIII. But when Magnitudes are continuously proportional, as 27, 9, 3, 1, the First is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second, and the triplicate to the fourth, and so on.

Double and duplicate ratio are very different; for Proportion is double or triple when one quantity contains another twice or three times. But Proportion is duplicate or triplicate when between several magnitudes there intervene two or three continued proportions. Thus, because between 27, 9, 3 there intervene two triple proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 3 the duplicate proportion of that which it has to 9. And because between 27, 9, 3, 1 there intervene three similar proportions, 27 is therefore said to have to 1 the triplicate proportion of that which it has to 9.

IX. Similar Figures are those that have their angles equal, each to each, and the sides about the equal angles proportional.

In these, moreover, the sides opposite equal angles are called homologous: [as in Figure 6, Theor., Pl. V] the side GE homologous to the side NL, and the side ED homologous to the side LH.

X. Reciprocal Figures are those that have their sides mutually antecedent and consequent.

That is, mutually double and half; triple and subtriple, etc., as in Figure 1, Theorems, Pl. V, are the Rectangles X and Y: for the Rectangle Y has the side GA double the side AD of the rectangle X, and reciprocally the other side AF half the side AB of the same rectangle X.

§. II.

p. 33

§. II.

Axioms.

I n place of Axioms I put most of the Propositions of Euclid’s bk. 5, of which

Geminus, the illustrious Mathematician, seems to have spoken in Proclus, bk. 3, ch. 1, where he says: Others have devised demonstrations even of indemonstrable things: they have tried to prove things that are known to all by less known Means.

I. If two quantities are equal to each other, they will have the same proportion to one third thing, or to equal things: as 8 and 8 contain 4 twice in the same way. (a)

II. If two things have the same proportion to the same third thing, or to equal things, they will be equal to each other. As, if the number 4 is contained twice by two numbers, these will be equal to each other, namely 8 and 8. (b)

III. Of unequal quantities, the one that is greater has a greater proportion to the lesser, or contains the lesser more times.

As the number 8 contains the number 4 more times than the number 6 does. And that which contains the same quantity more times is greater: and that which is contained more times is less. (c)

IV. Proportions that are equal, the same, similar to the same one (they signify the same thing by different names) are equal, the same, similar to each other. (d)

V. If single magnitudes have the same proportion to single magnitudes, all together will also have the same proportion to all together.

That is, twice the double will also be double to twice the half; three times the double to three times the half, etc.

Hence all the antecedents together are to all the consequents as the single antecedents to the single consequents: as, if 4 has to 2 the same proportion as 6 to 3, namely double: 4 and 6 together will also have a double proportion to 2 and 3 together. (e)

VI. Similar parts, that is, those that are contained equally, are to each other as the wholes containing them. That is, as 2 to 3, so twice 2 to twice 3; three times 2 to three times 3.

Hence if similar parts are added to or taken from similar wholes, what remains is similar. (f)

VII. If, as the whole to the whole, so the part taken away to the part taken away, the whole will also be to the whole as the remainder to the remainder. (g)

§. III

As, if from three times 4 and three times 2, in double proportion, you take away once 4 and 2, in double proportion, there remain twice 4 and twice 2, that is, 8 and 4, also in double proportion.

VIII. If equals are added to equal proportions, the wholes will be equal.

As, if to the two numbers 4 and 4, in double proportion to 2, there is added to each 6, which number is in triple proportion to the same 2, there will be 10 and 10 in equal, quintuple proportion to 2.

Hence, since multiplication is multiple addition, if equal proportions are multiplied by equals, the wholes will be equal: as, if two double proportions are each multiplied by a triple proportion, both will be sextuple.

Arguments about Proportions.

M athematicians, and also all Philosophers, use six modes of arguing for inferring

proportions, the truth of which is readily plain either of itself or from the Principles laid down.

I. Inverse, or converse, Ratio is the Change of the antecedent into the consequent, and of the consequent into the antecedent: e.g., as the antecedent 9 to the consequent 3, so the antecedent 6 to the consequent 2; therefore, by converting, as 3 to 9, so 2 to 6.

It is plain of itself: because if the antecedents contain the consequents equally, the consequents are also equally contained by the antecedents.

II. Alternate, or permuted, Ratio is the comparison of antecedent with antecedent and of consequent with consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by alternating, or by permuting, or conversely, as 9 to 6, so 3 to 2. (a)

It is plain from Axiom VI: because similar parts are to each other as the wholes, and the wholes as the similar parts.

In alternate proportion, however, the four terms must be of the same kind; for if the first two are of a different kind from the second two, the argument by alternation is not valid: because between things of a different kind there is no proportion. From definition III.

III. Compound, or conjoined, Ratio is the Comparison of the antecedent and the consequent, as of one thing, to the consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2: therefore, by composition, as 9 and 3 (that is, 12) to 3, so 6 and 2 (that is, 8) to 2. (b)

It is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are added, similar

(a) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 16.

(b) Eucl. bk. V, prop. 18.

p. 35

wholes also result. And proportional terms are those whose excesses are similar parts.

IV. Division of ratio is the comparison of the excess of the antecedent over the consequent to the consequent itself: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by division, as 6 (the number by which 9 exceeds 3) to 3, so 4 (the number by which 6 exceeds 2) to 2. (a)

This is plain from Axiom VI: because when similar parts are taken away, what remains is similar.

V. Ratio reversed, or conversion of ratio, is the comparison of the antecedent to the difference of the terms, as to a consequent: e.g., as 9 to 3, so 6 to 2; therefore, by conversion, as 9 to 6 (which is the difference between 9 and 3), so 6 to 4, which is the difference between 6 and 2. (b)

This is plain from the same Axiom.

VI. Equal ratio is the inference to equal proportions of the extremes from equal intermediate proportions: as if there are set down

On the one side 27, 9, 3;

On the other 18, 6, 2.

The argument runs thus: as 27 to 9 on the one side, so 18 to 6 on the other; and as 9 to 3 on the one side, so 6 to 2 on the other: therefore, from equality, as 27 to 3, so 18 to 2. (c)

And this indeed is called an ordered ratio, because the proportion of the first with the second, and of the second with the third, is compared in order on each side. But if this order is not kept, it is called a disturbed ratio: as if there are set down (d)

On the one side 12, 6, 2;

On the other 24, 8, 4.

The argument runs thus: as 12 to 6 on the one side, so 8 to 4 on the other; and as 6 to 2 on the one side, so 24 to 8 on the other: therefore, from equality in disturbed order, as 12 to 2, so 24 to 4. It is called a disturbed ratio because on the one side the proportion of the first with the second is compared, on the other that of the second with the third.

Each argument is plain from the definition itself and from Axiom 8, because in both cases the proportion of the extremes arises from equal intermediate proportions, whether these are taken in order or in disturbed order.

“Since, however, what has been said about proportions by the celebrated Author is apt to cause difficulty to young men, I have therefore thought it opportune to set these things forth and explain them again, perhaps more clearly.

If one quantity is referred to another, e.g., a number to a number, and attention is paid to the manner in which the former contains the other, or is contained in the other, that relation of the one to the other is called a Geometric Ratio; the number which is referred is called the antecedent, and the number to which it is referred is called the consequent of the ratio. But if the antecedent is divided

by the consequent, the quotient is called the exponent of the ratio. Now the Quotient, or Quotient number, is that which denotes how many times some number is contained in another. Thus in the ratio 8 to 2 the number 8 is the antecedent, 2 the consequent, and the quotient 4 is the exponent of the ratio; and 4 is the quotient because 2 is contained four times in 8.

If the antecedent equals the consequent, the ratio is one of equality, as 4 to 4.

If the first quantity contains the second twice, the first is said to be to the second in double ratio; if three times, in triple ratio, etc.; and the one that is contained is said to be in subdouble, subtriple ratio, etc. Thus, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to another of 4 feet in double ratio, and the line of 4 feet to the line of 8 feet in subdouble ratio.

The equality or likeness of ratios is called Proportion, and it is expressed in this way: 8 : 4 :: 6 : 3, or 8 : 4 = 6 : 3; that is, 8 is to 4 as 6 is to 3, or, e.g., a line of 8 feet is to a line of 4 feet as a line of 6 feet is to a line of 3 feet. These four terms, or numbers, are proportional, and this proportion is called Geometric because it is an equality of ratios. The following, however, is Arithmetic: 4 is to 3 as 2 to 1, because the excess of the first antecedent with respect to the first consequent is the same as that of the second antecedent with respect to the second consequent.

Two ratios, then, are equal to each other when the antecedent of the first contains its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second contains its own, or when the antecedent of the first is contained in its consequent as many times as the antecedent of the second is contained in its own. Thus the ratio 12 to 6 is equal to the ratio 48 to 24, and the ratio 3 to 6 is equal to the ratio 50 to 100. Two equal ratios, then, make up a Geometric proportion.

Two quantities are said to be in direct ratio when the first and third terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, and the second and fourth terms of the same proportion relate to another. Let us suppose, e.g., that Peter has 100 of wisdom and 100 of study, but that Paul has only 50 of Wisdom and 50 of study. Peter and Paul will have Wisdom in the direct ratio of their study: I shall say, therefore, that the Wisdom of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the study of Peter is to the study of Paul. In this proportion the first and third terms belong to Peter, while the second and fourth relate to Paul, as is evident. This ratio is therefore called direct.

Two quantities are in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio when the first and fourth terms of a Geometric proportion belong to one quantity, while the second and third relate to another. If Peter, e.g., has 100 of knowledge and 50 of study, and Paul has 50 of knowledge and 100 of labor, the knowledge of Peter and the knowledge of Paul will be in inverse, or reciprocal, ratio. I shall say, therefore, that the knowledge of Peter is to the knowledge of Paul as the labor of Paul is to the labor of Peter. The first and fourth

terms

p. 37

CHAPTER II

terms of this proportion belong to Peter, the second and third relate to Paul, as is self-evident.

The ratio which arises from the multiplication of several ratios with one another is called a compound Ratio. Thus, if there are the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5, and you multiply the antec. 8 by the antec. 3, and the conseq. 4 by the conseq. 5, the ratio of the product 24 from the antecedents to the product 20 from the consequents is said to be compounded of the ratios 8 to 4 and 3 to 5.

If there are several quantities, of which the first has the same ratio to the second as the second to the third, and the third to the fourth, then the first is said to have to the third the duplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Likewise it is said to have to the fourth the triplicate ratio of that which it has to the second. Thus if, e.g., there are four lines, of which the first is of 16 feet, the second of 8 feet, the third of 4 ft. and the fourth of 2 ft., and you ask the ratio of the first to the second, I shall say that it is double, or as 2 to 1. But if you ask the ratio of the first, of 16 ft., to the third, of 4 ft., I shall say that it is twice double, because it is compounded of the ratio of the first line, of 16 ft., to the second, 8, which is double, and of the ratio of the second, namely 8, to the third, 4, which again is double; whence the ratio of the first to the third is the duplicate of the ratio of the first to the second, or is twice double, or in a word quadruple. And the ratio of the first to the fourth, or 16 to 2, is the triplicate of the ratio of the first to the second. And so it must be compounded of the double ratio, which is that of the first to the second, and of the quadruple ratio, which is that of the same first to the third; and thus it is twice quadruple, or, in a word, octuple.”

Problems. H ere, besides the Problems selected from Book VI of Euclid, we add those

which teach a very useful way of enlarging or diminishing Figures in any Proportion whatever.

Problem I. (Plate IV. Fig. 1.)

To divide a line in a given Proportion.

L et the line AB be divided into five parts, just as the line AC is divided. Let them

be joined so as to make any angle whatever at A, and let CB be drawn. Then through the points at which the line AC has been cut let DE, FG, etc. be made parallel to CB, cutting the line AB. These divisions

will

p. 38

will divide the line AB in the same proportion as the line AC is divided. From Theor. II of this book.

Any line, however, such as AB, is divided more easily if it is to be divided into equal parts. For let an indefinite line AC be joined to it at any angle whatever, and at the other end, at an equal angle, the line BI (which by Theor. II, bk. I will be parallel to the line AC, because of the equal alternate angles); then from A toward C, and from B toward I, with any opening of the compass, let as many equal parts be cut off as you wish. The lines DL, FM, and the others drawn through the opposite points of section, will also divide the line AB into the equal parts sought. From the same.

Problem II. (Fig. 2.)

To find a mean proportional.

L et there be two lines AB, BC, between which a mean proportional is to be found.

Let them be joined into one line ABC; then, with the interval of half of AC, as from the point E, let a semicircle be made; then at the point B, which joins the two lines, let a perpendicular BD be erected, produced as far as the circumference; this will be the mean proportional sought. And the square on the line BD will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AB and BC. From Theor. IV and I of this book, cor. II.

Problem III. (Fig. 3.)

Given two straight lines, to find a third continued proportional.

L et there be two lines BD and DA, for which a third continued proportional is to

be found. Let them be placed at the right angle D, and joined by the straight line BA; then let AC be drawn perpendicular to the line BA, and let BD be produced until it meets the line AC at C. The line DC will be the third proportional sought; and the rectangle made of the lines BD, DC will be equal to the square on the line DA: from Theor. I, cor. 2.

Similarly, by placing the second and third at a right angle, a fourth continued proportional is found, etc.

Problem IV. (Fig. 4.)

To find a fourth proportional, even one not continued.

L et there be three lines AB, BC, AD, for which a fourth proportional, even one

not continued, is to be found. Let the first two, AB,

BC, be set out in one straight line, and let the third, AD, make any angle whatever with the first, AB; then let DB be drawn, and through C let CE be placed parallel to it, meeting the straight line AD, produced, at E. DE will be the fourth proportional. From Theor. II of this book.

To divide a line in extreme and mean ratio.

L et the line AB be cut in extreme and mean ratio, that is, by finding in the same

line the mean and the extreme proportionals. At A let a perpendicular AC be placed, equal to half of the whole AB; then let CB be drawn, and from it let CD be cut off, equal to the line CA; and let the remainder DB be transferred from A to E; and the line AB will be cut proportionally at E, so that the greater part AE is a mean proportional between the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Moreover, the square on the line AE will be equal to the rectangle of the whole AB and its smaller part EB. Because of its outstanding uses this was called by the ancients the Divine proportion. From Theor. VIII of this book, cor. I.

To make a Rectilinear figure similar and proportional to another.

L et the Rectilinear figure ABCD be divided into Triangles by drawing a line to the

opposite angles A, B; then let a Triangle EGF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ACB, according to Probl. XI, bk. I; and similarly let a Triangle EHF be made having angles equal to the Triangle ADB. And the whole Rectilinear figure EGFH will be similar and proportional to the Rectilinear figure ACBD. From def. IX and Theor. III.

Problem VII. (Fig. 7.)

To add, or to multiply, similar figures.

L et there be given three figures, circular or rectilinear, whose diameters or homol‐

ogous sides are AB, BC, DE. Let AB, BC be set at a right angle and produced indefinitely, and let AC be drawn; then let AC be transferred to BF, and DE to BG. The line FG will be the diameter, or homologous side, of a figure similar and equal to the three together upon the lines AB, BC, DE. If the lines AB, BC are taken as equal, the figure upon AC will be double the similar figure upon AB or BC; and when AC is transferred to BF, the figure upon FC (which is here understood to be drawn) will be triple; and when FC is transferred to BH, the figure upon HC (were it drawn) will similarly be quadruple the figure upon AB; and so on to infinity. From Theor. VI, cor. 3.

Problem

p. 40

Problem VIII. (Fig. 8.)

To subtract a similar figure from another, or to diminish it, or to enlarge it in any proportion

whatever.

L et there be two similar figures, rectilinear or circular, whose diameters or homol‐

ogous sides are AB, CB. Upon the greater line BC let a semicircle be made, within which let another line be fitted equal to the line AB; then let the straight line AC be drawn, which will be the side of the figure sought: the figure by which the similar figure upon BC exceeds the figure described upon AB. From the same Theor.

Hence it is plain how any figure whatever is to be diminished to a given proportion: e.g., let a third part be taken away from the figure described upon BC. Having made the semicircle, let BC be divided into three parts, and then at the intersection of one third, DC, let a perpendicular DA be erected; finally let AC be drawn. The figure upon AC will be the third part of the similar figure upon BC, and the figure upon BA two thirds of the same. From the same.

It is plain also how figures are enlarged in any proportion whatever. For let a figure be constructed one and a half times a similar figure described upon BD. Let half of the line, DC, be added to it; and when a semicircle has been described upon the whole BC, and the perpendicular AD erected, let AB be drawn in the semicircle; the figure described upon it will be one and a half times the similar figure described upon the line BD. From the same.

Problem IX. (Fig. 9.)

To make equal parallelograms upon a given line.

L et there be a parallelogram AC, to which an equal one is to be constructed upon

the given line CH. Let CH be placed in a straight line with the line DC, and let the parallelogram CI be completed. Then let the diameter ICE be drawn indefinitely. Let AD be produced until it meets the diameter; through the point of meeting E let EG be made parallel and equal to the line DH. And the parallelogram CG, constructed upon the given line CH, will be equal to the given parallelogram AC. From Theor. VI, bk. I, cor. 3.

Theorems.

welve Theorems are comprised in this chapter, selected chiefly from the

T sixth book of Euclid, in which are demonstrated first the Proportions of

Rectilinear Figures, then of Lines and of Figures in the circle, and also of the circles themselves,

Theorem I. (Plate V. Fig. 1.) Parallelograms and Triangles that have the same Height, or that are between the same Parallels,

are to each other as their Bases. (a)

Dem. If the base BA of the Parallelogram X is twice or three times equal to the base AF of the Parallelogram Z, the Parallelogram X will be twice or three times equal, that is, double or triple, of the Parallelogram Z, and so on to infinity, since Parallelograms of equal bases between the same Parallels are equal, from bk. I, Theor. VII: therefore Parallelograms of the same height are to each other as their bases.

Similarly the triangle X, half of the parallelogram X, will be double or triple the triangle Z, according to their bases.

Cor. I. If the base BA is double or triple the base AF, and the base GA is likewise double or triple the base AD, the whole rectangles X and Y, or their halves, the triangles, will be reciprocal and equal, because they are likewise double or triple the same rectangle, or of the half, the triangle Z, from what has just been demonstrated. And this is likewise plain of other Parallelograms. (b)

II. Hence it is plain that if four lines are proportional, as GA, AD, AB, AF, the Rectangle Y, which is made of the extremes GA, AF, will be equal to the Rectangle X, which is made of the means AD, AB. (c)

III. And if three lines are continued proportionals, that is, if the two means are equal to each other, as AD, AB, the Square X of the mean will be equal to the rectangle Y, which is made of the extreme lines AC, AF. (d)

IV. Rectangles of proportional bases and heights, as O and Z, are in the duplicate ratio of their sides: for if the base GA is double the base AD, and similarly the base BA is double the base AF, the rectangle O will be double the rectangle X or Y; but the rectangle X or Y is double the rectangle Z; therefore the rectangle O will be quadruple the rectangle Z.

Similarly, if the same bases are triple, the rectangle X or Y will be triple the rectangle Z, and the rectangle O will be ninefold of the same; and so on successively, always in duplicate ratio.

V. Hence the triangles O and Z, halves of rectangles, which have proportional bases and heights, also have the duplicate ratio of the bases and heights.

VI.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 1.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, Prop. 14, 15.

(c) Prop. 16.

(d) Prop. 17.

VI. And if the base BA is double the base AF, and the base GA triple the base AD, the rectangle O will have to the rectangle Z the ratio produced, or compounded, of the triple and the double of the same sides: that is, the rectangle O will be sextuple the rectangle Z, because it is triple the rectangle X or Y, which is double the rectangle Z. These things are demonstrated in like manner of all similar Parallelograms. (a)

If a Parallel is placed to a side of any Triangle, it will cut the two remaining sides proportionally.

(b)

Prep. For the demonstration, let ED, BC be drawn.

Dem. The Triangles EDB and BCE are equal, since they are on the same base BE and between the same Parallel DC; therefore, by Axiom II of this book, they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE. But the Triangles ABE, BDE have the same vertex E, and therefore the same height. Similarly the Triangles AEB and CEB have the same vertex B: therefore the base BD has the same proportion to the base BA as the base CE to the base EA. From the preceding.

Cor. I. Therefore, by alternation, as BD to CE, so BA to EA.

II. Therefore, by composition, as DA to AB, so CA to EA.

III. And if the line BE cuts the sides of the Triangle proportionally, it will be Parallel to the remaining side: for similarly the two Triangles EDB and EBC will be equal to each other, since they have the same proportion to the Triangle ABE as their bases, from the preceding Theor.; therefore, since they have the same base BE, they will be between the same Parallels BE, DC, from Theor. VI, bk. I, last cor.

Theorem III. (Fig. 3.)

Equiangular Triangles have their sides about the equal angles Proportional. (c)

Prep. Let the line GH be drawn, so that the side DG is equal to the side AB, and the side DH is equal to the side AC.

Dem. If the angle A of the Triangle ABC is placed upon the angle D, the base BC will fall upon GH (for the angles and sides are supposed equal); but the angles B and C are supposed equal to the angles E and F: therefore, by Theor. II, bk. I, in the cor., the line BC, or GH, will be Parallel to the base EF: therefore, by the preceding Theor., as the side DE to the side AB, so the side DF to the side AC.

But if the angle B is placed upon the angle E, the base AC will also become parallel to the line DF: therefore, as DE to EF, so AB to BC. The same will be shown if the angle C is placed upon the angle F.

Cor. I. A Parallel drawn to one side of a triangle, as GH to EF, cuts off a smaller triangle wholly proportional to the larger.

II. If the angles A and D are equal, and the sides about those angles proportional, the two triangles ABC and DEF will be wholly equiangular; for GH will be parallel to the side EF, by cor. 3 of the preceding Theor., and the triangle DGH will be as the triangle ABC. (a)

Theorem IV. (Fig. 4.) In a Right-angled Triangle the Perpendicular drawn from the right angle to the base divides the

whole Triangle into two triangles similar to the whole and to each other. (b)

Dem. I. The whole triangle ABC and its part, the Triangle ADC, have two right angles, CAB and CDA, by supposition, and therefore equal; but the angle C is common to both; therefore the remaining angle CAD is equal to the angle B, by Theor. III, bk. I; therefore, by the preceding Theor., these two equiangular triangles have the sides about the equal angles proportional.

Cor. I. Therefore the line AC is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its segment DC. For as in the whole triangle is CB to CA, so in the triangle ADC is the same CA to CD.

Dem. II. The whole triangle BAC and its other part ABD have right angles BAC and BDA, by supposition; but the angle B is common to both; therefore the remaining angle BAD is equal to the angle C: and so they are wholly similar.

Cor. II. Therefore AB is a mean proportional between the whole base BC and its other segment BD. For as in the whole triangle is BC to BA, so in the triangle BDA is the same BA to BD.

Dem. III. The two triangles ABD and ACD both have right angles at D; but the angle BAD is equal to the angle C, and the angle CAD equal to the angle B, from what has just been demonstrated; therefore these two triangles are wholly similar.

Cor.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 8.

Any similar Triangles whatever have the duplicate proportion of their homologous sides. (a)

Prep. From the equal angles let Perpendiculars AG, DH be drawn to the bases.

Dem. Since the angle B is equal to the angle E, by supposition, and the angles at G and H are right, by construction, the triangle ABG will be equiangular and proportional to the Triangle DEH, by Theor. III; therefore the right-angled triangle ABG will be to the right-angled triangle DEH in the duplicate ratio of the sides. By Theor. I, cor. 5.

The same is demonstrated, similarly, of the triangles ACG and DFH: therefore the whole triangle ABC is to the similar triangle DEF in the duplicate ratio of the sides.

Similar Polygons are divided into as many similar and proportional Triangles. (b)

Prep. Let lines be drawn from angles to angles, dividing the Polygons A and B into Triangles.

Dem. The angle E is equal to the angle L, and the sides about them are proportional, by the definition of a similar figure: therefore the Triangle GED is similar and proportional to the Triangle NLH. By Theor. III, cor. 2. By the same reasoning the Triangle GFC is equiangular and proportional to the triangle NMI: therefore, since from the whole angles G, D, C, which by supposition are equal to the angles N, H, I, equal angles have been taken away on either side, the triangles A and B that remain are also equiangular and proportional.

Cor. I. The whole Polygon A has to the Polygon B the duplicate ratio of the sides, since it is composed of as many proportional triangles, which have the duplicate proportion of the sides. From the preceding Theor.

II. Therefore all similar Polygons are to each other as the Squares and the other

proportional

III. Therefore, just as in a right-angled triangle the square of the base is equal to the two squares of the sides containing the right angle, so any similar figures whatever described upon the base of a right-angled triangle will be equal to the two figures together similarly described upon the sides containing the right angle, since they are likewise in the duplicate ratio of the sides. IV. If there are three continued proportional lines, as DC, HI, OP, then as the first is to the third, so is the rectilinear figure A, described upon the first, to the similar rectilinear figure B, described upon the second: namely, in the same duplicate proportion.

Theorem VII. (Fig. 7.)

If two lines cut each other in a circle, the Rectangle of the parts of the one is equal to the

Rectangle of the parts of the other. (b)

Prep. For the demonstration, let BC, ED be drawn.

Dem. The Triangles EAD and BAC are equiangular: for the vertical angles at A are equal in both. The angles C and D are equal, since they stand on the same arc EB, by Theor. II, bk. 2; and the remaining angle is equal to the remaining angle: therefore, by Theor. III, they have the sides about the equal angles proportional: namely, AD is to AE as AC to AB: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 2, the rectangle of the extremes AD, AB is equal to the rectangle of the means AE, AC.

Theorem VIII. (Fig. 8.) If, of two straight lines drawn from the same point C, one cuts the circle and the other touches it,

the Square of the tangent CB will be equal to the Rectangle of the whole secant CA and of its

part outside the circle, CD. (c)

Prep. From the center let a Perpendicular EB be drawn, and let AB, DB be joined.

Dem. The Triangles ACB and DCB are equiangular; for they have the angle C in common, and the angle CBD equal to the angle A in the alternate segment of the circle, by Theor. VI, bk. 2: therefore, as AC to CB in the whole triangle, so is the same CB to CD in the smaller triangle

CBD:

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 31.

(b) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 35.

(c) Eucl. bk. III, prop. 36.
