CBD: therefore, by Theor. I, cor. 3, the square of the mean CB is equal to the rectangle of the first and the last, CA and CD.

Cor. I. If the diameter of the circle is equal to the tangent BC, AC will be cut at D in extreme and mean ratio; for the square of the line AD, which is equal to the line BC by supposition, will be equal to the rectangle of the lines AC and DC, from what has just been demonstrated. (a)

II. And if from the line BC, equal to the diameter of the circle, CF is cut off equal to the line CD, the line CB will also be divided in extreme and mean ratio at F, according to Probl. V. For from what has been demonstrated, as the whole AC to the whole CB, so the part AD to the part CF, equal to the line CD: therefore, by Axiom VII, so also will the remainder DC (or its equal CF) be to the remainder FB.

Theorem IX. (Fig. 9.) The Square of the side of the Trigon inscribed in a circle is triple the Square of the semidiameter,

or of the side of the Hexagon. (b)

Dem. The Square of the Diameter is quadruple the square of the semidiameter, or of the side of the hexagon, since squares are in the duplicate ratio of their sides. It is also equal to the squares of the sides AM, MB, because the angle M in the semicircle is right: therefore, when the one square of the side MB is taken away, there remains the square AM, triple.

Cor. Since, moreover, the square ACBD inscribed in the circle is double the square of the semidiameter, because of the right angle at the center E, the square of the side of the trigon will be to the square inscribed in the same circle as 3 to 2, or sesquialteral.

Theorem X. (Fig. 10.) If the side of the Decagon, AB, and of the Hexagon, AE, or of the semidiameter, of the same circle, are put together into one line, EB, the whole line BE will be cut at A in extreme and mean

ratio. (c)

Theorem XI. (Fig. 11.) The Square of the side of the Pentagon, AC, is equal to the two Squares together of the side AB

of the Decagon and of the side FC of the Hexagon. (a)

Prep. Let the arc AC of the Pentagon, of 72 degrees, be bisected at B; whence the arcs AB, BC of the Decagon will each be of 36 degrees. Then let a perpendicular FD be drawn which bisects the line and the arc AB at D; whence the arcs AD, BD will each be of 18 degrees, and the whole arc CD of 54 degrees.

Dem. Since the whole angle F of the Pentagon is of 72 degrees, and the equal angles FCA, FAC are each of half of 108 degrees, the remainder to two right angles, they will each be of 54 degrees, as is also the angle EFC, whose arc DC is of 54 degrees: therefore, since the two Triangles AFC and EFC have the angles EFC and CAF equal, and also the angle C in common, they will be equiangular and proportional: therefore, as in the larger triangle is CA to CF, so in the smaller, CEF, is the same CF to CE; therefore the Rectangle made of the extremes CA, CE is equal to the Square made of the mean CF, the semidiameter, or side of the Hexagon. By Theor. I, cor. 3.

Again, since DF is perpendicular to AB, which it bisects, the sides AE, EB will be equal, by Theor. IV, bk. 1, and the angle ABE equal to the angle EAB, to which the angle BCA is also equal, because of the isosceles triangle ABC: therefore the two triangles ABC and AEB are also equiangular and proportional: therefore, as the whole AC to AB, so the same AB to AE: therefore the rectangle made of the extremes AC, AE is equal to the square of the side AB of the Decagon.

But

But the two rectangles made of the whole AC and of each of its parts are equal to the square of the whole AC: by Theor. X, bk. I, cor. 1; therefore the square of the side AC of the Pentagon is equal to the squares of the sides AF of the Hexagon and AB of the Decagon.

Cor. From which it follows that, if the side of the Hexagon, or semidiameter, and the side of the Decagon are placed at a right angle, the line subtending the right angle will be the side of the Pentagon to be inscribed in the same circle.

Theorem XII. (Fig. 12.)

Angles and sectors in the same or in equal circles are to one another as the arcs on which they

stand. (a)

Dem. If the arc CG is equal to the arc GD, the angle CBG will be equal to the angle GBD: from the definition of an angle, bk. 1; therefore the whole sector CBG, superposed, will coincide with the sector GBD, and will be equal to it. Likewise, if the arc CG is double the arc CP, the angle and the sector CBG will be double the sector CBP, and CBM triple the same, and CBD quadruple: therefore angles and sectors always have the same ratio as the arcs of the same or of equal circles.

Cor. I. Angles at the circumference in the same or in equal circles also have the same ratio as the arcs on which they stand, because they are halves of the angles at the center. From Theor. II, bk. II, and Axiom V of this book.

II. Circumferences, Chords and Arcs are to one another as the radii. For let the arcs CD, FE be similar, e.g. a sixth part of a circle: since the angle B is common, and the sides CB, DB are equal, as are also FB, EB, the triangles FBE, CBD will be similar: by Theor. III, cor. 2; therefore the chord CD will be to the chord FE as the radius CB to the radius FB; and, dividing the arcs equally at G and H, CG will be to FH as CB to FB; and, continuing the bisection, CP will be to FR as CB to FB: but to equal arcs correspond equal chords, by Theor. IV, bk. 2; therefore the arcs also have the same ratio as the radii; and all of them together, that is, the circumferences, are to one another as the radii.

III. Similar figures inscribed in a circle have to one another the duplicate ratio of the radii. For let FE, CD be homologous sides in similar figures inscribed in a circle: these have the duplicate ratio of the sides FE to CD; therefore, since FE is to CD as the radius FB to the radius BC, by the preceding Cor., the single Triangles, and the whole figures inscribed in the circle, will have the duplicate ratio of the radii FB, CB. (b)

Ee IV.

(a) Eucl. bk. VI, prop. 33.

(b) Eucl. bk. XII, prop. 1.

p. 50

E X P L A NAT I O N O F T H E A L G E B R A I C

IV. Circles also have the duplicate proportion of the radii; for the Triangles BCD and CFE have the duplicate proportion of the radii CB and FB, by the preceding Cor. Let the arcs be bisected at G and H. The similar Triangles inscribed, CBG and FBH, will also have the duplicate [proportion] of the radii. Likewise, the bisection being made again at P and R, M and N, all the similar triangles inscribed in the circle will have the duplicate proportion of the radii: by the preceding Cor. But the circles are equal to the whole sum of the triangles that can be inscribed in them (for if any space were left over in the circle, another triangle could be inscribed by bisecting the arc; and so the sum of all the triangles would not be understood to have been inscribed, contrary to the hypothesis); therefore circles are to one another in the duplicate ratio of their radii. Hence whatever was said in the Corollaries of Theor. VI on similar rectilinear figures must also be applied to circles. (a)

Moreover, just as Surfaces, which consist of a twofold dimension, namely breadth and length, have, if they are similar, the duplicate proportion of the Diameters, or of the homologous sides, so similar bodies, such as two whole spheres, have the triplicate proportion of the same, since they are made of a threefold dimension, namely breadth, length and depth. For example, if the Diameter of the earth is quadruple the Diameter of the Moon, the surface of the Earth will be four times quadruple, that is, sixteen times the surface of the Moon; and the whole terraqueous body will be four times sixteen, that is, sixty-four times, greater than the body of the Moon. Likewise, since the diameter of Venus appears as the tenth part of the diameter of the Sun, its apparent circle will be the hundredth part of the whole circle of the Sun; and so, when Venus comes between us and the Sun, it will appear like a spot on the Sun. And whoever knows these things has the most open access to all the natural disciplines.

P A R T I V.

§. I.

On Physics and its scope.

e begin the treatment of that discipline whose task is to in1

W quire into nature and its order and laws, and likewise its forces

and natural effects, and to investigate the origin and causes of

each single thing; which is therefore called Physics, and may be

defined: The faculty which is concerned with natural body, insofar as it is natural. It is

also called the Science of nature, namely the knowledge of those things which

make up the sensible machine of the world. For the physicist, says the illustri‐

ous Gassendi (a), is wholly occupied in exploring both that complex of all things

itself and each thing in particular, by inquiring, so far as is permitted, whether

it exists, and of what principles it consists, whether, and by what causes it has

been produced, and for

A2 what

(a) In the Proem to the Physics.

p. 2

what end it was made, whether, and with what forces and properties it is endowed, and other things of this kind; and once these have been seen through, then both the thing and the nature of things are deemed to be thoroughly known.

2 We said in the definition that Physics is concerned with natural body insofar as it is natural, namely insofar as it is the subject of sensible affections and capable of all those changes which we observe taking place in the world; and by this natural body is distinguished from the mathematical, and Physics itself from Geometry, which is likewise concerned with body.

3 The objects of Physics are Body, Space and Motion; what is understood by these I shall indicate in a few words. Whatever thing we can behold with the eyes, or grasp and feel with the hand, and which resists pressure, we call Body. The extension of the universe, in which bodies are placed and move freely, we call Space. The transfer of a body from one part of space into another we call Motion.

4 All the positions, motions, changes and actions of bodies which are observed by the senses, whether by one or by several, are called Phenomena. It is agreed that all bodies are moved according to certain laws or rules. A law of nature, moreover, is that norm according to which God willed certain motions to be performed always, that is, on all occasions; hence, e.g., every plant produces its own seed, from which a like plant, not a different one, is born again; hence every animal begets from itself one like itself. A heavy body freely left to itself falls downward of its own accord. By means of these laws we understand what happens naturally and what miraculously. For those phenomena are natural which are observed constantly in the same manner when bodies are placed on similar occasions; but there are miracles when phenomena occur contrary to those laws.

5 But if something happens according to the laws of nature, yet beyond what is usual, or contrary to what is owed to such a nature, it is called nonnatural: as a fever, which so agitates the beating both of the heart and of the arteries that they are said to be in a nonnatural state. What surpasses the forces and laws of nature is called supernatural. Thus if the Sun, e.g., while it is at noon, were rolled back toward the east, this is supernatural, because it cannot be brought about by any forces of nature, as is evident. There are, however, certain things which, even though they are above nature, can nevertheless be judged only by a man cultivated in good Philosophy and well practiced, whether they are natural or beyond nature. Hence we must judge cautiously of unusual things, lest we take for miracles things which are not such. This warning is most useful, so that we may meet the foolish multitude of the unlearned, and indeed also of those who, though learned in other matters, yet, because they are without good Philosophy, are prone to give credence to any chattering little woman who tells of some miracle.

§. II.

p. 3

§. II.

The usefulness of Physics. 6

T he dignity, certainly, and the excellence of Physics can be understood amply

enough even from this alone, that the study of this discipline extends as far as

nature itself. And indeed, who will deny that it is by far the worthiest thing now to

contemplate the vastness of the heavens and the mass of the bodies running their

courses in them by a fixed law, now to penetrate into the hidden recesses of the

earth, to search out the origin of metals and stones and the almost infinite variety of

plants and animals, and finally to consider the majesty of God shining forth in this

universe of things? Hence Seneca (b) valued this contemplation so highly that he did

not hesitate to say: unless I were admitted to these things (the more secret things of na‐

ture), it would not have been worth while to be born.

7 Then delight and the sweetest pleasure spring from this study of nature. For

whom would a science not delight in which there is never lacking the occasion both

of discovering and of contemplating new and wonderful effects, as so many shining

testimonies of the supreme Maker of things? Who could behold the most diverse

kinds of innumerable animals, terrestrial, aquatic, flying, insects, the wondrous vari‐

ety of the other things, their beauty and their fitness for definite uses, without a no‐

ble pleasure of mind? What of the fact that those very things which commonly fill

the unskilled with dread afford the physicist a most delightful spectacle? Thus, while

the rude multitude is shaken by an empty fear of eclipses, the Philosophers

This sun, and the stars, and the seasons that pass at fixed

Moments, there are some who, touched by no dread,

Can behold. (c)

8 Nay, they rejoice that so pleasant a scene is opened to them, and an occasion af‐

forded of weighing the nature of the heavenly bodies. The physicist beholds with a

tranquil mind the faces of Comets, which to others are horrifying. By the knowledge of

the nature of all things (says Tully (d)) we are relieved of superstition, freed from the fear of

death, and not disturbed by ignorance of things, from which very ignorance horrible terrors often

arise.

9 To these are added very many benefits, which spread from Physics through the

remaining disciplines and every use of life. For what benefits flow from Physics into

the most salutary art of healing? What great accessions has nautical science received

from the use of the magnetic needle, from the observed motions of the stars, from

the invention of the mariner’s compass card? I pass over

the

§. III

the advantages which clocks of various kinds, telescopes, microscopes, spectacles

and innumerable other things, which must be credited to Physics, afford to human

life.

On the Physics of the Peripatetics. 10

S uch advantages, however, and innumerable others which I silently pass over, you

will seek in vain in the School of the Peripatetics, if we may call Physics that dis‐

cipline in which most things have customarily been taught everywhere against the

observation of nature and against plain experiments. But it is a pleasure to hear the

excellent mathematician and physicist Tomás Vicente Tosca, the glory of our Spain and

a most distinguished ornament of the Congregation of the Oratory of Valencia. Let

them hear a Spaniard, those who, steeped in contemptible prejudices, falsely sup‐

pose that the Physics of the Moderns is cultivated only by heretics, and judge it impi‐

ous that it should be set before studious youth and commended to them: a race of

men born for the ruin and destruction of the good arts.

11 “I know not, certainly (so speaks the most illustrious Tosca (e)), I know not,

certainly, by what fate, and that an unhappy enough one, the School of the

Peripatetics has now for some centuries back been so given over to metaphysical

speculations that it seems to neglect physical things altogether: books come out dai‐

ly, to the point of nausea, which pursue the last fine points of the being of reason,

but pass over altogether the nature and causes of the wonderful effects of nature

that meet our eyes every day. Nothing was once held more pleasant (says Luis Vives

(f)) than the contemplation of this garden of nature: but now the inquiry into natur‐

al things is so entangled in metaphysical abstractions that upon them, as upon a

weak foundation, there rises nothing but a vast edifice of assertions and of dissent‐

ing opinions, or rather a cross is set up, on which minds are tortured rather than de‐

lighted by so great a pleasantness of natural things.

12 “It is surely most to be lamented by what windings those have made a

labyrinth of the whole of philosophy who treat physical things not physically, as is

fitting, but with metaphysical precisions remote from all sense and experiment; it is

to be lamented again that minds otherwise lofty, while they desire to satisfy their

hunger for knowledge, are fed for at least a whole three years on the empty food of

beings of reason alone, not without the greatest loss to youth, their minds being

held back, namely, lest they go on to better things.

13 “To

(e) In the Preface to the Physics.

(f) Bk. 5 De causis corruptarum artium.

p. 5

13 “To better things, I said. For who would doubt that the study of natural things is far more excellent than those metaphysical questions, not to say trifles, over which it is customary in the Schools to contend sharply in perpetual litigation, and for the most part about words? Certainly, when God willed to disclose to Job the incomparable eminence of his wisdom, he put to him a great many questions, and wonderful ones, taken from the storehouses of natural philosophy, as is manifest from the whole of chapters 38 and 39; but of those things which are made so much of in the Schools, not a word.

14 “He could, however, have asked him a great many things about the being of reason: namely, whether and how it exists, what its fabric is, what powers or what acts concur in its construction; whether, moreover, it can be produced by God, or by the Angels, or by the bodily senses? About precisions, too, he could have inquired whether they are only formal, or objective as well? About lacks, moreover, whether there are any? nay, whether there are even lacks of lacks? and likewise whether the essences of things are really distinct from their existence? But about these and other like things, deep silence.

15 “Moreover, in Wisdom, ch. 7, Solomon commends the knowledge bestowed on him by God, not because God taught him that huge crowd of formalities, distinctions and reflexions, but rather because he disclosed to him the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements, the beginning, and ending, and midst of the times, the alterations of their courses, and the changes of seasons, the revolutions of the year, and the dispositions of the stars, the natures of living creatures, and rage of wild beasts, the force of winds, etc.” Thus far Tosca. What do those men say to these things, who are little or not at all studious of physical things? Do they not deserve the rebuke of Isaiah (g): The work of the Lord you regard not, nor do you consider the works of his hands?

16 There will not be lacking, therefore, men who will try to throw you down at the very entrance and to call you away from the reflections you have undertaken, by dinning again and again into your ears and minds that this kind of Physics is new, obscure, and wrapped on every side in mathematical coverings; but, despising the raillery of the detractors, apply yourselves diligently to the most beautiful study of nature, and do not let yourselves be led away by the talk of the unskilled. It is true indeed that without the aid of Geometry no worthy progress can be made in Physics; but you have sufficiently experienced this aid in what has gone before, when you went through such Geometrical Institutions as were needed. For those Elements of Geometry set out above as briefly as possible suffice for a fuller understanding of our Physics.

§. IV.

(g) Ch. 5, v. 12.

§ . I V.

On the Study of Geometry.

17

C ertainly Geometry is necessary to the physicist; for, as the illustrious Caramuel

says: Those excel among the rest in the philosophical Schools who are versed in Geometry;

those who are ignorant of it serve: I speak from experience. Nor was it in vain that Plato

placed on the doors of the Academy the golden inscription by which he kept from

entering it those who were wholly ignorant of Geometry: Let no one ignorant

of geometry enter. And rightly indeed. Since, as Nature (says the most illustrious

Guglielmini (h)) is everywhere mathematical, it is the same to wish to fish out nature without

mathematics as to walk without legs, or for a craftsman to throw away all the instruments nec‐

essary for the work and nevertheless to promise his work.

§ . V.

The authors we shall follow. 18

B ut since it has been the custom of all physicists to indicate at the outset the sect

to which they had sworn, there will perhaps be some who demand this of us as

well, asking: Do we follow Descartes, or Leibniz, or Newton, or someone else? To them

we answer in these few words. We profess that our judgment is free, so that we will

swear to the sect of no Philosopher; for we think there has been no sect that saw

every truth, and none that did not hold something of the truth. Therefore to gather

into one body the truth scattered among individuals and dispersed through the sects,

this we judge to belong properly to our undertaking. But it is well, on the very

threshold, to set down the rules of philosophizing.

§. VI.

On the Rules of philosophizing. 19

W hile we try to explain phenomena and to investigate the laws of nature, it will

be necessary to attend scrupulously to the following rules of philosophizing

prescribed by the most illustrious Newton (i). The first is as follows.

20 No

(h) Dissertatio de Salibus, Preface. (i) Bk. 3 of the Mathematical Principles of Philosophy.

p. 7

20 No more causes of natural things ought to be admitted than such as are both true and sufficient to explain their phenomena. For if a cause is merely possible, it can never be held to be true, however apt and suited it may otherwise have been to producing the effect. That the same effect can arise from several causes is a matter beyond doubt; but of so many causes not more than one really exists and operates, and it alone is to be investigated by physicists, because it alone is the true cause of that effect. Those Philosophers are surely to be spurned who strive to derive natural effects from their own hypotheses and from causes feigned at pleasure, little concerned about the existence of those causes. Hypotheses, therefore, are in that case to be banished from Physics; for, as Musschenbroek very well says (j), whatever is gathered from them is inconstant; from them useless controversies are stirred up; phenomena are feigned so that the hypotheses may be strengthened and defended.

21 Unless perhaps we must agree with the most illustrious Perrault (k), who, not altogether unreasonably, rules on hypotheses very much in this manner. He contends that hypotheses bound by fixed laws are suited to the investigation of truth, being led by this reason: that from hypotheses laid down beforehand we strive in the most fitting order toward the thesis, and it is plain that a great many things which at present we hold as certain were once among the number of hypotheses. Now the laws by which the method of hypotheses ought to be restricted would chiefly be these, namely: Let the hypothesis flow from natural things and arise from phenomena observed again and again, but let no position be fashioned at whim, toward which nature herself is dragged by I know not what tricks; let the proposition, assumed not without foundation, correspond exactly not to one or another phenomenon only, but to all of that kind; let it, moreover, dissent from no phenomenon of another kind that has been ascertained and is of tested certainty, and likewise from no evident principle; finally, let it generate conclusions of such a kind as are held sober and consonant with the tenets of the saner Philosophers, and proceed by sure consequence from the assumed foundation of the doctrine. The second rule of philosophizing is this.

22 Of natural effects of the same kind the causes are the same. This rule is easily derived from the first. For (by the first rule) nature is simple and does not abound in superfluous causes; therefore to attribute effects of the same kind, or wholly alike, to different causes is altogether repugnant to the simplicity of nature. Thus the descent of heavy bodies in Europe and in America is to be attributed to the same cause. By like reasoning, since anatomical observations show the same instruments of respiration in all men, we rightly conclude that the cause of breathing is the same in each. But one must carefully beware lest from merely external characters we pronounce boldly on the perfect likeness of effects. Thus certain lethal plants imitate the external appearance of wholesome plants,

B but

(j) Elementa Physicae, vol. 1, ch. 1.

(k) Perrault, Essais de Physique.

p. 8

§. VII

but differ greatly from one another by a certain internal principle that is not easily

perceived. Which, to pass over other examples, is most true of water hemlock and

parsley. The greatest care must therefore be taken that we have all the parts of the

effects, and each of their conditions, certainly ascertained; for then this rule of anal‐

ogy is placed beyond all doubt. The third runs thus.

23 The qualities of bodies which cannot be intended and remitted (that is, neither in‐

creased nor diminished) and which belong to all bodies on which it is possible to make exper‐

iments, are to be held for qualities of all bodies universally. That is, those which persist al‐

ways the same and invariable in bodies, however the condition of time and place

may vary, and whatever change or alteration bodies may undergo; such as solidity

and figurability: for there are other qualities which can be intended and remitted,

and of this kind are gravity and the force of attraction. For when the distance of a body

from the center toward which it tends, either by gravity or by attraction, is dimin‐

ished, the forces of gravity and of attraction are increased, and they are diminished

when the distance is increased, as can be found by experiment in iron attracted to a

magnet. These are the rules of philosophizing which we shall use from here on.

Division of Physics. 24

F ollowing the method now accepted among men most practiced in teaching this

discipline, Physics has customarily been marked out in a twofold treatment,

namely under the name of General and of Particular. The General considers body tak‐

en generally and the principles of natural composites, and likewise comprehends the

phenomena pertaining to them, as also their causes. The Particular examines the sin‐

gle kinds of bodies and demonstrates their forces, properties and operations. We

shall perform both at once, since we neither ought, nor indeed are able, to be

lengthy.

Physics,

p. 9

PHYSICS, PART I

AND PRINCIPLES OF BODIES

D I S S E RTAT I O N I

CHAPTER I

O N T H E N AT U R E

On physical Body taken generally.

On the Nature of Body. The opinions of the Philosophers are

set out and refuted. 1

T he first thing to be asked in this dissertation would be whether bodies ex‐

ist, so that it might first be established that the thing whose nature we un‐

dertake to inquire into exists. But since our consciousness persuades us of their

existence, we propose this, as a kind of postulate, to be granted by our adver‐

saries, holding it for certain that a most certain matter is only made more ob‐

scure by a superfluous inquiry. Bodies, therefore, exist. But concerning their es‐

sence the opinion of Philosophers is not one and the same.

2 The excellent Philosopher René Descartes, wonderfully versed in the math‐

ematical disciplines, placed the nature of corporeal substance in extension; for

he says (l): we shall perceive that the nature of matter, or of body regarded in general,

does not consist in its being a thing hard, or heavy, or colored, or affecting the senses in any

other way, but only in its being a thing extended in length, breadth and depth: which

Aristotle also asserted, for in Bk. 3 of the Physics, text 43, body is, he says, that which

has dimension in every direction. But let us set out the state of the question. The

question, then, asks: what is the formal reason of physical body? that is, which

of all those attributes that belong to body (as impenetrability, extension, divisi‐

bility, etc.) is so first in the body itself that from it, as from a root, all the rest

proceed? For that attribute is the formal reason of the thing, through

B2 which

(l) Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 4.

p. 10

which the thing itself is what it is, and is first distinguished from all others. These things being laid down:

3 I say first, against Descartes and Aristotle: the essence of body is by no means placed in actual extension, or in threefold dimension. It is proved. Who will deny that God, Best and Greatest, can destroy the whole mass of air which is enclosed between the earth and the Moon? But then the very same extension would remain, and yet no corporeal substance would be left: therefore. But Descartes denies that this can happen: for he thinks that if, e.g., the air of this little room were destroyed, the walls themselves would touch one another, since those things are said to be joined which are separated by no intervening body; or he thinks that in this hypothesis a most manifest contradiction is contained, since that space would indeed be void, as is supposed, and at the same time not void, because there would always be threefold dimension in it, and therefore body itself.

4 But who does not see that Descartes here imposes upon us, since he proves the same by the same, and assumes in place of a principle what had been placed in controversy? For he contends that a void cannot be made by God for no other reason than that body would always remain in that space, extension, namely, remaining, which according to him is the essence of body; and that is the very thing under dispute. Next: although it is certain that two bodies touch each other when no other body lies between them, yet it is not necessary that those things touch which are separated by no body. Descartes, therefore, confuses physical body with mathematical body. But who does not see that what constitutes physical body must be one thing, and what constitutes mathematical body another; or that the nature of the body which is contained in our imagination alone is one, and that of the body which is also found in the very nature of things is another? Thus what constitutes a Geometrical line is that it have length without breadth; and yet the essence of a line which is found really and physically in the nature of things need not consist in length alone without breadth.

5 The Cartesians could indeed reply that mathematical body differs very greatly from physical body, but not by reason of extension, which is essentially common to both. But they ought also to take note of this: that then extension could no longer be held to be the complete essence of physical body, as they themselves contend; just as, because figure is common to the circle and to the triangle, it cannot be held to be the sole essence of either of them. Essentially, therefore, physical body must have something else, by which it is distinguished both from simple extension and from mathematical body.

6 Pierre Gassendi would have (m) the essence of body placed in actual impenetrability; against whom I say secondly: actual impenetrability is not the formal reason of physical body. Proof: the formal reason of body is not placed in that of which the body itself can be deprived

without

(m) Sect. 1, Phys., bk. 3, ch. 6.

p. 11

without ceasing to be body; but body can be deprived of actual impenetrability with‐

out ceasing to be body: therefore. Proof of the minor. It is certain that two bodies

can be compenetrated by divine power without their essence being changed: there‐

fore etc.

T H E O B J E C T I O N S A R E A N S W E R E D.

7

O bj. 1, for the opinion of Descartes: when threefold dimension is understood, all

the other things that are in body being cut away, body is understood; for spirit is

not understood, as is evident; and between body and spirit there is no middle: there‐

fore the formal reason of body is threefold dimension. The argument could very well

be turned back against the adversaries, and prove against them that the formal rea‐

son of body consists in impenetrability. Reply: I distinguish the antecedent. Body is

understood according to its more obvious property, I grant; according to its essence,

I deny; and I deny the consequent. Body is surely understood by the very fact that a

substance divisible into integral parts is conceived; and yet the Cartesians will not say

that divisibility into parts so belongs to body that it is in no way to be distinguished

from its formal reason.

8 Obj. 2. Whoever are willing to attend to the idea of body are forced to admit

that they conceive body in no other way than as a substance extended in every direc‐

tion: therefore the formal reason of body is not different from threefold dimension.

The argument proves too much: for in the idea of body not only threefold extension,

but also actual impenetrability presents itself. Reply: I deny the consequent; for since

the greater part of our ideas is acquired by sense [§. 14, Log.], and it is certain that the

inmost attributes of things become in no way known to us immediately through the

ministry of the senses [§. 29, Log.], it remains that the formal reason of body is not

that attribute of it which occurs to us in the idea of body that we drew in in the time

of infancy, but that attribute can most rightly be called only the more obvious prop‐

erty of body.

9 Obj. 3. St. Augustine, addressing Evodius, says (n): I ask you whether you think there

is any body that does not, in its own measure, have length, breadth and depth? ….. If you take

this away from bodies, in my opinion they can neither be perceived by the senses nor rightly be

judged to be bodies: therefore. Reply: these words must be understood of bodies as to

existence, since certainly without some extension no body could be sensible; but not

as to essence: just as body cannot indeed exist without figure, and yet no one would

say that its essence is placed in figure. We do not deny, however, that extension is one

of the properties of body; we contend only that it is not the first attribute in body.

10 Obj. 4. No body can exist, be seen, or be conceived without threefold dimen‐

sion: therefore extension is the formal reason of body.

The

(n) Bk. On the Magnitude of the Soul, no. 6.

p. 12

The consequent does not follow; because neither can any finite body be conceived without figure, nor man without the capacity for knowledge, and yet these ought by no means to pertain to their essence. You will say: if the essence of body is constituted in threefold dimension, the spirituality of the rational soul is most clearly proved, as was shown in the Psychology: therefore. Reply: in our opinion on the essence of body the argument for the spirituality of the soul has the same force; for just as, from the fact that the rational soul cannot have actual extension, Descartes rightly infers that it is incorporeal, so we, from the fact that the rational soul does not require to have extension, very well infer that it is of a different nature from body.

11 Obj. 5. When we wish to conceive in the mind that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we imagine a certain extension: therefore extension itself is conceived by us not as a property, but as the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent; and from the phantasm of our imagination the essence, or formal reason, of body is well gathered, I deny; is wrongly gathered, I grant; and I deny the consequent. The argument proves that matter was already existing before the creation of the world: for we conceive extension: therefore, according to the Cartesians, we conceive body: therefore that body was existing from eternity, which is absurd.

12 But the Cartesians insist: of nothing there is no extension, no property, no quality; but when we conceive that very nothing which was before the creation of the world, we conceive it as extended: therefore we conceive something, and not nothing itself, and consequently we conceive some body. But in this argument (as the Most Illustrious Pierre Daniel Huet (o) very well notes) Descartes is deluded: for he ought to have observed that properties, or qualities, are of two kinds, some positive, others negative; that of nothing there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. For we say that nothing is incorruptible, that nothing is like nothing, that nothing is contrary to being, that the world was created by God out of nothing, etc. But these properties are mere negations, namely of corruption, of difference from nothing, etc. Likewise, when we imagine that the wine which is contained in some vessel is reduced to nothing by God, no other body being admitted into the place of the wine, it must be said that the space which was occupied by the wine remains void, and that it will be of the same amplitude and extension as the wine was before; and we shall deservedly attribute extension to this void space, but a negative one: for when I say that that empty space which is inside the vessel is of one square foot, it will be just as if I said that in that space of a foot there is no body; and this extension of a foot, of the void, or of nothing, will be the negation of body in a space of a foot.

13 Obj. 6. A mode cannot be conceived without the thing whose mode it is; but extension can very well be perceived without, e.g., a stone: therefore extension is not a property or mode of body, but its very essence.

CHAPTER II

I distinguish the minor. The extension of the stone can be conceived without it,

I deny; extension taken generally, I subdistinguish: it can be conceived precisely

without the stone, I grant; without any body whose extension it is, I deny; and I

deny the consequent. You will say, for the opinion of Gassendi: as soon as some

actually impenetrable substance is conceived, body is conceived: therefore. The

consequent does not follow; for as soon as fire is conceived, some substance is

conceived which has actual heat, and yet no one would say that the essence of

fire is placed in actual heat, for the Babylonian fire, when applied, was without

burning.

Our opinion is set out and proved.

say, with very many of the Moderns: the formal reason of physical 14

I body is best constituted in natural impenetrability, or (what is the same)

in the natural exigency of occupying place impenetrably. Proof of the conclu‐

sion: the formal reason of physical body is rightly constituted in that

from which the other attributes are derived as from a root, as all agree; but such

an attribute is natural impenetrability, or, what is the same, radical impenetrabil‐

ity: therefore. Proof of the minor: from it flows the entitative extension of body;

for that is called entitatively extended which comprises several parts united

among themselves in such a way that the whole entity of one exists outside the

entity of another; but several things cannot be conjoined among themselves in

this way unless they are naturally impenetrable: therefore.

15 There follows solidity, by virtue of which bodies either cannot be com‐

pressed, or can be constrained by our forces only to a certain degree. Then mo‐

bility; because, if bodies did not resist bodies, we could scarcely think of the mo‐

tion which we experience in things. Then divisibility, measurability, and the capaci‐

ty to receive any figure whatever follow from natural impenetrability. Secondly: it

seems evident that such an exigency cannot be demonstrated of body a priori;

for there is nothing in body from which, as from a principle, or root, its natural

impenetrability could be deduced; for body is not impenetrable because it is ex‐

tended, but on the contrary it is entitatively extended because it is impenetrable.

T H E O B J E C T I O N S A R E A N S W E R E D.

16 Obj. 1. Impenetrability belongs also to Angels. For an Angel can be in

place in such a way that it excludes any body whatever from it;

therefore

p. 14

therefore impenetrability cannot be the formal reason of body. I distinguish the antecedent. If impenetrability is taken for the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, as it is taken in the question, I deny; if it is taken for a free power of non-penetration, I grant. The impenetrability of body is such that, because of it, a body cannot by the forces of nature subsist together with another in the same place, and by its very essence it always requires to occupy the place in which it exists with the exclusion of every other body. But an Angel is of such a nature that it does not fill place, although it can freely repel any body whatever, by its own force, from the place in which it is.

17 Obj. 2. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel: therefore body is not distinguished from spirit by impenetrability; and for that reason the formal reason of body is not well placed in natural impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent. Body is not impenetrable by an Angel through its own defect, I deny; by reason of the Angel, I grant; and I deny the consequent. Body by its nature seeks to exclude from its place everything that fills place. Hence, since a spiritual substance is not repletive of place, neither is it of such a kind that body could expel it from its place. Moreover, since it is evident from what was taught in the preceding place that the impenetrability which is in body does not belong to Angels, there can be no doubt that body is sufficiently distinguished from spirit by radical impenetrability.

18 Obj. 3. One body can by divine power be together with another in the same place: therefore body can be deprived of impenetrability, and so etc. I deny the consequent; for although some body may by a miracle be stripped of actual impenetrability, yet it always requires to have it, nor can such an exigency ever be taken away from it; in exactly the same way as, although actual heat may be taken away from fire, and downward motion from a stone, or be impeded by God, yet the power, nay even the exigency, remains, by which, once the obstacle is removed, those bodies would actually produce their proper effect.

19 Obj. 4. An extended thing can arise only from extended things: therefore extension is an attribute of body prior to impenetrability. I distinguish the antecedent: and these extended things are apt for composing body by reason of their impenetrability, I grant; and they are not so, I deny. For indeed, just as this does not prevent the extended thing from being, of its own kind, something composite, so it does not prevent the aptitude of the parts for composing it, namely their natural impenetrability, from being an attribute of the composite itself prior to its entitative extension: for natural impenetrability is nothing other than the natural exigency of occupying place with the exclusion of another, and the parts of body are rendered apt for constituting an extended thing through this impenetrability of theirs.

20 You will say: the principles from whose union the entitatively extended whole arises are not body if taken separately, but principles of body: therefore the formal reason of corporeal substance is not

different

p. 15

CHAPTER I

different from extension, but is extension itself. I deny the antecedent; because the

parts constituting the extended thing, taken separately, are material, or corporeal,

substance (for they are not spirits): therefore the formal reason of corporeal sub‐

stance is different from entitative extension: therefore, if the reason of material sub‐

stance is different from extension, the reason of body too will be plainly different

from it.

21 Obj. 5. The essence of body is explained better through the collection of all its

attributes than through natural impenetrability, so that body is called a substance by

its nature impenetrable, extended, divisible, mobile, and apt to receive any figure

whatever: therefore. I distinguish the antecedent: and this is the state of the ques‐

tion, I deny; and it is not, I grant. I explain the solution: however much the proper‐

ties mentioned may be proper affections of bodies, and, thus collected, may belong to

body alone, this does not prevent its being asserted that among those very ones listed

there is some one attribute which occurs in the first place in bodies, and from which

the remaining properties found in them flow. Certainly it cannot come into contro‐

versy that general properties so inhere in body that they in no way belong to a thing

distinct from it, since that cannot even be called into doubt; and this notion, as it is

obvious to anyone, so need not be discussed at length by a Philosopher.

On the Principles of natural body.

General notions of principles. 22

I ntrinsic principles of a natural composite are all those from which the composite itself is

essentially constituted. Thus the rational soul and the body are intrinsic principles of

man. These are either primary or secondary. Primary are those from which the composite

itself is so constituted that they themselves are in no way composed, together, of others into which

they could be resolved; or, as the Scholastics say, which are made neither from one another,

nor from others, but all things are made from them. Those are called secondary principles

which do indeed constitute a natural composite, but themselves too coalesce essentially from oth‐

ers. Thus the organic body is a secondary principle of man, since it so constitutes man

that it itself too, together with

C others

p. 16

others, is essentially composed. Moreover, the intrinsic principles of things are either metaphysical, or artificial, or sensible.

23 Metaphysical are those which, after the manner of metaphysical things, cannot be reached by sense, but only grasped by the intellect. Artificial are those which, disposed and conjoined by a certain wonderful artifice of nature, compose natural body in such a way that all its sensible affections and operations arise from the magnitude, figure, motion, etc. of the parts, and can be suitably explained from these. Sensible, finally, or Physical, are called those which can really be separated from one another by a true resolution of bodies, and be discerned with the aid of the senses. It is established among all Philosophers, the Ancients as well as the Moderns, that any natural composite which can be produced and destroyed by the forces of nature consists of a twofold essential principle; of which one is determinable and is called matter, the other determining, and is named form. For it is certain that natural changes of one composite into another as to substance take place: for who would deny that food, e.g., is changed into chyle, this into blood, and blood into the other parts of the organic body; of which one is surely converted into another on such terms that nothing sensible remains out of which each of them essentially coalesces?

24 Now it is certain that a composite which is changed by the forces of nature is neither made by creation nor reduced to nothing. It is certain, therefore, that there is something from which, as existing, all things are made, and which is therefore common to all; and this is rightly designated as the determinable principle, or matter. In a not dissimilar way, since, as is plain, natural composites differ from one another as to substance, but are in no way distinguished by that part which is equally common to all, it is made manifest that there is something else in bodies which is called the determining principle, that is, form. Wherefore, if matter is taken for the subject from which, as previously existing, natural composites are produced, and form precisely for that by which each composite is the very thing that it is, and is distinguished from the rest as to essence, it is plain indeed that no question can be raised concerning the existence of these principles between the Peripatetics and the Moderns. But just as these same principles, so taken, are contained in abstract notions and are by no means objects of Physical consideration, so they contribute nothing to explaining the nature, affections and operations of physical things.

25 The whole business, therefore, that this matter involves consists in this: that it be made plain what the physical nature of these principles is; namely, what physically is that from which, as pre-existing, as from a determinable subject, natural composites are produced by created causes, and what is that by which each composite is what it is, and is essentially distinguished from any other? The Peripatetics gave us nothing on this matter, content to have considered matter and form metaphysically. But the Moderns, having rejected the scholastic subtleties, are wholly engaged in setting out openly the physical nature of these principles; whence it appears how falsely the common Peripatetics

say

p. 17

say that neither matter nor form is admitted by the Moderns. These things, then, be‐

ing established, let us look at the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics.

The Metaphysical system of the Peripatetics is set out.

t must be supposed that any natural body can be considered in two ways: 26

I both inasmuch as it is generated, or, as the Peripatetics speak, in fieri, and

inasmuch as it has already been generated, or, as they themselves say, in facto

esse. The principles of natural body, inasmuch as it is generated, are three ac‐

cording to Aristotle (p): matter, form, and privation: for generation is a certain passage from

substantial non-being to that substantial being, in which passage three things necessarily

concur, namely the terminus a quo, or the privation of that being; that being which is

acquired, which is form; and that from which the thing constituted through that being

is made, which is matter. The principles of natural body already made, or in facto esse,

are only two, namely matter and form, as was said above. In addition, they say that

union is a certain form, or substantial mode, a part ut quo, whose office is to bring it

about that a certain complete substantial whole is constituted from matter and form.

The Thomists generally deny that this union is distinct from matter and form; the

others hold the contrary, and acknowledge it as a true modal entity. Nay, indeed,

there are some to whom another union of that very union, which they call unition,

seems to need asserting. But these things, like most others, are not of such impor‐

tance that they ought to be set out by me at greater length.

27 The Peripatetics teach, besides, that prime matter is a simple, incomplete sub‐

stance, the first foundation of corporeal things, and the first subject of natural trans‐

mutations. Aristotle defines it thus (q): matter of itself is neither something, nor a quantity,

nor a quality, nor any of those things by which being is determined; nor yet negations. Aristotle

could not have explained nothing itself with a better definition, as our Spaniard Don

Martín Martínez wittily says (r). It is not something, that is, of itself it is not a man, nor a

stone, nor wood, etc. It is not a quantity, that is, it has no determinate magnitude; nor a

quality, because it is neither hot nor cold, nor

C2 any

(q) This is the celebrated definition of matter handed down by Aristotle in bk. 1 of the Metaphysics,

(r) Filosofía escéptica en diálogos.

CHAPTER III

any of those things, etc., because it is not any form, whose office it is to determine a

being to this or that physical species. Finally, it is not negations, or privations of be‐

ings, because it is a positive entity.

28 From what has been said they infer: that prime matter is a subject indifferent

to many forms, and indeed not modal, but absolute; for if it were an accident, it

would be received in another subject, and consequently would not be the first sub‐

ject: that it is simple, that is, not composed of subject and form, for then it would

not be the first principle; this, however, does not prevent its being composed inte‐

grally of extended parts. They infer also that it is incomplete, that is, that it is or‐

dered to constituting a whole together with another substantial part: that it is in‐

generable and incorruptible; for since generation is the production of a thing from a

presupposed subject, and corruption the ceasing of a thing while the subject remains,

and since matter, which is the first subject, can neither be presupposed by itself nor

remain when destroyed, it can therefore neither be generated nor be corrupted. That

it is naturally indestructible, because God destroys no substance except at the de‐

mand of a stronger enemy, and there is nothing in things hostile to matter.

29 As regards form, they say that it is an incomplete substance, which as first act com‐

pletes and informs matter, so as to constitute natural body in a determinate species. It is called

incomplete, because together with matter it is determined to constituting the compos‐

ite; it is called act, because it determines the potency of matter to a certain comple‐

ment and to a certain species of composite: and it is called first act, that it may be dis‐

tinguished from accidents, which are acts of matter, but secondary ones. The

Peripatetics affirm that all composites consist of matter and form so explained. From

what has been said they infer: 1. that the specific difference of bodies is taken not

from matter, as being the same in species in all, but from form. 2. that substantial

form is produced anew in every generation, and destroyed in corruption (the rational

soul excepted), prime matter remaining, which is incorruptible. 3. that all forms (the

rational soul excepted) are educed from the potency of matter, either by a created

cause, if a proportionate one is present, or by God alone, as author of nature. So far

the system of the Peripatetics.

The System of Leibniz is very briefly set out and refuted. 30

L eibniz admits in nature some insensible force, and abstract beings: and for this

reason he is in the class of those who, as the principles of bodies, metaphysical, or

insensible, ones

have

p. 19

have laid down. The elements of all things, according to him, are monads, or simple, in‐

generable and incorruptible substances created by God. Every monad represents the

whole universe, and so is in a certain way all things; but just as we do not sufficiently

discern remote things with our eyes, so it comes about that not all the things that are

in any given monad are distinctly represented. His complete system was published in

the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (s). But who could grasp with his mind that any monad

whatever, that is, a being devoid of parts, represents the whole totality of things? Nor

is it my intention to reproach Leibniz with the use, in explaining his opinion, of

words beneath which no distinct idea lies, which Hartsoeker has done in full (t); nor to

show that the monadology is not far removed from the error of idealism, which has

been done expressly by Jac. Frider. Müller. It will be enough to have touched upon

these few things.

C H A P T E R I V.

Axioms altogether necessary for refuting or establishing systems

are set out beforehand. 31

B efore we approach the refutation of the system of the Peripatetics, we think we

must first set out certain universal axioms proper to Physics, deduced from the

general requisites necessary for establishing the system of any Science, which may

carry a torch before us, as it were, both in judging the systems of others and in con‐

stituting our own, and on which, as on foundations, the whole of Physics may hence‐

forth rest. They are, moreover, of this kind.

32 Axiom I. In Physics that system or opinion must be rejected as false which teaches or as‐

sumes anything contrary to Sacred Theology, or to sound metaphysics, or to certain experience.

Axiom II. That system is to be preferred to the others which is simpler, and explains the proper‐

ties, effects and phenomena of natural body from fewer principles. Beings, assuredly, are not

to be multiplied beyond necessity; likewise, what can be done by fewer things ought

not to be done by more, as all Philosophers agree. Wherefore neither the principles

of things nor the causes of effects are to be multiplied, unless an undoubted reason

demands it, as was said above [§. 20.]. Axiom III. That system is to be judged the better

which unfolds the more of the things that must be taken into consideration among Physicists. For

the whole of Physics is engaged in this: that the affections, effects, etc. of natural

things be explained, as many of them as possible, and as well as possible.

33 On

(s) Supplement, vol. 7, sect. 11, year 1721.

(t) Cours de Physique, bk. 1, ch. 1, art. 3.

p. 20

33 On the reason given for this axiom is founded Axiom IV. That system is to be

preferred to the rest which not only uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things,

but also sets forth in particular the nature of bodies, their affections, and the causes of effects,

as far as this can be done, perspicuously and lucidly. For general ideas produce only an

obscure knowledge of particular things, and do not explain natural things in the

best way, which is the task of Physics. Hence, if to someone asking, e.g., why does

heat rarefy bodies and cold contract them? the answer is given that this is the na‐

ture of heat, and that the nature of cold, a response unworthy of a Philosopher is

given. Similarly, to dispatch someone who asks about the various effects of nature

with the general term quality is the mark of a small and lowly wit, as the most illus‐

trious Rohault (u) says. Hence follows Axiom V. That doctrine excels the rest which as‐

serts or posits nothing that cannot be sufficiently grasped in thought or explained. For

Physics, as far as this can be done, ought to exhibit nature to us accommodated to

the powers of our intelligence, and to explain the nature of things with its wrap‐

pings removed.

34 Axiom VI. That system must prevail in Physics which pursues the doctrine of natur‐

al things in a manner suited to the nature and method of this discipline. To this may also be

referred, as certain further rules, the following, which are extremely useful. I. One

must not have recourse to the first cause, or God, when a second cause can be had. II. While

the sensible causes of effects are unknown to us, let no insensible and equally unknown cause

whatever be asserted. III. On those questions one must not dwell, or must altogether abstain

from treating them, whose solution either will never be found, or, if perchance it is found,

makes us none the more learned. IV. The same is to be said of those controversies which de‐

pend on the inscrutable counsel of God and are known to Him alone who made all things,

and which therefore, as Tertullian rightly says, are to be learned either from God or from

no one. These things being established,

C H A P T E R V.

The metaphysical system of the Peripatetics is refuted.

say, first: the principles of natural body, as they are set forth by Aristotle, 35

I serve almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy. The truth of

this assertion will be sufficiently plain if we consider that the principles of

natural body, namely matter and form, were only metaphysically

and

(u) In the Preface to his Physics.

p. 21

and in the abstract assigned by Aristotle, and that everything he asserts and determines about them is merely certain metaphysical abstractions, by which physical things are never sufficiently set forth; and so they contribute nothing to the knowledge of particular bodies or to the explanation of the various phenomena, and therefore serve almost nothing toward acquiring Physics, nor can they have a place in the system of Physics, by Axiom VI.

36 To make this clearer, suppose the following case. Let someone ask, e.g., from what, as from intrinsic principles, does a house come together? And let me answer that it comes together from the matter and the form of the house: that the matter, moreover, is that from which the house is made, and the form the act by which the matter is determined to compose a house. With this answer I have certainly spoken the truth, but I have not made the questioner more learned; and therefore he will rightly ask again what, namely, that matter is from which the house has been made, or likewise what that act is which is called the form of the house. We do not, therefore, come away from the school of Aristotle more learned in those things which pertain to the first beginnings of natural things; and therefore the metaphysical system of the Peripatetics serves almost nothing toward acquiring natural Philosophy, not because it is false, but on the contrary because it is too true, and teaches nothing beyond those things which cannot be unknown. For who can ever doubt that all composites are made of matter and form? But after we have learned these things we can give the cause of no phenomenon: therefore it serves nothing toward learning Physics thoroughly.

37 I say secondly: the Peripatetic system of the principles of natural body is to be altogether neglected in Physics. Proof: for if in natural Philosophy that system is rightly neglected in which natural things either are not explained or the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown, the Peripatetic system certainly cannot have a place in Physics, by Axioms III and IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected. The first part of this proposition, although it has already been proved by us above, is proved more fully and to the point of evidence. For suppose the question arises why fire, e.g., is endowed with certain qualities which we experience, while water, on the other hand, obtains other affections? You will receive no other answer from a Peripatetic than this: namely, that these things follow from the fact that fire has one substantial form, water another; and if someone insists by asking what those forms are, by what law they produce diverse effects and demand diverse accidents? these philosophers reply at once that this is the nature of the form of fire, that it requires such affections, and that on the contrary the nature of the form of water itself is another; which is indeed against Axiom IV.

38 The second part of the proposition is evident; for when a Peripatetic is asked why heat and cold, e.g., produce a diverse sensation? they point to no other cause than that these qualities are diverse, of an altogether diverse nature. But who will deny that by these little ways of speaking the phenomena of things are by no means explained, and that the unknown

matter

p. 22

CHAPTER VI

matter of the controversy is dispatched with an answer just as unknown? Therefore

in the Peripatetic system the unknown is set forth through the equally unknown,

and it uses general notions to explain the phenomena of things, contrary to Axiom

IV, and therefore it is to be altogether neglected in Physics.

39 Moreover, while the Peripatetics are intent solely on maintaining that sub‐

stantial forms perish and are generated, by what reasoning will they show that a

new substantial form, e.g. of fire, arises while all the same things remain by which,

once they are established, the same form is wont to be destroyed? The candle is the

same (I use the words of the most illustrious Casati (x)), giving out flame with the same

burning wick: you blow on it, the flame perishes; you blow again, the flame comes back to life:

the cause of the arising and of the perishing is the same, namely the same breath, the same dis‐

positions, the same subject, which is deprived of flame and receives flame. I pass over a great

many arguments against the Peripatetic system, especially those by which Henricus

Wiber vigorously assails matter and form (y). We by no means regard this system as

devised by Aristotle, but call it the common Peripatetic system, which might perhaps

more aptly be named Arabic, after the Arabs, the interpreters of the Stagirite. For

that Aristotle’s mind was far different is shown at length by Gassendi (z), Sturm [a],

Stephanus Pace (b), and others.

Artificial Systems. The system of the Atomists is set forth and

refuted.

ierre Gassendi, a celebrated man, wonderfully commended for his studies 40

P in Philosophy, and with him the whole school of the Atomists, holds that

the only principle of things is atoms. An atom, moreover, according to

these Philosophers, is a corpuscle that cannot be cut, or indivisible, yet

having figure and measurable in three dimensions, extended, solid and impenetra‐

CHAPTER VII

a prism, etc. They set forth the phenomena and changes of natural bodies through the

atoms thus explained. This is the most ancient system of Epicurus, renewed by the

most illustrious Gassendi. But he expunged the very many things which Epicurus had

impiously heaped up against God, Providence and Religion, and adorned the rest

most richly. For Epicurus posited atoms eternal, uncreated, infinite.

41 But Gassendi, and with him the more recent Atomists, acknowledge that

Epicurus erred when he admitted the atoms themselves as uncreated and mobile of

themselves; and he shows that this too was a mark of desperate madness in Epicurus,

that he believed the world to have been generated from a fortuitous concourse of

atoms and to be governed by no counsel of the Divine mind, or Providence; for, as

Cicero observed, there is nothing so hidden, so admirable and divine, that among

these men the throng of atoms does not accomplish it (c). Although, therefore, it

cannot be denied that a great many things in the opinion of the Atomists have been

devised happily and usefully, yet the system, or hypothesis, of the Atomists does not

seem acceptable as a whole, since it is altogether uncertain whether there can be cor‐

puscles of this kind which are extended and at the same time indivisible; and there‐

fore it is contrary to Axiom V.

The system of Descartes is set forth and refuted.

irst, Descartes (d) posits a matter created by God, simple, homogeneous, 42

F measurable in three dimensions, and extended everywhere. This matter

God divided into particles as nearly equal to one another as possible, cubi‐

cal, so that they touched one another on every side with an immediate con‐

tact excluding all void. On the parts thus divided God the Creator impressed a most

vehement twofold motion: one by which the individual portions were moved about

their own center, the other by which several together were moved about a common

center. To the portions of matter thus driven round in a circle Descartes gave the

name of vortices, from vertendo [turning]; and hence, secondly, he teaches that from that

agitation and twofold motion of matter, the angles of the particles having been worn

away, three elements of different kinds arose, of which the first contains the most

minute parts; the second, globules, into which the square particles were shaped once

their angles were removed; the third consists of the coarser parts, irregular, with vari‐

ous angles.

43 To exhibit this to the life, the interpreters of Descartes turn their attention to

the turner’s

workshop, where a globe is shaped out of a cube turned round very rapidly: for just

as, from the wearing of a cubic piece of wood, parts of three kinds appear — some,

namely, most minute; others again larger, but irregular, alike neither in figure nor in

bulk; and finally the globe itself is formed — so they compare the first element to

those smallest parts, the third to the larger ones, the second to the globe itself.

44 Thirdly, he lays down that these three elements are the matter of which all the

remaining bodies are composed: from the first, indeed, the Sun and the fixed Stars;

from the second, all diaphanous and fluid bodies; from the third, opaque bodies, such

as earth, air, and the remaining mixed bodies. The third element they also call striated

matter, that is, coarser matter. But let us now reject in a few words the Cartesian vor‐

tices, as unequal to the explanation of the phenomena, and unfit.

45 I say, therefore: the Cosmogony of Descartes (that is, the formation of the

world devised by Descartes), or the system of vortices, cannot have a place in

Physics. Proof: for in this hypothesis many things cohere poorly with one another,

and so the phenomena of nature cannot be explained in it in a connected order:

therefore. The antecedent is evident. For in the first place this system fails at that

first origin of the three elements. For if no void is possible, as Descartes would have

it, even by Divine power, then, when matter was divided into cubic parts and each of

those parts was moving about its own axis and about the center of the universe, it

certainly cannot be conceived how some empty space would not then be intercepted

between parts of this kind, a space, namely, that would not then be filled by any sub‐

tle matter, since this had not yet come forth from the wearing of the angles.

46 Moreover, it seems altogether necessary that, through so very rapid and con‐

tinual a motion and wearing, these elements devised by Descartes should lose their

nature, at least after some centuries: e.g., the globules would at length pass into sub‐

tle matter, and the branching heterogeneous parts of the third element into globules.

Therefore either some compensation had to take place, most difficult to explain and

nowhere (so far as I have seen) explained by Descartes by apt laws of nature; or the

machine of the world must have collapsed after more than six thousand years by now.

What do the Cartesians say to this?

The Newtonian system is touched upon lightly. 47

O f the system of the most illustrious Newton it is necessary to set forth some

things, though very briefly. It differs from the elements of Descartes, besides

other things, in the primordial particles of bodies, inasmuch as Descartes asserts

them to be friable, Newton hard and solid, so that they cannot be broken by any

forces of nature (e). Of the Newtonian system the principal

head

(e) Opticks, Qu. 31.

p. 25

head is the attractive force: by this they understand the virtue, or principle, of that action which cannot be explained by the ordinary forces of bodies, namely pressure and impulse; and the action itself by which bodies approach one another is called by them attraction. This they hold to be universal and mutual, both of great bodies and of the smallest particles of matter.

48 Some philosophers, the French especially, say that although Newton’s system would have vague and uncertain hypotheses driven out of Philosophy [§ 20], some of the Newtonians nevertheless do no less themselves, by admitting an attractive force. For they do not know whether a force of this kind is a cause or an effect, nor can they by its help give the reason of the phenomena. And as regards the first, the most illustrious Newton himself (f): “What I call Attraction may be perform’d by impulse, or by some other means unknown to me. I use that Word here to signify only in general any Force by which Bodies tend towards one another, whatsoever be the Cause.”

49 And elsewhere (g) he speaks thus: “I use the words attraction, impulse, or propensity of whatever kind toward a center indifferently and promiscuously for one another, considering these forces not physically but only mathematically. Hence let the Reader beware of thinking that by words of this kind I anywhere define the species or mode of action, or the physical cause or reason, or that I attribute forces truly and physically to centers, which are mathematical points, if perchance I should say that centers attract, or that there are forces of centers.” So that for this reason Nollet (h) said that attraction, once it passed from the hands of Newton to his followers, was greatly despoiled of its simplicity.

50 And as regards the second, namely that by the help of attraction the reason of the phenomena cannot be given, M. Pluche (i) strives to show it by very many arguments. Let them explain, he says, by the help of attraction: why does the huge mass of some building, which compared with a feather possesses an almost infinite attractive force, not draw to itself a little feather fluttering in the air? or why is a stone falling beside a tower attracted by the earth rather than by the tower, which is nearer? For although (as the Newtonians say) the attractive force of the earth exceeds any other attraction by an immense amount, who will deny that, if an increase is added to this virtue, it will act with a greater effort? Let there be added, then, to the attracting forces of the earth the attractive force of a steep mountain, as of a part joined to the terraqueous globe. What cause could there be why this sum of attracting forces does not accelerate the motion of a stone falling beside the mountain, and does not drive it on faster

51 Nor does it matter that the attractive force of the mountain is not sensible in

comparison with the other force, that of the earth; for, granting that it is held insen‐

relative to a body hanging in the air from the summit, and hence not far from a part

of the terraqueous globe; if it is regarded as conspiring jointly with the earth in the

same downward motion? Then: if the earth impedes every other attraction, how can

it happen that, in the presence of these forces, the surging sea is attracted by the

Moon? when yet the waters are both nearer to the earth, and also compose it as a

part of the terraqueous globe, and the mass of this globe exceeds that of the Moon.

But let what has been said suffice for you to have tasted the Newtonian system of at‐

would be impossible) to weigh it in its entirety in a few little pages: it is indeed a

mystery impenetrable to those who are not initiated in the higher mathematics. The

system of Newton is defended rightly and deservedly by very many most illustrious

and most weighty philosophers, whom you ought to consult if you are lovers of good

Philosophy.

The elementary, or sensible, physical systems,

and the chemical system.

52

T here were some of the Ancients, called Elementarians, who said that one element

only was the first principle of natural things. Of these Thales of Miletus held wa‐

ter, or the moist, to be the principle of things (j); Xenophanes, earth (k); Anaximenes, air

(l); Heraclitus, fire (m). Others laid down two elements. Among the Moderns, Eller,

Fellow of the Berlin Academy, holds water as the passive principle, from which air

and earth come to be, and fire as the active (n). The principal system of the

Elementarians was founded by Empedocles. He took as prime matter the four common

elements, namely earth, water, air,

and

(j) In Plutarch, On the Opinions of the Philosophers, bk. 1, ch. 3.

(k) Sextus Empiricus, Against the Physicists, bk. 1, sect. 360.

(l) Plutarch, bk. 1, ch. 3.

(m) Plutarch, loc. cit.

(n) Dissertation on the Elements.

p. 27

and fire, but as their form, their combination [o]. Others held otherwise: for nothing (as Cicero says) can be thought up so absurd that it has not been said by some one of the philosophers.

53 Chymia, which by the Moderns is also called Chemia, that is, the art of resolving bodies, is said to have been invented by Hermes, and is therefore also called Hermetic. It was greatly illustrated, not only with a view to preparing medicines but also to explaining the principles of natural things, by Theophrastus Paracelsus, called the Father of the Chemists. The chemists, then, are the Spagyrists, or Empirics, who are occupied with the analysis of bodies and seek nothing else by their art and operations than to unfold the principles joined and bound together in mixed bodies and, once unfolded, to subject them to the senses themselves. The object of this art is every sensible body, and it is divided into three classes, or kingdoms, or families, as they themselves speak, namely the animal, the vegetable and the mineral. And what they draw out of these, chiefly by the help of fire and through menstrua, or dissolvents, those are for them the principles of bodies, according to their axiom: that anything is constituted of those parts into which it is resolved. Their principles are numbered five, namely Mercury, Sulphur, Salt, Water and Earth. The first three are called active, the last two passive.

54 Mercury, or spirit, is a subtle, penetrating and volatile liquor, which usually comes out of bodies first when fire is applied; on which, according to its greater or lesser dose, the growth and corruption of bodies depend; and from which the motions of all mixed bodies immediately proceed. Hence it is plain that the mercury of the chemists is a substance far different from quicksilver, which is otherwise also called mercury. Sulphur they call a certain fat, oily substance, through which mixed bodies that abound in it are able to catch flame. Salt is a savory substance [because it is the origin of savors], which can be diluted by water and liquefied by fire. It is divided into fixed and volatile, acid and alkali: the former does not fly off in the fire, though it is dissolved and melted; the latter flies off and is dissipated by heat. It is called acid because, placed on the tongue, it affects and twitches it with a certain sense of sharpness known to all. Alkali is that which is of a looser texture and of a taste as it were burning, and broken up by many passages; whence, if it is mixed with an acid, it produces a great ebullition. Therefore every body is called alkaline which cannot be mixed with an acid without exciting a great effervescence.

55 Water, which is also called phlegm by the chemists, is a fluid substance, extremely moist, odorless, insipid. Earth, lastly, the damned earth, which is also called caput mortuum, is not much the concern of the chemists, who almost neglect it; it is a dry, fixed, insipid, solid and powdery substance, which remains after the said liquors and the fixed salts have been extracted. These are the five elements of the chemists, which

are
