CHAPTER IX

are admitted by them as the principles of bodies. Here I note in passing that the op‐

erations of the chemists are by no means to be neglected, nor indeed to be held of no

account. For it must be confessed, as Du Hamel says [p], that Physics has taken great

increases from the labors and experiments of the chemists. Hence many arts very

useful for life have flowed. What is to be determined about the system of the

Elementarians and of the chemists we shall see later.

Our doctrine on the internal principles

of bodies is set forth. 56

I say, first: The physical nature of matter seems to consist in this, that it is a sub‐

stance impenetrably extended, consisting of primordial parts that are most

minute, and these homogeneous as regards substance, but unequal and diverse as re‐

gards bulk, figure, motion and like affections. Proof, by parts. The physical nature of

the matter of natural bodies is placed in that by which it has the capacity, as first sub‐

ject, with a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite, and which it is

known to have both by reason and, so far as is permitted, by the experience of the

senses; but by this very fact, that matter is a substance impenetrably extended, it has,

and is understood to have, whatever is required for it to be able, as first subject, with

a form supervening, to constitute a natural composite: therefore. The minor is plain:

for, this being established, it is capable of motion and rest, of varied disposition,

composition, texture, and other affections of this kind; from which results, as will be

plain hereafter, the substantial form with which it constitutes the natural composite.

57 The second part of the proposition is evident: for since matter in the composi‐

tion of bodies is understood to be something first, as belongs to the notion of a first

principle, it is therefore rightly asserted to consist of primordial particles. That these

particles are most minute the stupendous divisibility of bodies, to be weighed here‐

after, demonstrates to evidence; but now, in confirmation of this matter, we shall em‐

ploy only two experiments.

58 The most illustrious Boyle observes [q] that one grain [*] of copper, dissolved

in

spirit

[p] Tract. 1, General Physics, Diss. 3, ch. 5.

[q] De mira subtilitate effluviorum, ch. 3.

[*] An ounce contains 480 grains.

p. 29

spirit of sal ammoniac, imbued so great a quantity of water with a blue color, and that a conspicuous and saturated one, that it contained 256806 parts equal to that little grain. The most learned Fr. Francesco Lana testifies [r] that as much gum lac as would suffice to fill a walnut shell tinges with an intense color such a quantity of water as is enough to imbue a thousand paper leaves on both sides with the same color. Since, then, on any one leaf a thousand millions of colored points can conveniently be marked, there will be on all those leaves 1,000,000,000,000 visible colored points, distinct from one another. These things certainly prove that the parts of matter are most minute. Next, that these smallest parts are unequal in their magnitude, and diverse in figure and motion, is manifest from this, that this inequality and diversity of the most minute parts must be asserted in order that the sensible qualities and operations of any natural body may be rightly and conveniently explained.

59 These most minute parts of bodies, finally, can certainly be homogeneous, and not diverse as regards substance, since it is by no means required that they be substantially diverse in order that from their union bodies may emerge whose sensible qualities are diverse from one another, and whose operations are quite dissimilar. For composites can be made from those primordial parts of matter whose sensible qualities and operations are quite diverse from one another, although the parts themselves differ not at all from one another as regards substance: for since they are of unequal magnitude and diverse figure, they can be artfully disposed among themselves in diverse ways; finally, some of them can be moved in diverse directions within the whole that they constitute, and others be at rest in it, which quite suffices for bodies endowed with dissimilar qualities to be capable of being composed of them: therefore those parts can certainly be homogeneous.

60 I say, second: The essential, or substantial, form of natural bodies devoid of life, if it is regarded physically, is nothing different from that disposition, congruence and proportion of the particles of which the bodies themselves are composed intrinsically and as to their essence. Proof: given a certain disposition, proportion, etc., of the parts of matter, and everything else taken away, a corporeal being, or a substantial composite specifically distinct from others, is understood perfectly well: but by substantial form nothing else is understood than that ground by which this composite is actually such, specifically different from others, and by reason of which it has these special effects and properties: therefore. The major is proved by the example of a plant: given precisely a certain disposition, organization, etc., in the particles of matter, an excellent account is had of how the nutritive sap is sucked up, distributed, etc., and why such a vegetating body is a plant and not a stone, etc., without there ever being need to recur to anything else in order to explain these phenomena, these attributes of the plant: therefore.

61

(r) Magisterium naturae et artis, vol. 1, tract. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 3.

p. 30

61 The same reasoning holds in the remaining bodies. For if (as Du Hamel rightly says (s)) we wish to designate the form and species of gold, we shall adduce its properties: that it is the most ductile of all, that it is not dissolved in aqua fortis as silver is, etc. And a skilled goldsmith, when he has seen those qualities come together in some body, will not doubt that it is true gold, nor will he be anxious whether there is in it some absolute form of gold. For were that form withdrawn, so long as those endowments remained, it would be pure gold: and the same is the reasoning for all bodies; therefore the essential, or substantial, form of bodies devoid of life is nothing different from a certain aggregate of sensible qualities, which arises from a certain disposition, motion and other affections of the parts of matter. To these is added that, from a substance extended, impenetrable, mobile, divisible, yet everywhere like itself and uniform, things most dissimilar can spring up if it is variously configured, determined, modified.

62 For just as from the varied drawing of little lines, dissimilar only in situation, posture and figure, all the letters of the alphabet come forth, which, variously placed, make innumerable words, and can be permuted in such a way that, having made the calculation, the excellent geometer Tacquet (t) does not hesitate to affirm that a thousand millions of writers could not in a thousand millions of years write out all the permutations of the 24 letters of the alphabet, even if each of them finished 40 pages daily: so too the homogeneous parts of matter, disposed in diverse mode, figure and situation, and connected and combined in diverse order, produce that incomprehensible variety of things which the Infinite Creator has displayed in reality, and which so many most acute men who have lived since the founding of the world have not been able to attain even in thought.

63 To these arguments greater strength accrues from the analogy that exists between the mode of operating of nature and that of art; for the works of both, however great the difference that separates them, yet agree wonderfully in this, that in both the ground by virtue of which they are composites in a certain class of corporeal things, and both are and come to be, falls back on certain modifications, coordinations, motions and textures of the parts of matter, and consists in the complex of qualities and affections of this kind. Now, from the axioms established above, our system of the physical nature of matter and of form must be confirmed.

64 That system is to be preferred which is simpler and explains the properties of a natural body from fewer principles (Axiom II). Likewise, that which unfolds more of the things pertaining to Physics, and expresses the reasons of the phenomena not merely by general notions, but sets forth the nature and affections of bodies specifically and to the capacity of the mind (Axiom III & IV). In which, finally, nothing is asserted or assumed that it would never be possible sufficiently to comprehend in thought or to explain

(Axiom

(s) General Physics, tract. 1, Diss. 1, ch. 2, Concl. 2.

(t) In Verdries, General Physics, Tract. 1, §. 3.

p. 31

(Axiom V). And such is our system, inasmuch as it excludes the multiplicity of so many semi-substances and, when nature is considered, lays down a homogeneous matter: in which (as will be plain in the course of the Physics) the nature and affections of bodies and the causes of effects are rendered in a way accommodated to our understanding, and by distinct notions; which, finally, repudiates abstruse mysteries never to be explained, as everyone will understand from the discussion of the systems: therefore it is necessary that our system should prevail in Physics.

65 From what has been said you will infer I. That in our opinion form is not an absolute entity, but something modal and relative: for that texture, proportion, combination, etc., of the parts of matter, in which form consists, are mere modes. You will infer II: that if this name substance is taken for a being existing by itself, the essential form of natural composites devoid of life (for we are speaking only of these) is not entitatively a substance, as is self-evident. You will infer III, that the said form, properly speaking, is neither produced, nor made, nor generated, as the Angelic Doctor excellently says in very many places; for everything that is made, says St. Thomas (u), is always a composite, but form is not a composite. We are by no means speaking of the rational soul, which is truly and properly the form of man, and is created by God alone.

66 Material form, therefore, or essential form, is not produced, nor made, nor generated, but the composite is: for since the said form is nothing else than that disposition, proportion, texture, etc., and these are nothing else than something modal, form cannot be made except improperly, inasmuch, namely, as it is so denominated from the production of the composite; for when the parts of matter are joined, variously disposed, etc., which is for the composite to be composed or generated, there are necessarily in them those presences, dispositions, etc., which we call form; form, therefore, is not made otherwise than insofar as the composite is made or generated, which can best be set out in an artifact. You will infer IV. that for form to be contained in the potency of matter is nothing else than that the parts of matter can be variously disposed and conformed. You have an analogy in a statue, which, before it is made from wood, is contained in that wood in potency, inasmuch, namely, as the wood can be formed into a statue.

67 You will infer V. That matter and form are really distinguished, not indeed entitatively, since form is not an entity but something modal, as we have said, nor by the major real distinction, but by the minor real distinction, or modal distinction. When the idea of one thing positively and completely excludes the idea of another thing, then we say that they are distinguished by a major real distinction; thus body and soul are distinguished. The minor, or modal, real distinction is that which is found between a thing and the mode of the thing itself, as the distinction of body from figure, which has already been stated in the Ontology too. But everything that does not subsist by itself

CHAPTER X

is not properly a being, but a mode of a being, since to subsist by itself belongs no less to

a substance, or thing, or being, than to inhere belongs to an accident, or mode of a being.

By inescapable arguments drawn from Tosca (x), substantial

forms that are absolute entities, as they are commonly defended

by the Peripatetics, are struck from the roll of Philosophy.

68

I say, first: substantial forms of bodies devoid of life, such as are absolute entities,

entitatively distinct from matter, and incomplete substances in the Peripatetic

sense, are of no use in Physics, and can be of no help for explaining the causes of

natural things, and accordingly ought to be banished far from Philosophy. Proof.

For what experiment will be assigned that has ever been explained by their help?

What have they contributed to understanding the impressions of the air, or the ac‐

tions of earth, sea or fire? What phenomenon of nature has ever been set forth by

the help of these same forms? Turn over, for all I care, the authors who have toiled

at uncovering the hidden secrets of nature, and you will find none who has called in

the help of the said forms to accomplish it: therefore.

69 I say, second: the said substantial forms by no means agree with the princi‐

ples of natural Philosophy, especially the Aristotelian. Proof 1. Every entity existing

in the nature of things, and which is outside God, is produced; but such substantial

forms, if they were given, would exist outside God in the nature of things: there‐

fore they would be produced; but they are not produced: therefore they do not ex‐

ist. The subsumed minor is proved, 1. because this is the express doctrine of

Aristotle and of the Angelic Teacher. For the first, in bk. 7 of the Metaphysics, ch. 8,

text 26 & 27, proves at sufficient length that the form is in no way made, but only

the composite, and concludes the proof of this matter thus: it is manifest, therefore,

that neither the species is made, nor whatever the form ought to be called; which afterwards,

in ch. 12 of the same book, text 32, he extends to accidental forms as well.

Moreover,

in

(x) Philos., vol. 3, bk. 1, tract. 3, prop. 35.

p. 33

in bk. 1 of the Physics, text 64, he says: It is manifest from what has been said that everything that is made is always composite. The Angelic Doctor defends this very point in the places cited [§. 65]. Indeed, this very thing is shown most clearly also by the testimony of Cicero, who, since he knew Greek to a marvel, and understood Aristotle and Plato and the others, whom he had read attentively, much better than even all the common Peripatetics gathered into one, says in more than one place that the Peripatetics and the Academics differ in names but agree in substance; and since it is clearer than daylight that the Academics in no way admitted such substantial forms, we must say that Aristotle, in expounding physical things, never took refuge in such forms.

70 Proof 2. Whatever is produced outside God is produced either by creation or by generation; but substantial forms are produced neither by creation nor by generation: therefore. The minor is proved as to its second part: if forms were generated, they would be made out of something existing in them; but this can be nothing else than matter: therefore they would be made out of matter existing in the forms themselves: therefore the forms themselves would coalesce out of matter and form. I will frame the same argument about the form of the form, and so on to infinity: therefore, to avoid an inconvenience of this kind, it must necessarily be said that form is neither generated nor made, and consequently is not an absolute entity, as the Peripatetics contend.

71 They reply: the form is truly not made when the composite whose form it is is generated, but is educed from the potency of matter, and therefore is not created. But against this: for to be educed from the potency of matter does not befit a form that is entitatively a substance: therefore either that form is not entitatively a substance, or it is created when the composite is produced. The antecedent is proved: that a form is educed from the potency of matter is nothing other than that it is so made that it is necessary, at least in the natural order, that a subject exist in which it is produced and conserved: therefore a form which is educed from the potency of a subject necessarily depends on it in becoming, in being, and in being conserved, which is the same as saying that the form inheres in the subject; but to inhere in a subject befits only a physical accident, because a physical accident inheres in a subject and depends on it, at least by the forces of nature, in becoming, in being, and in being conserved: therefore, taking substance as it is taken by the Peripatetics, namely for a being existing by itself, a form that is a substance in this sense cannot be educed from the potency of matter. For to exist by itself and to inhere in a subject are wholly opposed modes of existing, as is evident.

72 Proof 3. Every substantial entity really distinct from others can properly be made and generated; but form, according to Aristotle and St. Thomas, cannot properly be made and generated [§§ 65 & 69]: therefore it is not a substantial entity, but only a mode modally distinct from matter. Proof 4. If the said entitative forms were given, they would be annihilated in the destruction of the composite; but they are not annihilated: therefore. The major is proved: an entity which ceases to be according to its whole being is annihilated,

E2 but

p. 34

T H E A R G U M E N T S O F T H E P E R I PAT E T I C S A R E A N S W E R E D

but the said forms, in the destruction of the composite, cease to be according to

their whole being: therefore.

73 They reply that the said forms are not annihilated although the composite is

destroyed, because their subject remains. For annihilation is the ceasing of a thing

with no subject remaining; destruction, on the contrary, is that in which the subject

always remains, as is clear from the definitions. But against this: for these very defini‐

tions are arbitrary, and by no means consonant with common notions. For who, un‐

less he clings tooth and nail to Peripatetic prejudices, would not grasp that a thing

goes into nothing when it no longer exists in the nature of things? And what does it

matter that the subject (namely a wholly different thing) remains, so that we should

use the word not of annihilation but of destruction? as though there were in reality

some difference whether we speak in this way or otherwise. We shall therefore be of‐

fering mere words, and Philosophy will not be advanced a nail’s breadth by these cir‐

cumlocutions and logomachies.

74

O bj. 1, against 1. It implies a contradiction that the parts of matter should be ho‐

mogeneous, or of the same nature, and should differ from one another as to fig‐

ure, bulk, etc.: therefore either they do not differ from one another, or they are not

of the same nature. I deny the antecedent: for although the parts of matter do not

differ as to substance, since all are homogeneous, they differ nevertheless in their art‐

ful dispositions, and no repugnance is found in this: for all admit that very many mol‐

ecules, or parts, of gold, certainly of the same nature, can by art differ in affections of

this kind, while some are made cubical, others spherical, etc.

75 Obj. 2. If the parts of matter differ from one another as to bulk, figure, etc.,

then matter is not indifferent to receiving all forms: therefore it will not be a deter‐

minable principle. The antecedent is evident: for one body, e.g. air, by the very fact that

it has dissimilar properties, must also comprise particles, by which it is constituted,

different from those of fire. Reply: by the very fact that the most minute parts are

apt for a most diverse combination among themselves and demand none in prefer‐

ence to another, it is sufficiently understood that matter is indifferent. The four and

twenty letters we use differ in figure and magnitude; yet who would deny that of

themselves they are indifferent to being gathered into definite words, or to being

bound by no laws, to being constrained into verses by the laws of meter, or to com‐

posing a more freely flowing speech? We by no means contend that it belongs to the

notion of matter that the very same parts which are in one composite should, with

no change at all supervening, constitute any other.

76 Obj. 3. It belongs to matter to be the first subject of all natural changes, and of

bodies of incredible variety and discrepant

from

p. 35

from one another; but matter, which is everywhere of the same kind and not of diverse nature, cannot accomplish this: therefore. I deny the minor. For all variety must be derived from the varied disposition, combination, etc., of matter, that is, from form. Thus from the juices of the earth, by the mere percolation of their parts transmitted through the fibrils of a tree, bark, flowers and fruits are born. From foods likewise chyle, blood, bones and flesh, which differ greatly from one another, are formed by the mere transposition of parts, a new order, etc. Accordingly the variety of bodies coheres most aptly with a matter homogeneous as to substance.

77 You will insist. If the parts of matter are supposed homogeneous, from their addition and conjunction there would not result some new essence, but a certain homogeneous integral whole, which would not be of a different nature from one part of it; just as, when we add water to water, we do not make another essence, but extensively increase the same essence of water that is found in any drop; but this is against experience: therefore. It is confirmed: if a musician joined two voices like each other in all respects, he would by no means make a diapason; for this it is necessary that they be of diverse nature, the lower, namely, double of the higher: therefore the same must be said in our case.

78 To 1, I deny the consequence: for in order that a composite specifically different from others may be produced, it suffices that the parts of matter be of diverse nature, not indeed substantial, but only modal; that is, it suffices that they be diversely figured, diversely extended, etc.; which is very different in the addition of water to water: for what is added is of altogether the same nature as the other, namely of the same figure, of the same state, namely of fluidity; and from the addition no new combination is made, no new texture, and consequently no new form and essence, but only the same water becomes more extended.

79 The confirmation of the argument, however, rather confirms our opinion; for the voices that compose a diapason do not differ essentially, but only accidentally, namely in quantity and motion: for the lower is greater and moves more slowly, the higher shorter and quicker; for the diapason, or octave, consists in this alone, namely that the lower voice moves twice as sluggishly as the higher, so that the latter performs two vibrations in the time in which the lower completes only one. Just as, therefore, the species of this consonance, the diapason, coalesces from the combination of voices diverse only in motion and magnitude, so from particles of matter diverse in magnitude, figure, etc., all the species of things can arise.

80 Obj. 4. If we say that matter is a substance consisting of parts diverse in bulk, figure, etc., it is not the essence of matter that is explained by us, but body itself: therefore. The antecedent is proved: it is the nature of matter that it is not complete; but the particles of which matter consists are complete: therefore. I distinguish the minor: they are complete in the character of matter, I grant; in the character of a natural composite, or sensible body, I deny. By us only the essence of matter physically considered is set forth:

in

p. 36

in the character of matter it is something complete; but in the character of sensible

body it is not completed except by the form, which arises from a certain complex, or‐

der and proportion of the parts.

A RG U M E N T S AG A I N S T T H E S E C O N D C O N C LU S I O N .

81

O bj. 1, the principal argument of the Peripatetics. In the Sacrament of the Altar

the accidents of bread and wine remain, but the substantial form of bread and

wine does not remain: therefore the substantial form is something besides a certain

aggregate of accidents. I distinguish the major: the accidents remain, taken in the

Peripatetic sense, for accidental forms, or absolute qualities inhering in a subject, I

deny the major; in the Theological and Dogmatic sense, taken for species, which in an

ineffable and plainly miraculous way deceive us, I grant the major. And, having round‐

ly granted the minor, I distinguish the consequent: the substantial form is something

besides a certain aggregate of Peripatetic accidents, I let the consequent pass; be‐

sides the aggregate of accidents such as are so called by the Moderns, that is, besides

the texture and combination of the molecules of corporeal matter, I subdistinguish:

where such a texture and combination is really given, I deny; where it is not really

given, but nevertheless so appears to the senses as if it were truly given, I grant.

82 The matter comes back to this, that we understand the accidents of bread and

wine in the Most Holy Sacrament of the Altar not to be true corporeal qualities, ab‐

stracted from the body of the bread and wine and left without a subject connaturally

proper to them, but mere appearances (if I may so speak), or species of bread and

wine, under which the most true Body and the most true Blood of Christ the Lord

lie hidden. We, therefore, taught by the Orthodox faith, deny that the substance of

bread and wine lies beneath them after the consecration; but, taught by Philosophy,

we shall deny that those things which appear are true accidents.

83 It is, therefore, a Dogma of the Catholic Faith that in the Venerable

Sacrament of the Eucharist the body and blood of Christ the Lord exist truly, really

and substantially. So it was expressly defined in the Council of the Lateran (y), in that

of Constance (z), in that of Florence (a) and in that of Trent (b), against Berengar,

Calvin and other impious Innovators, who dogmatize no less falsely than wickedly

that Christ the Lord is contained in the Eucharist only in sign, or figure, or virtue. It is

also a Catholic Dogma that by virtue of the Consecration there takes place a real

conversion of the whole substance of the bread into the body, and of the whole sub‐

stance of the wine into the blood, of Christ the Lord; which altogether wonderful

and singular conversion the Catholic Church transubstantiation

most

(y) Under Innocent III, ch. 1.

(z) Sess. 8.

(a) In the Decree of Union.

(b) Sess. 13, ch. 1, & Can. 1.

p. 37

most aptly calls. This transubstantiation, moreover, as the celebrated Theologian Honoré Tournely (c) excellently says, has no example in nature, because it is singular; nor can it be comprehended by human reason, because it is wonderful; it lies wholly hidden in the mysteries.

84 It is also altogether most certain that the most Sacred body of Christ the Lord (and the same must be said of his blood) is in the Eucharist Sacramentally, namely in such a manner as, although we can scarcely express it in words (as the Council of Trent wisely admonishes), we must nevertheless most steadfastly believe to be possible to God (d). That mode of existing, indeed, has no example in created things, and is full of miracles, and is therefore deservedly called Sacramental, that is, a mode which belongs to the Sacrament alone. Let these things that have been said suffice for the Peripatetics to see that the most Sacred Dogmas of our Religion are kept safe and sound by us.

85 But since they leave no stone unturned to brand the opinion of the Modern Philosophers on non-substantial forms as heretical, and to persuade the unlearned that the Catholic Dogma of Transubstantiation is overthrown once the opinion of the Moderns is posited, it is worth the trouble to add some things, so that they may see that they have no right whatever to think us guilty of violating the faith. In the first place, then, I should have to count very many Catholic Philosophers who most steadfastly defend the opinion on forms in the very words in which it has been set forth and proved by us, without their Works ever having been proscribed by the Church; nay, they have been approved with the highest praise by great Theologians. Let it suffice to name some. Klaus, Macko, Regnault, Paulian, Scherffer, Lanis, Corsini, Hamel, Purchot utterly explode the substantial forms of the Peripatetics. From the family of the Minims, Maignan, Saguens and Jacquier; from the illustrious family of the Minors, the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia, who suffices for a thousand; from the Congregation of the Oratory of St. Philip Neri, the celebrated Tomás Vicente Tosca, and very many others from the French Oratory.

86 What of the fact that this doctrine is publicly defended throughout all Europe, and at Rome especially, in the Universities and Colleges, before the Roman Pontiff himself? Let us now hear the illustrious Melchior Cano. I think (says the celebrated man) that the testimony even of many Scholastic Theologians, if other learned men contend against them, is of no more weight for producing belief than their reasoning; that is to say, that in a Scholastic disputation a Theologian ought not to be overwhelmed by the authority of the greater number, but that if he has a few Men with him, provided they are weighty ones, he can surely stand against very many (e). Among the Theologians, moreover, there are not a few who expressly teach that the opinion of the Moderns on non-substantial form agrees perfectly with what the Church holds concerning the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist, and that it can therefore, without harm

to

(d) Sess. 13, ch. 1.

p. 38

to Religion and with the Faith secure, be defended by a Catholic man. So the celebrated Robert Holcot (f), of the illustrious family of the Preaching Fathers. So the most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly (g). So the most learned Prelate Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (h). So the celebrated Lodovico Antonio Muratori (i). So Father Vanrroy (j). So the most renowned light of the Augustinian Order, Lorenzo Berti (k). So the celebrated Noël Alexandre (l).

87 But it is better to hear the most learned Theologian of the illustrious family of the Preachers, Hyacinthe Serry [m]: “Why should I relate other things” (says the celebrated man)? “Are the systems of the recent School to be subjected to the rash censures of certain Theologians? Most philosophers now, following Descartes, place the essence of physical body in the extension of quantity, and hold that substance itself is in no way distinguished from quantity; and the Church, as I know for certain, permits them to philosophize thus. Why then do you brand them with censures? And those whom the common Mother cherishes as sons, do you curse as heathens and publicans, because they seem to you perhaps to shake the faith of the most holy Eucharist? Your study and zeal for the House of God I praise highly and commend: but I would have it be according to knowledge. You will be by far a better Theologian if you reconcile the system permitted by the Church with the faith of the Eucharist.

88 “This will perhaps be done not unfittingly if you say that the conversion of the substance of bread which is wont to take place in the Sacrament of the Eucharist has been defined by the Church, but that the mode of the change has not been so defined; and that the Mystery stands just as well if, the substance being changed together with the quantity, only the external sensations produced in our senses remain (as Descartes thinks), as if, the substance alone being changed, the true quantity remains with the other accidents, as the Peripatetics judge. And that for this reason the Fathers of Trent used the word species for what remains when the substance has been taken away, when they could have named them accidents: namely, so that by the word species they might signify simply those sensations which both Cartesians and Peripatetics profess to be produced in our senses alike, whether the quantity, being undistinguished from the substance, perishes, or, being distinct, does not perish. If you do not say this, but charge the Cartesians with violating the faith until the Church passes sentence against them,

you

you are not a Theologian but a most audacious censor; you fight not for the Faith but for preconceived opinions; you contend not for the Church but for the Aristotelian School.” Thus far the most Eloquent Theologian. What do the Peripatetics say to this? Let them see to it themselves.

89 “For it is not enough” (says the celebrated Cano) “for passing sentence of heresy to have touched upon the heresy itself by suspicion; but a certain comprehension is needed, so that we may judge of errors without error” (n). “Let the Peripatetics therefore cease” [I use the words of the celebrated Muratori] “to leave no stone unturned whereby they may defame the Modern Authors of new opinions, though these have nothing at odds with our Holy Religion, and tear their books to pieces, proscribe them, and present them to the Supreme Tribunals of the Church to be pierced through” (o).

90 Further, it must not be passed over in silence that that opinion too is held by many Peripatetics to be heretical which denies that quantity is really distinguished from corporeal substance. This censure, then: is it true or false? If true: then the Most Eminent Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church Pierre d’Ailly, Auriol, Ockham, Biel, Melchior Cano, who deny that real distinction of quantity (p), are heretics, which surely no sensible person will say of such great Men: then likewise all those Scholastics are heretics, especially of the School of the Scotists, who think the quantity of bodies is to be placed not in their entitative extension but in their impenetrability, chiefly for this reason, that extension is not an absolute accident really distinct from corporeal substance, but substance itself is of itself entitatively extended, that is, with every accident excluded.

91 Then the Subtle Doctor himself is a heretic, who (q) steadfastly maintains (as the celebrated Fortunato da Brescia says) [r] that continuous permanent quantity consists in extension, that is, in the order of the parts in the whole, as Father Hiquaeus, the Commentator of Scotus, says. But if that censure is false (as in truth it is): then that one too must by the same right be held entirely false which the very same men pronounce on the opinion that denies absolute accidents. For what the Church understood by the name of species, or what at length their physical nature may be, has nowhere been handed down by her, just as it has nowhere been defined by her either that quantity too is comprehended under the name of species.

92 Nor let the Peripatetics say that the Council of Constance (s) defined against Wycliffe and John Hus that there are accidental forms in the Eucharist. For that is false: for, as the celebrated Verney says [t], it is established from the Historians that Wycliffe never said that there are no accidents in the Eucharist, but that under the accidents is the substance of bread, and not Christ.

This error, then, the Council condemned; it did not say that the existence of accidents in the Peripatetic sense is a Dogma.

93 It is therefore established by Faith that under the species of bread and wine which present themselves in the Eucharist there is contained, not the nature and substance of bread and wine, but the true Body of Christ the Lord. But that the aforesaid species are absolute accidents, as the Peripatetics contend, the Church has nowhere defined: nor has any question of this kind ever been raised in the Church; nay rather (u), I nowhere read that the existence of the species in the Eucharist was doubted, which no one but a blind man or a madman could have denied. And so much on the Venerable Sacrament of the Eucharist. Let us dissolve the other arguments of the Peripatetics.

94 Obj. 2. If a natural composite devoid of life were composed essentially of particles of matter differing among themselves only in mechanical affections, it would not be one per se but one per accidens, as consisting by no means of an act per se and a potency per se: but this is false, just as it is also manifestly false that there is no difference whatever between natural and artificial composites: therefore. Dist. maj.: it would not be one per se, if by this name is understood a whole made of a double semi-substance, I grant; if a whole is understood which is primarily and per se intended by operating nature, I deny the maj.; and in the same way dist. the min.; I deny the conseq. In the opinion of the Moderns, which is also ours, the natural composite is one per se, and is more than sufficiently distinguished from the artificial one.

95 For it is one, because it is undivided in itself and divided from everything else. It is one per se, because the particles which constitute it are united together by the diverse intention of operating nature: whereas in an artificial composite the parts which constitute the artificial whole are coupled together by the direct intention of the artificer. It also consists of an act per se and a potency per se. For the mechanical affections are in matter by the direct intention of nature, and by the same intention they determine the matter itself to constitute a composite one in species. Nor do I think that anything else can be understood by the name of potency and act per se without a manifest begging of the question, as I shall say below.

96 Inst.: every natural composite is one substantial whole: therefore its essential form must be entitatively a substance; for otherwise it would in no way be distinguished from an accidental composite. Dist. antec.: it is one substantial whole, that is, intended per se by nature, I grant; in another sense, gratuitously devised by the Peripatetics, let it pass; and I deny the conseq. I call a substantial whole, then, that which, whatever at length the essence of the component parts may be, is regarded by operating nature primarily and per se when it acts; an accidental whole, on the other hand, that which either is not regarded by nature, as an effect by its cause, but only by art; or is regarded by it not primarily, but secondarily

only

(u) So the above-praised Verney, De Re Metaphysica. Rome, printed by Generoso Salomoni.

p. 41

only, and as it were for the sake of another thing directly willed by it. Thus a house, e.g., since it is made only by art, is an accidental whole. For the rest, these and other instances of the kind which fill the writings of the Scholastics rest on principles which are neither known from the terms themselves nor demonstrated from others, but which, first devised according to arbitrary hypotheses, were soon believed rather than known, when they had been entered on the authority of others in the register of axioms.

97 For what, I ask, do those words mean: One per se, a whole per se, a substantial whole? What do these mean: act per se and potency per se, or a whole being composed of act per se and potency per se? For if by the name of one per se, etc. a composite is understood which arises from a double semi-substance, what is in question is assumed as if certain, or the same is shown by the same, as they say. For to say a natural composite is one per se is just the same as to say a natural composite arises intrinsically from a double substance, or the form of any natural composite is entitatively a substance. But if by the name of one per se is meant that which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, it is plain that nothing can legitimately be inferred from this which would in the least favor establishing the existence of the forms of the Scholastics.

98 Obj. 3: one natural composite is distinguished substantially from another: but to be distinguished substantially is the same as to be distinguished by an entity which is a substance: therefore its essential form is entitatively a substance. Dist. maj.: it is distinguished substantially, that is, essentially, or in respect of something pertaining intrinsically to their essence, I grant; that is, by an entity which is a substance, I deny; and the conseq. For substance can be taken in two ways: first, for the essence of a thing; second, for an entity which does not need a subject in order to exist. Taken in the first way, those things are distinguished substantially which differ among themselves by something pertaining intrinsically to their essence. Taken in the second way, those things differ substantially which are discriminated among themselves by an entity that is a substance. That natural composites differ essentially is certainly true; that their difference arises from the form, all admit; but that they are distinguished substantially, namely by a form which is entitatively a substance, this must be proved by the Peripatetics, not assumed without hesitation as though it were most certain. For in this lies the question, as is plain.

99 Inst.: things that differ by a form which is entitatively an accident differ accidentally: therefore, for natural composites to differ substantially, they must differ by a form which is entitatively a substance. Dist. antec.: things that differ by a form, etc., differ accidentally, if that form does not pertain to the essence of the things compared with one another, I grant; if it pertains to their essence, I deny; and the conseq. For no one is unaware that a white thing, e.g., differs no less essentially by whiteness from everything that is not white than a man

F2 is

p. 42

is distinguished essentially by rationality from that which is not a man. And the reason is that whiteness pertains intrinsically to the essence of a white thing no less than rationality does to the essence of man. Artificial dispositions, therefore, although considered in themselves they are accidents, nevertheless, because they essentially constitute a natural composite, bring it about that the composite itself is distinguished essentially, or substantially, from any other.

100 They urge: a natural composite is essentially a substance: therefore its form cannot be an accident; for it cannot happen that a substance be composed of an accident. Dist. antec.: it is essentially a substance by reason of the matter, I grant; by reason of the form, if it lacks life, I deny; and the conseq. A natural composite devoid of life, then, is not a substance except in the way in which man is called a corporeal substance; namely, just as man is not a corporeal substance except by reason of matter, and by no means by reason of form, so a natural composite which lacks life is a substance not by reason of form but only by reason of matter; and just as it is not repugnant that man should consist intrinsically of body and spirit, so it implies no contradiction that a natural composite should be essentially composed of substance and accident as of parts.

101 Obj. 4. If a form which is entitatively a substance is taken away, there is no longer any substantial generation: for matter is not generated: therefore a form which is entitatively a substance must necessarily be admitted. Dist. antec.: there is no longer any substantial generation, if by this name is understood the production of a composite whose form is a substance, I grant; if by this name is meant a composite which is regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, I deny the antec. and the conseq. For just as a natural composite can be regarded primarily and per se by operating nature, and so be one per se and a substantial whole, although its essential form is not entitatively a substance, so this very thing does not prevent its production from being rightly called substantial generation. But if this does not please the Scholastics, let them prove that substantial generation occurs in nature in the sense in which they themselves take it: for otherwise they hold as certain what is in question.

102 “To show,” says a most renowned man (x), treating of this matter, “that this argument is a mere begging of the question, we need only lay bare the equivocation that lies hidden in the word generation. For if by generation we understand the natural production of a new whole in nature, such as is the production of a chick from an egg, then rightly and deservedly it must be said that in this sense there is generation; but from this it could not be inferred that substantial forms also exist, since the disposition of the parts effected by nature is able to produce these new wholes and these new natural beings. But if by the word generation

is

(x) The author of the Art of Thinking, pt. 3, ch. 19.

p. 43

is understood, as is commonly done, the production of a new substance which had never existed before, namely of a substantial form, the very thing will be supposed which is in question, since it is clearer than daylight that one who denies substantial forms cannot grant that nature produces such things. Nay, so far is anyone from being driven by this argument to admit substantial forms, that he ought even to draw from it a wholly opposite conclusion, in this manner: if there were substantial forms, nature could produce anew substances which did not exist before; but nature does not produce such things anew; for such a production would be a kind of creation: therefore there are no substantial forms.” Thus far the praised Author.

103 Obj. 5. There is in every natural composite, not even excepting those which lack life, an active principle of diverse operations; but this principle cannot be anything but a substantial form, as it is taken by the Scholastics: therefore we must admit a form of this kind in every composite. Reply by denying the min.: for the active principle, if any exists in natural composites which lack life, is nothing but the subtler portion of those corpuscles of which the composite itself essentially coalesces: for there is no purely corporeal operation in nature which is not wholly accomplished through the motion of the subtlest corpuscles.

104 They say: it is evident that there is in each natural composite a force by which they recover their congenital qualities. For it is plain that heated water recovers its former coldness as if of its own accord: therefore some substantial principle, wholly different from the artificial dispositions of matter, must be admitted in them. Reply by denying the antec.: for it is manifest that the parts of a tree’s bark, if they have been somewhat scorched by a torch brought near, no longer recover their power of attracting moisture; that an egg violently shaken becomes wholly unfit for incubation; that an apple bruised in some part gradually rots. Nor does the example of heated water prove anything. For, as we shall say in its place, the recovery of coldness arises from without. But if it sometimes happens that some composite recovers lost qualities, we judge that this is to be derived solely from the living substance which is in it.

105 Obj. 6. Prime matter is not a physical and substantial act, because it is pure potency; but this act is the form: therefore prime matter is entitatively not the form: therefore the substantial form is entitatively distinguished from matter. Granting the whole argument, I deny the last conseq.; for although prime matter in itself is entitatively not form, yet from this it by no means follows that the form is entitatively distinguished from matter; for since the form is not an entity but a mode, it is only modally distinguished from matter.

106 Obj. 7. If form were nothing entitative, but only modal, creatures would produce nothing anew, and there would be no created agent,

but

p. 44

but this must not be said: therefore. Proof of the conseq.: for a created agent does not produce matter anew, since it presupposes it; nor the form, which is neither generated nor produced: therefore it produces nothing. I reply that created agents produce neither matter nor form, but only the composite: for creatures, as St. Bonaventure excellently says (z), only bring it about that what was in one mode comes to be in another mode.

107 Obj. 8. Each natural being devoid of life has its own peculiar operations; e.g., in fire is found a particular operation of heating, and so of the rest; but operations of this kind cannot arise from matter, which of itself is inert and has no operative force, and is the same in species in all natural composites: therefore they proceed from the special form of each: therefore this is something entitatively distinct from matter. Dist. min.: the aforesaid operations cannot arise from matter considered in itself, I grant; from matter as modified, I deny; and the conseq.

108 Obj. finally: once our opinion is posited, there is no difference between alteration and generation; but there is one, for in alteration only qualities are produced, in generation a substantial form must be produced: therefore the substantial form is a semi-substance distinct from matter, as the Peripatetics maintain, following the opinion of the Arabs, against the doctrine of Aristotle. Reply: I deny the maj.: for in alteration the same sensible body remains which was there before, since only a few accidents perish from it and a few newly arrive, as when water from hot becomes cold, or when wax from yellow becomes white, or from soft hard. But in generation either all the accidents perish, or, if some remain, they are not enough for the sensible body to be called the same: e.g., when wax has been dissolved into smoke, it cannot be called the same body, although perhaps certain accidents which were before in the wax, e.g. the odor, remain in the smoke, because these few accidents are not enough to constitute wax.

109 Inst. If the matter stands so, generation and alteration are not distinguished except according to more and less; but more and less do not change the species, as the common axiom of the Schools has it: whereas diverse forms constitute diverse species: therefore the substantial form of a body devoid of life is not an artificial disposition of the parts. Dist. min.: more and less do not change the species where only a few accidents perish, I grant; where all or nearly all perish, I deny. But when a new form is given, nearly all the accidents which were in the former subject are destroyed, and new ones succeed, as when from wood comes fire, from wax smoke, etc. Hence a new species then results; for smoke is of a different species from wax, and fire from wood; for those things are judged to differ among themselves in species in which there appears so great a diversity

that what has been proved essentially of the one need not belong to the other. Let

these things that have been said suffice.

On the Secondary, or Sensible, Principles.

efore we propose our opinion, it is useful to affirm that three of the com110

B mon elements, fire, water and earth, seem nothing different from as many

principles of the Chemists, namely mercury, phlegm and caput mortuum. And

as regards mercury, Willis (a), Sennert (b), Boerhaave (c), Lémery (d) and many others

assert that the mercury of the Chemists is that principle which is elemental fire, or a

certain most subtle substance, wholly different from air, and from flame and common

fire; but that water is not discriminated from phlegm, nor earth from caput mortuum,

the Authors praised above show, with others. This laid down, let the conclusion be:

111 The sensible principles of bodies, besides the four common Elements, are

rightly held to be also the twin principles of the Chemists, salt and sulphur. Proof:

from the fact that the said principles can be drawn out of individual bodies by means

of resolution; which indeed, as regards vegetables and animals, no one will call into

controversy who has observed the manifold operations of the Chemists and the di‐

verse condition of the parts dissolved by them. An obvious experience in the burning

of green wood declares this very thing: for the spirituous and most agile particles, re‐

leased as it were from their bonds, are roused into flame and, torn away from the

rest, fly off entirely; the sulphurous, or oily, ones feed the flame, and are gradually

raised up, concreting into the part of soot; the saline ones partly go off into smoke,

sharply stinging the eyes, partly settle in the ashes; the watery ones burst forth at the

very beginning like the tiniest buds, to be dispersed into vapor; earth, finally, remains

as survivor once the salts have been drawn out.

112 This very thing can be demonstrated of the mineral kingdom by the example

of iron. The celebrated Boerhaave (e), speaking of iron dissolved in Rhenish wine,

says: this is the highest remedy known to me so far in the art

and

(a) De Fermentatione, ch. 2.

(b) Works, ch. 11.

(c) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 1.

(d) In the Chemistry.

(e) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 445.

p. 46

and in nature for restoring the haematopoietic force (namely the force of converting chyle

into blood) to the human body, whenever this arises solely from the weakness of over-lax

solids, and from a not very light, watery, cold and inert character of the humors. He adds that

the medicinal power of metals is demonstrated chiefly by this experiment: for by no

virtue of anything vegetable or animal, by no rule of diet, will anyone bring about in the said

case what is accomplished by this Mars.

113 These things surely indicate that there reside in iron certain peculiar endow‐

ments, an active and at the same time subtle substance, to which the Chemists give

the name of spiritus rector, and which we, consistently with what was said above,

think to be the elemental fluid of fire, bound up in a certain ratio, quantity and tex‐

ture with the other principles constituting iron: at least the same solution shows

that such a principle is present in this metal; and hence we deduce by legitimate rea‐

soning that water likewise is comprised in it, as being what all kinds of salts give off

in evaporation. Sulphur is perceived from the odor of iron growing hot under

pounding: finally, both its very hardness and the vitriol contained in iron, which is it‐

self made up of earthy molecules, show that it is compacted of earth.

114 Finally, it will easily be shown convincingly that air is a sensible principle of

bodies, if it be ascertained that those things belong to air which are required for the

character of an element of mixed bodies. For in almost every analysis of composites,

among the rest, aerial particles betray themselves: there is scarcely any humor, says

Boerhaave, with whose parts air does not mingle itself, scarcely any solid from which it cannot

be drawn out by some art; these things being established, we deduce that the sensible

principles of corporeal things are rightly held to be mercury, which we do not distin‐

guish from fire, or the most subtle fluid; then air, salt, sulphur, water and earth.

The arguments are answered.

115

O bj. 1. The Elements of the Chemists are not found in mixed bodies in the form

in which they themselves set them out to us: therefore they ought not to be

sensible principles of bodies. The antecedent is proved: for fire by its action brings

it about that the parts of a body show themselves after the resolution in another

form and state than they were in the mixture; and therefore they must be consid‐

ered as new substances, as it were, produced by fire: therefore. Reply by denying the

antec. of the proof: for, as we shall say in its place, the whole nature of heat consists

in a swift, disturbed and expansive motion impressed on corpuscles; and nothing

else is effected but, first, an expansion, then a disturbed agitation of the parts in the

body, when it conceives heat. Moreover it is evident that by means of the disturbed

and expansive motion of the corpuscles which enter the pores of a natural compos‐

ite no new substance can be entitatively produced, but only that the texture is loos‐

ened and the bond dissolved by which the component particles of the composite it‐

self are held united together; and therefore the destruction of a natural composite,

which

p. 47

which is effected per se by the action of fire, or heat, consists not in the production of some new substance, but only in the dissolution of the bond by which the component parts are tied together.

116 I said that fire, or heat, effects nothing else per se, when it destroys a natural composite, than to dissolve the component parts. For I do not deny that it happens not rarely that some new substance, which had not been in the composite, is produced by the action of heat. But this is entirely per accidens; for a new substance comes to be if the heat is more vehement than the dissolution of the parts requires. For the particles, agitated beyond measure by too great a heat, are so mingled together, those of diverse kinds, that new concretions emerge from it, and hence new substances seem to be produced; but this does not prevent the aforesaid substances from being found in mixed bodies; for from bodies of the same species salt, sulphur and mercury, likewise of the same character, are perpetually extracted, which would surely not happen with such constancy if those substances were produced entitatively by heat; for what is effected by chance happens rarely.

117 Obj. 2. If salt, sulphur and mercury are secondary principles of the composite, the principles will be plainly innumerable, namely as many as there are species of those same things; but this is absurd: therefore. Maj. proved: for, to make mention of salt alone, there will be nearly as many salts differing from one another as there are composite bodies; for salt extracted from ash wood is caustic, that is, it corrodes by burning the flesh to which it is applied; extracted from other woods, it is not so: therefore. Dist. maj.: the principles from which the essential difference of the things themselves is taken will be plainly innumerable, I grant the maj.; those by which they are specifically distinguished, I deny the maj.; and dist. the min.: it is absurd to constitute as many principles by which things differ as there are species of the things themselves, I deny; to constitute as many genera of all the principles as there are genera of composites, I grant the min.; and I deny the conseq.

118 But from this argument nothing is gathered which does not utterly overturn the Scholastic hypothesis of principles. For the Scholastics posit as many genera of essential forms, or formal principles, as there are composites that differ from one another in species.

119 Obj. 3. Iron too must be admitted among the secondary principles: therefore. Proof of the antec.: for in the ashes of very many plants granules are found which go to the magnet and are fused by means of a burning mirror, no otherwise than iron filings, which at length flow together into metallic spherules, as the most renowned Geoffroy attests (f): therefore. The argument proves only that the component parts are bound to one another by so tight a bond that, even when divided into the most minute parts, they retain and preserve the integral nature of iron; but it does not prove that iron must be admitted among the secondary principles of bodies; for, as is attested by

G the

(f) Histoire de l’Académie Royale, 1704, p. 37.

p. 48

the great Boerhaave, iron coalesces out of the very principles which are established by us, so that this metal has its place not among the principles or elements, but among mixed bodies.

120 And what forbids us to say, rather, that in the very act of combustion the fatty, saline, vitriolic-acid and earthy parts, which are the elements of iron, fused into one and joined together, coalesced into true iron? So that, consequently, the extraction of iron from ashes and clay is a true making of it. An argument for this may perhaps be what the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris (g) record: namely, that those composites which burn less readily and give off smoke more copiously, such as herbs and the harder woods, yield iron in their ashes in greater quantity than those which flare up suddenly and give off a more brightly shining flame.

121 Nor perhaps is the origin to be sought elsewhere of the granules of iron which, drawn out of a calcined human calculus by the most renowned Lister, were exhibited to the Royal Society of London (h). So that for this reason the most renowned Boerhaave opportunely came down to this opinion: If any metal, he says, is changeable, if any destructible, it will certainly be this one (i). Yet it will not be permitted to affirm the same of the elements established by us, concerning every resolution universally. For no one is unaware that it is wholly preposterous to draw a general consequence from singular cases, in which circumstances sometimes intervene.

122 Obj. 4. It is established by experience that sulphur especially, and mercury, are resolved into earth and water, as the most renowned men Du Hamel (j) and Du Clos attest: therefore sulphur and mercury are not of that condition of which they must necessarily be in order to be rightly and deservedly held for principles of things. Passing over the antec., I deny the conseq. For since those are laid down as secondary principles of a natural composite, their composition from others does not prevent them from being legitimately held for principles of this kind. However the matter may stand, then, concerning the composition of salt, sulphur and mercury, our assertion will be safe by this alone: that any natural mixture whatever, when it is corrupted by the action of heat, is resolved into earth, water, salt, etc., by their mere separation.

123 Obj. 5. Our opinion being posited, it follows that any particle whatever of a mixture is mixed of salt, sulphur, etc., and so to infinity; but this is repugnant: therefore. Reply: if the talk is of absolutely any particle that is in the mixture, it is true that each of them does not consist of all those things from which the mixture itself essentially arises. But to will that there is no particle in the mixture which is not mixed is just the same as begging the question. For to ask whether a natural mixture is so composed of earth, water,

salt

(h) Journal des Sçavans, 1719, p. 378.

(i) Elementa Chemiae, vol. 2, p. 447.

(j) Vol. 4, Philosophia, ch. 20, no. 9.

p. 49

salt, etc., that the particles of those substances are formally in it, what else is it but to ask whether any natural mixture whatever is of such a nature that there are in it some particles which are not mixed?

124 Moreover, the argument must also be answered by the Scholastics. For if there can be no part in a mixture which is not mixed, there could also be no essential part in a composite which is not essentially composite: therefore matter and form must necessarily be composed essentially of other principles, which likewise must be essentially composed of others, and so on, so that it would be true, namely, that there is no part of a composite which is not composite; but this is absurd: therefore it is absurd also that there is absolutely no part in a mixture which is not mixed. Finally, note: not all the sensible principles are found in every composite, nor always in equal quantity, since experience teaches us that some bodies abound in salt, e.g., but contain less oil and mercury; in others earth holds the chief place; of others the greatest part is sulphur.

125 Obj. 6. Only the four common elements should be laid down as principles of natural body: therefore the Chemical ones are superfluous. Proof of the antec.: there must be as many elements as there are first and principal qualities; but these are four, namely heat, cold, moisture, dryness: therefore. I distinguish the maj. of the proof: if from those qualities alone all the affections, forces and phenomena occurring in composites can be derived, I grant; if they cannot be so, as in truth they cannot, I deny; and the conseq. For, as Sennert (k) argues excellently, an alteration and injury arising from manifest qualities cannot kill a man as suddenly as poisons do. Moreover, poisons in the least quantity can lie hidden unharmed in the body, and at length after a long time put forth their forces.

126 Thus a tiny quantity of the saliva of a rabid dog can remain unharmed in the body and protect itself against the action of our heat, and at length, after not only six but even many more months, induces most grievous changes in our body. And what we have said of poisons can be said of very many other things, whose forces are far greater and nobler than that they could be referred to the first qualities. Who will conveniently reduce the actions of the magnet to the first qualities? Who, again, will derive the manifold colors, odors, flavors, etc. from the said four qualities? These four elements alone, then, endowed with as many qualities, do not settle the matter.

127 Nor does it avail to say that from the mixture of several things it mostly comes about that forces emerge which were not at all present in the miscibles before the mixture; for we grant indeed (says the praised Sennert) that there is more in the composite than in any simple taken separately. Meanwhile it does not follow that there is more in the composite
