than in all the simples which enter into the composition. If several colors are

mixed, there arises indeed a color other than all the simples taken separately,

but still only a color; never, however, from colors mixed in whatever way, will

there come an odor, or a flavor, or another quality of a different species. So the

temperament made of the four first qualities is indeed something other than

the simple qualities taken separately, yet no other quality of another species

arises from it; and however the first qualities are mixed, never will a color, or

any other quality differing in species, come from them.

On the properties of bodies.

he principles of bodies having been established and their nature set 128

T forth, those affections now come to be weighed which are derived

most proximately from the nature of body; and they are magnitude,

figure, situation, divisibility, and above all motion: for a substance by its nature

impenetrable acquires a certain mode of extension, or magnitude, and is divisi‐

ble into parts; it likewise obtains some figure, and a position among other ex‐

tended substances; and finally it is understood to be endowed with an aptitude

for motion and rest. Moreover, it must be in place and time, of which

Physicists are also wont to treat. We shall give the more useful things.

O N T H E M A G N I T U D E O F B O D Y.

It is shown in what the magnitude of body formally consists.

think it certain that the magnitude of a body formally consists in that 129

I by which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or un‐

equal to it; just as by the name of quality is meant that by reason

of

p. 51

130 I say, first, against many Scholastics: the magnitude of body does not

CHAPTER II

of which one thing is called similar or dissimilar to another. This established:

consist formally in its impenetrability. Proof: it is plainly established that any two

bodies agree in impenetrability in such a way that, if they are considered in re‐

spect of it, one can in no way be discerned from the other: therefore either the

magnitude of body is not formally placed in impenetrability, or any two bodies

whatever are equal to each other; but this manifestly opposes the truth: there‐

fore the magnitude of body by no means consists in its impenetrability.

131 I say, secondly: the magnitude of body is nothing different from the enti‐

tative extension of the body itself. Proof: the magnitude of body is formally that

in respect of which one body, if compared with another, is said to be equal or un‐

equal to it; but it is by entitative extension that one body is said to be equal or

unequal to another: therefore the magnitude of body is nothing different from

its entitative extension. The maj. is evident: for two bodies a palm in length are

judged equal for this reason, that the extension of both is the same; whereas bod‐

ies of which one is a palm and the other two palms in length are called unequal,

because the extension of both is not the same, but the one is exceeded by the

other in respect of it. Confirmation of the concl. It is agreed among all that rar‐

efaction is motion toward greater, and condensation motion toward lesser quanti‐

ty; but rarefaction is motion toward greater extension, and condensation toward

lesser: therefore.

132 They reply: the magnitude of body consists indeed in extension, but in

solid, or impenetrable, extension. But against this: because, when impenetrabili‐

ty is prescinded and extension alone is posited, the foundation of equality and in‐

equality is had: therefore impenetrability in no way pertains to the formal notion

of magnitude; just as, for altogether the same cause, it is certain that the hardness

of a body does not concern magnitude. Surely hardness does not pertain to the

formal notion of magnitude for this reason, that two bodies can be unequal and

at the same time equally hard: therefore neither does impenetrability concern

magnitude in any way, since two bodies can be unequal and at the same time

equally impenetrable.

On the Figure and Situation of bodies.

he extension of any body is limited by terms, or surfaces, which en133

T close the matter proper to the body. That order and position which

the surfaces bounding the volume of the body have among themselves

is

p. 52

is called figure, by which a body is said to be spherical, cubical, etc. The exterior conformation of a body, then, is called figure, which namely does not pertain intrinsically to the nature of the thing, and can be common to altogether diverse bodies; but the figure of the parts themselves, constituting a body definite in its kind, which in wax, e.g., must doubtless be other than in iron, is called configuration. Situation is a certain posture, order, combination, texture, or artificial disposition of the molecules themselves in the whole which is intrinsically constituted of them.

134 The surfaces of bodies can be varied in altogether manifold ways. This prodigious variety of figures, moreover, is confirmed by innumerable experiments of the Physicists, of which we shall select the more useful. Keep some drops of the best vinegar on a fragment of glass for some hours, so that they partly evaporate; then look at them through a microscope: you will observe innumerable salts, nearly all pointed. If you keep vinegar in some vessel exposed to the air for some weeks, and more quickly in summertime, you will see with the microscope innumerable, as it were, most tiny eels running about hither and thither. From these, however, it is plain that the sharp taste of vinegar draws its origin not from the eels, as some have thought, but from diverse salts.

135 Put a drop of pure water on glass, and in it dissolve thoroughly a little common salt reduced to powder; after all the water has evaporated of its own accord, observe the drop with the microscope: you will see the salt reduced into crystals of cubical figure. If you dissolve sugar in the same way, you will observe crystals of nearly round figure. Richard Mead, in his Mechanical Account of Poisons, placed upon glass a very small part of the venomous juice which is emitted from the tooth of a viper when it bites, and in a short space of time it was changed into most slender and extremely sharp crystals, which were so rigid that they remained for a month without any change. From the figure and hardness of this poison, then, is to be derived its untamable nature, which sometimes scarcely yields to remedies opportunely applied. If a portion of crushed pepper is kept for some days in a vessel full of water, innumerable animalcules of diverse kind and diverse figure are observed with the microscope.

136 Insects figured in other ways are detected in stagnant water into which bits of cut hay, of chaff and of various plants have been thrown: certain animalcules are seen like globules, others longer and turning themselves round in a circle; in some, feet are distinguished; some are seen ringed like worms; and, in a pleasant spectacle, the greater are often observed to pursue the lesser so as to devour them.

137 If you collect the parts emitted spontaneously, or drawn out of bodies by art with the help of fire, you will notice that they are of the same nature, and produce the same effects, as the bodies themselves. Thus the vapor of water, collected, gives water; the vapors of sulphur and of camphor restore sulphur and camphor anew. But these things would not happen if the parts of bodies did not

have

p. 53

have, and when released did not preserve, the same figure. The parts of water and of other vapors can be observed if bodies evaporate in a small room closed on all sides, into which only a ray of the sun passes to illuminate the vapors. In this way it became known that the parts of water are perfectly round. Many other things worth noting are found in the writings of Leeuwenhoek, Robert Boyle, Martin Lister, Erasmus Bartholin and John Freind, which Authors you will be able to consult when you have the means and the leisure.

138 Since, then, any part whatever of matter, or of body, has its peculiar figure, necessarily, while the parts of some body are actually separated, its surface must be increased. For when the parts are disjoined, and each is contained by its own surface, because it has figure, those internal surfaces of the body by which the parts touched one another become visible, and, together with the old surface under which the whole body was contained, compose the entire surface of the body cut into parts. When, therefore, a body is divided into several parts, its surface is increased while the same mass, or solidity, remains. Wherefore, since the same matter remains and the surface of the body is increased by the continued separation of the parts, the surface will acquire a greater ratio to the matter of the body.

139 From this, moreover, are explained several phenomena which are very often observed when some fluid, such as air, fire or water, acts upon bodies. The action of fluids follows the ratio of the surface of the body; for the greater the surface of the body, the greater the quantity of fluid that acts upon the body. Hence it is excellently explained why a wind which cannot lift a cubic foot of marble carries up in a moment of time several cubic feet of sand to a remarkable height, namely a weight a hundred times greater than the first. For a cubic foot of sand is the same as a cubic foot of marble cut into as many parts as there are grains of sand; but the wind can exert a greater force on marble in powder than on a cubic foot of the same; it will therefore lift a cubic foot of sand, nay several feet of sand, and will not be able to raise a whole foot of marble.

140 In the same way is explained the very great medicinal force of quicksilver, or mercury, for driving out stubborn diseases. A drop of mercury is easily resolved into innumerable most tiny globules, as will be plain if you throw upon it the rays of the sun collected by a concave mirror or a crystal lens. Wherefore its surface will quickly be increased to a wonderful degree within the body, and, this being increased, the mercury will more easily be driven by the fluids of the body into the vessels, and with the force acquired will expel the morbid matter from them; or it will easily open for itself an entrance into the smaller vessels, and so will at least deplete them, whence the circulation of the fluids will become more unimpeded, by which the body recovers from long-lasting diseases. Mercury, then, does not operate by its own weight, as most think, but by its divisibility.

141 From the figure and situation of bodies many phenomena can be explained

and

p. 54

and these no less useful than pleasant to know, of which we shall set forth only some, so that from those which are now to be set forth by us very much light may come to what we shall afterwards say on Statics and Hydrostatics. All bodies, then, are seen to have a certain gravity; hence it comes about that stones, e.g., descend until they are held up by meeting other bodies. They begin to be held up, moreover, when their center of gravity is prevented from descending. The center of gravity, moreover, is the point placed in any heavy body by which, if the body is suspended, all its parts will keep whatever situation you have given them, and so will be in equilibrium. E.g., if a staff or an iron rod is suspended by a thread at its middle part, and each part of it is in equilibrium, that point from which it will be suspended will be its center of gravity, since its parts on either side will be of equal weight.

142 But if that rod is not everywhere homogeneous, that is, of the same nature, suppose if in one part it is of iron and in the other of wood, its center of gravity will not be in the middle of its extension, but will recede from it toward that part of the matter which is denser. Wherefore the center of gravity and the center of magnitude, or of extension, do not always coincide in the same point, but only when the matter of the heavy body is homogeneous: e.g., in an iron globe the center of extension, or its middle point, which is equally distant from the individual points of the surface, can also be conceived as the center of gravity, since the matter in the iron globe is everywhere homogeneous.

143 Now, when a heavy body tends downward, namely to the center of the earth, which they therefore call the center of heavy things, since all heavy things strive toward it, its motion, or descent, is directed along a certain line on which the center of gravity always stands; and for this reason it is called the line of direction, and is defined: the straight line which is understood to be stretched from the center of gravity to the center of heavy things. Now the Axioms are these. First: A heavy body resting on another remains at rest, if the body on which it lies prevents its center of gravity from being moved downward. For since the whole gravity of the body is as it were collected in one point, it cannot happen that the body moves downward if its center of gravity cannot move downward.

144 Second: a heavy body resting on another slips, if its center of gravity is not supported by that on which the body itself rests. For if the center of gravity is not supported, nothing prevents the center itself from tending downward, as the law of nature requires, and consequently the whole body from moving downward. A heavy body, then, can never fall unless its center of gravity falls. But that center cannot fall as long as the body is so placed on a horizontal plane that the line of direction is conceived to pass within its base. Third axiom: The center of gravity of any heavy body cannot ascend except violently; for it is against the law of nature that a heavy body should tend upward as it were of its own accord.

Let

p. 55

145 Let a heavy solid A rest on the horizontal plane D E (Fig. I) by its plane surface m n x, and let its line of direction a b fall within its base m n x. I say that it can then in no way happen that the body A slips downward. For it is evident that the center of gravity a is supported by the plane D E on which the body A rests; but a body cannot fall if its center of gravity cannot move downward [§. 43]: therefore the body A will not fall down. But let there be another body H G (Fig. II) whose line of direction Cd falls outside the base F G; it is understood that it will at once fall toward the side e, because, while the whole body is carried with a circular motion about F, its center of gravity C is continually descending: therefore it must needs fall [§. 144]. Moreover, the center of gravity C is not supported by the plane D E, since the line of direction Cd runs outside the base F G: therefore it is necessary that the body H G should tumble down [§. 144].

146 Hence the reason appears why some leaning towers do not fall, such as those of Bologna and Pisa, observed by me while I was traveling through Italy in the year 1767. The Bologna tower is square, 130 feet high (1). The Pisa tower is round, 138 feet high. The plumb line of the Bologna tower stands off from the base by an interval of 9 feet, while the plumb line of the tower of Pisa runs outside the base over a space of 15 feet. Yet they remain firm and stable, because the line of direction of each is within the base, and therefore neither can tumble down. Hence it also follows that slender bodies, such as a needle, for example, can by no means stand upon their point, for its base is too narrow; whence any inclination, however slight, any impulse of the air, however small, suffices for its line of direction to run outside the base.

147 Hence it is also gathered why a bucket A (Fig. III) full of water, suspended from a rod B C laid on a table, does not fall, provided another rod G D is set upright below the handle and against the end C of the first rod, perpendicular to the bottom of the bucket. For since both rods together with the bucket make one and the same body, the bucket cannot fall without the end B of the rod B C being raised, describing, namely,

the arc B L. But it cannot be raised without the center of gravity i, which is in the bucket, describing at the same time the arc i M, which it cannot describe without ascending upward against the tendency of heavy bodies (Axiom 3, §. 144): therefore the bucket will not be able to fall, but will necessarily hang motionless from the rod.

148 By means of the motion of the center of gravity it is also explained how it can happen that a body, while ascending, continually descends, which at first sight seems a Paradox. Let a triangle A B C (Fig. IV) be constructed of three pieces of wood, whose base C B is equal to the axes of two cones joined together by their bases G F. Under the base C B let two supports C D, B E be placed, shorter than the radius of the base of the cones G F. If those two cones are set upon the extremity A, they will seem to ascend into C B, where the elevation is greatest; yet the center of gravity will descend.

149 That this may be understood more plainly, consider the plane A B b (Fig. V) in which the center of gravity a of the two cones is found. This center is raised above the horizon by as much as the line a b, which is equal to p F. If the cone advanced upon F D, the center of gravity a would describe the line a p parallel to the horizon F D. But the cone in the IV. figure moves along the two planes B A, A C in such a way that its vertex x x is in B C, or in C (Fig. V): therefore in the motion of the cone the center of gravity a describes a C, that is, it continually descends, so that when it arrives at C, its center of gravity will have descended by as much as is marked by p C; but the motion of bodies is determined by the motion of their center of gravity: therefore if the center of the cones descends, as has been demonstrated, the cone must ascend. It is necessary, then, that the double cone should ascend along the two planes of the IV. figure.

150 The knowledge of the center of gravity and of the line of direction is suited to explaining many other things. A man, for example, who sits in such a way that his legs make a right angle with his thighs, and his thighs too are at a right angle with his trunk, will not be able to rise unless he first inclines his shoulders or draws his foot back, so that the line of direction may fall within the base of the feet. If a man stands touching a wall with his shoulders and heels, and resting on the ground only with the tips of his feet, he will not be able to bend himself unless he puts a foot forward; otherwise, when he bends, he must needs fall, because the line of direction then falls outside the base.

151 But it is enough to have touched on these things lightly: for if it were my intention to report all the things that are derived from the figure and situation of the parts, almost all the phenomena both of nature and of art would have to be heaped together here: for nearly all qualities arise from the figure and situation of the parts.

Chapter

p. 57

CHAPTER III

On the divisibility of bodies.

hat divisibility is an affection proper to all bodies, as it is beyond 152

T doubt, so it ought by no means to come into question here; the

Physicists consider only this: how far does that divisibility extend? This

contemplation is indeed of the highest moment in Physics, and for

that reason the modern Physicists have instituted very many experiments and

have illustrated this subject in published writings. But can matter, body, or the

physical continuum be divided to infinity, or must one at last come to a stop at indivisible

parts? It is a controversy which, as Fr. Regnault says (m), has from the very rise

of Philosophy tormented famous and most elegant wits without fruit. We shall

approach the matter with this design: that, having set forth the state of the

controversy, we may candidly expound what can seem certain in it.

153 That, then, is called a continuum which results from parts so joined that

their extremities are one, that is, belong to altogether the same substance, as

are the parts of wood, which compose the same single substance of the wood.

That, however, is called contiguous whose extreme parts are together, as when

hands, or two bodies, touch each other. The parts of some composite are also

said to be placed in succession, or placed side by side, when particles of another

body, e.g. of air, lie between them, as are the grains in a heap of wheat. Those

parts are called aliquot which, repeated some number of times, exactly equal

the whole. Thus the foot is an aliquot part of the fathom, because, repeated six

times, it exactly equals the fathom.

154 Those parts are called aliquant which, repeated any number of times,

never exactly equal the whole, but either exceed it or fall short of it: thus a part

four feet long is an aliquant part of the fathom, because if it is taken twice it

exceeds the fathom, while taken once it does not yet equal it. Proportional parts

are those which decrease in continued proportion; thus the fathom can be di‐

vided into two halves, and either of these into two others, and so on. The

Peripatetics and very many Cartesians judge the parts of the physical continu‐

um to be divisible to infinity. Those who follow Epicurus and Gassendi defend

the contrary opinion.

155 The defenders of the first opinion argue thus. Everything extended is

divisible into parts; but every body, however thin, is always

H2 extended:

(m) Entret. Physiques. Entret. I.

p. 58

extended: therefore every body is always, and to infinity, divisible. The Epicureans reply by distinguishing the major: everything extended taken mathematically, they grant; taken physically, they deny. That is said to be extended mathematically which is considered only by reason of its dimensions, without regard to the condition and nature of the extended subject; that, however, is called extended physically which is considered as a certain physical substance endowed with a definite nature and condition. Whatever is extended can be divided mathematically and by the mind, but not always in reality itself and physically, since there can be a certain simple substance not composed of parts, namely the atom, which is the first subject of which all sensible bodies consist, and the last into which they are resolved. Thus far the Epicureans and Gassendists.

156 These, moreover, argue thus against the Peripatetics: If matter were divisible to infinity, a tiny body, such as a grain of wheat, would contain within itself infinite parts in act, for a body is conceived as divisible only into those parts which it contains; but this is manifestly contradictory: therefore matter, or the continuum, is not divisible to infinity. The Peripatetics reply by distinguishing the major: if matter were divisible according to aliquot parts, a tiny body would have, etc., they grant; if it is divisible only into proportional parts, each of which includes infinitely many others within itself, they deny. You have the state of the question.

157 But all these things (as Purchot and Klaus very well observe) (n) are of such a kind that, if only the reasons, and not the replies, are weighed, they seem on both sides to carry the force of demonstrations. So that it may therefore be permitted to pronounce this one thing: it is uncertain whether corporeal magnitude can always be divided, or whether all its division at last terminates in indivisible parts; which we assert all the more fittingly as we know the more certainly that for the advancement of Physics it is altogether the same whether the parts of the continuum are posited as indivisible or as divisible to infinity; for, for the principles of natural body and for explaining the phenomena in general, it suffices to show that any bodies whatever can be split into parts so minute that reason itself is astonished, which is to be proved by us as clearly as possible in the following proposition.

158 I say, therefore: bodies are actually divided, and can be divided, into utterly minute parts in an altogether stupendous manner. First, indeed, the diffusion of odor furnishes an argument of the extreme subtlety to which an odoriferous substance can attain. Beyond what we have said (§. 58), let an example be the calculation which Fr. Lana Terzi (o) carries out of the smoky exhalations that issue from a tiny grain of incense and occupy every point of a small room. The said Father therefore, supposing a room 20 feet long, as many wide, and rising to a height of 15 feet, affirms, having made the calculation, that the particles

of

(n) Pt. 2, General Physics, no. 128.

(o) Magist. Nat. & Art., Tract. 1, bk. 1, ch. 1, Obs. 4.

p. 59

of smoke actually contained in the room will be 75,000,000,000,000, all of which, though previously shut up in one tiny grain of incense, are nevertheless still so many that they can affect a man’s sense of smell.

159 Fill the vial A (Fig. VI) with a bent neck, which is called an Aeolipile, with rose water or any other fragrant water; put a fire under it, or the case B, in which there is spirit of wine with a lighted wick; the water will soon evaporate through the slender neck, and the odor will be diffused through the whole room, however large. After two or three minutes remove the vial from the fire and stop it up: the diminution of the water will scarcely be sensible, so that a very small quantity of it has been dispersed through the whole air of the room. Now, by a calculation made by the learned Fr. Giovanni della Torre (p), a man most perspicacious in searching out the secrets of nature, it has been ascertained that that very small portion of water which evaporated in the space of three minutes is resolved into 3,583,180,800 particles sensible to the nostrils, which truly surpasses all comprehension.

160 The odors of the fragrant fields of the island of Ceylon are carried toward approaching ships even at a distance of ten leagues. A tiny particle of musk so imbues other larger bodies — clothes, gloves, books — with its odor that they keep the odor for a very long time, and yet continually never cease to give off odoriferous parts. Many similar things are related by Boyle, Keill, ’s Gravesande, and other Physicists. Since, then, with so many odorous particles perpetually flowing off, no sensible loss of substance can be observed in many cases, these effluvia will have to be incredibly subtle.

161 Secondly, it is shown from tinctures. The said Boyle relates that he found by experience that if a grain of copper, dissolved and mixed with spirit of wine, is poured into a lamp whose wick, made of plume alum, is not consumed, a flame tinged with a blue color is produced for a whole half hour; and so new particles of copper continually succeed one another and produce the same color in the flame: so that we cannot sufficiently wonder by what means that particle of copper could have been cut up so minutely as to supply always new color, that is, always new particles.

162 Thirdly, the same is proved from the ductility of gold; for, as the most celebrated Physicist Réaumur (q) testifies, a cubic ounce of gold is beaten out by the gold-beaters into more than five hundred times a hundred thousand square leaves of the utmost thinness; but, what altogether surpasses every power of the imagination, if one of these leaves is wrapped round a silver cylinder and covers its whole surface, and the cylinder is then drawn gradually through several successively narrower holes until it is reduced to the thickness of a very fine thread, or of a hair, the surface of this very long thread will nevertheless appear gilded everywhere, which

certainly

(p) Elem. Physic., vol. 1, no. 135.

(q) Memoires de l’Academ., 1713.

p. 60

certainly cannot happen, as is shown when the calculation is made, unless a single grain of gold is extended to about two leagues.

163 Fourthly, an abyss of minuteness in matter is demonstrated from microscopic observations. Fr. Lana Terzi (r) relates that he observed a very white animalcule which had been invisible to even the most perspicacious eyes, and which, placed under a microscope magnifying twenty-seven million times, appeared equal to a grain of wheat: with a very swift motion it scarcely covered the length of a grain of wheat in twelve seconds of time. What, then, must be the wondrous subtlety of the steps, of the feet, of the eyes, of the pupil, of the blood, of the animal spirits in an animalcule of this kind! The same must be said of those very fine animalcules which are seen in cheese with the help of a microscope. How tiny, moreover, is the pupil of those animalcules, through which nevertheless far finer rays of light pass? How tiny are those parts which can be called animal spirits? If we consider these things, we must needs confess that something greater, and more than our faculty of imagining can present to us, lies hidden in the smallest things.

164 That most skillful investigator of Nature, Leeuwenhoek, observed in water kept for some days, with the help of an exquisite microscope, very small animalcules, thousands of which do not exceed the size of a globule of common sand. Now since any animalcule whatever is an organic body, let us weigh for a little how delicate and subtle must be the parts necessary to constitute it and to preserve its vital action. It is not easily conceived how in so narrow a little space there can be comprised the heart, which is the fount of life, the muscles necessary for motion, the glands, the stomach and intestines, and innumerable other members without which an animal cannot exist. Moreover, since each of the members mentioned is also an organic body, they cannot lack other parts necessary for their actions. They will therefore consist of fibers, little membranes, tunics, veins, arteries, nerves, and similar little canals, whose minuteness far surpasses the powers of the imagination. But almost infinitely smaller than these must be the parts of the fluid which runs through the little canals, namely the blood, the lymph and the animal spirits. What prodigies in the meanest animalcule, and what proofs of the Divine Omnipotence!

165 Nor do the works of nature alone manifestly demonstrate the admirable subtlety of matter: the most celebrated works of art also prove the same, and must with full justice fill us with admiration. The distinguished Derham (s), Fr. Klaus (t) and Sigaud de la Fond (u) relate that Oswald Nerlinger fashioned out of a peppercorn a cup in which were set twelve hundred little ivory cups, each of which was furnished with a stand

166 And these few things, out of the many that could be added, which we have

and adorned with a gilded rim, so much space being still left over that four hundred

put forward to show the extreme divisibility of the continuum and the minuteness of

matter, we conclude with those words with which Pliny (x) begins his treatment of

insects: that the nature of things, namely, is nowhere more to be found than in the smallest

things. We acknowledge also, and profess with the great Augustine (y), that God is so

C H A P T E R I V.

On the porosity of bodies.

y the pores of bodies we understand the intervals, cavities and openings, 167

B whether visible or invisible, which occur everywhere in all bodies, whether these be

fluid, or soft, or hard. Pores arise, moreover, from the joining together of the

smallest corpuscles that constitute visible bodies. For these, on account of their fig‐

ures, can scarcely ever be so joined that they fit one another altogether and leave no

cavities and openings to be occupied by some subtle matter foreign to the body.

Imagine, e.g., that the smallest corpuscles which compose some body are spherical:

then every three spheres will touch one another in three points and will leave a trian‐

gular space in the middle; wherefore there will be in the body innumerable triangular

pores of this kind, filled with some very subtle matter.

168 It will be the same if the smallest component corpuscles are laid down to be

of other figures, except that pores of very different figures as well must necessarily

arise from the joining together of those corpuscles. Pores, moreover, are for the most

part so very small that they are not perceived by the senses. We must not, therefore,

abide by the judgment of the senses in determining how much solid matter is found

in any body. For it can happen that two bodies equal in bulk seem to contain the

same quantity of matter beneath their surface, and yet in one of the two scarcely any

matter is found. These things laid down,

169 I say: all bodies, whether large or small, hard as well as liquid, are pierced

through with innumerable pores. Proof: the greatest porosity of those bodies must be

admitted which experiments made in each body

demonstrate:

(x) Natural History, bk. 11, ch. 2.

(y) Bk. 21, Against Faustus, ch. 5.

p. 62

demonstrate: but very many experiments show that all bodies are pierced through with innumerable pores: therefore. The minor is proved; and, to begin with diaphanous bodies, their very great porosity is more than sufficiently established from the fact that they transmit light, whereas, if these bodies were not pierced through with innumerable pores, they would deny passage to the rays of light. Wherefore air, water, glass, crystal, diamond and the other pellucid stones must be filled with innumerable pores; for pellucidity cannot be understood unless an easy passage lies open for the rays of light to the opposite points of the surfaces. Hence it is evident that crystal, e.g., contains almost nothing whatever of solid matter.

170 Now, since the smallest parts of all bodies appear in some measure pellucid, as is observed with the microscope, it follows that opaque bodies too are not devoid of their pores; for if the smallest parts of which they grow together are porous, the bodies composed of those smallest parts must also be porous. Let us now speak of particular bodies.

171 That woods, however compact and hard, are porous is argued by the manner of their nourishment, which could not take place unless the woody fibers were perforated, so that, namely, they can allow passage to the sap ascending from the roots. Earthenware vessels, though baked and hard, are so porous that they easily drink in the particles of a liquid poured into them, and keep its odor a very long time. There are also thick and compact stones which transmit water, and from them are made mortars through which water is strained, that it may be purged of its muddy parts. Magnetic effluvia pass through wood, glass and metals: for if iron, or small fragments of steel, are placed on some plate of glass, wood or metal, and the magnet is moved in any way whatever below the plate, you will see the iron stirred by the motion of the magnet.

172 The hardest marbles, too, are penetrated by very many fluids, by spirit of wine, by spirit of turpentine, as the most distinguished Dufay testifies in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (z). The most distinguished Homberg (a) discovered that a salt extracted from mixtures of quicklime, distilled vinegar, saltpeter, sea salt and common sulfur penetrates iron no otherwise than water permeates paper.

173 The most distinguished Réaumur likewise shows a method of preserving fresh eggs, and suggests this plan: that the very small and innumerable pores existing in the shell of the egg be covered over with a coating that cannot be dissolved by water and has such consistency that it is not loosened by the particles which strive to burst out of the egg and would evaporate. Suitable for this use will be mutton fat, wax heated until liquid, or common varnish laid on several times. Certainly Nollet (b) found by experience,

he

(z) Memoires de l’Academ., 1728, 1732.

[a] Histoire de l’Academ., 1713.

(b) Leçons de Physique, vol. 1.

p. 63

he writes, that eggs were preserved in this way even for the space of six months, without being spoiled by even the least unpleasant taste. This practice serves those who sail the sea for a longer time, and also for bringing into our kingdoms foreign birds, which would not be carried alive across so many stretches of land and sea without the greatest trouble.

174 I will also describe for you, so that the porosity of bodies may appear more clearly, the ink which is commonly called sympathetic by the Chemists. It is usually prepared in this way. Let one ounce of litharge be taken and mixed with five or six ounces of distilled vinegar, and let it be filtered through paper in the usual way. This liquor, which is called by the Chemists vinegar of Saturn, or impregnation of Saturn made with distilled vinegar, is to be used for tracing characters, which you will no more perceive than if you had written with water; but if another liquor is applied, to be prepared by an artifice presently to be described, the characters at once become visible. Let one ounce of orpiment therefore be taken and mixed with two ounces of quicklime; let water be poured onto the mixture: there will be had a second liquor, with which some paper inscribed with the characters previously traced is to be moistened; even with a hundred sheets of paper placed in between, the particles of this liquor at once pass through the many sheets of paper, and you will read, splendidly black, the characters which before escaped the eyes, and you will marvel.

175 But you will marvel more that quicksilver itself also passes through the pores of wood: for if a little cylindrical vessel C B A (Fig. VII) is made, and a glass tube about three feet long, furnished with a screw E at D, is inserted into it, which is filled with quicksilver through an opening in the base of the little vessel fitted with a wooden screw, then, the little hole at D being opened and the screw E removed, so that the pressure of the external air upon the quicksilver may not be intercepted, the mercury bursts out through the pores of the wood at G F in a delightful spectacle; and if the part G F from which the quicksilver flows out is observed with a microscope, little round holes arranged in order present themselves, to be looked at with no less delight, as Thümmig reports in the Institutions of the Wolffian Philosophy (c).

176 The porosity of fluids too is easily gathered from the fact that certain fluids imbibe one another. Let a vessel be filled to a height of three inches with oil of vitriol, let as much water be added to it, then let it be closed, so that nothing may evaporate in their effervescence: when the fermentation has subsided, you will have not six inches of height, but a smaller number. Moreover, if within any vessel there are two inches’ height of sand, and you mix with them two inches’ height of water, you will have not four, but only two inches of matter. I should be long if I wished to describe here all the phenomena that could adorn the present subject.

177 I will only note that it sometimes happens that some bodies afford passage to certain effluvia and deny it to others: which must be thought to happen both from a certain peculiar configuration of the pores,

I and

(c) Instit. Philosoph. Exp., §. 247 ff.

p. 64

and from the size and figure of the effluvia. Thus, if oil extracted from wax and

quintessence of sulfur, both certainly very odorous, are carefully kept in a glass

flask, even though you shake the flask a great deal or warm it before the fire, they

nevertheless give off no exhalation, even of the faintest odor. And if odors do not

penetrate glass, let us cease to wonder if the less subtle parts of water do not en‐

ter the pores of glass, as has been proved by a most splendid experiment by the

very learned men of the Florentine Academy.

178 Manifold, therefore, is the necessity and use of pores in nature. First, in

the generation of plants, while the little seed of the plant is unfolded by the heat

and moisture entering it; similarly in the production of animals: namely, a hen sit‐

ting on an egg hatches the chick by no other means than by the heat that enters

and penetrates the pores of the shell. Secondly, in nourishment, since through

them suitable nourishment and juices are sent off to the single parts. Thirdly, to

omit the rest — fermentations, namely, various rarefactions, magnetic motions

and other effects, for producing and explaining which these minute interstices

contribute wonderfully — they are of the greatest use for excreting harmful and

superfluous humors in animals, which is effected by perspiration, of which we

shall treat in the following chapter. And thus far of porosity, which is a property

common to all bodies.

T H E A RG U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

179

O bj. 1. If all bodies are pierced through with innumerable pores, then we do

not know the absolute weights of bodies: for the quantity of matter is un‐

known, and hence also the weight, which is proportional to the quantity of mat‐

ter; but this seems contradictory: therefore. I grant the major, deny the minor:

for no perfectly solid body can be found, as is manifest from what has been said;

and if one could indeed be found, the quantity of matter in each body, and hence

its absolute weight, would at once become known, namely by comparing some

given portion of matter with an equal volume of different bodies.

180 Wherefore, since such a perfectly solid body is nowhere found, those idle

Philosophers indulge in superfluous conjectures who attempt to determine the

quantity of matter by fictitious hypotheses; nay, it is most probable that this

whole universe consists of a very small quantity of matter. But you will say: at least

gold will be a perfectly solid body: therefore what we have said thus far is false. I

deny the antecedent: for gold of itself transmits water, not to say mercury, whose

parts are doubtless subtler, as the most distinguished Martini testifies (d); for a

hollow golden globe filled with water, and then, with great force

compressed,

(d) Instit. Philosoph. Rat., vol. 1, no. 59.

p. 65

compressed, exuded water on every side, and dripped everywhere with innu‐

merable tiny droplets as though bedewed, although the gold itself meanwhile

had cracked in no part of it. Moreover, gold is very easily penetrated by the

very fine particles of aqua regia, which could not happen unless it had pores.

181 Obj. 2. If the porosity of bodies were so great, the organs of the senses

would perpetually lead us into error, and God, Best and Greatest, would per‐

petually deceive us by false sensations; but this illusion is contrary to the

Divine veracity: therefore. I deny the major: for very many fallacies of the sens‐

es can be called back to examination and corrected by philosophical reasoning,

and the senses must not be rashly believed, as we said in the Logic. The judg‐

ment of truth is not in the senses, says St. Augustine. God, Best and Greatest, there‐

fore by no means drives us into the error of the senses; for it pleased his infi‐

nite Goodness to grant to men only those cognitions which can lead to the just

uses of this life and to the ultimate end, namely eternal life.

C H A P T E R V.

On the transpiration of bodies.

he effluvia of a body are said to be certain very subtle corpuscles 182

T which burst out of the pores of the body and are scattered in every

direction as if in a circle. The motion, moreover, by which a body

emits effluvia is called Transpiration. For a body is said to transpire

which exhales a very subtle substance. The Atmosphere of a body is the space oc‐

cupied by its effluvia diffused as if in a circle around the body itself; so that, if

the body X (Fig. VIII) diffuses outside itself effluvia which fill the space A B C

D and hence surround the body itself, the space comprised by the outermost

surface A B C D will be the atmosphere of that body (namely, the sphere of its

exhalations, or of vapor). All bodies, therefore, which emit effluvia are endowed

with an atmosphere. These things being established,

183 I say, therefore: there seems to be scarcely any mixed body in nature

which does not either continually transpire, or (though it is not the same thing)

from which certain outflowings do not fly off. I said that to transpire and to

emit outflowings are not the same: because the first belongs only to bodies en‐

dowed with animal or vegetable life, the other also to those devoid of life. It is

proved by observations and experiments. For just as there is no sensible body

which lacks pores and which does not contain something of a very subtle sub‐

stance, so likewise none

I2 seems

p. 66

seems to exist from whose pores some portion of its substance does not continually burst out of its own accord, or is not carried off from it by the impetus of another body running against it. But let us prove this very thing specifically of different bodies. As regards animals, it is plain from the sagacity of dogs, which follow a wild beast even when it is far away by the effluvia left along its path; it will be still more plain from the observations of Sanctorius and Dodart to be adduced below. The Physicists affirm the same of plants, with Fr. Lana Terzi and Malpighi.

184 Truly no other reason is given why plants, while the air is very hot, droop and wither, but, when the air has cooled, begin to flourish and revive, than that this hidden expiration, brought about by the heat, robs the plants of a huge quantity of corpuscles; whence it comes about that the fibers are exhausted and slackened, lose their firmness, and, through the lack of the corpuscles and of the spirits which sustain the little tubes of the fibers, are at length forced to yield to the forces of gravity; which shines forth most of all in the heliotrope. Not to mention to you the odor which vegetable bodies above all diffuse in every direction.

185 As regards very many mixed bodies, e.g. wine, spirit of wine, and others of this kind which abound in active substance, it is evident that, if they have been exposed to the free air for a considerable time, such mixtures are much weakened, a manifest sign that much active substance has been lost through the flying off of a very subtle vapor. That the weight too is in some cases sensibly diminished, the said Fr. Lana Terzi (e) shows by many experiments. Of camphor that eminent man Robert Boyle (f) speaks thus. When I had weighed camphor in an exact balance, in the space of a few hours it suffered a visible loss of its weight through the flying off of corpuscles: he also records a remarkable evaporation which he observed in apples, as well as in bodies covered with a firmer integument, such as eggs, which became manifestly lighter from day to day, and in other bodies which he had kept long in the balances, observing the decrease of their weight.

186 Effluvia emanating by exhalation for the most part retain the same color, taste and odor which the bodies themselves from which they fly off possess. Thus, to omit the rest, Fr. Lana Terzi confesses that when he was preparing a salt from wormwood and touched his tongue with his hand, although his hand had previously in no way handled the wormwood, he nevertheless perceived exactly the same taste which belongs to the plant itself, namely from the exhalations of the salt adhering to his hand. Another, who had taken every day a very little spirit of vitriol mixed into his drink, noticed that the keys he carried with him, well polished to brightness, had contracted blackness and rust, although they had never been touched by this spirit. A girl afflicted with jaundice imparted the color of a citron to the clothes she wore and to the silver coins she carried for use.

From

(e) Magist. Nat. & Art., vol. 2, bk. 2, ch. 1, exp. 129, no. 1.

(f) De atmosphaera corpor. consist.

p. 67

187 From what has been said it is inferred, 1. That there is scarcely any mixed body which is not surrounded by its own atmosphere. For every body that emits effluvia is endowed with an atmosphere. It is inferred, 2. That there exists no mixed body whose internal, subtler particles are not affected with a continual motion, although a motion of this kind may be very slight and can hardly be perceived by the senses. For since the ethereal matter, placed in continual motion, permeates even the most compact body, plucks away its fine parts and excites a certain exhalation, it seems evident that there is in bodies an intestine agitation of certain subtle parts; nor does this come to rest in those smallest particles alone which first flow out through the body, but others too receive an impulse; for the subtle matter, having entered through the pores and being agitated, continually urges and impels other particles that form the sides of the pores, whence it comes about that it plucks away now this, now that particle from the rest of the body and, the bond being broken, carries it off with itself.

188 It is inferred, 3., with Robert Boyle (g) and Lana Terzi (h): that there is no natural composite all of whose parts are entirely at rest. It is plain both from what has been said and from this, that since there is no body which is not at length corrupted as if of its own accord, there is certainly none of these whose internal, subtler parts are not continually moved. But let us say a few things about insensible transpiration in the human body from the most learned Sanctorius (i).

189 Sanctorius was the first to reduce the insensible perspiration of the human body to calculation, having spent 30 years in observing it; from his observations it has pleased us to note down some things. Insensible perspiration carries off more from the body in the space of 24 hours than all the sensible evacuations together in 15 days. This is aphorism 4 of Sect. 1 of the Medicina Statica of Sanctorius. Healthy men in winter transpire 50 ounces within 24 hours; likewise, within the same time, out of 8 pounds of food taken, perspiration carries off 5 pounds. Aphor. 6. The quantity of insensible perspiration suffers some variety according to the variety of nature, region, season, age, and diseases. Aphor. 7. Any cold, even the slightest, which we suffer while sleeping at night, impedes perspiration. Aph. 50. One of the frequent causes which in summertime impede perspiration is frequent agitation of the body in bed. Aph. 51.

190 In summer, if the body lies uncovered, perspiration is checked, whence heaviness of the head and a feeling of the body being broken. Aph. 113. Placid sleep so favors perspiration that in 7 hours 50 ounces of digested perspirable matter are often exhaled in robust persons. Sect. 4, Aph. 1. I should copy out the whole volume of Sanctorius if I wished to set forth all his most useful observations. There will perhaps be men, plain strangers in Physics, who will confidently

assert

(g) De absolut. quiete in corporib., Sect. 6 ff.

(h) Magist. Nat. & Art., vol. 2, bk. 3, ch. 1.

(i) Medicina Statica.

p. 68

assert that there is little or no usefulness in these matters; but again I say to you: do not be led by the talk of the unskilled. Let us, however, return to the point from which we digressed.

191 The most distinguished Dodart (j), Member of the Royal Academy of Paris and physician to the King of France, established by experiments carried out over a space of 33 years that transpiration is far greater in youth than in any other age (k). From what has been said it is manifest that a very rapid change takes place in our bodies, and that the hardest parts of our body are subject to this perpetual vicissitude; and indeed there is no bone in the animal body so hard, so compact, that it is not nourished, and hence that it is not changed, and does not lose part of itself and recover a new one.

192 Who, then, will not marvel at the hand of Almighty God, which in the structure of our body has disposed so many very subtle instruments necessary for nourishment and evaporation! But let us contemplate a little more attentively the single stages of human life and the different states of our body; for these things have more usefulness than quarrelling sharply about the appetite of matter and other trifles of the common philosophy. In childhood the parts are very tender, abound in water, and are perforated with innumerable little canals, which anatomical injections indeed demonstrate in the bones, membranes, cartilages and tendons, and in the skin itself. Hence it comes about that the force which is the principle of motion in the animal body extends the softer parts more easily. With the progress of time the parts become more robust and are solidified, and this goes on until at length the forces of the heart are no longer sufficient for extending the solids.

193 Nevertheless the cellular tissue still remains easily flexible and in many places admits fat and blood; hence adults become fatter up to a certain time, and yet they do not grow. In advanced age the cellular tissue becomes thicker, the bones of old men stiffen, the excretory vessels are compressed, the secretions are diminished, the blood is dried up and deposits a kind of earthy humor in the single parts of the body. Hence all the parts are observed to be harder; hence bony crusts are found on the surface of the bones, and above all in the vertebrae.

By

(j) In Ozanam, Recreat. Mathematiques, vol. 3.

(k) Of the same Dodart the said Ozanam relates a fact not unfittingly to be brought forward here: namely that at the beginning of Lent Dodart weighed 116 pounds and 1 ounce, then spent the time of the holy fast living chiefly on legumes. Then on the Saturday of Holy Week, examining the weight of his body again, he found that it did not exceed 107 lb. and 12 oz.; that is, in the space of 46 days he had lost 8 lb. with 5 oz., namely the 1/14 part of his substance. Having afterwards resumed his accustomed manner of living, after 4 days he had gained 4 pounds in weight. Whence it is plain that in 8 or 9 days he would have recovered the integrity of his former weight, and that what is dissipated by fasting is thus easily repaired.

p. 69

By these stages we proceed to old age and to death itself. At length this fragile

machine of our body is dissolved, to be repaired again and recalled (God grant

it) to a better and eternal life. And thus far of transpiration.

O bj. 1. If all mixed bodies continually transpire, it will come about that they

gradually decrease in weight and bulk; but this is contradicted by very

many experiments: therefore. Secondly: through the very pores of the human

body the fluids necessary for life would also burst out; but this is not to be said,

for then a man would never have good health: therefore. To 1. I deny the major,

Therefore the Divine Goodness is to be praised again and always, which so

composed the admirable structure of our body that we might live, and live as

long as God himself willed, to pass thereafter to immortal life.

196 Obj. 2. It is of faith that all men will rise again in their own flesh, to be

set before the Tribunal of the Divine judge, so that the good may be rewarded

and the wicked consigned to punishment; but this cannot be reconciled with

the transpiration of the human body; for how will those particles of the body

which continually vanish through insensible transpiration grow together again

into the same body? Therefore. I deny the minor: for although the matter of

our body has flown off through insensible transpiration, although it has even

passed into the substance of a carnivorous beast or of a barbarous man, God

will discern it and restore it to the body whose it will be. Not all the particles

which from birth until death constituted our body through its different ages

will rise again with us; for then we should be raised up as monsters of enormous

size.

197 God will restore to us that size which he himself has decreed, about

which size faith indeed teaches nothing; but it is in no way foreign to reason,

nay, reason itself demonstrates, that Almighty God can gather the scattered

particles of matter which made up each man’s

substance

p. 70

CHAPTER VI

substance through the whole course of life, and pick them out, and recall them to

whatever size he wishes; and what may be lacking to anyone, He will supply who

was able to make even out of nothing whatever he willed, as St. Augustine says (l).

The resurrection of bodies is the work of the divine power alone, whose causes

and reason one would investigate rashly. It must therefore be held altogether with

sure faith that at the coming of Christ the Lord all men shall rise again with their

bodies, and shall give an account of their own deeds; and they that have done good

shall go into life everlasting, and they that have done evil into everlasting fire (m).

On the Rarefaction and Condensation of bodies.

body is called rare which under great dimensions contains little matter; dense, 198

A however, which has much matter under small dimensions; thus water filling

half a little vessel and boiling when brought near the fire is called rare,

because for so great an extension as it then has there is in reality little aqueous

matter; wax, on the contrary, first heated and afterwards cooling, is dense, because

it contracts into a smaller space. Hence rarefaction is the motion by which a body, the

same quantity of matter remaining, is extended into a greater space. For if something of

the same matter is added, e.g. water to boiling water, it will not be rarefaction but

augmentation. Condensation is the motion by which a body is reduced to a smaller space

without anything of its matter being taken away; for if anything is taken away from

wax, e.g., it will not be condensation but diminution.

199 A rare and a stretched body agree in this, that under a greater extension they

contain little matter; they differ, however, in this, that the stretched body requires

to be brought back to a smaller extension, but not the rare body, precisely, that is,

on account of its state of rarity. Similarly a dense and a compressed body agree in this,

that under a small extension they have much matter. But the compressed body re‐

quires a greater extension, not, however, the dense, namely by reason of its density.

The compressed body requires a greater extension: for the particles composing it

have been reduced to a smaller space by an extrinsic cause; but the dense body is so

constituted by some intrinsic cause that it does not require a greater extension;

and this cause can be the binding together, the new interweaving and the fixing of

the particles composing that body; and once this is in place, even

with

(l) In the Enchiridion, ch. 20.

(m) From the Creed attributed to St. Athanasius.

p. 71

with no restraint applied from outside, they do not regain their former extension. These things being thus established,

200 I say: the rarefaction of bodies consists in this, that the pores of the body are dilated; condensation, however, in this, that the same pores are constricted; upon which dilatation there follows an entry of particles and of insensible corpuscles, as upon the constriction their expulsion. Proof: a body is said to rarefy when, its matter not being increased, its volume grows and occupies a greater space; to be condensed when, its matter not being diminished, its volume decreases and the body fits a smaller space [§. 198]; but it is evident that the volume of a body is increased without its matter growing, by the very fact that the pores in it are dilated, and that the volume of a body decreases without anything being taken away from its matter, by the very fact that the pores are narrowed: therefore. That in the physical sense, moreover, there cannot be rarefaction without the entry of insensible corpuscles, fiery, ethereal or others, is plain; because, since (as will be said) there is no sensible void, and so every sensible space is full of some very subtle matter, it follows that when the pores are dilated, the bulk of the whole body being sensibly increased, this matter, being very subtle, enters and fills them. One must reason about condensation in the same way, proportionally.

201 Confirm.: In physical matters that opinion is to be preferred to the others which is easy to grasp, does not bring in mysteries almost surpassing the human intellect, and in which an account is most easily given of the phenomena occurring in the motion of rarefaction and condensation [Axiom. III, IV & V, §§. 32 & 33]; but such is our opinion: therefore. The minor will shine forth both from what has been said thus far and from the solution of the objections, and is also proved by induction from experiments and by their explanation. For it is explained why water congealed into ice occupies a greater space than in its natural state. The Florentine Academicians, to examine this exactly, chose a glass tube closed at one end, which they filled with water to half its height, then immersed it in finely crushed snow until the water was turned into ice; whereby it came about that the dilated water rose in the tube and occupied a greater space in it than when it was fluid.

202 Moreover, with a most exact balance they examined the weight of water before freezing, and of the same water once frozen, and found that the unfrozen water weighed more than after freezing. The reason of these things, moreover, is this: since the particles of water on one side adhere to one another by congelation and embrace one another more tightly, they leave on the other side innumerable and quite notable pores, which are filled chiefly with aerial matter; and since this cannot escape through the narrower pores of the water that is freezing, it is dilated; whence it comes about that ice, which is a kind of aggregate of coagulated water and of air thus dilated and enclosed in those little bubbles, becomes more extended than the water itself was before freezing.

K 203

p. 72

203 For while the air is dilated and does not burst out, the whole bulk of the

water in which it is contained must necessarily be increased; and consequently, be‐

ing set under a greater bulk and containing the same matter of water, but deprived

of very many particles, especially fiery ones, it becomes lighter. I think, however,

that water, if it could exist separated from the little bubbles under the same vol‐

ume, would be rendered heavier after freezing; for it is plain that hail, in which no

little bubbles appear, is heavier than rain water, since it sinks in it, whereas, on the

contrary, common ice, full of conspicuous little bubbles, floats on the same water:

for out of water condensed a little and air very greatly dilated there is made an ag‐

gregate lighter than the water before freezing. I omit many other things which are

set forth from these with no trouble at all. Let us now discuss in a few words the

difficulties drawn from various phenomena.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

204

O bj. 1. On our opinion no fitting account can be given of the phenomena ob‐

served in a vessel which is made of copper, has the shape of a pear or an apple,

and has for its little stem a tube ending in a tiny opening; this vessel is called an

Aeolipile. Filled with spirit of wine to a certain quantity and set upon a fire, it will

exhibit a fountain of spirit of wine leaping up, and if you bring a candle near it, the

liquor springing out will be set alight (Fig. IX). Similarly, if it is filled to half with

water and set near coals, it will throw out vapor through the little canal with great

vehemence and noise (Fig. X): nay, the vapor will drive the water contained in the

Aeolipile to a height of 20 feet. These things being established, the argument is

formed thus.

205 If rarefaction takes place through the dilatation of the pores, then, when

water or spirit of wine is rarefied in the aeolipile, the little vessel itself must neces‐

sarily be rarefied just as much, since it is nearer to the fire than the liquor con‐

tained in it; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Nor are several other

things explained more aptly: as that a glass globe (Fig. XI), full of a drop of water or

of spirit of wine and closed on all sides, bursts with a crash when brought near the

fire; similarly, that chestnuts not cut open, put into live coals, burst with a noise; es‐

pecially since it cannot be said that the external air, which would have to rarefy the

water, permeates the pores of the glass globule. But these arguments can be ex‐

plained without difficulty. I indeed assert that the aeolipile is somewhat dilated,

and also rarefied, by heat; but since it is more solid and consists of more compact

matter, it has parts more cohering and fixed into one another; whence, for its pores

to be rarefied as much as the liquor contained, a greater force of heat is required

than that which suffices for dilating the pores of water or of spirit of wine, bodies,

namely, that are liquid and therefore cohere less among themselves.

206 Nor

p. 73

206 Nor can the other phenomena be explained any less easily. Certainly the bursting of a glass globe arises from the rarefaction of water, or from vapor. The bursting of chestnuts thrown into the fire is likewise brought about by moist particles shut up within the shell, which are rarefied by the heat and seek an outlet. Nor should you wonder that so great a force is attributed by us to vapor, since it is established that rarefied vapor has a greater force than gunpowder, which, shut up in a like little glass globe and of the same weight as the drop of water, does indeed shatter the globe, but with a far smaller crash; and since, moreover, it is known from Nollet (n) that water converted into vapor forms a volume 14000 times greater.

207 Obj. 2. In condensation subtle matter is excluded; therefore no subtle matter is then introduced. I deny the consequence: for since the subtle matter which is introduced joins and binds the parts of the body more tightly to one another, it is the cause of the pores being contracted, and consequently of the other subtle matter, which was contained in them, bursting out; but what is excluded is more than what is newly added, and therefore the dense body occupies less space than it occupied before condensation. The other arguments which the Scholastics are wont to raise are very easily dissolved by distinguishing a twofold signification of rarity and density: one in which this twin change of bodies is taken metaphysically and insensibly, the other in which it is taken physically and sensibly.

208 Obj. finally: when a spark of fire falling on a heap of gunpowder kindles and rarefies it, that motion or rarefaction can proceed neither from the dilatation of the pores nor from subtle matter. For what is it that impels that matter, or agitates it with such force that by mere contact it imparts so great an agitation to the gunpowder? Whence comes its force, so that it throws down citadels themselves, as we see in mines? I reply that this effect is to be referred chiefly to the dilatation of the pores and to the elastic force of the kindled powder; for the kindled powder, which demands a greater place, pressing against the walls on every side, bursts out on the side where it is less resisted: the successive dilatation of the powder increases the force of the percussion. The force of the powder by which it propels a ball from a cannon is also to be attributed to the fiery particles, joined with the elasticity of the air and of the niter; for these so many springs strive in every direction with the utmost force, and since the resistance of the ball is less than that of the hinder part of the cannon, it therefore hurls even a ball of several pounds to a notable distance. And of such great effects in the powder the principal cause is saltpeter, on account of its elasticity; whence, as Kircher says, if a cannon is filled with powder made of sulphur and charcoal alone, without niter, and the powder is kindled, it will not expel the ball from the cannon, the spring, namely, being wanting.

On the Fermentation of bodies.

ermentation seems to be nothing other than an intestine motion of a mixed 209

F body, by which its subtler and more active parts loosen its texture, attenu‐

ate the coarser particles, and agitate them in such a way that a certain ef‐

fervescence and ebullition is observed in the whole mixture. The explana‐

tion of fermentation can best be derived from two principles, namely from acid and

alkaline salts: for since the particles of an acid salt, on account of their rigidity, in‐

trude themselves only with violence into the pores of an alkaline salt and into alka‐

line materials, the ethereal matter impelling a great part of them, and compress the

fiery and airy particles lying hidden in the pores, it comes about through these vio‐

lent concussions, with the spring both of the fire and of the air coming to their aid,

that the passages into which they rapidly rushed are broken open, and that the alka‐

line particles are impelled by the help of the rarefied air and of the fire and are scat‐

tered in every direction; and this scattering of the diverse parts is followed by that

swelling observed in fermentations which, if it forms something like bubbles of va‐

por, is called ebullition, and if it is joined with sensible heat, effervescence.

210 In general it can be said that that intestine motion of fermentation is excited

by spirituous particles which, contained and compressed within coarser and more

solid ones, burst out, when these are scattered and cut to pieces, as from an opened

prison, unfold themselves more freely, and by their motion agitate the other parts,

variously mix them together, and disturb them. But I am pleased to note, following

Father Regnault

(o)

p. 75

(o), the fermentation of fulminating powder.

211 Fulminating powder is a mixture composed of three parts of niter, two of salt of tartar, and one of sulphur, each reduced separately to powder and then mixed together. This, put in an iron spoon over a candle or live coals and heated to a certain degree, is suddenly dissipated with a horrible detonation, and sometimes bursts the spoon. The action, namely, of the fiery corpuscles insinuating themselves carries the spicules of the niter into the salt of tartar, and the dilatation of the internal air brings about that violent agitation from which the detonation arises. Father Regnault gives as the cause of the bursting of the spoon that the force of the powder is not only borne in every direction, but is moreover driven into the spoon by the resisting upper air, the more powerfully the greater the speed and vehemence with which the dissipated powder strikes and moves the air. From these things the phenomena of fermentation are explained.

212 First: if spirit of niter is poured onto mercury or tin, an effervescence and a very hot ebullition will follow; for the acid particles of the spirit of niter, aided by the spring of the internal air, rush rapidly into the alkaline particles of the mercury or of the tin; hence they communicate agitation in every direction, whence effervescence, ebullition, sensible heat. Secondly: if oil of tartar is mixed with spirit of niter in which iron filings have previously been dissolved, the fermentation will take fire; for the acid particles communicate motion and agitation in every direction to the alkaline ones, and this motion is greater than that which is produced by simple heat; this motion in every direction, moreover, is produced by the spirit of niter, which meets in the iron filings a great many obstacles that must be overcome by it. Other explanations of the phenomena can be seen in the Dictionary of Physics published in French by Father Paulian (p).

213 Thirdly: the fermentation of quicklime when water is poured on it arises for this reason. In the making of lime the heat breaks the fibers of the stone, enlarges the pores, and makes new ones; these interstices and pores are filled with subtle matter and fiery corpuscles; then, when the lime begins to cool, the outer air penetrates into its many passages and is condensed by more and more air coming in after it; and so, if water is poured on, it violently pervades the very dry lime, and by its agitation the fiery particles and the mineral salt lying hidden in the pores and left behind after calcination are loosed and freed from their prison; whence, the little fires acting with greater force, and the acid particles of the salts also thrusting themselves into the pores of the alkali, the parts of the lime, forced to yield, are separated and scattered: hence the effervescence and sensible heat. On this matter, among others, Willis (q), Boerhaave (r), François Bayle (s) and Father Lana (t) may be consulted.

214 Hence, fourthly, can also be explained the phenomenon of the burning powder, which is also called the pyrophorus powder. Let powdered alum be put in an earthen dish with a third part of its weight of honey, or flour, or sugar, and, the dish being set over coals, let these powders be stirred for a long time until they are thoroughly dried and turn dark. Then let them be pounded in a mortar and dried again, and this until the parts of the powder no longer unite but remain separate. Then let this powder be put in a small long-necked matrass (u), which is buried up to the neck in sand; the matrass being lightly stopped with paper, let the vessel be exposed to a fire increased by degrees, until the lower part of the neck glows red and no more smoke comes forth; when the fire is put out, let the powder be placed in a phial well closed, so that it is not exposed to the air, and kept for use.

215 The property of this powder is that even the smallest portion of it, exposed to the air, takes fire spontaneously, without noise. In the course of time, however, it loses this force, and when it does not take fire quickly, it often takes fire when it is moistened with the breath. The reason of these things is given. When it is exposed to the fire to be roasted, it is then intimately pervaded by the fire, and acquires the power of retaining fire, as an alkali does. As soon as it is exposed to the air, it draws in the air’s moisture, and so the latent, compressed fire acquires the force of expanding itself and is rendered sensible, as in lime moistened with water; hence in the course of time it loses this force, because the fire flies off; and if there has not been too much moisture in the air, it takes fire when moistened with the breath.

216 I cannot, however, pass over the different chemical vegetations that belong to this subject. Among these the most celebrated are the tree of Mars and the tree of Diana, or Philosophical tree. The first is set forth by Lemery the son in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (x). Into a glass vessel (Fig. XIII.) in which there are iron filings, pour spirit of niter upon them; a huge effervescence and ebullition will arise. The spirit will be tinged with an intensely red color on account of the dissolved iron, and many red fumes will arise. When the effervescence, by which the parts of the iron are raised to the upper regions, has subsided, throw into the liquor oil of tartar per deliquium; a moderate effervescence will arise, by which the liquor will be greatly swollen; a little after, on its sides and on the lip, countless branches and shrubs will arise, which without any visible effervescence will rise above the liquor and the lip, and fall down on the outside, as is shown in the figure. In another vegetation Lemery employed, in place of the spirit of niter, a spirit produced from the red vapor which spirit of niter gives off in effervescence, and he used this in another experiment to dissolve iron, and a more distinct vegetation

arose,

It is composed of a glass phial A (Fig. XII.) with a long neck, with another small phial B luted to the first: the liquor ascends into B, returns again into A, etc., and through this circulation it is attenuated and deposits its dregs at the bottom of phial A.

arose, because the red vapor is imbibed by the sulphur of the iron, which divides the iron more quickly and into smaller parts.

217 That these phenomena may be explained, it must be observed that spirit of niter divides iron into very small parts and associates itself with them, and these parts are the smaller the more the spirit abounds in the sulphur of the iron. That sulphur, moreover, can divide metals is well established. Now let oil of tartar, which is an earthy alkali, be added: the parts of the nitrous acid do not cohere so closely with those of the iron that they cannot enter with their points into the cavities of the alkali; hence arises the effervescence, which the bubbles of air continually bursting from the liquor display. Since, however, the acid parts are united with the iron, they cannot rush into the alkali with very great force, and therefore the effervescence is not so sensible as that which arises if oil of tartar per deliquium is put into simple spirit of niter; but in our experiment the acid particles of the niter partly enter the alkali, partly cohere with the particles of the iron.

218 The particles of the iron, however, pressed by the acid and by the alkali, are divided still more, and the sulphur of the iron is attenuated and rendered more volatile, so that it carries with it and lifts upward with very great impetus toward the surface of the vessel the particles of iron united with the saline ones; and these, as soon as they are freed from the liquor, cohere in a determinate manner and, having become dry, take on the figure of shrubs.

219 The tree of Diana is produced easily and expeditiously by the method handed down by Homberg in the Memoirs of the Royal Academy of Paris (y). Take four drachms of silver filings (z), and let an amalgam (a) be made with two drachms of mercury, without fire. Dissolve the amalgam in four ounces of aqua fortis, and throw the solution into a vessel with 18 ounces of common water; then shake the water, and put it away in a well-stopped phial. Whenever you wish to use it to produce the tree, take an ounce of this water and put it in another phial; into this put a common amalgam of gold or of silver of the size of a pea, which should be semifluid, or of the consistency of butter: after two or three minutes threads will begin to come forth from the amalgam that has settled to the bottom of the vessel, which will put out lateral branches, will grow little by little, and will be formed into small silver shrubs, as is depicted in Figure XIV; and within a quarter of an hour this, together with the amalgam to which they adhere, will harden and become white. Behold the tree of Diana made in a short time, which was formerly completed only by a long operation.

220 That this vegetation may be explained, it must be noted that the water can no longer be fit for any further vegetation, and that the pea of amalgam is not diminished in weight after the operation. These things being laid down, it is certain that the silver

When the solution has been diluted by the water, the parts of the niter are no longer

associated with the silver ones with very great force, and therefore, when a new amal‐

gam is put into the water, they are borne toward it and leave the parts of silver and of
