around it together with the mercurial and silver parts. This is confirmed by the diver‐

sity of the shrubs: for if the silver and the mercury have been pure, most beautiful

trees arise.

221 If the solution is too dilute, the trees will be produced more slowly, but the

branches will be more conspicuous. If the solution is stronger, then the trees will

arise denser and less perfect. If the amalgam put in, of the size of a pea, is hard, it will

be dissolved by the solution, and the tree will arise as in Fig. XV. A vegetation is also

made by means of rainwater, which can be very well explained on our view. In rainy

and thundery weather collect a determinate quantity of water running down from a

roof. Keep it: after several days it will deposit a greenish matter to the height of two

lines, which in hot weather, or when placed near a fireplace, will swell, will produce

bubbles, then filaments and green branches, some of which will rise as far as the sur‐

face of the water; when the heat ceases they will settle again to the bottom; when the

heat returns they will sprout again.

222 Each branch will have at its extremities bubbles of air, as though they were

fruit. This vegetation, unless perhaps you prefer (which I allow) that very true seeds

fall to the earth together with the water, is easily explained by means of efferves‐

cence; for the matter is first inflated, and on account of the effervescence air is ex‐

pelled, which is visible, and this raises and distributes the matter into branches and

shrubs, which, on account of their charming green color, wonderfully imitate the nat‐

ural vegetation of plants. These things are rather curious. You will find many others

in the celebrated Authors often praised by me.

On Time.

erhaps someone might suspect that the order of things has been disturbed 223

P by us here, in that among the properties of bodies we also enumerate the

nature of time and of place; but since the motion of bodies cannot be con‐

ceived unless the nature of time and of place has also been accurately

known, therefore, since we are going to say a great many things below about Motion,

which can be considered a universal affection of bodies, we shall seem to be doing

something quite

in

p. 79

in keeping with our plan if, before we explain the nature, the laws, and all the properties of motion, we embrace very briefly (the subtleties of the Schools being set aside) those things concerning time and place from which some light may shine forth for explaining the rest more conveniently.

224 Time, then, to begin with it, is indeed very easily conceived, but can scarcely be explained or defined by us. “For what,” says the great Augustine (b), “what do we mention more familiarly and more knowingly in speaking than time? And we understand it, surely, when we speak of it; we understand it also when we hear another speaking of it. What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to one who asks, I do not know: yet I say confidently that I know that if nothing passed away there would be no past time, and if nothing were, there would be no present time.” Aristotle, however, wishing to define time, says that it is the number of motion according to before and after (c). This definition is deservedly wont to be censured by the Moderns; for it can more probably be said that motion itself is the number and measure of time, since we are certainly accustomed to number or to measure the duration of time by some motion, such as that of a clock or of the sun.

225 Things, moreover, are subject to time not only when they are moved but also while they are at rest, and are contained in some time; and therefore time ought to be called equally the number and measure of motion and of rest; and just as time is called by Aristotle the number of any motion whatever, so it ought also to be called the number of any rest whatever. What of the fact that the number or measure of things is not the thing itself numbered or measured, just as the fingers by which days are numbered are not the days themselves, nor is the ell by which cloth is measured the cloth itself? — to omit many other things, which can be seen in the Philosophia Sceptica written in the Spanish language by Doctor Martínez (d). Hence the Aristotelian definition of time is deservedly censured as faulty, or obscure, or rather false.

226 More clearly, then, time can be described as the successive duration of mutable things; from which definition is understood the notable difference between eternity and time: for in eternity no parts can be distinguished, since it embraces all the differences of times in an admirable way; whence it is quite fittingly defined by all Theologians, with Boethius: the whole, simultaneous and perfect possession of interminable life. We, indeed, by no means possess this mortal life of ours all at once: for what has passed was indeed possessed by us, and what remains to come will be possessed, and only that fleeting instant which is present to us is possessed by us; and just as a sphere rolled over some plane always touches it

227 But to the immortal God the whole of His interminable life is so present that

created, permanent being, dependent on God, and by its own nature incorruptible. Such is the

duration of an Angel and of the rational soul.

It is shown what the place of bodies is.

ristotle, in Physics 4: place is (he says) the first immobile boundary of the sur228

A rounding body, that is, the first and interior surface of a body containing

another body. This interior surface is called concave, and the exterior con‐

vex. Here is an example. The terraqueous globe is circumscribed on every side by the

air: here three things are to be considered, the air itself, its concave surface, and the

convex surface of the terraqueous globe, which is contiguous to the concave surface

of the air. Aristotle therefore says: the place of the Earth is not that surrounding air,

nor the convex surface of the earth, but that concave surface of the air which sur‐

rounds the earth. Descartes embraced the opinion of Aristotle. For he too expressly

teaches (f) that the external place of a body can be taken for the surface which most

closely surrounds the thing located.

229 This surrounding surface he calls the external place, so as to distinguish it

from the internal, namely from space, which in his opinion is distinguished from the

substance of the located body not in reality but by thought alone. For in truth, says

Descartes (g), the extension in length, breadth and depth which constitutes space is plainly the

same as that which constitutes

body.
