body. On the other hand, St. Augustine formerly agreed with Democritus and Epicurus (h): for place, says the Holy Doctor, is in space, which is occupied by the length, breadth and height of a body. Not otherwise do Gassendi (i), Newton (j), Keill (k) think about place, and, in short, all the Moderns, to whom nothing is more at heart than to swear by the words of no master. Having laid down these few things, then, I shall say briefly what I think should be held about the nature of place. For nothing can legitimately be determined in this matter unless what is certain is first distinguished from what is uncertain.

230 I hold as certain, in the first place, that no body really exists which does not exist in some place. Whether, however, it can be brought about by Divine power that some body should exist nowhere, let the common Philosophers, who take the greatest delight in the philosophy of possibles, weigh in the scales. I likewise hold as an ascertained matter that place is not in a place, and so that place is not one of those things that exist in a place. For if it were so, by the same reasoning the place of the place also would be in a place, and so on to infinity. It is ascertained also that none of those things which are moved locally can be held for the place of bodies. For only that which exists in a place can be moved locally. I judge, finally, that the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves singly so exist that they fill one part of it altogether equal to their extension, are moved in it while it is itself wholly immobile, and by it, primarily and of themselves, mutually exclude one another, so far, namely, that several cannot by any means be placed together in the same part by the forces of nature. For all admit that bodies fill the place which each occupies, that they equal it, and that they are on that account impenetrable, because each of them excludes another from that place in which it is. By the name of space nothing else is understood but a negative extension, wholly immobile according to its threefold dimension, in which existing bodies are now placed, and which, if they were reduced to nothing, they would leave behind. This negative extension is called by St. Augustine a spacious nothing, by others an interval. These things being laid down:

231 I say 1. Space is really to be admitted, if it is shown to be possible. It is proved: for since space is not something real and positive but a pure nothing, it cannot be the term of a productive action; therefore, if it does not exist, it certainly cannot be possible either, since what does not really exist and is possible can be produced, at least by God. Wherefore either space is not possible, or, if it is possible, we must necessarily say that it really exists.

232 I say 2. Space is possible in which no body at all exists. Proof: God could, before He founded the machine of the World, have created only two spherical bodies, and have placed them in such a way

L2 that

(h) Bk. of 83 Questions, q. 20, and bk. 4 on Genesis, no. 34.

(i) Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

(j) Principia, Schol. to Def. 8.

(k) Introductio ad veram Philosophiam, lect. 2 and 6.

p. 82

that they touched each other. In this no repugnance, not even the least, appears. Let there be, then, two such bodies A, B (Fig. XVI.), which touch each other at the point C. Since, therefore, it is a most certain thing that the contact of two spheres can take place at one point only, it remains evident that the two bodies A, B will touch each other only at the point C, and consequently that their convex surfaces will be distant from each other, or that a straight line can be drawn from the point a to the point b, and so of the others. Between such convex surfaces, however, no body would really be had, since it has been supposed, namely, that only the two bodies A and B were created by God: therefore between those surfaces there would then be a pure interval, or space; and therefore space is possible in which no body at all exists.

233 I say 3. Space is really to be admitted, namely a negative extension, altogether different from corporeal substance. Proof: space is really to be admitted if it is shown to be possible [§. 231.]; but it is established with mathematical evidence that space is possible [§. 232.]; therefore it is really to be admitted. Moreover, the existence of space is clearly gathered also from the fact that the extension of the world is not infinite. For it cannot be finite unless outside its bounds there is space which could be occupied by other bodies. That the world is by no means without limits is the opinion of all those who hold it for an ascertained matter that no being besides God is infinite. From what has been said it becomes manifest that all bodies exist in space, that each fills one part of it, plainly equal to its extension, and that they are moved in it while it is wholly immobile.

234 It is established also that, since any two bodies really resist each other, it seems that something must necessarily be admitted in which, while one of them exists, the other can by no means be by the forces of nature. That this, however, is nothing other than space seems perspicuous, since, even if no surrounding surface whatever existed, nay, if one were impossible, any two bodies would be naturally impenetrable, inasmuch as they would still be bodies. I do not deny that secondarily and accidentally two bodies, because they are impenetrable, cannot be contained by one and the same concave surface; but space, in which bodies exist, is the only thing from which the bodies themselves primarily and of themselves, by reason of their natural solidity, mutually exclude each other.

235 I say 4, against the Peripatetics: bodies are not in a place because they are circumscribed by the concave surface of another body. Proof: if it were so, that body which is contained by no circumambient surface would exist nowhere: therefore, since the outermost Heaven is comprehended by no external body, it really is outside its own nothingness without existing in any place; but it is false that a body can exist without being somewhere [§ 230.]: therefore bodies are not in a place because, etc. That the outermost Heaven, moreover, is nowhere, once the opinion of Aristotle is admitted, none of the Scholastics can deny without most openly opposing Aristotle himself. For this is what the Prince of the Peripatetics

(l)

p. 83

(l) has: Heaven is not somewhere, nor in any place, since no body contains it. Wherefore, as

the most illustrious Gassendi says (m): it is wonderful to tell into what straits the

Peripatetics are driven, who, while they are unwilling to abandon the surface, are forced to deny

place to the noblest body, and at the same time the most ample, to which reason persuades us to

assign the principal place.

236 It is confirmed: once the opinion of Aristotle is laid down, it must be said

that a body exists in the same place as long as it is contained by the same circumam‐

bient surface, which is false; for from this it follows that the same body can at the

same time exist in the same place and be moved locally, as is evident in the case of

water contained in a glass vessel. For it is moved together with the vessel when the

vessel itself is carried elsewhere, and yet the surface by which it is circumscribed is

not changed: therefore a body is not in a place because, etc. 2. The concave surface of

the surrounding body also exists in a place, and it too is moved at the same time

when the body is carried elsewhere: therefore the place of bodies cannot be set in it

without our being forced to say that place is not locally immobile, and that place itself

at the same time exists in a place, contrary to what we have said [§. 230.]

237 I say 5. The place of bodies is the space occupied by the bodies themselves.

Proof: each body really exists in space, fills one part of it equal to itself, and is moved

in it while it is wholly immobile [§. 230.]; but by the name of place nothing else is un‐

derstood than that in which each body is in this manner [§. 230.]: therefore. It is con‐

firmed: the place of bodies is to be set in that in which the bodies themselves so exist

that each, by reason of its natural solidity, primarily and of itself excludes any other

whatever from that in which it is [§. 230.]. But this is nothing but the space which

each occupies [§§. 233 and 234]: therefore. Secondly: the concave surface of the sur‐

rounding body cannot be held for the place of the contained body [§. 235]; but when

this is rejected, space alone remains which can be taken for place: therefore the place

of each body is space itself.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

bj. 1, against the third conclusion, with Descartes: space is called exten238

O sion in length, breadth and depth; but this is not distinguished from

body: therefore. I distinguish the major: space is called extension, etc.,

negative, I grant; positive, I deny; and I distinguish the minor: positive extension is

not distinguished, etc., I grant; negative, I deny; and the consequence. Body is not

any extension whatever, but a positive and solid one, and divisible in such a way that

its parts can be torn from one another and entirely separated. Space, on the other

hand, is indeed called

extension,

(l) Bk. 4 of the Physics, text 45.

(m) Sect. 1 of the Physics, bk. 2, ch. 6.

p. 84

extension, but negative, penetrable, and altogether indiscerptible: for body and space claim for themselves attributes not only diverse, but so contrary that it is impossible to conceive them as one thing and as inhering in the same subject. The greatest difference of body from space, therefore, consists in this: that every body indeed has the three kinds of spaces (that is, of dimensions), yet not whatever has the three kinds of spaces is body.

239 Obj. 2: Space is either something real or a pure nothing. If the second: then it is wrongly called extended, measurable, etc., because of nothing there are no properties. If the first: then something besides God is immense and unbounded; but this is absurd: therefore there is no space. I reply that space is not something real and positive, but, as St. Augustine says, a spacious nothing. It can be called real inasmuch as it does not depend on the intellect. For with no intellect thinking, the points a, b (Fig. XVI.) are distant from each other. Space is called extended, measurable, etc., in plainly the same sense in which a shadow is called extended and measurable, inasmuch, namely, as an extended and measurable body can be placed in that space. Of nothing, moreover, as we have said [§. 12], there are no positive properties, but many negative ones. Since these things are so, it is vainly asked by the Scholastics whether space is a substance or an accident. For it is manifest that only the real and positive is that which can rightly be divided into substance and accident. Nor does it help them that space is not something feigned by the intellect, for neither is a shadow anything of this kind, and yet none of the Scholastics will say that it is a substance or an accident. Nor does it stand in the way that space is called imaginary, as though it depended on the imagination; for it is so called because we imagine its dimensions after the manner of corporeal dimensions, which fall under the senses.

240 Obj. 3. Against the fourth and fifth: it is an undoubted thing that place must be something real, but space is not of this kind: therefore. I distinguish the major: something real, namely not feigned by the intellect, I grant; that is, some positive being which can be produced by a real action, I deny; and, the minor being distinguished by the same solution, I deny the consequence. For it is true that place cannot be something altogether imaginary, but from this it does not follow that it must be some real positive being: for it would follow either that some real being could exist without being anywhere, or that place itself also exists in a place. That reality, therefore, is in space which can legitimately belong to place.

241 Obj. 4: place is said to receive the locable thing, to contain it, and to be filled by it; but these things do not belong to space, but to a positive being: therefore. I distinguish the major: and to be filled by it exactly as a vessel receives a liquor, contains it, and is filled by it, I deny; in such a way, namely, that the sense is that the thing exists in the place, and indeed so that nothing of the thing itself is had outside the place, and that, speaking of bodies, it does not allow the place to be occupied at the same time by another thing, I grant; and I distinguish the

minor.

p. 85

minor: these functions do not belong to space if it is taken in the first way, I grant; if

it is taken in the second way, I deny; and the consequence. The solution is manifest.

242 Obj. finally: a body is referred to the things which are around it; that is, we

judge that a body is in the same place as long as it keeps the same distance from the

surrounding bodies: therefore this relation will be the place of the body. I distin‐

guish the antecedent: it is referred so that its situation may be defined, I grant; so

that we may be certain that the body itself is in a place, I deny; and the conse‐

quence. The situation of a body is nothing else but a certain respect resulting from

the fact that the body itself has a certain position among those things with which it

is compared, and which are regarded as immobile, and holds a determinate distance

from them; but it is false that the body must be referred to the surrounding bodies

in order that it may be certain to us that it exists in a place. For just as it does not

depend on them in order to be outside its own nothingness, so it has no need of

them in order to exist in some place. Therefore the Moderns divide place into abso‐

lute and relative; the first they call that part of space which the body occupies. The

second, which we have just called situation, they also call apparent and sensible. From

what has been said the following Corollaries are deduced.

243 First: The absolute place of bodies is nothing real and positive. For space is nothing

of this kind. Second: A body can change its absolute place without changing its relative

place. For a man sitting in a ship which is moving keeps the same situation in it, as is

evident; but at the same time he continually changes his absolute place, since to‐

gether with the ship in which he is his body occupies a different part of space at

each moment. Third: The division of place into natural and violent is to be understood of

relative place only. For since space is perpetually uniform with itself, it is all the same

to a body whatever part of it it holds, and therefore any absolute place whatever is

natural to a body. On the contrary, a body is in a violent place if among other bodies

it does not keep that situation which it ought to keep so that that disposition of

them may stand which God established at the beginning of time. Thus the earth

would be in a violent place if it existed above the water, since the constitution of the

world requires that it be held below it.

C H A P T E R I V.

On the Vacuum.

aving set forth the nature of place, it remains for us to say some things 244

H about the vacuum. Hence it will be more openly established, what we

demonstrated in the preceding chapter, that a negative extension,

namely space, in which each and every body is, must be admitted.

245

p. 86

245 A vacuum or void, taken properly, is called a space comprehended by surfaces and as it were bounded, in which there exists absolutely no body, whether fluid or solid, whether conspicuous or inconspicuous, by which it is filled. I said deliberately taken properly, for in common speech a vessel is also wont to be called empty which is occupied by no body conspicuous to us, although it is filled by an inconspicuous one. From this definition the following Corollaries are deduced. First. There is no vacuum if no space exists within the universe which is not occupied by some body. Second. Nor is a vacuum sufficiently proved from the fact that all sensible bodies whatever are demonstrated to exist in space. For all can be in space without intercepting some portion of it which is occupied by no body: but conversely, and let this be the third Corollary, it is proved that space exists, if a vacuum is shown to exist or to be possible. For by this very fact it is manifest that a negative extension exists.

246 The vacuum is wont to be divided by Philosophers into the coacervate and the disseminate. The first is some notable space within the circuit of the universe, occupied by absolutely no body. Disseminate vacuums, on the other hand, is the name given to the little spaces intercepted by the corpuscles of water or of air, which are no longer filled with air or other body, but are wholly empty, or altogether devoid of every body; or very small, insensible little vacuums shut up within the texture of matter, almost as, between a great many grains of wheat, there lie very small spaces in which there is nothing of wheat. Three questions about the coacervate vacuum are wont to be weighed by Philosophers. First: is it possible? Second: does it really exist in the world? Third: can it be obtained by the forces of nature alone? That the coacervate vacuum is so repugnant that it cannot be had even by Divine power is the most open opinion of Descartes (n). The contrary, however, is held by all those Moderns with whom it is a settled principle that body is distinguished from space.

247 The celebrated Newton, by no means content with having taught that the coacervate vacuum is not repugnant, thinks that that vacuum really exists in the world, as may be seen in his own works (o). These things being laid down:

248 I say 1.: the coacervate vacuum is not so repugnant that it can by no means be had by Divine power. This is against Descartes. Proof: God can reduce to nothing every body contained in some vessel, and at the same time prevent another from succeeding; but in this way a coacervate vacuum would be had: therefore. The major is established: for no vessel so needs to be filled by a substance that, unless some substance is in it, it could by no means exist in the nature of things. Moreover, of two things really and entitatively distinct, God can annihilate one and conserve the other, just as He can annihilate Peter while conserving Paul. But Descartes denies the major, for this reason, namely, because then it would necessarily

come

(n) Pt. 2 of the Principles, no. 16.

(o) Bk. 2 of the Principia, sect. 7, Schol. to prop. 40, p. 356, London ed., and p. 371 of the Opticks.

p. 87

come about that the sides themselves would not be distant from each other, but would plainly touch each other. On the contrary, however: for I hold it certain that the sides of that vessel cannot touch each other without its figure perishing; and who will deny that God, the Best and Greatest, can reduce to nothing all the substance contained in the vessel without the figure of that same vessel being changed in the least, since, as experience witnesses, the figure of the vessel itself depends in no way at all on the substance which fills the vessel?

249 It is also false that those bodies touch each other between which no body is really interposed. For the physical contact of two bodies requires not only that no body be had between them, but also that none, not even the smallest, could be interposed between them without their being moved from their place. That this may be more openly evident, consider Fig. XVI. It is certain that it is wholly repugnant that those two spherical bodies A, B should touch each other along their convex surfaces: therefore the points a b, e d, m n, x y will not be contiguous to one another; but then nothing real and positive would be had between them: therefore it is false that two bodies touch each other by the very fact that nothing real and positive, or no body, really exists between them.

250 The celebrated Antoine Le Grand (p) is therefore mistaken when he says: A possible substance cannot be an actual medium dividing and separating bodies; since it is perspicuous that in that hypothesis the points a, b of the globes A, B would be really distant from each other only through a possible substance. Nor does what he objects help him, namely that nothing in the world would then be united, for this reason, to be sure, that between the parts of a body which are united some medium is possible which might separate them. It does not help, I say, because for two things to be really separated from each other it is not enough that some medium be possible between them; it is further required that some medium be possible between them such that, if it were really interposed between them, they would not be forced to change their situation. Thus the points a, b of the globes A, B are really distant from each other, because, although in the hypothesis made above they intercept nothing real, they can nevertheless intercept it without obtaining a situation different from the one they have. Nor does it help the Cartesians to reply that in the proposed case of the vessel body still remains, since extension, namely, remains, which according to them is the essence of body. For, as we have already said [§. 4.], this is a most open begging of the question, and it can be very strongly attacked, following Tosca (q), in this way.

251 For if, as Descartes would have it, that space which in the aforesaid hypothesis would necessarily be left within the vessel were a real body, certainly it would either be produced anew when the air was destroyed, or be brought there by God from elsewhere, or else it was already there. Not the first, nor the second, for both are against the hypothesis made; for it is supposed

M that

(p) Institutio Philosophiae, pt. 4, ch. 13, no. 9.

(q) Philosoph., vol. 3, p. 254.

p. 88

that God does not substitute another body within the vessel: therefore it will have to

be admitted that it always existed there, and consequently that it was penetrated

with the air; but the penetration of one body with another is, even according to

Descartes, naturally impossible: therefore it will also be impossible that that space

left behind is a real body: therefore it is void.

252 I say 2.: a coacervate vacuum does not really exist in the world. Proof: the ex‐

istence of a coacervate vacuum in the world can neither be proved by experience nor

demonstrated by reason: therefore it does not really exist. Proof of the antecedent:

not by experience, for those experiments which are wont to be brought forward to

persuade us of it by no means prove the existence of a vacuum, as we shall see later;

nor is its existence shown by reason, for the arguments which are reckoned the prin‐

cipal ones are of no strength, as will be evident from the solution of the arguments:

therefore.

253 I say 3.: a coacervate vacuum cannot be had in the world by the forces of na‐

ture. Proof: for since, from what has just been said, there is really no notable space

within the circuit of the universe occupied by no body, no notable space can be de‐

prived of every body unless either the body which was in it is reduced to nothing, or

it comes about that the same place is filled at the same time by two bodies; but it is

manifest that neither can be done by the forces of nature: therefore a coacervate vac‐

uum cannot be had in the world by the forces of nature.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

bj. 1, against the first: not even by Divine power can it come about that 254

O there is a vacuum when there is actually a body; but in the case of the

vessel there is actually a body: therefore. Proof of the minor: what exists

and is not a spirit is a body; but space in the vessel exists and is not a

spirit: therefore. I distinguish the major: what exists and is not a spirit is a body, if it

exists by a physical and real existence, I grant; if it is only equivalent to a physically

existing thing, I deny; and the consequence. Space, however, where it is posited as

empty of every body, although it does not exist by the physical existence that belongs

to bodies, nevertheless exists in such a way as to be in a certain manner equivalent to

a really existing body, inasmuch as it is endowed with the capacity of receiving one.

255 Obj. 2. In that case the sides of the vessel would be joined: therefore not

even by Divine power would there be a vacuum. Proof of the antecedent: in that case

no real interval would intervene; but those things really touch each other between

which no real interval lies: therefore. I distinguish the major: no real interval would

intervene, if by this name is understood a really existing body, I grant; if there is un‐

derstood the capacity of receiving a body, or a body which could be interposed, I

deny; and, the minor being distinguished in the same terms, I deny the consequence.

In order that two bodies should not touch each other and should be distant from one

another, it is enough that, while they remain unmoved, some body could be inter‐

posed, even though none is actually interposed;

for

p. 89

for by that very fact they must exist in remote and distant places, as has been demonstrated by us above.

256 Obj. 3, against the second, with the great Newton: if there is not actually a coacervate vacuum, then the spaces of the heavens would have to be actually full; but they cannot be full, for thus the motion of the comets and planets would be retarded; nay, ever since the beginning of the world, from which they have been moving, their motion ought to have been growing languid: therefore. I deny the minor and its included proof: for in order that the stars may continually pursue their motion, nothing else whatever is required than that the matter filling the planetary heaven should not sensibly resist the stars. Moreover, the substance of light, diffused on every side through the circuit of heaven, in which the globes of the planets and comets are moved, does not, according to the excellent Newton himself, bring it about that their courses are disturbed, or that the motion itself grows gradually languid: therefore by the same reasoning those spaces of the heavens could be filled with another body, most fluid and most subtle, without the perennial motion of the stars being either disturbed or retarded even in the least. These things, however, which we have said about the coacervate vacuum do not prevent us from admitting the disseminate vacuum with the celebrated Gassendi.

257 For it is more probable that very slender spaces are interspersed among corporeal things, to which we give the name of disseminate vacuum, since it is perspicuous that the most subtle matter itself, which pervades all things, is interrupted by empty spaces of this kind. For since it is most fluid, and not perfectly continuous, it must consist of particles touching one another at very few points and really dissociated; and those interstices are filled by no body. For if some subtler substance is asserted, one of two things must follow: either this matter of which we are treating will not be the most subtle, or, since the same difficulty recurs once this subtler fluid is admitted, the doctrine of matter divided to infinity and decreasing in fluidity will have to be admitted. Finally, if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies, no local motion could take place in the nature of things. For in order that some body be moved, e.g. through the air, it is necessary that the moving body push the air in front of it into another place; but it could not push it into another place if there were no little vacuums interspersed among bodies: therefore. The major is evident: for (as Tosca argues) a body cannot be moved without entering into the place of the air in front of it; but it cannot enter into it while the air in front persists there, for otherwise there would naturally be penetration: the moving body must therefore push the air in front of it in order to be able to move. The minor is proved: for the moving body cannot push the air in front of it into another place unless there is a place, forward or backward, upward or downward, or at the sides, that can be occupied by that air which is to be pushed; but if no little vacuums exist, there is no occupiable place, since all are full: therefore.

258 Obj. 4, against the third: that celebrated experiment which is called Torricellian

M2 because

p. 90

because Evangelista Torricelli is asserted to have been the first of all to perform this experiment. Let there be a little glass tube A C (Fig. XVII.), hermetically sealed at one of its ends, and let its length be greater than two and a half feet; let it be filled with mercury, then let the mouth through which it was filled with mercury be stopped with a finger; let the tube, thus closed by the finger, be inverted, and let its end, together with the stopping finger, be put into some vessel also well filled with mercury; after the immersion let the finger be removed and the mouth of the tube opened, and at once the mercury will descend from the tube into that vessel, not, however, all of it, but it will remain in the tube itself up to the height A E, which varies with the variety of time and place: therefore the upper part of the tube, E C, left by the mercury, is altogether empty: therefore a coacervate vacuum can be had by the forces of nature alone.

259 I reply that it is false that the upper part of the tube left by the mercury is filled with no substance whatever. For since glass is furnished with innumerable little pores, as we have already said, the mercury cannot desert any part of the tube without the most subtle ethereal substance entering the pores of the glass and filling that part of the tube. Certainly that upper part takes on heat if it is brought near a fire, and is suffused with light, which would by no means happen if there were no substance there: for a vacuum, since it is nothing but the absence of body, is not capable of heat or of light; and light cannot be propagated unless either a substance is diffused through that space, or the substance which is already in it is most strongly urged in a straight line by the luminous body, as we shall demonstrate when we come to speak of light. Besides, if the part C E is altogether empty, I should like to know why the whole tube is not emptied? For it is not contrary to nature that the whole should become empty, if it is not contrary to the laws of nature that the part C E should exist plainly empty.

Physics

p. 91

ON MOTION

D I S S E RTAT I O N I

CHAPTER I

PHYSICS,

PA RT T WO.

On the local Motion of bodies.

On the nature of Motion, and incidentally on Rest.

n Time, Place, and the Void we have now said enough: we now approach 260

O local motion, about which the Scholastic philosophy, little concerned, ei‐

ther looked at it only in passing or even omitted it altogether, so that it

should therefore be a wonder to no one if, the science of motion having

been neglected through so many ages, Physics made almost no progress. Certainly, if

there is anything in the nature of things that ought to have been investigated above

all by all Philosophers and treated most accurately, that, in the judgment of all the

wise, is motion, since, as Aristotle (r) admits, it must be that if motion is unknown, na‐

ture is unknown. Wherefore it is altogether to be wondered at that, although the said

Philosopher made so much of the knowledge of motion, it was investigated so negli‐

gently by those who enrolled themselves under Aristotle’s name; for a custom pre‐

vailed in the Schools that the constitution and nature of motion were treated only

under certain metaphysical precisions, its admirable phenomena being forgotten,

without knowledge of which nearly the whole of Physics must remain in darkness.

We, therefore, in this Part of Physics shall treat of motion more fully, together with

the Moderns.

261 That there were once some who not only called the existence of local motion

into doubt but even openly denied it, such as were Parmenides and Melissus, Sextus

Empiricus is witness. But since it is so certain that motion really occurs in nature,

and so

evident

(r) 3 Phys., text 1.

p. 92

evident that it could be called into doubt only by one who can speak without moving his tongue, I consider it a sin to spend even the least bit of time, and to bestow even the slightest effort, on demonstrating the existence of motion, imitating that man who, when questioned about motion, answered nothing, but rose and walked, mocking the sophist’s fallacy by evidence itself. The existence of local motion being thus placed beyond all hazard of doubt, we shall briefly inquire into its nature.

262 Motion is defined by Aristotle: the act of a being in potency toward a new place, insofar as it is in potency toward it. It can, however, be described more clearly: the passage of a body from place to place, or: the state of a body which is actually carried from place to place, or the continual acquisition of place. For a body is said to be moved locally when it passes from one place into another in such a way that it ceases to be in the one because it is made present to the other. For local motion, therefore, it is necessary that the movable cease to be present to one place from the fact that it is made present to another. Local motion is divided into absolute and relative. Absolute motion is the migration of a body from one absolute place into another, or from one part of space into another; relative motion is the migration of a body from the vicinity of those things which are around it and are regarded as if immovable, into the vicinity of others which are likewise considered as entirely at rest.

263 Thus a man sitting in a ship is moved with absolute motion while the ship is carried along by the winds, but not at all with relative motion, if he is referred to the parts of the ship. He is moved with absolute motion, since he successively occupies one part of space after another; but he is not moved with relative motion, since he keeps the same distance from the parts of the ship. Descartes, just as he admits no place other than the relative, so acknowledges no motion but the relative. But besides the relative, an absolute motion too must be admitted, as is proved by the same reasons by which it was shown that, besides the relative place, an absolute place, namely space, must be admitted.

264 Rest is the permanence of a body in the same place; and indeed, if a body remains always in the same relative place, the body rests relatively; but if it remains always in the same absolute place, the body rests absolutely. Wherefore a body can rest relatively and be moved absolutely, as happens to a man who sits in a ship while it is driven by its sails. Conversely, a body can be moved relatively although it rests absolutely: as if someone walks in a ship toward one part with exactly the same velocity with which the ship is carried toward the opposite part; for because of the man’s twofold equal motion, the one contrary and proper, the other common — namely the one by which the man walks, which is proper, and the other by which he is carried along, which is common — it comes about that he always stays in the same absolute place.

Chapter

p. 93

CHAPTER II

On the properties of motion, and on its divisions.

265

T here are three properties in all motion from which we can discern most of its

differences: namely determination, celerity, and quantity. Determination is the di‐

rection of a body that is moved toward one part rather than another, or toward a certain term.

For since a body can be moved in any direction whatever, in order that it be moved

it must be directed toward a certain region. While a body pursues its direction it

traverses a space, which can be regarded in two ways: physically, namely, and mathe‐

matically. In the former acceptation, what is considered is the whole place which the

movable thing successively occupies according to its every dimension. Thus (Fig.

XVIII.) the sphere A, moved perpendicularly to the line B C, traverses physically a

space which is conceived as a right cylindrical body D E. Taken in the latter sense,

that space is the line of direction m n, in which, if account is taken of the length, and

so of the time in which the motion is performed, the space traversed will be repre‐

sented by it.

266 Just as a body is said to be moved with simple motion when there is only one

power that determines it to motion, but with compound motion when it is deter‐

mined to motion by several powers at once, and indeed according to different direc‐

tions, so direction is twofold: one simple, the other compound. The simple depends on

one impression only, as the descent of the globe A (Fig. cited); the compound pro‐

ceeds from several impressions. Thus if the globe E (Fig. XIX) is impelled at the

same time by the globe A in the direction A F and by the globe B in the direction B

D, the globe E will follow neither of these, but will keep to the diagonal line E G.

267 Celerity, or velocity, is that affection of a movable by which it runs through a

given space in a given time; whence it corresponds to the dimension both of space

and of time, and so is the relation which space has to time. For if two bodies pass

through the same space in different times, that one proceeds with greater celerity

which reaches the goal in less time, while that which arrives at the same goal in a

longer time goes with less celerity. Conversely, if two bodies measure out unequal

spaces in exactly the same time, we declare that the one which described the greater

space went more swiftly, and the one which traversed the smaller space less swiftly.

From

p. 94

268 From this it is easily understood that in the concept of velocity two other concepts are contained, the one of space, the other of time, to such an extent that, the time remaining the same, if the space described is increased or diminished, the velocity of the motion is also proportionally increased or diminished; while, the space traversed remaining the same, if the time is increased or diminished, the velocity in turn is diminished or increased in the same ratio. Wherefore to those who ask, what is velocity? the answer must be that it is the relation which the space described has to the time elapsed meanwhile, and so its measure is had if the space described is divided by the time consumed in describing the space; or, what is the same, the quotient of the space which a body runs through with uniform motion in a certain time, divided by that time itself, best designates the value of the celerity with which the body is moved in that time.

269 Thus if the movable A described 20 feet in a time of 4 minutes, and the movable B described 40 feet in a time of 5 minutes, the velocity of the movable A will be of 5 degrees, the velocity of the movable B of 8 degrees. That is: the space described by the movable A in any part of time is to the space described by the movable B in the same part of time as 5 to 8. Let us suppose also that the body A has run through 20 leagues in the space of 2 hours, and the body B 100 in the space of 4 hours: I say that the celerity of the body A is to the celerity of the body B as 10 (which is the quotient of 20 divided by 2) is to 25 (which is the quotient of 100 divided by 4); that is: by as much as 10 is less than 25, by so much is the celerity of the body A less than the celerity of the body B.

270 This is to be understood only when bodies are moved uniformly; for if the motion is non-uniform, since the body is not moved with the same celerity during that whole time, that variable celerity cannot be designated by a constant quantity. A body, moreover, is said to be moved uniformly if it is moved continually with the same celerity, namely, if in equal times it runs through equal parts of space. It is said to be moved non-uniformly if the celerity of its motion is not always the same, namely, if in equal times it is carried through unequal spaces. Thus the motion of the body A will be uniform if it runs through 5 feet in the 1st minute, then 10 feet by the 2nd, then 15 feet by the 3rd, and so on. Conversely, its motion will be non-uniform if in the 1st minute it is carried through the space of a foot, but in the remaining ones through a space not of a foot, and not by a constant law at all times, but with the magnitude of the space always varied non-uniformly.

271 That motion is accelerated whose celerity is continually increased; retarded, that whose celerity is continually diminished. If in equal times equal increments of velocity are added, the motion is called uniformly accelerated, just as, if they fall away in that proportion, it is named uniformly retarded. And these are the chief divisions of motion. There follows now the third property of motion, which is called quantity; but before we explain it something must be said about Forces.

272 Force is the faculty or power which either induces motion in a body,

or

p. 95

or would induce it if an obstacle were removed; and this, following the most learned Leibniz, Philosophers divide into living and dead. They call that force living which actually induces motion in a body, as is gravity in a descending stone; that force, on the other hand, they say is dead which actually lacks its effect, but which, if an obstacle were removed, would drive the body to motion, as is the same gravity in a globe held up by a thread, which rests so long as it is held up, but when the support is removed at once begins to descend downward. This same force is also called initial force, conatus or nisus toward actual motion.

273 By quantity of motion (which the Moderns also call momentum) we understand the force or impetus which bodies, out of the state of rest, can exert against obstacles set against them; and so, in defining the quantity of motion, attention must be paid both to the velocity with which the body is moved and to the mass, or quantity of matter, of the body itself. For let there be two bodies A B having equal quantities of matter, and let them be carried against an opposed obstacle with equal velocity: each body will exert the same impetus against the obstacle, for there is no cause why the one should exert a greater force than the other, since both the masses and the velocities are supposed equal; and if the impetuses are equal, the motions, or quantities of motions, will likewise be equal.

274 But, the equality of the masses remaining, make the body A be carried more swiftly and the body B more sluggishly: then the impetuses of the bodies A and B exerted against the obstacle will by no means be equal, but the impetus of the body A, which is moved more swiftly, will be greater, and the greater, the greater the velocity with which it is carried against the obstacle. And since impetus and motion are one and the same, it follows that the motions, or quantities of motion, of two bodies A and B whose masses are equal are to each other as the velocities of those same bodies. But if, the equality of the velocities remaining, the masses of the bodies A and B are supposed unequal, neither will the impetuses exerted by them against the obstacle be equal, but the impetus of that body will be greater which contains the greater quantity of matter, and the greater, the greater the quantity of matter; whence both the impetuses and the motions of equally swift bodies will be in the ratio of the masses.

275 From these Theorems there follows directly the third, which runs thus: the momenta, or quantities of motions, of bodies whose velocities as well as masses are unequal have a ratio compounded of the simple ratios of the velocities and of the masses. So that, therefore, when a twofold motion of any bodies whatever is proposed, it may be understood which of those motions must be held the greater or the smaller, first the gravity, or mass, of each body must be accurately ascertained, then the velocity, or celerity, with which each is moved, or the spaces which are traversed by each body; then, the mass of each body being multiplied by the celerity of the body, the product of them will exhibit the quantity of motion which belongs to each body: and this

N very

p. 96

very thing is stated thus in the geometric manner: The quantity of motion, or momentum, of a body is rightly expressed by the product of the celerity multiplied into the mass.

276 The quantity of motion, therefore, is not to be estimated from the celerity of the movable alone. For since motion belongs both to the whole body and to each of its parts, it cannot, as we have already said, be estimated otherwise than by multiplying the mass of the body into the velocity. For let, e.g., the mass of the body A be 4, its velocity or celerity 6. In this case each part of the body A will have 6 degrees of celerity, and consequently also 6 degrees of impetus or motion: the impetus, therefore, or force of the whole body will be equal to 6 degrees of impetus repeated four times; or, what is the same, if 4 is multiplied into 6, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 24. Likewise let the mass of the body B be 3, its velocity 8; let 3 be multiplied into 8: the quantity in the body B will be 24. From which it can easily be understood that the same quantity of motion is found in each movable. The momentum of a given body can therefore be regarded as a rectangle whose base represents the mass of the body itself, and its height the body’s celerity. For a rectangle arises from multiplying the base into the height, as was said in Geometry.

277 But if the gravity in the body A is 4, the velocity 5, and the mass in the body B is 3, the velocity 8, the quantity of motion in the body A will be 20, in the body B 24: whence the quantity of motion will be greater in B than in A. From this, moreover, it can easily be deduced that the quantity of motion itself must correspond to the motive power; and therefore, if a certain force is required for a body of 1 pound to be thrown to a distance of 100 feet, a power twice as great will be required for it to be thrown in the same time to a space of 200 feet. Just as, by the same reasoning, it appears most manifestly that if a body of 10 pounds is thrown in some determinate time by a certain force to a distance of 30 feet, exactly the same force and impetus will be required for a body of 20 pounds to be thrown through a space of 15 feet.

278 And therefore, universally, the motive power will be the greater, the greater the quantity of motion in the body that is moved; and the quantity of motion will be the greater, the greater the gravity or mass of the body, and at the same time the celerity with which it is moved. Thus in the former example, since the quantity of motion is the same in each body, it manifestly appears that each of them will be moved by an equal force or power; but if, as happens in the other case, the quantity of motion is greater in one of the two bodies, whether this inequality arises from the gravity or rather from the celerity, a greater motive force or power is also required. All of which must be observed most accurately, since from this, as from a most abundant source, almost the whole of Statics and Mechanics is derived, as we shall show in what follows when occasion is given.

279 From what has been said it is manifest that the force or impetus, or motion, or momentum (for all these are one and the same) of any body can be increased in three ways. 1. By increased velocity, an example of which we have in the iron balls which engines of war, by the force of gunpowder,

discharge

p. 97

discharge against the walls of besieged towns, which balls strike the walls themselves with great impetus because of the great velocity with which they are carried. 2: By increased quantity of matter; an example of which we have in battering rams and other machines of war which were in use among the Ancients; for these, although they advanced most slowly, yet had an immense mass, and so afforded great use for assaulting walls. 3.: By increased velocity and quantity of matter together, in which case the impetus becomes immense, since the increment comes to the momentum from a double cause, namely from the velocity and from the mass.

280 But since not a few of the things said in this chapter can cause difficulty for young students, it is helpful to set before their eyes some examples of the equality and inequality of impetuses, and to demonstrate them again, and also to propose more clearly the rules of velocities and of the quantity of motions.

281 As to the first, let there be two straight lines A B, C D (Fig. XX.), divided into as many equal parts as you like, e.g. into nine. On the first line let there be supposed a body of one foot, on the second another body of one foot, perfectly homogeneous with the former; then let these bodies be supposed to run through, within the same time, the same number of parts of their lines. In this hypothesis I say that the motive forces applied to those movables are perfectly equal to each other. For the effects produced are altogether alike, and consequently their productive causes must be judged altogether alike.

282 Again, let there be two other bodies carried along two other equal lines, such that the body of three feet, such as is shown by f g h, is moved along the line A B with three degrees of velocity, while the other, of one foot, is carried along the line C D with nine degrees of velocity.

283 I say that the impetuses applied to those bodies are likewise equal to each other: which I show thus. Impetuses, or forces, or quantities of motions are equal to each other when their effects are equal: but in this example the effects are equal. For the effect of the first power is to carry the body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B, namely as far as the point 3; and the effect of the second motive power is to carry, in the same time, the body of one foot through nine equal parts of the line C D, or as far as the point 9: but these effects are equal.

284 For to carry a body of three feet through three equal parts of the line A B is to bring it about that each body of one foot composing the body of three feet runs through three equal parts; or it is to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of that line. Now to bring it about that three bodies of one foot each run through three equal parts of space is the same as to bring it about that a single body of one foot runs through nine equal parts of space; since on either side nine equal parts of space are traversed

N2 by

p. 98

by a body of one foot: therefore the effects are alike: therefore their productive

forces are equal.

285 Finally, let there be two other homogeneous bodies, such that the bulk of the

one is six times the bulk of the other, and let both be carried with equal velocity. In

this hypothesis it is evident that, to carry the six-foot body, a power six times more

intense is required than to carry the body six times smaller in bulk. But let the Laws

of velocities and of the quantity of motions proposed by us above be set out again

more clearly.

RU L E S O F V E L O C I T I E S .

286 I. W hen the spaces run through by homogeneous bodies are equal to each other,

and the times within which they were traversed are likewise equal, then the

velocities are equal to each other. II. When the spaces run through are unequal, but

the times equal, then the velocities are to each other as the spaces run through. III.

When the spaces run through are equal to each other, but the times unequal, then

the velocities are to each other reciprocally as the times; that is, the shorter time in‐

dicates the greater velocity, and the greater the smaller. IV. When the spaces run

through are unequal to each other, and the times likewise unequal, then the velocities

are to each other as the quotients of the spaces divided by the times.

R U L E S F O R T H E Q UA N T I T Y O F M O T I O N S .

287 I. I f the masses or homogeneous bulks are equal to each other, and their velocities

are likewise equal, then the quantities of the impetuses applied to those movables

are equal to each other: because in this case the effects are perfectly alike, as was

proved. II. If the homogeneous bulks or masses are equal to each other, and their ve‐

locities unequal, then the quantities of motions, or of impetuses, are to each other as

the velocities. III. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their ve‐

locities equal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the masses, or

bulks. IV. If the homogeneous bulks are unequal to each other, and their velocities

likewise unequal, then the quantities of impetuses are to each other as the products

arising from the multiplication of each bulk by its velocity.

288 The rules just prescribed, both about the velocities of movables and about

the quantities of impetuses, must be regarded as the foundations of the whole sci‐

ence of machines, or of that part of Philosophy which, with help borrowed from

Geometry, supplies us with the apparatus of various machines. How useful this part

of Physics is, and how much it serves for knowing very many phenomena of nature

and

p. 99

CHAPTER III

LEMMA

and explaining them, only one who is plainly a stranger to Geometry and

Physics could deny; so that for this reason I have judged it altogether necessary

to deliver to you this most useful and most delightful part of Physics once I

take up the discussion of Statics. Do not let the difficulties of these matters

frighten you, for the difficulty will be compensated by the usefulness. Besides

which, I bend all my efforts to this, to show you a very easy road; nor will you

strike any rock, if you apply your mind attentively and with serious meditation

to contemplating the truths.

On the Newtonian laws of Nature. 289

P hilosophers call a law of nature a most universal rule which has place in all the vi‐

cissitudes and changes of natural things. And since every vicissitude of nature

proceeds from motion, it comes about that the exercise of the laws of nature

shows itself chiefly in the motions of bodies. Since Philosophers had disputed

much about these laws of nature, at length Newton reduced everything that had

been said before on this argument to three principal heads, which today are

commonly called by Philosophers the Newtonian Laws of Nature.

290

M otion, so far as lies in itself, is directed along a straight line, nor does it desert it un‐

less it is turned aside from it by some extrinsic cause. The reason is that the

straight line is the shortest of those which can be drawn from point to point, or

from the term from which to the term to which, and is also the simplest: for it is

not divided into various species, as the curved line is: therefore motion along a

straight line is shorter and simpler; but nature in all things affects brevity and

simplicity, undertakes nothing in vain, rejects superfluities, and works all things

with the greatest possible economy: therefore motion is directed along a

straight line rather than along another. This being established, before we pro‐

pose Newton’s Laws of motion, some things must briefly be said by us about

the force of inertia. By this name we understand that force in each body by which

every body, so far as lies in it, perseveres in its state either of rest or of motion, or a certain

force implanted in matter, by which it comes about that each body strives to maintain and

preserve its own state.

291

p. 100

291 For if a body rests, that rest in the body would last forever, if no impetus were made upon it. And likewise a body once moved would be moved perpetually, and would suffer no retardation from the resistance of the medium. For every body that is moved is moved in a medium resisting it; whence the body cannot continue its motion except insofar as it overcomes this resistance; and it cannot overcome it except by dividing and separating the parts of the medium, nor can it separate these parts except by spending against them some part of the impetus which it had for moving itself; since, therefore, the impetus is gradually diminished in the movable, its celerity must be diminished proportionally, and at length be reduced to nothing.

292 But beyond this resistance of the medium there is also in the body another Resistance, namely insofar as the body, in order to preserve its own state, struggles against the impressed force. For when the body B at rest receives a blow from the moved body A, the body B is not moved without the body A losing something of its force; wherefore there is in B a force breaking the impetus of the body A, which is called the force of resistance. These things being supposed, the first Newtonian law is usually proposed thus: Every body perseveres in its state of rest, or of moving uniformly and in a straight line, unless it is compelled by some impressed force to change that state. This law is founded on the force of inertia, because of which it comes about that individual bodies strive to preserve for themselves that state in which they are actually placed.

293 A body at rest will never cease to rest of itself, but in order that it be placed in motion an external force must intervene. Conversely, a body that is moved will never cease to be moved, if we suppose the resistance of all the surrounding bodies overcome and reduced to nothing. Nor are the common Peripatetics to be heard here, who teach that moved bodies by their own nature affect rest, or also tend from motion to rest, contrary to what their Prince Aristotle (a) teaches, led chiefly by this reason, that they see the motion of thrown stones gradually grow languid and at length cease altogether. For if thrown stones at some time desist from motion, this must indeed be imputed to a double cause. The first, because, driven downward by gravity itself, they at length strike against the earth. The second, because the air resists their motion; for if a stone were thrown in a vacuum, and moreover if it were destitute of all gravity, without doubt its motion would never grow languid, but would last forever.

294 Setting aside, then, the consideration both of gravity and of resistance, projectiles must not only be moved forever, but must be moved in a straight line and uniformly. For at the beginning they are without doubt moved along a straight line [§. 290.]; and if at the beginning the course is rectilinear, then, because of the force of inertia, which makes bodies always preserve for themselves the state in which they are placed, projected bodies will perpetually persevere

in

(a) Bk. IV, Phys., text 69.

p. 101

in that course, and will never deflect from the rectilinear path. For if they described a curve, they would then be changing their direction at every moment, which conflicts with the inertia of matter, because of which it cannot assign itself any determination. That they must be moved uniformly, moreover, comes from the same force of inertia; for in order that the motion be accelerated or retarded, a new force must come in which either helps or hinders that motion, a force which, however, we suppose removed.

295 Besides: a body is of itself so indifferent to motion and rest that, if it once rests, it rests forever, but if it has once been placed in motion, it is moved perpetually: therefore, if it has once been determined to motion, it will not return to rest by itself alone; or if it rests, it will not be roused to motion by itself alone: therefore, once incited to motion, it will need a new determination in order to be called back to rest, and conversely. Moreover, a body which was created spherical by God always perseveres spherical, and one that is once square always maintains its figure, until this figure is changed by some cause: therefore likewise a body which once rests will always rest.

296 From what has been said you will gather, 1.: that a body cannot be understood to be carried around a square, a pentagon, or any other polygon whatever, unless at each angle occasional causes of the changed determination of such a body are conceived. For after that body has described one side, it would be understood to be carried along the same line continued, unless there were an obstacle turning it aside along the second side; and so on consequently at the end of each side. Since, therefore, the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of sides indeterminate in number, if some body is moved circularly, there must be conceived either perpetual obstacles, or the same one continued, by which the determination of the movable is perpetually changed.

297 But that you may understand more clearly that the circle must be conceived as a polygon consisting of infinite sides, consider the circumference of a circle (and what we are about to say of it can be applied without any trouble to all the other curves), and understand described in it first a triangle, then a square, afterwards a pentagon, then a hexagon, and finally a decagon, all of them, however, regular.

298 It is manifest that of all the figures now described the triangle departs most from the circumference of the circle; for the square comes somewhat nearer to it, the pentagon somewhat more, the hexagon still somewhat more, and the decagon indeed much more. But if you understand a regular figure inscribed in the circle consisting of infinite, that is, indeterminate sides, each of which is nevertheless as small as possible, then its declination from the circumference of the circle will be null; and so the perimeters of the circle and of the other curves can be held as rectilinear figures of infinite sides, each of whose sides is infinitely small.

299 Imagine now a body moved in the circumference of a circle, and

then

p. 102

then it will in truth be moved in a rectilinear figure of infinite sides, each of which is infinitely small. Therefore, if in the first particle of time the body describes one of these sides, thereafter, every external force being set aside, it ought, because of the force of inertia, to be moved uniformly along that same side produced further, which side touches the circle. Wherefore, if we see some body revolve in the circumference of a circle, it must be said that there is some force acting perpetually on the body, which draws it back from its rectilinear course and gradually bends it into the remaining sides of the polygon.

300 This force of a body of receding from the center is called centrifugal; that by which the body seeks the center, centripetal: both are called by the common name central. Hence you will gather 2. that a body moved circularly and afterwards left to itself, or with the obstacles removed, must be carried along the tangent of the circle, which is the small side continued; whence is deduced this general rule, which is the foundation of the whole system of the world: A body moved circularly strives at every moment to recede from the center of its motion; and indeed the more vehemently, the more vehemently it is agitated. This rule is confirmed by experience.

301 For if you have whirled a stone, e.g., circularly in a sling, as soon as you let go one cord of the sling it will slip away now upward, now downward, now horizontally, now in any other determination, according as the tangent begins from that part of the circumference in which the stone was left to itself; and moreover that stone runs out the farther, the more vehemently it was whirled round. But if a body is moved in an infinite circle, or also in a straight line, into which an infinite circle in any case passes, then, since the deflection of the tangent from its circumference is null, as is plain, there will likewise be no centrifugal conatus, or force of receding from the center.

302 But you will say: a body once placed in some state must of itself persevere in that state; but a body moved circularly was placed in some determinate state: therefore, left to itself, it will always be moved circularly. I deny the minor. For a body whose determination is continually changed should not be said to be placed in some determinate state, but rather should be said to be placed in a perpetual change of state. Now the determination of a movable moved circularly is perpetually changed, as evidently appears when a body is moved around some polygon.

303 You will insist: the determination of a movable along a circular line should be called its single state just as much as its determination along a straight line. I deny the proposition: the difference is that the beginning of translation is a straight line, but not a curved line. For the beginning of motion is translation from point to point. Now that translation can be made without deflection, and so along a straight line, as was proved.

304 From what has been said it follows that, although it is natural, that is, consonant with the laws established by God, that some body carried

and

p. 103

and left to itself be moved in a straight line, it is nevertheless no less natural that the same body, first carried along a straight line, should afterwards be moved away from its determination as often as obstacles occur to prevent its being moved in a straight line. The permanent disturbance, therefore, or inflection of motion in a body which is moved along a circular line, is against the natural requirement of the initial motion impressed along a straight line, according to which the body at each instant begins to move itself; but this disturbance or inflection is not against nature, because the nature of a motion already begun does not require absolutely not to be disturbed, but only not to be disturbed in the absence of some obstacle which requires the disturbance. But let us now propose the second law of nature.

305 The second law is: the change of motion is always proportional to the motive force impressed, and is always made along the straight line along which that force is impressed. For since motion is generated in bodies by motive force, this is certain, that the motion begotten in a body is proportional to the motive force itself, to such a degree that, if some force generates a certain motion in a body, a double force will generate a double motion, a triple force a triple one; and generally, one force which is to another force as the number 100 to 1 will generate a motion which will be to the motion begotten by the other force as the same number 100 to 1; but for this to be true, equality of the times is postulated. That the motion must be made along a straight line has already been demonstrated above.

306 There follows the third rule: To action reaction is always contrary and equal. That is, to the action destroyed the resistance is always contrary and equal. That this law may be understood, let us suppose a horse having a force as 100 drawing a stone tied to a rope, which has a resistance as 50. I say: the horse does not draw the stone with the force which it has as 100, but with a force as 50. The rule, thus understood, is demonstrated: for while some body acts on another, its force tends to overcome the resistance of the second. The acting body, therefore, will not spend all its force, but only that part which is required for overcoming the resistance of the second body. The portion of the motive force which it spends is called Action, and the resistance which the other body opposes is called Reaction. Action, therefore, will have a contrary and equal reaction, which is the 3rd law of motion.

307 There are some who think that the falsity of this law can be shown from this, that, if it were accepted, no motion would ever take place in nature. For let the body A be moved toward the body B at rest. Now, if the reaction of the body B on A is as great as the action of A on B, no motion will follow in B; but we see that it is moved; therefore it is false that reaction is equal and contrary to action. Bah, what a rotten sophism! For in reasoning of this kind there is nothing that ought not to be rejected. For this law of nature does not hold that the resistance is equal and contrary to the motive force, but the reaction to the action, two things which are enormously distant from each other. Force is all the efficacy which there is in a body for acting, speaking absolutely.

O Action

p. 104

Action, however, is only that portion of the motive force which the body spends

while it acts. Bodies, therefore, do not always spend all the force they have in produc‐

ing an effect, but only that which is required for equalling the resistance of the body

tending in the contrary direction; and so motion must indeed be made through a

force as great as the excess of the action over the reaction, or resistance, has been.

308 The objection, therefore, is futile. For in order that two bodies acting on

each other should rest, it is required not only that the actions be equal, but also the

forces applied by them. They will rest, namely, when they have equal forces and apply

all the force they possess; for in this case, since nothing of their forces remains to

them, and these are supposed equal, they will destroy each other mutually, and no

motion will arise. Thus, if a horse wishes to draw a weight equal to the whole force

which it possesses, it will certainly strive to move the weight with its whole force; but

since this weight is equal to the force of the horse, it will destroy that force, and no

motion will arise. But if the weight is less than the horse’s force, then it will apply

only that part of its own force which equals the resistance of the weight to be over‐

come, and thus, since a portion of force still remains to it, it will carry the weight

along with it.

309 It will not be out of place to note here, since we shall use the name of elastici‐

ty in many places, that by the name of elastic motion we mean that by which bodies

stretched, compressed or bent are restored to their former figure and situation once

the power stretching, compressing or bending them is removed. This force of bring‐

ing itself back to its native state we honor with the name of Elasticity, elastic virtue, or

elater; and if this restitution is accomplished with the same force by which the body

was moved from its state, the elasticity is called perfect; otherwise it is called imper‐

fect.

C H A P T E R I V.

On the Laws of Motions which have place in the collision of

bodies.

s soon as Physicists seriously turned their minds to investigating the 310

A phenomena of nature, it was at once discovered that nature proceeds by a

certain path and always by certain laws; but the constancy of nature ap‐

peared chiefly in the collision of bodies, inasmuch as this is carried on by

certain perpetual laws. Since René Descartes had judged the knowledge of these laws

exceedingly useful for tracking down the most hidden secrets of nature, he spent no

mediocre study in searching them out. And would that he had given us truer laws!

For he would have raised on more stable foundations the edifice

which

p. 105

FOR THE SECOND CASE. 314

which we have seen partly totter, partly collapse, not without some detriment to his

name. Warned by his example, we shall strive to bring forward truer ones.

311 When one body runs into another, it imparts motion to it in the collision:

nature accomplishes this by certain laws, in which the principles of Dynamics are con‐

tained. It must be noted, however, that the collision of two bodies can take place in

three ways. First: if one runs into the other entirely at rest. Second: if they are carried

toward the same part, but with unequal velocity, such that the one which is moved

faster overtakes the other with its motion, or impels it. Third: if they meet each oth‐

er from opposite parts. Now since the ratio of motions is one in non-elastic, or inert,

bodies (under which name both perfectly hard and perfectly soft bodies are compre‐

hended), and another in elastic ones, we shall propose the laws of each kind observed

in collision. And of the first, indeed, for the threefold case, we give three laws ex‐

pressed in as many Propositions by Nollet (b).

L AW S O F M O T I O N I N T H E C O L L I S I O N O F B O D I E S

D E V O I D O F E L A S T I C I T Y.

F O R T H E F I RS T C AS E .

312

I f a body at rest is impelled by another, the celerity of the impinging body is divided between

both in proportion to the masses.

313 Namely, since the impelling body imparts motion to the one at rest solely in

order to remove the impediment to its own motion, and since for this to happen it is

necessary only to share out the force in proportion to the mass of each — for if the

bodies taken together are understood to be divided into equal parts, and the whole

motion likewise into as many equal parts, and equal parts of motion are assigned to

equal parts of each body, it will be plain that in this way it comes about that equal

parts of the two bodies, endowed with an equal quantity of forces, will follow the

same direction with equal celerity, without some being an impediment to the motion

of others — accordingly, if a body runs into another at rest and equal to it in mass, it

will communicate to it half of its velocity; if the other is half as large, two thirds; if

double, it bestows on it one third part of its celerity.

I f two bodies are carried toward the same part with unequal celerity, whether their masses

are equal or unequal, when the collision is completed they continue their motion along the

same direction with a common celerity

O2 which

p. 106

FOR THE THIRD CASE

which, however, is less than the celerity of the impelling body, but greater than that of the im‐

pelled body was before the impact.

315 For if they were carried toward the same part with exactly equal celerity, and

so had the same distance between them, the two bodies, compared with each other,

would have to be regarded as if at rest. Since, therefore, they are supposed to be car‐

ried with unequal celerities, these bodies behave no otherwise than if the one moved

faster tended, by the force of the respective celerity by which it exceeds the other,

into this one as entirely at rest. Wherefore the same must follow as in the former

case.

316

I f two bodies with contrary motion meet each other, the motion is extinguished either in both

or at least in one. If after the collision some part of the motion has survived, each will be

moved toward the same part, according to the direction of the one which was endowed with the

greater force, such that the quantity of motion common to them is equal to the excess of the one

over the other before the collision.

317 Namely, if the quantities of motion before the collision are equal, since they

are diametrically opposed to each other, it will come about that in the impact they

destroy each other. Hence Fr. Regnault thinks that this same rule holds only in soft

bodies, but not in hard ones, because these seem to have to be reflected after the im‐

pact just like elastic ones, since no compression of the parts is effected. (c) But with

the most illustrious Fortunato da Brescia we think that this happens in bodies of

both kinds; (d) for although, if a perfectly hard body runs into another similar one

entirely at rest, it rebounds after the impact, as we said above, what happens here is

yet a very different thing; for a hard and immovable plane only prevents the incurring

body from pursuing its motion in its own direction, and brings it about that the di‐

rection of the incident body is changed in the impact; but it by no means extinguish‐

es any impetus in it by a contrary force, as happens when two bodies meeting each

other from opposite sides collide. If the forces before the collision were unequal,

their equal parts, since they are opposed to each other, destroy each other in the col‐

lision: and therefore the body which is the stronger will act with the excess of its

forces on the other as on one at rest, and accordingly (by the Law of the first case) they

will proceed with equal celerity.

318

A n elastic body, when it runs into another of the same nature, equal and at rest, remains

immobile once the collision is completed; but the one which was at rest is moved after the

impact along that direction, and with that very celerity, with which the incurring body was

carried before.

319 For since the masses of the bodies are equal, if the celerity of the incurring

body is = 6, half of it is communicated to the one at rest in the impact, the other

part remaining to the impelling body (by the Law of the first case): which is what

would happen if the bodies were destitute of elater. But since the elastic motion

corresponds to the compression, this to the percussion, and the percussion to the

direct motion which the body obtains in the collision, therefore the half celerity

acquired in the impact is doubled by the equal restitution of the compressed parts:

accordingly the impelled body, once the collision is completed, will be moved with

celerity = 6, namely with the velocity = 3 communicated in the impact, and with

the celerity = 3 supplied by the elater. The incurring body, on the contrary, since it

retains half of its celerity, while at the same time the compressed parts after the

impact restore themselves with equal celerity but in the opposite direction, must

therefore have its motion extinguished, and must rest after the impact.

320 Law II. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, likewise elastic, but of smaller di‐

ameter, which is at rest, each is carried toward the same part once the collision is completed;

but the celerity of B will be greater than the celerity of the body A.

321 Let A run with celerity = 6 into B, which is half of it as to mass, and at rest.

Since A imparts to B celerity in proportion to the mass of each, and so, since it is

double of B, one third of its celerity, that is: the celerity = 2 (by the Law of the first

case of non-elastic bodies), these degrees, because they are doubled by the restitution

of the elater, will make B be moved after the impact with celerity = 4 along the di‐

rection of A. The body A, on the other hand, the celerity = 2 having been trans‐

ferred into B, loses as much elastic motion in the contrary direction: it therefore

follows the other only with celerity = 2.

322 Law III. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, of greater diameter, of the same

nature, and at rest, B will be roused toward the direction along which A was carried before

the impact, but A will go back after the impact.

323 Let A be half of B as to mass, and let it run in with celerity
