= 6 (by the said law): it will transfer two thirds of its celerity, that is: = 4; two degrees of

celerity therefore remain in A. Now since the elasticity corresponds to the motion

communicated in the collision, and this is of four degrees, by the force of the elastic

motion A would therefore go back with a celerity of four degrees. But since two of

these are cancelled by as many degrees of celerity which remain from the direct mo‐

tion and yield in the opposite direction, for that reason the body A goes back after

the impact with a celerity of only = 2.

324

L aw I. If an elastic body follows another equal to itself and of the same nature toward the

same part, they will be carried after the collision in the same direction, with their celerities

exchanged.

325 Let A be moved with celerity = 4, and B, following the same direction, with

celerity = 12: since these bodies behave just as if A were at rest and B were moved into

A with celerity = 8, or with that part of its celerity by which it exceeds the celerity of

the one going before, therefore in the collision the body B will impart to A half of

this celerity of its own, that is: four degrees (by the Law of the first case of non-elast. bod.).

This celerity = 4 is doubled by the force of elasticity and becomes = 8; the same,

added to the celerity of four degrees before the collision, is = 12. The body B, on the

contrary, having communicated in the impact four degrees of celerity out of the eight

which were in excess, loses four again by the force of the elastic motion tending to‐

ward the contrary part, so that only the celerity = 4 remains to it as surviving.

Wherefore after the impact A will be carried with celerity = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12, B with

celerity = 12 − 4 − 4 = 4; that is: with their celerities exchanged, they will pursue their

motion in the same direction.

326 Law II. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, of the same nature, but of smaller di‐

ameter and moved more slowly, once the collision is completed A will continue its motion more

slowly, and B, describing the same line, more swiftly.

327 Let A (which as to mass is double of B) be supposed to be carried with celeri‐

ty = 6, and B with celerity = 3. Since bodies of this kind behave just as if they were at

rest and the body A ran in with only the relative celerity = 3, therefore A bestows in

the collision one third part of this celerity, = 1, which celerity is doubled by the force

of the elastic motion, so that after the impact the body B is carried with celerity = 3 +

1 + 1 = 5. The body A, on the contrary, having communicated one degree of celerity

through the collision, and, of the remaining five, one being extinguished again

through the restitution of the elater in the opposite direction, will be moved after

the impact with celerity = 6 − 1 − 1 = 4.

328 Law III. If an elastic body A runs into another, B, likewise elastic, of greater diameter

and moved more slowly: after the impact it will go back.

329 Let the body A be moved with celerity = 19, the body B with celerity = 4, and

so let the relative celerity of the body A become = 15. And let A, as to

mass,

mass, half as great. In the impact this will impart to body B a velocity = 10, namely

two thirds [by the law stated]: this velocity, increased by just as much again through

the restitution of the spring, will cause body B to proceed with a velocity = 4 + 10 +

10 = 24; but body A, retaining after the collision 4 + 5 degrees of velocity of direct

330

L aw I. Two elastic bodies of the same diameter, meeting each other from opposite sides with

equal velocity, rebound after the impact with the same velocity; the same holds if the

masses of the two bodies meeting are in the inverse ratio of their velocities.

331 This is evident; for their whole force is extinguished in the direct line, but in

the restitution it is restored again. They rebound, therefore, with the velocity with

which they were borne. Again, if body A, whose mass is = 3, and body B, whose mass

is = 2, meet each other in such a way that the velocity of the former is = 4, that of

the latter = 6: since the whole force of each is given back in the restitution of the

parts, body A will go back with a velocity = 4, body B with a velocity = 6.

332 Law II. Two elastic bodies of equal diameter, meeting each other from opposite sides

with unequal velocity, rebound after the impact with their velocities exchanged.

333 Let body A run with a velocity = 6, B with a velocity = 4. Since the equal ve‐

locities with which the bodies are borne in opposite directions cancel each other,

the whole velocity of body B will be destroyed in the impact, and the velocity of A

itself will be = 6 − 4 = 2. Now half of this is communicated to body B, as though to a

body at rest; but in the direction in which A itself was moving, that is, the direction

in which B must be reflected. Therefore after the impact no more than a force = 1

will remain in A in the same direction. Further, since the compression is = 4 + 1, the

restitution of the parts must be exacted with the same force; yet under this law, that

since in A there remains a velocity = 1 toward the opposite side, this destroys the

fifth degree of velocity which it would have had for going back. But body B, since it

acquired four degrees of velocity for rebounding by the force of the velocity with

which it first met the other: obtained one degree of velocity, going back along the

same line, from the excess of the greater velocity of the other body, and, on account

of the compression of one simple degree that was made, is increased once more by

one degree of velocity along the same line; for that reason body A will rebound with

a velocity = 4, body B with a velocity = 6, and so with the velocities exchanged.

334 Law III. If body A, of greater, and B, of smaller diameter, both elastic, meet each oth‐

er directly with equal velocity: B will always rebound after the impact; but A will sometimes

continue its motion, sometimes stand motionless after the collision, sometimes be reflected.

335 B

p. 110

335 B rebounds, since in the restitution of its parts it recovers the whole force it

had lost; and it is endowed with a force twice as great as that which body A commu‐

nicated in the impact. A will sometimes be moved along the same line; for it can happen

that the force with which it ran directly into the other body is greater than the forces

of the spring. Sometimes it stands still; for it happens that the force with which the

compressed parts restore themselves is equal to the direct motion surviving after the

impact, and that they extinguish each other altogether. Sometimes it is reflected: namely,

when it happens that the restitution by the force of elasticity of the parts exceeds

the force that is left over from the direct motion after the impact.

336 More on these rules of motion was given by John Wallis (e), for hard bodies;

for elastic ones by Wren and Huygens, confirmed afterwards by Mariotte, whose

Machine Nollet also adapted: Father Regnault likewise pursues these matters perspicu‐

ously (f). Finally the distinguished Fortunato da Brescia treats them at length (g), ex‐

tending Law III of the second case for elastic bodies somewhat more widely.

C H A P T E R V.

On Reflected Motion, and its laws.

ince the motion impressed on any body is not extinguished at once, but per337

S sists for some time in the mobile, as will be explained below, it must neces‐

sarily happen that if the body itself, before the motion and the impetus im‐

pressed on it by the cause is extinguished and perishes, falls upon some solid, immov‐

able body, as upon a wall, it does not indeed lose its motion, but, since it cannot pro‐

ceed any further according to the former direction of the motion, it is turned toward

the opposite side; and this affection of motion is called Reflection, or the regress of a mo‐

bile body rebounding from another body which it can neither penetrate nor push forward; as if,

e.g., a ball, which is indeed capable of reflection, is thrown against a wall: since it can

neither pass through it nor drive it forward, it is at once reflected. And the laws of

this reflection are these.

338 I. If some body falls perpendicularly on the surface of another solid, immovable body

along the straight line GB (Fig. XXI.), it rebounds, also perpendicularly, along the same line

GB, since there is no greater reason why it should be directed rather along another

straight line deflecting from the said one than

along

CHAPTER VI

along that very one. II. If that body falls obliquely on the surface of another body, as if

a ball falls at the angle ABD (same Fig.) on the line, or surface, DBE, it will so re‐

bound on the other side, along the line BC, that there is formed the angle EBC, which is

called the angle of reflection, equal to the angle DBA, which is called the angle of

incidence. Hence that celebrated principle, that the angle of incidence is always

equal to the angle of reflection. It is demonstrated: nature always operates by short‐

er lines; therefore a body in motion that is capable of reflection, falling on a re‐

sisting body, falls and is reflected along shorter lines; but the lines AB, CB,

which are the lines of incidence and of reflection and form equal angles, are

shorter than the two others AF, FC, and than all the rest that can be drawn be‐

tween the same end points [from Geometry]: therefore the ball will describe the

shorter and equally inclined lines AB, CB, rather than the longer and unequally

inclined AF, FC.

339 The perfect equality of the angles of incidence and reflection can be

maintained only if the reflection takes place on a very highly polished surface,

and neither roughness nor the situation of the parts stands in the way of this

equality, nor is the motion of the mobile body in any way diminished in the

contact, or percussion. For if the surface is rough and uneven, or distorted in

any way whatever, the mobile body will be twisted aside from it, rebounding in

various ways according to the varied situation of its parts, or their roughness.

But where it is a question of the reflection of light in mirrors, since that reflec‐

tion takes place in clean and polished bodies, it can be taken as a principle, so

to speak, that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

On Refracted Motion and its laws.

hat we have so far set forth about the reflection of motion and 340

W its laws will certainly bring a great deal of light also to the things

that remain to be said about the other property of motion,

namely refraction. For just as, if some mobile body falls on anoth‐

er body that is immovable and impenetrable, it loses its former direction of

motion and acquires an entirely new one; so too, when a mobile, passing from

one body, runs into another body of unequal resistance or density, it does in‐

deed penetrate it, but is so bent and inclined that it acquires a new direction of

motion; whence refraction is very well defined: the inflection, or curving, of motion

by which a mobile body, on account of the greater or smaller resistance of the body which

it enters obliquely, from the straight line which it was describing

P is

p. 112

is deflected. We said which it enters obliquely, because if it fell perpendicularly, it would not be inflected at all, but would tend straight on.

341 But so that this may be understood more clearly and explained more accurately, let there be conceived a ray of light AB (Fig. XXII.), which, propagated in the air, falls obliquely on the surface of water CD; for this ray, as soon as it enters the water, is so inflected that it bends away from the straight line BE, which it would describe with straight motion if it always found the same density, and approaches the straight line BG, which is conceived as perpendicular to the surface CD.

342 But if the ray had issued from the point F, placed in the water, then on reaching the surface of the air it would no longer describe the straight line FH, but would rather be so inflected along AB as to recede not only from the point H, but also from the perpendicular BI itself. Hence in Dioptrics these are assumed and shown as the most certain laws of refractions: If a ray passes from a rarer body, or medium, into a denser body and medium, its motion will be so inflected as to approach the perpendicular; but if from a denser into a rarer, it recedes from the perpendicular itself.

343 But if not a ray of light but any other body, as e.g. a ball of lead or of ivory, were to descend from the air into water with an oblique motion, it would so inflect its motion as to recede from the perpendicular, just as, conversely, if it came out of water into air, it would approach the perpendicular. Therefore the motion of light and that of another body must be distinguished most accurately, lest refraction be thought to be performed by one and the same law in light and in other bodies. But for what reason all bodies whatever, if you except light, must be so refracted as to recede from the perpendicular will easily be understood if it is observed that water, as a denser body, resists motion more than air, which is lighter, and that therefore the motion impressed on the ball becomes in some degree more sluggish while it is entering the water.

344 And since it is easily detected by experiment that water resists perpendicular motion more than horizontal, of the two motions of which the oblique one is composed the perpendicular will become more sluggish, and the horizontal will be increased, and so the ball will recede from the perpendicular. But since a ray of light moves more easily in water, crystal and other bodies whose pores, or solid parts, are more stable, than in air, inasmuch as the parts of the air and the interstices formed by them are agitated by a perpetual flux, the ray itself will meet less resistance in water than in air, and so will be refracted by approaching the perpendicular.

Dissertation

DISSERTATION II

CHAPTER I

S TAT I C S ,

or

On certain particular motions

of solid bodies.

Preliminary notions are proposed.

aving set forth the various kinds of motions, we must explain certain 345

H peculiar motions of heavy solid bodies. In this treatment everyone

will understand how widely the elements of motion, and their use for

the conveniences of human life, extend, so that it ought to seem a

wonder to no one that the greatest effort has been spent on this subject by most

excellent men. Relying, therefore, on certain principles of the Mathematicians,

and with a previous knowledge of them, we shall survey Statics with a philosophical

eye. Let there be, then, an unfolding of the notions in order.

346 Statics is that part of Physics which discourses on the equilibrium of heavy

bodies. If it is concerned with the weight of solid bodies, it is called Geostatics, or

Statics without any addition; if it treats of fluids, it is named Hydrostatics. We shall

treat of the former first, with the most distinguished Michael Klaus, and then pur‐

sue the other, after general notions have first been indicated.

347 Power is the name given to any cause producing motion. Weight is that

which is moved by the power, or resists motion. In what sense living force and dead

force are to be taken we indicated above [§. 272.]. To distinguish the matter more

carefully here, some call the moving force joined with actual motion, whatever it

may be, living force; but that which merely sustains a weight, with only some striv‐

ing toward motion impressed on it, they hold for dead force. Momentum is usually

the name given to the force of a gravitating mass. Equilibrium is the equality of

momenta with one another, and their mutual compensation.

P2 348

p. 114

348 Homogeneous bodies are those all of whose sensible parts are of the same nature; heterogeneous, on the contrary, those whose parts are diverse as to nature. Heavy bodies, whether fluid or solid, are held to be homogeneous when their gravities are proportional to their volumes; but heterogeneous heavy bodies are those which are not allotted gravities proportional to their volumes.

349 One center is that of heavy bodies, another of gravity, another of magnitude, another of motion. The first is the common center of the universe and, in comparison with terrestrial bodies, the center of the earth, to which they are borne. The second is that point, placed inside or outside the body, about which parts of equal momenta, or equiponderant parts, stand on every side, as, long before Father Schott (h), Pappus of Alexandria (i) and Stevin (j) had more or less explained. Thus in bodies that comprehend all their parts united, the center of gravity is placed within the bodies themselves; but in a ring, a half-ring, a concave sphere or hemisphere, it is constituted outside, e.g. at the intersection of the diameters, a point from which a body suspended, even by thought alone, maintains equilibrium. The third, which is also named the center of figure, is that point in the magnitude, or extension, such that, if some plane, freely imagined, passes through it, the body is divided and cut into equally great parts, whether they are of the same weight or of different. This coincides with the center of gravity in regular homogeneous bodies, but is different in irregular and heterogeneous ones. The center of motion will be set forth a little below.

350 The line of direction of heavy bodies is the straight line drawn from the center of gravity of the body itself to the center of heavy bodies, and perpendicularly to the horizon [§. 143]. It has obtained this name because it directs the descent of heavy bodies, so that the center of gravity, and the heavy body itself, never departs from it. It is also called the diameter of gravity, because, passing through the center of gravity, it divides the body into two equiponderant parts.

351 The beam is the name given to a straight, rigid and inflexible line which can revolve most freely about one point of itself that is altogether immovable. Such is the line AB (Fig. XXIII.), if it is conceived as entirely rigid and void of weight, and freely revolvable about the immovable point F.

352 The center of motion is that immovable point about which weights suspended from the extreme points of a rigid line can move freely. Such (Fig. cit.) is the point F, if the weights A and B applied about it, while it stays altogether unmoved, can be moved. This point is also usually called the point of suspension, because the bodies hung from it, altogether immovable as it is, hang freely together with the beam. The same point also goes by the name of center of the fulcrum; for the Greeks it is called Hypomochlion, as if you were to say:

placed

placed under the lever; because, namely, it rests upon a rigid line, which is also called

the Mathematical lever, or line of the lever. Weights hung from the extreme points of

the same beam, when about the point of suspension they sustain each other under

such a law that neither can overcome the other and move it from its place, are said

to be set in equilibrium. Hence bodies are designated equiponderant which, hung from

the same beam, stand in equilibrium; but non-equiponderant if one prevails over the

other: whence the latter is named preponderant. The notions of the rest will be pre‐

sented more conveniently in their own places. From these is deduced the following

C O R O L L A R Y.

353

A body suspended from an immovable point does not rest unless its retaining

cord coincides with that straight line which, drawn from the point of suspen‐

sion, hangs perpendicularly over the horizontal plane. For let the pendulum recede

from the perpendicular AC (Fig. XXIV.) to B: since the straight line AC, passing

through the point of contact C and perpendicular to the tangent bd, passes, when

produced, through the center e (k); and since it is the least of all the straight lines

that can be drawn from the same center to the tangent (l), it will be less than the

straight line ae: and therefore also less than eB. Wherefore a heavy body placed at

B will stand farther from the center of heavy bodies than at C. But heavy bodies

strive to come as near as they can to the center of heavy bodies: therefore the pen‐

dulum will not come to rest at B, nor, for the same reason, in any other place than

at C; that is, it will not rest unless the thread coincides entirely with the perpendic‐

ular AC.

354 Conversely, moreover, when a heavy body is at rest, the plane on which it

stands perpendicularly will be parallel to the horizon. From this shines forth the ar‐

tifice of exploring, by means of a pendulum, whether a plane is parallel to the hori‐

zon or, on the contrary, inclined. Heavy bodies standing with a plane surface on a

horizontal plane remain unmoved if the line of direction falls within the base; but

they collapse if that same line strays and falls outside the base [§ 145]. The reason is

manifest: for in the former case the line of direction is sustained by the underlying

plane; not so in the other. Moreover: if in the former case the body ABDC were to

topple (Fig. XXV.) while the line of direction EF is contained within the base CD,

it would have to be turned and revolved about the extreme point D of the base, and

so the center of gravity E would have to ascend along the arc EG above the hori‐

zontal line EH, which conflicts with the action of the gravitating cause, and does

not happen except when forces opposing gravity are at work. But where (Fig.

XXVI.) the line of direction KL runs out beyond the base DC, the center of gravi‐

ty K can descend along the arc KM below the horizontal straight line KN,

p. 116

without anything obstructing it. Since, therefore, it is not hindered from descending, the heavy body must necessarily fall along that same arc.

355 From the consideration of the center of gravity it is likewise deduced why those things stand erect more firmly and more securely which rest on a broader base; and so why we ourselves, while we stand on both feet, remain safely, but on the contrary totter easily when supported on one alone; for in the former case the base is ample enough, and twin props sustain the body; but in the second it is narrow, and much narrower still when we press the floor only with the heel, so that the line of direction easily runs out beyond the base. Hence too are derived the rules of dancing, of walking, and of regulating the motions of the body. The very conformation of the animal body shows this same principle of equilibrium: the paired parts, distributed equally, occupy the sides, so that they are separated from the middle by an equal interval, while the single parts hold the middle place. Nor is this equilibrium evident in men only, but in brutes as well. For the wings of birds add an equal weight to them on either side: those which are allotted a longer neck are also furnished with longer feet, which they stretch out backward in flying; while they take their rest supported on one foot, they hide the head under the wing that lies crosswise opposite. We pass over countless things of this kind (m).

356 It is likewise seen from this doctrine why bodies touching a horizontal plane, even at a single point, remain in that place only when the line of direction passes through that point. In this way a homogeneous sphere BC (Fig. XXVII.), placed upon the plane MN parallel to the horizon, stands unmoved; for its center of magnitude a coincides with the center of gravity, and the straight line aE drawn from the center to the point of contact E is perpendicular to the tangent and to the plane MN (n): hence the line of direction passes through the point of contact, or base. But since (Fig. XXVIII.) the straight line xa, which is drawn from the center to the point of contact a, is perpendicular to the inclined plane AB, and so cannot stand perpendicularly on the horizontal plane DB: therefore the straight line xe, which hangs perpendicularly over the horizon and is the line of direction, cannot pass through the point of contact a, or base: the sphere therefore will come to rest at no point of the inclined plane. Here you have a phenomenon common enough, but a cause not commonly enough known.

CHAPTER II

P R I N C I P L E O F S TAT I C S I

P R I N C I P L E O F S TAT I C S I I

On the Principles, or fundamental Laws, and the Instruments

of Statics.

ext to be set forth are the principles, or Laws, of Statics, of very 357

N wide use indeed, from which is derived the diverse relation among

themselves of heavy bodies hung up. The chief of them, moreover,

and the foundation pertaining to Geostatics as well as to Hydrostatics,

namely: that the quantity of motion of a given body is the product of the weight, or mass,

multiplied into the velocity, we have already weighed elsewhere [§ 276]. One thing

alone remains: that, this being established, we unfold the rest, which rest upon

it as on a base, and embrace them all in few words, looking only to this, that we

treat chiefly the principal heads of the doctrine, in a manner suited to the un‐

derstanding of Beginners and in keeping with the plan and brevity of our

Elements. Let them follow, then, in order.

358

T he velocities of two heavy solid bodies hanging freely from the extremities of the same

beam are directly to each other as their distances from the center of motion.

359 For it is well established that body B (Fig. XXIX.) cannot be moved

along the arc BD without body A being depressed at the very same time along

the arc AC. But the velocities of two bodies set in motion are to each other as

the spaces traversed by them in the same time [By the Laws of velocities]: there‐

fore the velocity of body A is to the velocity of body B as the arc AC to the arc

BD. But the former arc is to the latter as the distance AE to the distance BE, or

as the radii of the circles, as is known from Geometry: therefore the velocity of

body A is to the velocity of body B as AE to BE, that is, as their distances from

the center of motion E.

360

H eavy bodies whose weights are equal, and which are placed, hung up, at an equal

distance with respect to the center of motion, remain in equilibrium. If the weights

are unequal and the distances equal, they do not remain in equilibrium, but the one that is

endowed with the greater weight

will

p. 118

P R I N C I P L E O F S TAT I C S I I I

will be depressed. If the weights are equal and the distances unequal, they do not stand

balanced, but the one that is removed further from the center of motion preponderates.

361 The first part is evident: since bodies equal in weight are posited, and

an equal distance from the center of motion is had, and so an equal velocity of

each (for since, by Princip. I, the velocities are as the distances, if these are

equal the velocities too must be equal), therefore the quantity of motion in

both is equal, or the momenta are equal: they will therefore stand unmoved in

equilibrium (by the Def. of equilib.). The second part is shown: since the distances

of the bodies are posited equal, the velocities are likewise equal. Therefore

their momenta are as the weights (for since the weights of bodies are as their

masses, and the quantities of motion of two bodies driven with equal velocity

are as their masses, they will also be as their weights). Wherefore the momen‐

tum of the one that is greater in weight will exceed the momentum of the oth‐

er; and, the equilibrium being removed, it will preponderate. The third part too

is clear: since the distance of one body is greater than the distance of the other,

the velocity of the former will likewise be greater than the velocity of the latter.

But the bodies are equal in weight. Therefore the momentum of the body more

remote from the center of motion will be greater than the momentum of the

other: they will therefore not persist balanced, but the one that is removed fur‐

ther will also preponderate more.

362

B odies of unequal weight, hung on a beam at unequal distances, obtain equilibrium if

the distances from the center of motion are reciprocally as the weights themselves,

that is: if the one that is endowed with the smaller weight is as much farther from the cen‐

ter of motion as the other (with which it is compared) is heavier and less distant from the

same center.

363 For let body A (Fig. cit.) be of twice greater mass than B, and let them

be so hung that the distance AE is to the distance EB as body B to A, that is:

let body B be twice smaller than the other, but stand twice as far removed from

the fixed point E: it is manifestly clear that A and B stand in equilibrium if the

quantity of motion in the one equals the quantity of motion in the other, that

is: if the momenta are equal. But these are equal by the very fact that their dis‐

tances from the center of motion are in the reciprocal ratio of the weights; for

since the velocities of the weights A and B are directly to each other as their

distances AE and BE, the velocity of body B is twice as great as the velocity of

body A. Let the former be called = 2c, the latter = c; the mass of body A = 2m, of

body B = m. So that hence this reciprocal proportion necessarily holds, 2c : c =

2m : m; since, therefore, the momentum of body B equals the product that aris‐

es from the double velocity multiplied into the simple mass,

it

p. 119

ON THE BALANCE

it will be = 2cm. But the momentum of body A is the product of the mass twice as

great multiplied by the simple velocity, that is: = 2mc, which is evidently the same.

The bodies will therefore stand in equilibrium. From these principles is taken the

rationale of weighing instruments, or Statical ones: the chief of them are held to be

the Balance and the Steelyard.

364

T he balance, or scales, is the best-known instrument of Statics, by which the un‐

known weight of a given body is explored by taking another of known gravity.

Several parts are distinguished in it. The first is the beam AC (Fig. XXX.), namely a

rigid rod divided into two parts AB and CB, equal both in length and in weight,

which are called the arms. The second is the handle DB, to which the beam is so fit‐

ted, by means of a small axle passed through the center of motion B and through

the holes of the handle, that it can move freely about the holes of the handle as

about a center. The third is the tongue x, which is fixed immovably at right angles to

the middle point of the beam: it is also called the trutina, examen, or argumentum of

the balance, because it shows either the parallelism of the beam with the horizontal

plane or its inclination. The fourth are the pans E and F, which, hung from the ex‐

treme parts of the beam, receive the weights.

365 For this whole Statical organ to be exact, it is necessary, first, that not only

the arms but also the threads from which the pans are suspended be equal in

weight. Secondly, it is required that the pans too be of equal weight. Thirdly, that

the friction upon the beam be, as far as can be done, slight and almost none.

Hence, to lessen the friction, the axle inserted in the tongue is made cylindrical,

and the hole in the tongue round, so that the contact may turn out smaller. Indeed,

if the axle ends in an edge on the side where it touches the tongue, the motion of

the beam will be quicker. Moreover, the following belong in general to the perfec‐

tion of the balance. Let the arms be longer; for an inequality of the weights, which

in shorter arms is sometimes scarcely discerned by sense, betrays itself very easily

in longer ones. Let the tongue likewise be made longer, for a not dissimilar reason.

The pans are better suspended from little metal chains than from threads, inas‐

much as the temper of the air sometimes acts upon threads in various ways.

366 As regards the more excellent use, that balance is to be preferred to the

others whose center of motion is above the straight line from whose extremities

the bodies to be weighed hang: whence, other things being equal, all require that

the center of gravity of the beam be placed a little below the center of motion. The

use of the balance is very well known, so that there is no need to mention anything

about it. A defect is brought into the balance chiefly by the inequality of the arms;

for, their inequality being posited, the bodies which, placed on the pans, are in

equilibrium will be not of the same but of unequal weight, as

Q (from

p. 120

O N T H E S T E E LYA R D

(from Princip. III.) is clear. This fraud (indeed, every fraud) in deceitful balances

is detected by making an exchange of the weights in the pans, as Father Schott

teaches: for if (he says) that which was before in equilibrium in the right pan, when now

placed in the left pan, preserves the equilibrium, it is a sign that the balance is exact. But if

it happens that by this exchange of the pans the same bodies appear now equal, now un‐

equal, it is manifest that the balance is deceitful and unjust. (o)

367

T he steelyard, the Roman or Chinese Stater, is a weighing instrument comprised

of unequal arms (Fig. XXXI.). Four parts are counted in it: namely the rigid

rod, or beam, AB, divided into the unequal arms BD and AD, of which the longer,

BD, is divided into parts equal among themselves, ab, bd, de, etc., each of which

equals the distance of the point D from the point A, or the length of the shorter

arm. These parts are divided again into other smaller parts, equal among them‐

selves, for determining minute quantities. The handle ED, enclosing the tongue, to

which the beam is fitted by means of an axle, as in the balance. The pan, or hook, is

hung from the extremity of the shorter arm, so that the body to be weighed can

be placed on it or suspended from it. The counterpoise N is movable hither and

thither, and is therefore called the runner of the steelyard.

368 For this instrument to be exact it is required that the shorter arm, to‐

gether with the hook, equal the weight of the longer arm when the counterpoise

is removed: or, if that is not done, that the longer arm be divided into propor‐

tional parts, a division that is found by trial. Steelyards have this advantage over

the balance, that the weight even of large bodies can be explored by means of

them with a single weight, and that a fairly small one; although in this the scales

excel, that in them we can discern even small particles of an ounce, and more

conveniently, and in our regions we usually do so; not so with steelyards. The

weight of a given body is examined with this instrument by the following law:

the body M, whose weight is being explored, being hung on, the counterpoise N

is set at that place of the longer arm at which it obtains equilibrium with the

body to be weighed; equilibrium being now established, the hung body has the

same ratio to the counterpoise that, reciprocally, the distance of the counter‐

poise from the center of motion has to the distance of the hung body from the

same, or to the shorter arm: namely, if the counterpoise N is of one pound, and

its distance Dm is to the distance DA as 4 to 1, the body M will be of four

pounds.

369 The reason of this is abundantly clear (from Princip. III of Statics). But

if

(o) Magia universalis, pt. 3, Mag. Stat., Syntagm. 3, Pragm. 3, toward the end.

p. 121

DISSERTATION III

if, further, the momentum at the point m is increased, so that, if that force were

made such as to exceed the weight of a hundredweight, a weight of four hundred‐

weight suspended from the hook F would be lifted by it: if the momentum were

placed in a more remote part, the hung body would be raised more easily still. And

hence, since a power applied to the arm of the steelyard is endowed with so much

greater force the farther that arm is stretched out, it is plain that forces can in this

way be increased without limit: so that for this reason the Syracusan Mathematician

Archimedes, not without a foundation established by the laws of Statics, promised

Hiero that he would move the earth from its place, if there were some place outside

it on which to stand.

370 Moreover, several defects can creep into the steelyard; for if the shorter arm,

taken with the hook or pan, does not keep equilibrium with the other arm when the

counterpoise is removed; likewise if the parts into which the longer arm is divided

are unequal, or lack the due measure, the steelyard will always be deceitful: indeed,

since it can deceive those who use it on other heads as well, and it is not so easy to

detect the deceit, the distinguished Wolff says (p) it is better that it be banished from

common life.

MECHANICS,

or

The doctrine of Machines.

echanics, or the Machinal science, hands down the principles and laws by 371

M which a power, of itself unequal to sustaining and moving a body, can be

rendered fit by the aid of certain machines either to sustain it or even

to move it. Whence a mechanical machine is the name for that through which a power

applied to it is rendered fit for sustaining or moving a body, neither of which it could

accomplish. One machine is called simple, another compound. The former does not co‐

alesce out of several, each of which would separately suffice to produce the effect: the

latter arises out of other simple ones fitted to each other by a fixed law.

372 In this place there now comes to be set down the single principle of the

Machinal science, a general one indeed, by which alone it has pleased us to embrace

the several principles that others have established here.

Q2 Principle

(p) Elem. Mechan., §. 778.

p. 122

PRINCIPLE OF MECHANICS

ON THE LEVER

373

P ower and weight must be so applied to a machine that they cannot be moved together

unless the power moves more swiftly than the weight: and indeed under this law, that

the velocity of the power have a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocal‐

ly, the weight itself has to the force of the power: and the greater this ratio is, the more easi‐

ly will a slight power move a huge body.

374 For let the force of the power be = p, and the weight to be moved = P,

the velocity of the power = C, and the velocity of the weight = c. If the velocity

of the power has a greater ratio to the velocity of the weight than, reciprocally,

the weight to the force of the power, it will be C : c > P : p; and therefore the

product, or momentum, of the power, pC, will be greater than the momentum

of the resisting weight, Pc. The heavy body will therefore be moved by the pow‐

er. Since, further, the product pC turns out the greater the more the ratio C : c

exceeds the ratio P : p, it follows that a huge body can be moved, by means of a

machine, the more easily even by a slight power, the greater the ratio of the ve‐

locity with which the power is endowed to the velocity of the weight is than the

ratio that holds reciprocally between the weight and the force of the power.

From which indeed it at once shines out that this saving in lifting weights by

machines is joined with some loss of time, which nevertheless ought rightly to

be counted among the gains. This being established, let us weigh the machines

for a while, so far as is necessary for the purpose of Physics.

375

T he lever, the first machine of Mechanics, is an oblong stake consisting of

solid material, which is conveniently employed for moving huge weights

more easily. Three things are distinguished in it, namely: the moving power, or

momentum; the resistance, or weight to be sustained or moved; and finally the

fixed point on which the lever rests, immovable: this is called in Latin fulcrum,

by the Greeks hypomochlion, by Vitruvius pressio. But since these three points can

be disposed in the lever in a threefold manner, a threefold kind is therefore usu‐

ally distinguished.

376 The first is when the fulcrum holds the middle place between the power

and the weight, such as the lever AB (Fig. XXXII.), where the fulcrum C is in‐

termediate between the power B and the weight A. The second kind is when the

fulcrum C (Fig. XXXIII.) is found at one extremity, the power A at the other

extremity, and the weight B holds the middle. The third is had when the power

A (Fig. XXXIV.) occupies the middle between the fulcrum B and the weight C.

The lever of the first kind they call heterodromous; of the second, homodromous;

that of the third kind they refer to the homodromous.

In

p. 123

ON THE WHEEL AND AXLE

377 In the first kind of lever, by as much as the distance CB exceeds the dis‐

tance AC, by so much does the power B exceed the resistance of the body A: and

so, if the distance between the fixed point and the power is ten times greater than

the distance of the weight from the same point, and the body A is of a hundred

pounds, then, provided the power B is equivalent to a little more than ten pounds,

it will lift it; yet in such a manner that while the power, in descending, covers a

space of about ten inches, the weight is raised through an interval of only one inch.

The same holds in the lever of the second kind; for by as much as the distance AC

exceeds the distance BC, by so much more efficaciously will the power overcome

the resistance of the weight. In the third kind of lever there is only this advantage,

that the moving power can move a lighter weight with a greater velocity: which is

not without its utility when a saving of time is sought.

378

T he wheel and axle, the second machine of Mechanics, is an instrument suited to

lifting weights, in which the cylinder hi (Fig. XXXV.), which they call the axle,

sustained on either side by the props k, l, has placed around it a drum, me, which

they call the peritrochium: in its circumference are fixed round rods, ac, bd, which

are called spokes, or scytalae, by which the power applied turns the peritrochium

with the axle, and lifts the weight by means of a rope wound round it. Elsewhere

the name peritrochium is given to that circular plane itself, in place of which the

scytalae are substituted. If the scytalae are joined to an axle having a horizontal po‐

sition, it is called a Windlass; but if the axle is set up perpendicularly, it is named a

Capstan. The use of windlasses is very great in mines. The capstan has this advan‐

tage, that several men together can be applied to each of the scytalae without hin‐

dering one another.

379 This machine is referred to the lever of the first kind; indeed, in reality it is

a perpetual lever. For the hypomochlion is in the middle of the axle, namely at the

point m, or f; indeed, points of this kind are rightly conceived through the whole

axle: the moving power placed at a or b has the distance am, or bm, from the fixed

point: the resistance is constituted at the point e of the surface of the axle itself,

and is distant from the fixed point f only by the semidiameter of the axle, ef.

Whence, by as much as the distance am exceeds the distance ef, by so much more

easily does the power at a overcome the resistance at e: and therefore, the greater

the scytala is to be, the more the forces of the power increase. And from this same

principle are deduced the force and efficiency of wheels whose motion is driven by

treading, or by the inflow of water, likewise of the sails that are turned round by the

wind in mills, and of other instruments of that kind.

On

p. 124

O N T H E P U L L E Y.

380

T he pulley, the third machine of Mechanics, is an instrument consisting of one

or several little wheels revolving about their axles, which are fixed somewhere,

by which, with a rope wound round them, which is called the ductarius, weights are

drawn in. If only one little wheel is employed, it is called a simple pulley, and

monospastos; if it is composed of two, three, four or more, it is called, according to

their number, dispastos, trispastos, tetraspastos or polyspastos.

381 A simple pulley revolving about an immovable axle does not increase the

forces of the moving power; for as much as the weight D ascends (Fig. XXXVI.), so

much does A descend, and so the motions both of the weight and of the power are

equal. Wherefore its whole advantage lies in this, that the direction of the power is

changed, while, namely, by the aid of the pulley the power is moved downward

which would otherwise have to be moved upward for the weight to be raised.

Moreover, in the descent of the power, the forces grow from the very weight of the

moving body. Finally, the rope rolled round the wheel is less worn by friction.

382 It is plain, moreover, that the pulley BC is a perpetual heterodromous lever;

for the fixed axle L, about which the little wheel revolves, is like a fulcrum, around

which the power and the weight, which behave just as if they were applied to the

extremities of the diameter CB, are moved together. If the simple pulley (Fig.

XXXVII.) is movable, since A, the extremity of the diameter AaD corresponding

to the immovable point F, is the fulcrum on which the rope rests by means of the

pulley, the power is placed at the other extremity of the diameter, D, and the

weight, finally, in the middle, a; and so, since a pulley so arranged is a lever of the

second kind, and the distance of the power from the fulcrum is to the distance of

the weight from the same, namely DA to Aa, as 2 to 1, it is clear (from the preced‐

ing Chapter) that there will be equilibrium if the power is to the weight as 1 : 2. But

the weight will be moved by the power if the latter is to it in a greater ratio than

subduple: for supposing it is as 4 : 6, since the distance DA is double the distance

Aa, and then since the power moves twice as fast as the weight (by Princip. I of

Stat.), the velocity of the power will therefore have a greater ratio to the velocity of

the weight than, reciprocally, the weight itself to the force of the power, namely 2 :

1 > 6 : 4, and so the weight will then be moved by the aid of the movable pulley (by

the Princip. of Mechan.). The former pulley is called monospastos of the first kind; this

other, monospastos of the second kind.

383 In the Dispastos, one little wheel of which is immovable and the other mov‐

able (Fig. XXXVIII.), the power P moves twice as fast as the weight M; for the

lower little wheel cannot ascend from a to D unless the power P descends through

a space = Da + bx, that is, through double the space covered by the weight.

Therefore, by means of the dispastos, the power will move

the

p. 125

the weight, if it is to it in a greater ratio than 1 : 2, and so the power is rendered dou‐

ble by it; and it is helped just as much as by the monospastos of the second kind.

Wherefore, since all increase of the moving power is to be derived from the movable

little wheels, and this force grows by as much as its velocity exceeds the velocity of

the weight, for that reason in the trispastos (Fig. XXXIX.) the power is tripled, since

indeed the little wheel MN cannot be raised from d to b unless the power P, in de‐

scending, covers a space triple the height db, that is: unless three segments of the

rope equal to the height db are drawn in. Thus in the tetraspastos the power is quadru‐

pled, in the polyspastos it is multiplied many times over.

384 Whence by means of the polyspastos a huge weight will be lifted with a slight

power employed, if the ratio of that power to the weight is greater than the ratio of

unity to the number of little wheels constituting the polyspastos. Wherefore, given the

value of the power = 10, and the number of little wheels likewise = 6 (Fig. XL.), the

product will express the value of the weight to be sustained by the power applied to

this machine, = 60; and this weight will be carried upward if a little greater force of

the power is added. Specifically, the part AB of the polyspastos is the upper pulley, and

the part CD the lower pulley; each is named rechamus in Vitruvius.

O N T H E PA N C R AT I U M .

385

T he Pancratium, the fourth machine of Mechanics, is a complex of several toothed

wheels associated by a certain artifice and under such a law that the teeth of one

are inserted into the little teeth of another wheel revolving about its own axis, where‐

by it comes about that, when one is moved about its little axle, all the others are set

in motion. This machine is named Glossocomum by Pappus (q), and, on the same wit‐

ness, it was either invented or explained by Hero of Alexandria, for which reason it is

commonly called Hero’s Glossocomum. Its form and construction are various: it will be

enough to have sketched one, from which it may appear how greatly the forces are

increased by a composition of wheels of this kind (r).

386 Let there be (Fig. XLI.) a Pancratium composed of four axles with toothed

wheels. Let the larger wheels have, as to diameter, the ratio to the smaller of 10 : 1,

and let the ratio of the number of teeth be the same. Let the handle AB, or radius, to

which the power is applied, be ten times longer than the radius of the little wheel C;

the velocity of the power will be to the velocity of the wheel C as 10 : 1. On the sec‐

ond axle the greater wheel D, furnished with ten times more teeth than the little

wheel C, is turned once while C meanwhile revolves ten times. To the same axle is

joined a little wheel E, equal to the former

C,

(q) Mathematical Collection, bk. 8, at prop. 10.

(r) Father Schott, Magia universalis, pt. 3, Magia Thaumaturga, ch. 1, exhibits Pancratia constructed

in various ways.

p. 126

ON THE INCLINED PLANE

C, which completes its revolution in the time in which the wheel D is turned round.

Let the teeth in the wheel F likewise be ten times more numerous than the little

teeth of the little wheel E, so that the latter must revolve ten times before F is borne

once round its axle and carries off with it the attached wheel G. Finally the wheel H,

itself too having ten times more teeth, will turn once with the axle IH and the cylin‐

der K, which is contained by the same diameter as the wheel C, and which, revolving

about the axle IH, lifts the weight by means of a rope.

387 This series and proportion of revolutions being posited, the velocity of the

power A will be to the velocity of the little wheel C as 10000 : 1000; the velocity of

the latter to the velocity of the little wheel E as 1000 : 100; that of this one to the ve‐

locity of G as 100 : 10; finally the velocity of G to the velocity of the cylinder, and of

the weight L, as 10 : 1. Wherefore this proportion holds (ex aequo ordinata): the veloci‐

ty of the power A is to the velocity of the weight L as 10000 : 1. And hence, by the

aid of this machine, a force able to lift one pound is rendered fit for lifting 10000

pounds. Indeed, by means of the Glossocomum the power can be increased by such

increments that, as the most distinguished Father Schott has demonstrated by calcu‐

lation, with this machine compounded of twenty-four larger wheels the earth, even if

it were made wholly of gold, could be raised on high from its place by a power weigh‐

ing 125 pounds (s).

388

A n inclined plane is a plane surface forming unequal angles with the horizontal

plane on which it stands. It is counted among the Mechanical machines on this

account, that huge weights are either sustained or lifted on it more easily. Wherefore

the laws by which the forces of moving bodies are increased by the aid of this plane

come to be weighed a little; but before this let it be noted that the weight with which

a body placed on an inclined plane strives to descend, and which must be overcome,

is called the respective weight; but the whole weight of a body resting on no prop, the

absolute weight.

389 If a heavy body (Fig. XLII.) placed on the inclined plane ABC is sustained by

a power acting along the direction DK parallel to the plane, the power will be to the

absolute weight of the body as the height of the plane AB to its length AC. For let

lines be drawn: one, DE, from the center of gravity to the point of contact with the

plane; another, DF, expressing the direction of gravity, or of the absolute weight, DH;

and finally a third, EF, perpendicular to the line DF: there result the three points of

the bent, or angular, lever DEF, whose hypomochlion is E, the power D, and the

weight F (for it is all one whether the power at K or at D

be

(s) Place cited, Mach. 2.

p. 127

be understood to be placed; yet let the whole weight be thought of as rightly collect‐

ed in the one point F of the line of direction D F). Therefore the power in D is to the

weight in F as F E to D E, and, on account of the similarity of the triangles D E F

and A B C, D : F = A B : A C. But if the power acts along the direction R I (Fig.

XLIII.), parallel to the base M N, so that the weight may be sustained by it, it is nec‐

essary that the power be to the weight as the height of the inclined plane to its base.

390 For when the perpendicular Q T has been erected upon the direction R I, the

angular lever T Q S will again be had, so that the power I can be conceived to be in T

and the weight R in S, the same things, namely, being supposed that we assumed

above. Hence the power I will be to the weight S as S Q to T Q; that is, on account of

the similar triangles R Q S, S Q O, O P N and L M N, T : S = L M : M N will hold.

Hence a slight power will raise a weight along an inclined plane if its ratio to the ab‐

solute weight of the body is greater than that which holds between the height and

the length of the plane. And hence, in general, the forces of the power for sustaining,

or drawing, a heavy body upon an inclined plane are increased the more, the greater

the length of the plane is made than its height: and so, if the height were infinitely

small, or the plane horizontal, an infinitely small sustaining power is required. From

the inclined plane are derived the Screw and the Wedge.

O N T H E S C R E W.

391

T he screw is an inclined plane carried round on the surface of a cylinder, namely

when the cylinder is furrowed into equal and parallel spirals, which we call helices.

It is joined, moreover, as a double one: one formed on the exterior surface I K (Fig.

XLIV.), the other on the interior surface L M; the former is called the male screw, the

latter the female screw: each is made in such a way that the hollow spirals of the latter,

cut into it, fit exactly the projecting spirals of the inner cylinder, and the helices re‐

ceive each other mutually. The ratio by which forces are aided by means of the screw

is contained in the following laws.

392 Since the screw I K is an inclined plane encircling the surface of a cylinder,

and the direction of the power applied to the screw L M is parallel to the base of the

inclined plane, the power will be in equilibrium with the weight (by what was said on

the inclined plane) if the former is to the latter as the distance between two helices

nearest each other is to the circuit of the screw, or the periphery of the circle which

the power describes. Wherefore a huge body will be moved by the forces of a slight

power applied to the screw, if the periphery of the circle run through by the power

has a greater ratio to the distance of the nearest helices than the weight to the pow‐

er: since, namely, the velocity of the power will then have a greater ratio to the veloci‐

ty of the weight than the weight itself has to the power: and so the momentum of the

power will exceed the momentum of the weight and of the resistance.

R Whence

p. 128

ON THE WEDGE. 395

Whence it comes about that screws are the stronger, the closer to one another their

helices are cut, the circuit of the cylinder remaining the same.

393 If a screw is joined to a toothed wheel in such a way that by its revolution the

little teeth of the wheel are driven and the wheel is turned round, it is called the per‐

petual or endless screw, because it can be turned without end. (Fig. XLV.) If the power

is applied at A, it will complete one circuit of the screw while the wheel F E is ad‐

vanced by the interval of only one tooth. The power applied at A must therefore be

revolved as many times as the wheel F E is furnished with teeth, in order that a com‐

plete revolution of this wheel be obtained; and so that the axle E H may complete an

entire revolution, and hence that the weight G hanging from it may be raised

through a space equal to the periphery of the axle. Wherefore, if the wheel F E is

supposed to be furnished with a hundred teeth, and the periphery described by the

radius A B contains the periphery of the axle H E ten times, the velocity of the pow‐

er will be to the speed of the weight as a hundred times the periphery of the circle

described by the radius B A to once the periphery of the axle H E, that is, as 1000 to

1. Hence, by means of this machine, a force able to sustain one pound will establish

equilibrium with a weight of a thousand pounds; and it will raise it if it obtains a

greater ratio to it than 1 to 1000.

394 Finally, a peculiar screw deserves to be pointed out in this place, which re‐

ceived the name Archimedean from that same author. (Fig. XLVI.) It is defined by the

cylinder A B, around which a tube is wound in the manner of spirals, a tube more

conveniently made of lead; the extreme part A can be turned about the axis by means

of a handle; the other, B, having the orifice of the tube attached, is sunk under water,

and the whole cylinder is inclined to the horizon at an angle of about half a right an‐

gle. These things being set up, when the screw is turned round, the water entering

through the orifice of the tube is raised step by step, by the revolution of the ma‐

chine itself, through the spirals as through so many inclined planes, and is at length

poured out at A.

T he wedge is a quadrangular pyramid ending in an edge. (Fig. XLVII.) The plane A

D F B is called the base, A B the breadth or back, a A or a B the height, a C the

length, C E the edge of the wedge. The power usually applied to this machine is either

striking or pressing, and by means of the wedge it splits and tears apart even the

hardest bodies.

396 Most derive the force of the wedge from the inclined plane (the illustrious

Fortunato da Brescia (t) objecting altogether, a controversy on which we shall settle

nothing certain), regarding it as composed of two inclined planes A C, B C: and since

it is all the same whether the body is moved over the inclined plane or the plane is

thrust forward under the body to be moved

and

(t) Phys., pt. 2, §. 2147. See Fr. Schott, Mag. Mechan., Syntagm. 5.

p. 119

and moreover the direction of the power which drives bodies apart by means of the

wedge is parallel to its length, they infer therefore that the power is to the force of

the obstacle as half the breadth, or thickness, of the wedge is to its length, that is: ½

A B : a C. Hence, since in a sharper wedge the height has a smaller ratio to the

length, if this same is supposed to remain, a sharper wedge will on that account sepa‐

rate the parts of an obstacle more strongly than a blunt one.

397 Let these things said about the common machines suffice. From them innu‐

merable others are composed for various uses; if desire for these should hereafter

take hold of anyone, let him consult, among others, chiefly Leupold (u), Varignon (x),

and the description, drawn up at length, of the Machines approved by the Paris

Academy of Sciences (y). It is our task to teach, not artisans and builders of ma‐

chines, but Physicists, those things which they can neither be ignorant of without

disgrace nor ought to dwell upon too long, hastening on to other matters. It will help

only to observe a very few things for the knowledge of these.

R E M A R K O N T H E D O C T R I N E O F M AC H I N E S .

398

S ince, wherever three points are found, in one of which a moving power is applied,

to another of which a weight to be overcome corresponds, while the third is that

about which the motion is performed, there we can fittingly set a lever before our

minds (either a curved one, in which the points are disposed along a curved line, or an

angular or bent one, where the points are set in straight lines composing an angle), and

there the doctrine handed down about it has its place; and since this holds in a great

many things, motions of quite different kinds can therefore be clearly unfolded from

the nature of the lever. Borelli certainly shows that all the motions of animals are ex‐

plained from the knowledge of the lever (z). Indeed the forces of very many instru‐

ments are derived from this: scissors, or pincers, represent a double lever of the first

kind, whose fulcrum is the little pin; the power is applied to the extreme parts of the

arms; the body to be cut makes the resistance.

399 Likewise a stick to be easily broken over the knee exhibits a double heterodro‐

mous lever. For the hands impress motion on each extremity; the fulcra are those

parts of the leg on which the stick rests; the resistance to be overcome occupies the

middle place between these points of contact. Whence it follows that bodies are cut

apart by scissors the more easily,

R2 the

(x) Nouvelle Mechanique.

p. 130

both the longer the arms of the handle are, and the closer the body comes to the little pin; and again, that this stick is broken the more readily, the farther out the parts by which it is grasped extend. The reason is also given, from the nature of the heterodromous lever, why a mill driven by the wind or by the inflow of water turns the faster, the farther the sails or spokes are stretched out. For the impact of the air flowing against them, or of the water, acts as the moving powers; the axle, which the sails or wheels surround, takes the place of the hypomochlion; the stone has the role of the load.

400 Nor by a dissimilar law does the homodromous lever make plain to us the force of oars; for the oar rests on the water as on a fulcrum, the ship to be moved forward holds the part of the weight, the hands that of the power: for that reason it happens that the vessel is propelled the more easily, the farther the rower is from the thole-pin and the closer the thole-pin is brought to the water. From this same principle the forces of the rudder are derived: likewise it is deduced why a ship runs forward the more swiftly, the higher the yard is raised on the mast. For the wind filling the sails stands in the place of the power, the ship for the weight, the lowest part of the mast for the fulcrum. It is explained also why a nail firmly fixed in a board is easily pulled out by a forked hammer taking hold of its projecting head. For the hammer represents a lever of the second kind, whose handle the moving power drives; the board, against which its other end is pressed, is the fulcrum; the nail holds the part of the load to be raised. For the same reason a knife fixed at one end to a table cuts the more strongly, the closer to the point of attachment the thing to be divided is applied. Similarly we grind even harder foods more strongly with the molar teeth than with the so-called incisors; for the former are nearer the fulcrum than the latter.

401 II. To the wheel and axle are referred the elastic springs of portable clocks, and the conical screw to which the chain is attached; and from the principles of this mechanical machine the construction of the parts of automaton animals was ingeniously devised. In this artful structure the spring of the steel lamina S (Fig. XLVIII.), coiled round in a spiral, plays the part of the power, while by means of the little chain it drives the toothed wheel which it has joined at the extremity F, the screw A B, and the wheel on whose revolution the motions of the rest in the clock depend: the resistance to be overcome by the spring is therefore the revolution of the wheel E, and so of the others; the center of motion, or fulcrum, is found in the axle A B itself.

402 Now, since the elastic lamina, when fully coiled, being stretched more strongly, has a greater force when it begins to unwind itself, and this force is continually diminished in the very course of the unwinding, while the resistance, on the other hand, remains constantly the same (for the difficulty in moving the wheels of the clock does not decrease), the little screw-shaped axle which the chain surrounds is therefore fashioned not into a cylinder but into a conical form; whereby it comes about that, while the spring acts upon the axle at the beginning of its unwinding, the chain embraces its narrower part K L, but as the unwinding proceeds the chain reaches the wider circuit of the axle, F or O.

Therefore

p. 131

Therefore, for overcoming the resistance, which is always the same, the power continually retains the same momentum; since, namely, there is an equal compensation, so that, while the forces of the spring are unimpaired at the beginning, its momentum is tempered by a diminution of velocity; while, that is, the power, applied through the chain and acting, is at the beginning brought nearer to the fulcrum B; whereas afterwards, on the contrary, the breadth of the axle brings it about that, though the power indeed decreases of itself, it is nevertheless removed farther from the fulcrum, by the radius, namely, of the spirals F or O, and so its speed is increased.

403 Wheels and axles, without doubt, are also the keys which we use to wind the springs of clocks or to raise their weights, and which, according to the varying position of the clock, will give now a windlass, now a capstan. The gimlet too is an instrument of this kind; although, on account of the spirals twisted round its point, it has something of the screw mixed in, and on account of the sharpness in which it ends, something of the wedge.

404 III. The pulley, in which Descartes boldly declared (a) that it seemed to him foolish to look for a lever, since, used by itself, it increases the forces of the power very little, is joined to similar ones, as we have already taught; and this is done under the law that either some hang over others, as the figures above showed, or the little wheels, equal in size, are set beside one another in a position parallel to each other (Fig. XLIX.), a construction which is very convenient, especially when the narrowness of the space in which the machine is to be placed does not admit another arrangement. In the use of pulleys those who treat of them advise that it be observed that all the parts of the hauling rope always be parallel to one another. And since the rope must be bent less in larger pulleys than in smaller ones, the former are on that account superior to the latter. But since the number of ropes is not increased by the size of the pulleys, and besides certain inconveniences present themselves in larger little wheels, which arise from their greater weight, from the stronger friction on the axles, etc., it is therefore clear that that law does not hold universally. Further, to diminish the friction either of the pulley about its little axle, or of the wheel and axle within its case, or within the holes which are called chelonia, it will be expedient to form the holes of the little wheels, or the cases, not round but out of three or four convex circular arcs; for the little axle, turning round, will touch these arched surfaces in fewer points (b). Pulleys joined with the wheel and axle compose a machine of very frequent use, which is called the Crane, and whose most convenient construction is described by Musschenbroek (c). The windlass with a polyspast yields another kind of machine, which they call the gin.

IV.

(a) Letters, pt. 2, letter 24.

(b) See the illustrious de la Hire, Mechanique, Prop. 63.

(c) Essai de Physique, §. 542, saying that it was invented by Mr. Padmore at Bristol in England; and described by Desaguliers, vol. 1, p. 179, Cours experiment.

p. 132

405 IV. A toothed wheel, if its teeth project along the direction of the radius, is called stellate; if they are perpendicular to the radius and turned downward, pectinate; but if vertical, crowned.

406 The axle which often turns a toothed wheel round is furnished with teeth, either cut into it or inserted, that is, with pegs, and is named the lantern, or the runner of the wheel. In this instrument it is to be noted that, since the teeth of the axle must perform their function more often than the toothed wheel, especially one of many teeth, and are on that account worn down more, they must be made firmer than in the toothed wheel. Care must besides be taken that the same teeth of the wheel are not always engaged with the same peg, or tooth of the axle itself; but that, different ones being inserted among different ones, it may come about that, being worn against one another in various ways, they may attain the more nearly to equality of motion: which is effected if the teeth acting on one another are of such a number that one does not exactly contain the other, as if the wheel comprises 60 teeth, the axle 7 or 9. (d)

407 V. Not only experiments but reason too, relying on the principles established before, proves that heavy bodies let down along an inclined plane accelerate their motion uniformly; for along an inclined plane neither the force of the cause of gravitation nor the continued motion of the mobile itself is stopped; hence at each single moment a new impulse from the gravific fluid is added, by which the respective velocity is continually increased in the proportion which holds between the absolute and the respective gravity (f). Hence, just as bodies falling freely acquire at the end of their fall that force by which they could be raised to as great a height as that from which they fell, so it is necessary that bodies descending along an inclined plane possess the same forces, the resistance of the medium and of other bodies being set aside: for, these being supposed, since the velocity acquired at the end of the fall is not destroyed in the body if nothing presents itself to the falling body except that alone which changes its direction, it is a consequence that the force obtained in the progress of the descent is spent upon the ascent.

408 From this doctrine the motion of pendulums, and its physical reason, are derived: for if the arc which a pendulum runs through in its descent is regarded as composed of infinitely small straight lines, that is, as of inclined planes contiguous to one another, C A, A B (Fig. L.), of infinitely small length, whose bend, or angle A, only changes the direction, the heavy body, in traversing the arc, will acquire that velocity by whose force it could ascend to a height equal to it. The friction of the thread at the point of suspension, indeed, the parts of the holder itself, which are not entirely flexible, and the resistance of the air gradually take something away from the force of the motion all the while: for that reason, unless some cause conserving the oscillations is added, the arcs continually decrease; nor is the hung weight raised altogether to the height of its descent, but only to one equal to it so far as the senses can tell.

VI.

(d) See Krafft, Praelect. Phys., pt. 2, ch. 2, §. 83.

(f) See Introduct. facil. in doctrin. de motu by Fr. Erasmus Froelich, ch., Prop. 4 ff.

409 VI. The screw, which is usually fitted up in many ways, is employed for a

NOTE

great many uses. Forces are increased very much by its means, and indeed with such

an increase that Fr. Schott relates, from Münster, that whole wooden houses were

moved by the help of screws (g). This advantage is besides found in them, that they

sustain the weight by themselves even when the power is removed, provided the he‐

lices of each receive one another mutually and are pressed against each other; so the

power can meanwhile rest and recover itself without loss. Yet the great friction of the

parts in this machine makes its use less convenient: a defect which is remedied by

putting grease between the windings of the spirals. The same Schott advises, besides,

that it be observed that, so that the screw may be more durable, the nut should com‐

prise several spirals; for if it has only one, then the mass of the weight to be raised,

resting on that one alone, easily causes it damage (h).

410 VII. To the wedge belong various manufactured things: knives, swords, scis‐

sors, gimlets, and others like them; indeed, the efficacy of the molecules composing

natural bodies is derived from the nature of this mechanical machine: namely, of

acrid and corrosive poisons, such as sublimate of mercury, arsenic, aqua fortis, etc.,

which act like wedges.

411

I n mechanical machines ropes are wont to be, and must be, employed in manifold

ways: and as they are aids for moving masses of bodies by means of machines, so

they very often add no small part of hindrance. Fr. de Lana (i) worthily enlarged this

treatment of Mechanics; the illustrious Amontons (j) was the first to work it out by

an elegant method, and he showed that it matters greatly to know the measure of

this resistance, pointing out that, for the most part, the resistance to be overcome by

the moving power can be increased by one third part solely from the stiffness of the

ropes: which he demonstrated by experiments through the following theorems. I.

That the resistance depending on the stiffness of ropes increases in the direct ratio

of the weights, or forces, stretching them. II. That this same resistance is increased

besides, all other things being equal, in the proportion in which the diameter of the

ropes grows. III. That ropes are folded with the more difficulty, the smaller the cylin‐

ders or pulleys which they surround: although this resistance does not grow in that

very proportion in which the diameters are diminished. To these remarks of the

Author the most illustrious Nollet added experiments and illustrations (k).
