o remedy the defect of touch in exploring the heat and cold of bodies, 598

T the more recent Philosophers invented that instrument which is com‐

monly called the Thermometer, or thermoscope, which we use as a criteri‐

on for discerning the degree of heat and cold in bodies. There are sev‐

eral forms of it, and as it were species. Its first invention is attributed to Cornelis

Drebbel, a Dutchman; Sanctorius afterwards brought it to a better condition; the

Florentine Academicians added greater perfection, after whom they are named

Florentine thermometers. All these are constructed with most highly rectified

spirit of wine. The mercurial thermometer was invented by Daniel Fahrenheit,

and is therefore called the Fahrenheit Thermometer. The most distinguished

Réaumur found a method of making thermometers of spirit of wine which corre‐

spond to one another by so constant a law that, placed in the same spot, they

mark the same degree of heat. We do not wish to dwell on explaining the con‐

struction of the thermometer. It has been explained most clearly in his periodical

sheets (p) by our fellow American Don José Ignacio Bartolache, Doctor of

Medicine, and for a four-year term Holder of the Principal Chair of Medicine in

the Royal and Pontifical Academy of Mexico, etc., a man who has deserved excel‐

lently of Mathematics and of the whole of Medicine, an outstanding cultivator of

the Sciences and of the Liberal Arts. Fig. LXI exactly represents the Fahrenheit

thermometer.

599 That

(p) Mercurio Volante sobre asuntos de Física y Medicina, no. 3.

p. 189

599 That nothing of use may be lacking to you, I shall add something on the Hygroscope and the Barometer. The Hygroscope, which is also usually called the Hygrometer, is an instrument by which the humidity and dryness of the air are explored, and their increases and decreases are made manifest. It is usually constructed in this way. Let a hempen rope, or a gut string A B (Fig. LXII), whose one end A is fixed in the wall, be stretched over the small wheel B; from the other end of the string let a weight D hang, with an attached index E. To the same wall let there be fixed a plate a b divided into equal parts, to which that index corresponds: since, as experience testifies, the length of a hempen rope and of gut strings is diminished while they take up moisture, and on the contrary they become longer while they are dried out, the index D will rise higher when the humidity of the air is increased, and will descend when it is diminished. By this ascent and descent, therefore, the increase and decrease of the humidity and dryness by which the air is affected will become known to us.

600 There is no one at all among the Moderns who doubts even in the least that air is heavy. For it seems all too plain that the suspension of mercury in Torricellian tubes comes from the external pressing air. Add that it is most certainly established that a glass globe, for example, full of air, is heavier than itself emptied of air. Nor did Aristotle himself shrink from this opinion. For he had said, bk. 4 On the Heavens, text 29: all things have gravity except fire; and ibid., text 30: all things in their own region, even the air itself, gravitate. There will perhaps be someone who thinks that the air is heavy on account of the vapors and exhalations with which the air itself abounds. But I should like him to notice that, if vapors and exhalations are heavy, the air too must be heavy, so that, namely, the vapors themselves and the exhalations can be suspended in it and float in it most freely. For a fluid which lacks all weight cannot sustain solid and heavy bodies.

601 From the weight of the air, therefore, the Barometer took its origin: that is, an instrument which we are accustomed to use as a criterion for exploring the changes in the gravity of the air. The Barometer consists of an inflected tube A C D (Fig. LXIII) full of mercury and immovably fixed to a flat board A D. At the side of the tube there is a scale, of which one portion E F is divided into inches, the beginning of the division being taken from the surface a b of the mercury standing in the open lower orifice C D of the tube. For from here is reckoned that height to which, by the force of the pressure which the external air exerts on the surface b of the standing mercury, the mercury itself is sustained through the tube up to the stretch A C. Further, the single inches of the scale are usually subdivided into their lines, so that even the small changes which the height of the mercury undergoes may be discerned more exactly.

602 The use of the Barometer lies wholly in this, that it may be recognized day by day how great the gravity of the incumbent atmosphere is. Therefore the higher the mercury has stood in the Barometer, the heavier the atmosphere is to be judged, and the lighter, the lower the mercury has been in it. And today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to its yesterday’s gravity as today’s height of the mercury in the Barometer is to yesterday’s

height;

p. 190

CHAPTER I

height; so that if, for example, yesterday the mercury remained suspended in the tube

A C of the Barometer (same Fig.) at the height a e, but today it stands suspended in it

at the height a B, today’s gravity of the atmosphere will be to yesterday’s as the

height a e is to the height a B. But enough of these things.

On the Qualities perceived by Smell, Taste,

and Hearing.

In what does the smell of bodies consist?

hese things being supposed which have been said about smells [§. 158. 603

T ff.], I say: smell in first act, or as it is in bodies, consists in a substantial

and most subtle effluvium of the odorous body, and this effluvium is the

particles of the volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance of the odorous body, which,

configured and determined in a certain manner and torn away from odorous bodies,

enter the cavities of the nostrils with the air as their vehicle while we breathe in, and

variously push and stir the nervous fibrils distributed through the organ of smell.

Prob. by parts. The first is established from this, that it cannot be conceived how a

bodily organ could be affected and stirred without a real contact of parts: but the

fibers of the nerves are irritated, pressed and plucked by smells: therefore. For women

(as Boerhaave says (q)) at the mere smell of musk and amber at once fall into a faint. The same

odorous things cause exacerbations in epileptics. The most distinguished Boyle (r) reports

that he knew a man of firm health, but of a very sanguine temperament, who felt vio‐

lent headaches from the smell of musk; another who suffered a not dissimilar dis‐

comfort from the sweet fragrance of damask roses

(s).

(q) Praelect. Academ., on smell.

(r) De insig. efficacia effluvior., ch. 6.

p. 191

(s). These things, however, and very many others cannot be explained except through a substantial effluvium of the odorous body.

604 The second part is proved: for it is established from chemical experiments that only those bodies are odorous which are endowed with a volatile sulphureo-mercurial substance, and that those smell more intensely which abound more in a substance of this kind: therefore. The third part, namely that these particles are configured, is most plainly established. For it is altogether certain that the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium are formally odorous through that by which they can tickle the nervous fibers of smell; but it is established that these nervous fibers are not moved by the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium except inasmuch as the corpuscles themselves are endowed with a certain size and affected with a certain figure, since reason demonstrates that a purely mechanical effect, such as that motion of the fibers is, can be ascribed only to a mechanical cause: therefore.

605 The last part is proved: for no smell is perceived unless air is drawn in through the nostrils. Spirit of sal ammoniac, which most powerfully affects our nostrils, (says the praised Boerhaave (t)) placed at the nose will do nothing at all as long as we either breathe out, or at any rate do not breathe in. For unless air is drawn in through the nostrils, the corpuscles of the odoriferous effluvium, which are dispersed through the air and float in it, cannot run into the nervous fibers of the nostrils and tickle them as is required for exciting the sense of smell. Moreover, on our opinion the phenomena of smells are explained most clearly. First: heat excites smell in bodies, cold prevents it. For by heat the sulphureo-mercurial substance of which the body consists is separated from the coarser particles and is very greatly attenuated. The pores of the body are likewise dilated, whence the portion of volatile substance that is in it easily bursts out and is diffused in every direction. On the contrary, cold constricts the pores of the body and retards and prevents the intestine motion of the parts.

606 Secondly: By rubbing and friction those hard bodies become odorous which seem inodorous; and those which are odorous breathe out a more intense smell. For by rubbing the texture of the body is loosened and its pores are dilated, and the sulphureo-mercurial substance that is in them is stirred to a truly great motion. Thirdly: Very many things which, taken separately, smell very little, give off a powerful smell if they are mixed. Sal ammoniac and alkaline salt, each of them inodorous, breathe out a most powerful smell in the very mixing. For from the mixture there follows a fermentation, and hence the dissolution and evaporation of those subtle particles in which smell consists. So also orpiment and quicklime, each an inodorous body, when mixed in water and boiled, breathe out a foul and repugnant smell. But, to say a few words

Bb about

Lana Terzi reports many other things in the Magisterium Naturae et Artis (from which, as from a treasury, not a few Physicists have relieved their own poverty: would that they were as dutiful in rendering the author his deserved honor as they are ready to appropriate what belongs to others!)

(t) Loc. cit.

CHAPTER II

about the specific difference of smells, only two kinds can be distinguished, namely

the pleasant and the troublesome.

607 A smell is pleasant if the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium so answer to the

organ of smell that its fibers are moved by them in an orderly and gentle way. On the

contrary, a smell is troublesome if the nervous fibers of smell are harassed and twisted

in a perturbed way by the corpuscles of the odorous effluvium. Hence the reason why

the same smell is agreeable to one person and disagreeable to another, as also why

the same smell neither always pleases us nor always displeases us, seems to be sought

only in the different disposition of the organ of smell. For there is no doubt that,

when the temper or texture of the nervous fibers of smell is changed, it must neces‐

sarily come about that the fibers themselves are not always moved in the same way by

the impact of the same corpuscles.

608 But you will say against our conclusion: if smell consists in a substantial out‐

flow, etc., the weight of a body would be continually diminished by a long emission of

smell; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. I deny the min.: because, as expe‐

rience itself testifies, the weight of an odorous body, of camphor for example, does

decrease even sensibly, as we have observed with the most distinguished Boyle [§.

185.]. Nor can the weight of an odorous body decrease on account of the odorous

evaporation unless the matter of the body is diminished for this cause, and conse‐

quently unless the smell of the body consists in a substantial effluvium of it. For the

rest, no one will deny that the smell which a body spreads can consist in an effluvium

without its weight decreasing sensibly, if he has clearly seen the subtlety of those cor‐

puscles from which all sensible bodies first arise. Very many things on this matter

have been said by us in §§. 158 ff. and §. 185.

In what does the taste of bodies consist?

bservation first. Those bodies are savory which abound in salt, and the 609

O greater the quantity of salt they contain, the more savory they are. On

the contrary, those are altogether insipid which contain nothing at all, or

almost nothing, of saline substance. This can be confirmed even from the

fact that there is nothing savory from which salt cannot be extracted and which,

once the salt is extracted, is not rendered insipid; likewise nothing insipid which does

not become savory when salt is mixed in. Observation second. The taste of no solid

body is perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the

help of the saliva. Hence those things are altogether insipid which the teeth cannot

grind and the saliva cannot dissolve, such as metals, stones, etc. Observation

third:

p. 193

third: although solid bodies are savory, no taste at all is perceived if the tongue is either too dry or swollen with too much moisture. Observation fourth: savory bodies become more savory with heat, but on the contrary become altogether insipid if they grow excessively cold. Things that are very cold, says the most learned Boerhaave, are not tasted, nor does any taste remain when the tongue is exquisitely cold. These things being laid down,

610 I say: Tastes in first act, and as they exist in the body, consist primarily in saline particles of the savory body, affected with a certain size and figure, which, dissolved by the saliva, can pervade the cuticle that clothes the organ of taste and agitate in various ways the nervous papillae protruding beneath it, and pluck, squeeze, prick or soothe them according to their various modification. Prob. by parts. The first, from observation first: for if the taste of bodies did not arise from saline particles, neither would those bodies be insipid which are destitute of salt, nor would those be savory which abound in salt. I said that tastes consist primarily in particles of salt. For there is no doubt that a sulphureous substance too contributes very much to tastes, since experience demonstrates that the force of the saline particles is diminished not a little by sulphur: hence it is brought about by it that the organ of taste is not always changed in the same way by the saline corpuscles.

611 But that they must have a certain size and figure, Prob. For only by reason of the size and figure with which they are endowed can those corpuscles enter the little pores of the tongue and pluck those fibers of the nerves which immediately constitute the organ of taste. It is manifest indeed that a mechanical effect has only a mechanical cause; but it is established that the saline corpuscles have formally that they are savory from that from which they have formally that they can tickle the nervous fibers of taste: therefore. But that they are of such a kind as to be able to be dissolved by the saliva is established from observation second. The varieties of tastes are comprised in this pair of lines:

The tastes are Salty, Fatty, Sweet and Acid;

Sharp, and Insipid, Austere, Harsh, Bitter. Some hold that Insipid is not properly a taste, but the negation of taste.

612 The conclusion is confirmed: on our opinion a reason is given for those things which we observed about tastes at the threshold. First: the taste of a consistent body is not perceived unless the body itself is ground by the teeth and dissolved by the saliva. For the saline particles of a body cannot change the organ of taste unless they are separated from those with which they are mixed in the body itself, and are so dissolved by the saliva that they can enter the pores of the tongue. Secondly: the taste of no solid body is felt if the tongue is too dry or swollen with too much moisture. For when moisture is lacking, the menstruum is wanting by which the saline substance of the body

Bb 2 may

p. 194

CHAPTER III

may be dissolved and conducted to the organ of taste. But excessive moisture dimin‐

ishes the ratio of the dissolved body to the dissolving vehicle, and therefore little or

almost no change of the sense organ takes place. Moreover, if the nervous papillae of

the tongue swell with excessive moisture, they are unfit to take on motion from the

impact of the saline particles, and hence for the sensation of taste to be excited in us.

613 A reason is also given for observation fourth. For heat brings it about not only

that the saline particles are dissolved, but also that they rush more strongly into the

sensorium of taste and move it more powerfully. On the contrary, cold not only pre‐

vents the dissolution of the saline particles, but also retards and even stops the mo‐

tion of those which have been dissolved, and, by constricting the little pores of the

tongue, prevents them moreover from entering those very pores and pressing and

plucking the nervous fibers of taste. It is to be noted at the end that taste acts ac‐

cording to the various disposition of the organ. Hence, because not all men have the

same temperament, nor is the texture of the nervous fibrils the same in all, the same

taste is neither agreeable to all nor troublesome to all. Similarly, because of a changed

disposition of the organ, it happens that a taste which had been agreeable to us be‐

fore pleases no longer. Whence the Spanish proverb has gained currency: sobre gustos

no hai disputas [there is no disputing about tastes].

On Sound, and its principal affections.

hose who wish to explain clearly the nature of sound consider one sound 614

T in the sonorous body, another in the medium through which it is transmit‐

ted. The former they call primitive sound, the latter derivative. The center of

sound is said to be that point from which the sound is diffused and reaches

the ears. Direct sound is that which is carried straight from the sonorous body to the

hearing. Reflected sound is called that which is thrown back from an obstacle into

which it runs, and from it reaches the ears. It is certain that only those bodies are

sonorous which take on a tremor if they are struck. This tremulous motion is beyond

all doubt in strings, from which sound is drawn out by a tremulous agitation. In larg‐

er bells, and in many other bodies, this tremulous motion is quite sensible. That

when the air is removed no sound is perceived, although the sonorous body be plied

with strong blows, has already been said by us in the Logic (§. 107). These things be‐

ing established,

615 I say: Sound as it is regarded in the sonorous body, or primitive, consists in a

tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body;

but

p. 195

but as it is in the medium through which it is transmitted, and hence derivative sound, it is placed chiefly in a tremulous motion of the air, which arises from the tremor and quivering of sounding bodies and is propagated all the way to the organ of hearing. The first part is demonstrated. Only those bodies are sonorous which, when struck or vibrated, take on a tremor, and hence which consist of elastic parts fit for performing very swift vibrations; but by that very fact primitive sound consists in a tremulous motion of the smallest parts of the sonorous body: therefore. The major is established, since we have found by experiments that those bodies which are more elastic, and hence fitter for tremulous motion, are also more sonorous. Thus, because tin is stiffer than lead, silver more than gold, steel than iron, for that reason the one is more sonorous than the other; and it is commonly known that bodies consisting of excessively flexible parts are destitute of sound. Moreover: we know that bells, by the mere contact of a hand applied while they are sounding, give back a diminished sound, because the tremulous motion is in some part impeded.

616 The second part is proved: namely, that bodies are not sonorous through a tremor, or vibrations, that are total, but through particular ones, that is, through a tremulous motion of small parts; which the distinguished men Perrault (u), Carré (x) and de La Hire (y) discovered, whereas formerly bodies were thought to be sonorous through total vibrations. The thing is proved by common experiments. I shall use only two. If a musical string is struck rather vehemently with a bow greased with tallow, even though total vibrations are bound to occur, it gives no sound; but if a bow made rough with pitch or resin is drawn over the same string, a sound is clearly perceived: but no other reason can be given for this than that the bow coated with resin is roughened and as it were obtains little teeth, with which it rubs and agitates the smallest parts of the string, which the bow made slippery with tallow cannot graze: therefore. Secondly: if the ends of a pair of flexible, elastic fire tongs, pressed together by the fingers, are suddenly released, either no sound is heard or a moderate one, although the arms of the tongs are set into a vibratory motion by their elasticity; yet they sound clearly if they are struck with a hard body: therefore the tremulous motion of small parts produces primitive sound.

617 The 3rd part is proved: by derivative motion we understand that which is apt to strike the organ of hearing: but such is the tremulous motion of the medium, and chiefly of the aerial particles: therefore. The major is established: for since the sensation of sound does not arise in us unless the organ of hearing is changed by the sounding body, and it cannot be changed by it immediately, since it is not immediately touched by it, for that reason it must be changed through an interposed medium. But that this medium

is

(u) Essai de Physique.

(x) Mémoires de l’Académie, 1709.

(y) Mémoires de l’Académie, 1716.

p. 196

is above all the air is plain, first, from its nature: for since it is endowed with a notable elasticity, it has the aptitude that its particles nearest the sonorous body are repelled by the small vibrated parts of that body, and these urge others, and still others more remote, until at length an impression is made on the organ itself and the sound is perceived; next, the same is clear from the fact that no sound is perceived when the air is removed: therefore derivative sound, etc.

618 We have said that derivative sound is placed in the tremulous motion chiefly of aerial particles: for that air is not the only medium through which sound is transferred, very many experiments made by Mr. Nollet (z) and others clearly prove. Thus water seems a body quite fit for taking on a tremulous motion, since experience testifies that fish in fishponds are very often called together by the sound of a bell to food prepared for them.

619 The nature of sound having been examined, let us weigh its principal affections, as far as we may. The celerity of sound, or its diffusion through a certain space in a determinate time, is rightly reckoned among its principal affections. Various learned men have tried to observe it carefully, as can be seen in Musschenbroek (a). At length, according to the more celebrated observations, it was fixed at 180 French perches in the interval of one second; but because there was still controversy about this very result, a more exact inquiry into this matter was for that reason entrusted by the Royal Academy of Sciences of Paris, in the year 1738, to the most distinguished men de Thury, Maraldi and de La Caille. These, then, chose for their operations a line 14636 perches, or toises, long, and found, first:

620 That sound, in the space of 1 second, both by day and by night, in rainy as in clear weather, covers 173 perches or toises, as we have said elsewhere. 2: that a wind blowing along the same line which the sound runs through either retards or accelerates it in proportion to its own celerity, that is: a contrary wind retards the sound, a following wind furthers it. 3: that the celerity of sound is always constituted by such a law that it runs through equal spaces in equal times. 4: that the intensity of sound, or its force, changes nothing in its celerity; for although a more vehement sound is diffused farther than a weaker one, the latter nevertheless runs through 173 perches in 1 second just as the other does (b).

621 The reason of which seems to be this: that since the impression, e.g., from a cannon, is stronger, the nearest aerial particles, by approaching the neighboring ones more on account of the greater force, do indeed cover a greater space; yet in order to restore themselves to their places again, they must have just as much space once more: but the particles of air less impelled by a pistol, just as they make less space in going forward on account of the smaller force, so in going back they run through less. From these things it now follows:

622 The

(z) Leçons de Physique, vol. 3, lesson 11, exp. 4.

(a) Comment. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 3, p. 113.

(b) Mémoires de l’Académie, 1738.

p. 197

622 The knowledge of the uniform celerity with which sound is carried is very useful for determining the distances of places where geometrical operations cannot be applied: namely, for measuring straits of the seas, mouths of rivers, the distance of a siege trench from a bulwark, etc. That is, if between the discharge of a cannon or of a musket and the hearing of the sound the seconds are counted, then, since each corresponds to a distance of 173 perches, and these are multiplied by the number of seconds, the distance of the place in which the cannon was discharged will be had (understanding the distance along the straight line along which the sound is diffused); thus, if 10 seconds elapse between the fire seen and the sound perceived, the distance will be 1730 perches. Moreover, it will also be possible to measure the celerity of the wind; for since a following wind furthers the sound, if from the celerity increased by the wind you subtract the 173 perches corresponding to each second, the remainder will show the celerity of the wind.

623 Reflection is a singular affection of sound. That is, sound, no otherwise than any other motion, changes its direction when it strikes an obstacle, and according to the general law of motion is so reflected that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. But nothing is more admirable in the reflection of sound than the resonance which is called Echo, and which takes place when the air, variously agitated by the sounding body and falling on an opposite body, is thrown back with exactly the same modification, so that this repercussion presents to the ears almost the same sound as the direct sonorous rays produce. But not every reflected sound, sent back from an obstacle into the ear, brings it about that an Echo is formed: certain conditions, namely, must be present.

624 And first, indeed, it is required that the distance of the hearer from the obstacle from which the sound returns be such that the organ of hearing is perfectly changed beforehand by the direct sound before the reflected sound reaches it: the reason of which is that, if the time which intervenes between the impact of the direct sound and that of the reflected sound is not distinct, only one motion and change of the organ will be excited by both sounds, or at least the subsequent one will follow the prior with such haste that they can by no means be discriminated; and hence also only one sound will be perceived by us. This coincidence of the direct sound and the reflected sound nevertheless makes the sounding body heard better.

625 It is required, secondly, not only that there be a reflection of the voice and of the sounding body from a due distance, but also that the reflection be of such a kind that by its force the voice leaps back from certain as it were vaulted passages, windings and cavernous grottoes, so that the sonorous vibrations, collected through obstacles of this kind, reach the ear after the prior ones, which first set the air in motion, have already ceased: the reason of which again is that, if any reflection whatsoever, and every one at all, sufficed for this resonance, an Echo would always exist; but it is established by experience that a repercussion occurs only when the direct voice is carried into obstacles bristling with various passages, ducts and windings. Memorable is the

Echo

p. 198

Echo of the Villa Simonetta near Milan, where a voice sent from a window against the

opposite parallel wall, 33 paces distant, is repeated twenty-four times, nay even thirty

times. It has pleased me to note these things from Fr. Klaus. Celebrated examples of

Echo throughout the world are reported by Fr. Kircher (c), Sturm (d) and others.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

626

O bj. 1: The sound of a trumpet is heard from more than a hundred paces, al‐

though the motion of the air stirred by the trumpet is scarcely perceived from

two paces: therefore sound is diffused as far as the motion of the air cannot reach. I

reply by denying the conseq., and I say: when a trumpet sounds, the tremor of the air

reaches the same distance to which its sound extends; but this motion of the air,

since it is only tremulous and composed of very minute vibrations, is altogether im‐

perceptible to the sense of touch, for on account of its tenuity it does not suffice to

change that sense; it is perceived, however, by the sensorium of hearing, on account

of the exquisite texture, proportioned to this, which it has, by reason of which it is

affected by such slight percussions.

627 But that the tremor of the air runs out to the same distance which the sound

reaches is plain from experience; for when a cannon is fired, windows, especially glass

ones, even a thousand or two thousand paces distant, tremble, and they do not trem‐

ble before the sound of the explosion is heard; and since such a tremor can only

come from air impelling them, it becomes evident that the tremor of the air is insep‐

arable from sound and reaches the same distance with it.

628 Obj. 2: If, inside a glass phial hermetically sealed, a little bell is struck by

some artifice, the sound is perceived; but this would by no means happen if sound

consisted in a vibratory motion of the air: for the air enclosed within the phial can‐

not pass through the glass so as to drive the external air all the way to the ear: there‐

fore. I reply that whenever any sound is excited, not only the air but also the other

bodies are stirred with a certain tremulous motion: for we frequently experience

that, when the thicker strings of a musical instrument sound and the larger pipes of a

pneumatic organ sing, the tables, the seats, nay even the very floor on which the said

instruments stand, tremble. What wonder, then, if, in the case of the objection, when

the air enclosed in the phial vibrates, the glass itself is stirred with a similar tremor,

as experience testifies? For if the phial is gripped by the hand, a deaf, as it were, and

very dull sound is heard, namely because the vibrations of the glass are in part pre‐

vented by the applied hand.

629 Obj. 3: If our opinion were true, we could not at once and at the same

time

(c) In the Phonurgia.

(d) Phys. Elect., vol. 1, p. 659 ff.

p. 199

time perceive different sounds, as of voices, bells, etc.; but this is contrary to experience: therefore. Proof of the major: the air cannot be set in motion at the same time by different motions together; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear. I reply by denying the proposition. For the tremulous motion of the air also consists of its own small motions; hence, when the alternating percussions of different bodies are communicated to the same organ, the air can be stirred by different motions in the same sensible time; and the same must be said of the drum of the ear, and consequently different sounds can be perceived in the same sensible time.

630 You have an example in standing water: if you throw little stones into different parts of it at the same time, you will surely see the whole of it ruffled into swelling ripples in the manner of a circle, which, continually spreading themselves out, intersect one another without any disturbance whatever. Likewise, therefore, in our case the vibrations excited by different sounding bodies run all the way to the ear without any disturbance, and affect it in different ways, whence it comes about that different sounds are perceived at the same time.

631 Obj. 4. If sound consisted in the aforesaid vibrations, we could not measure the distance of a sounding body by hearing: therefore. I reply: since the vibrations in the air are formed in the manner of a circle, and the air is rippled in waves in every direction, at the center of which circle the sounding body stands, hence the farther vibrations of this kind recede from the center, the greater the circumferences they make, and consequently a smaller portion of them, or a smaller arc, affects the more remote air than the nearer; hence the particles of air that strike are fewer, and at the same time less united; they therefore impress a smaller affection on the sense the farther one stands from the sounding body; and by means of this greater or smaller affection the distance of the sounding object is perceived.

632 Obj. finally: according to the more probable opinion, a low sound consists in slower vibrations, a high one in swifter vibrations; but the vibrations of the drum of the ear must be isochronous, or of the same duration, as are the vibrations of the same string equally stretched: therefore the same sound would always be heard as to low or high, which is contrary to experience, especially since the same body, keeping the same tension, cannot be set now into slower, now into swifter vibrations. Reply: by denying the supposition, namely that the drum of the ear always keeps the same tension. For the drum of the ear performs for hearing nearly the same office that the crystalline lens performs for sight.

633 For just as the crystalline lens receives the rays of light in such a way that by the force of its convexity it projects them onto the base of the retina with due distinctness, and to accomplish this changes its convexity to greater or smaller according to the different falling-in and different incidence of the rays: so also the drum of the ear is so constituted that, according to the different falling-in of the vibrating air, it now increases its tension, now diminishes it; so that, just as the crystalline lens increases or diminishes its convexity by

Cc expanding

p. 200

of the ear increases or diminishes its tension through the action of a twin muscle, by

which the drum is either drawn tight or slackened: you have an analogy in the mili‐

contraction by the first projection of the rays, to receiving which and to projecting

them inward it straightway adapts itself, so the drum of the ear is determined to in‐

creasing or diminishing its tension by the first impulses of the air; whence it comes

about that it very easily accommodates itself to swifter or longer-lasting ones, and

On visible Qualities, or

on Light and its properties.

The nature of light, both primitive and derivative, is inquired

into.

luminous body is said to be that which is such by its own nature that it 635

A emits light. That, on the other hand, is called illuminated which does not

have from itself the light with which it shines, but receives it wholly

from without. Thus flame, for example, burning coals, and above all the

Sun are luminous bodies. Illuminated, on the other hand, are all those things which

are visible to us when the sun or a flame is present, invisible when the luminous

body is taken away or extinguished. Primitive light is that affection through which a

body is formally luminous. Derivative light is that affection which, diffused through

a medium from a luminous body and propagated all the way to the eyes, brings it

about that surrounding bodies, otherwise invisible, are seen. These things explained,

636 I say first: light as it is regarded in a luminous body, or primitive light, is

rightly made to consist in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of that

body. Proof: primitive light is rightly made to consist in that

which

p. 201

which is always joined with light itself in a body, and on which light so depends that, when it is posited in bodies, light is at once had in them and they are made luminous, whereas when it is taken away light straightway perishes; but always joined with light is a most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the body, so that there is no luminous body in which a motion of this kind is not detected; and as soon as the subtler parts of bodies are driven into agitated motion, light is emitted by them, but it is extinguished as soon as the agitated parts are brought back to rest: therefore primitive light consists in a certain most agitated motion of the subtle parts of a body. The minor is demonstrated part by part most plainly.

637 And as to the first part, namely that all luminous bodies are endowed with such a motion, it is altogether most certain. For in flame and in burning coals a vehement motion of the parts is visible; likewise that putrefying bodies, putrid fish, wood corrupted by rot, which emit light, are agitated by an intestine motion of the parts is manifest from what has been said elsewhere, since fermentation and putrefaction cannot be explained without motion and agitation of the parts. The other part too is clear, namely that bodies emit light as soon as their subtler particles are set in motion.

638 “Do not all bodies (says the most distinguished Newton (e)) which abound with terrestrial parts, and especially with sulphureous ones, emit light as often as those parts are sufficiently agitated, whether this be done by heat, or by friction, or by percussion, or by putrefying, or by some vital motion, or by any other cause whatever? As sea water, the back of a cat stroked obliquely with the hand in a dark place, wood, flesh and fish while they putrefy, the vapors from putrid waters which are commonly called ignes fatui, glowworms and the eyes of certain animals by a certain vital motion, the Bononian phosphorus agitated by the rays of light, and certain liquors mixed with one another whose particles come together with an impetus, as oil of vitriol distilled from an equal weight of niter, and then mixed with a double portion of oil of cloves or of aniseed?”

639 But there are countless things that make this truth manifest, and the consideration of electrical phenomena demonstrates it to evidence. The last part is shown quite easily: for no one is unaware that, when the motion of the parts ceases, light is not spread from bodies; that flame is extinguished when the inflamed body is compressed; that light in burning bodies, for example in coals and in red-hot iron, vanishes when they are plunged into water, by which the agitation of the parts is stopped.

640 I say second: derivative light, or lumen, is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line. Proof, part by part. And first, that light is a corporeal substance is made

Cc 2 evident

(e) Opticks, query 9.

p. 202

evident from this, that it shares in the affections of a body: for, first, while it passes from one medium into another, it is refracted. Second: falling upon an opaque surface, it is reflected toward the opposite side. Third: propagated light can be gathered and, as it were, condensed into one point, if it is received by a concave mirror or a convex lens, in the point which they call the focus, in which it produces a heat so intense that it sets on fire, after a few minutes, any combustible bodies placed in that spot, melts and dissolves metals and all fusible things, and turns into glass those which are least liable to liquefaction and abound in salt, as may be seen in the Acta Eruditorum of Leipzig (f), where a great many things are related of the concave mirror which, from its inventor D. Tschirnhaus, is called the Tschirnhausian. (g)

641 Fourth: light strikes the organ of sight, and by its abundance or vehemence (just as an excessive crash offends the ear) it disturbs it, nay hurts it greatly; but all these things manifestly prove a corporeal, or impenetrable, substance: therefore. And indeed, as the distinguished Gassendi argues very well (h), just as a ball driven against a wall rebounds from it, because, since it is a body, it cannot pass through a place occupied by a body, so a ray of light driven against a body is struck back by it, because that body occupies the place with its bulk; for it is a constant rule that natural effects of the same kind have the same causes, as we have said [§. 22.]. Next, that it is a most subtle substance is evident from this, that it enters the pores of glass most easily. What of the fact that the structure of the tiniest animalcules demonstrates the tenuity of light? For if the animalcules themselves, as we have already said [§. 164.], are of such tenuity, if their eyes and the pupils of them are of so slight a bulk, how much smaller must the matter of light be, so that it may glide into the eyes and the pupil and easily permeate these organs?

That

(f) For the year 1687, month of January, p. 53.

(g) But since the gathering of the rays, and hence the powers of mirrors, increased by their aid, depend on their concave figure, therefore any material whatever is suitable for a burning mirror, provided it can be polished exactly. Hence, on Wolff’s testimony, the celebrated Dresden craftsman Gärtner constructed great burning mirrors of wood, which were said to surpass the Tschirnhausian ones in effectiveness. Indeed Zahn [in Wolff, Elem. Catoptr. §. 223.] relates that a mirror was made by Neumann by which metals were rendered fluid, out of rather hard paper with straw glued onto it. Nevertheless, the texture of the material from which mirrors are prepared must be so constituted that it sends back the rays of light and does not absorb them, as happens in black bodies. For that reason the distinguished Boyle, by means of a mirror which he made in the form of a burning glass out of black marble, could not burn wood set in the focus, even though the sun had fallen upon the mirror for quite a long time, as Musschenbroek relates [Essai de Physique §. 975.].

(h) Sect. 1, Phys., bk. 6, ch. 2.

p. 203

642 That the motion of those corpuscles is very swift is proved, first, from the very swift diffusion of light. Second, it is demonstrated from that astonishing force of the burning mirror of which we have spoken [§. 640.]: for since a force of this kind is that very force by which those corpuscles are moved, and this arises from the product of the mass into the celerity [§. 275.], the mass of each of those corpuscles, being most slight, as indeed it is, cannot give them a force as great as we have seen it to be unless they are moved with the greatest celerity; and so it is necessary that they be moved with the greatest celerity. Finally, we have it ascertained by experiment that this motion is rectilinear: a luminous ray let in through a very small hole into a dark chamber is always propagated in a straight line, and falls upon the point opposite the little hole along a straight line: therefore light is a most subtle substance, affected with a very swift motion along a straight line.

643 I say 3: the propagation of light, or derivative light, or lumen, is not rightly explained by a fiery outflow emanating from luminous bodies. This is against the distinguished Gassendi and Newton. Proof: if it were so, a medium once lit up would remain illuminated even when the luminous body was taken away. For the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium itself, even though the luminous body from which they were emitted is no longer present to it; but it is false that the medium remains illuminated when the luminous body by which it is lit up is taken away: therefore. Next, the light spread by a candle in a small room, or by the sun through the air, ought to become the more intense the longer the body is present there; for since the luminous body emits new corpuscles of light at every moment, it is necessary that in the same part of the medium through which the light is diffused the corpuscles always become more abundant, and therefore the light more intense; yet each of these conflicts with experience.

644 Each of these reasons is strengthened by the comparison that the distinguished Gassendi uses to explain his opinion about light: for he says that light is produced just as odors are, namely by the emission of slender corpuscles; but it is certain that an odor is preserved even when the body spreading the odorous molecules is taken away; it is likewise certain that an odor is made continually more intense and more lively in the same part of the medium the longer the presence of the bodies from which the odorous corpuscles emanate lasts: therefore light is not rightly placed in a substantial effluvium of the luminous body.

645 The Newtonians say that the medium, once lit up, does not remain illuminated when the luminous body is taken away: because, although the corpuscles of light do not need the presence of the luminous body in order to be preserved in the medium through which they have been diffused, they do need it in order not to cease being moved in it, and therefore in order to show the medium itself lit up to us.

646 But against this, argues the most distinguished Fortunato da Brescia: for no projected body needs the presence of the projector in order to persevere in the motion that it received from it; but it goes on being moved even if the projector

fails

p. 204

fails after impressing the motion on it: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light need the presence of the luminous body, lest the motion which they received from it should perish in them. Moreover, neither the corpuscles of sound nor those of odor so depend on the sounding or odorous body from which they emanate that they can be moved, and excite sensation in us, only in its presence: therefore neither do the corpuscles of light so depend on the luminous body that they should come to a halt in their motion and be rendered wholly unfit for exciting the sensation of light in us as soon as the luminous body is no longer present to us.

647 But if someone should say that the corpuscles of sound can be moved even when the sounding body from which they were emitted is absent, because their motion is perturbed and spreads through the air in every direction, whereas the corpuscles of light can be moved only when the luminous body by which they were darted forth is present, because their motion is rectilinear: against this it is urged that, just as the perturbed motion of corpuscles does not need, in order to be preserved, the presence of a body moving them in a perturbed way, so neither should the rectilinear motion of corpuscles need, lest it perish, the presence of a body vibrating them along a straight line. For the reason of each motion is altogether the same, namely the independence of the body moved from the mover, so that it retains the motion it has once received, whatever that motion may be. Nay, so far is the duration of a rectilinear motion once impressed on a body from depending on the duration of the mover, that among the laws of nature this is one: every body once set in motion is always moved along a straight line, so long as it is not compelled by some external cause to change its direction [§. 294.].

648 But hence none of those who hold for certain that the substantial effluvium of the luminous body, in which they make light consist, needs some notable interval of time in order to reach us from the sun and the other stars, can deny that it will come about that light remains in the medium through which it has been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it is produced is taken away. For it is evident on this hypothesis that light is preserved in the medium independently of the luminous body for that whole time which elapses while it travels from the luminous body itself to us. For if it is supposed that one hour is required for light to be propagated from the Sun S to the earth T (Fig. 117.), it is evident that the light diffused from S remains in the space from S to T even if, within that interval of one hour, the Sun S, which emitted that light, ceases to exist.

649 Since, then, the distinguished Newton (i), ’s Gravesande (k), Musschenbroek (l) and many others besides hold that light comes from the sun to the earth in the space of seven or eight minutes, and hence

that

(i) Princip. Philosoph. Mathem., bk. 1, Schol. to prop. 96, and also Optic., bk. 2, prop. 11.

(k) Elem. Phys. §. 2155.

(l) Comment. in Exp. Acad. del Cimento, pt. 2, p. 184.

p. 205

that it needs the space of some hours in order to reach Saturn from the sun, and then

us from Saturn, and the space of some months in order to be propagated from the

fixed stars all the way to the earth, I think that all these will readily grant that light

can by no means be made to consist in a substantial effluvium of a body, since at the

same time it would be granted by them, what is plainly contrary to experience, name‐

ly that light itself is preserved for a notable space of time in the medium through

which it has once been diffused, even when the luminous body by which it was pro‐

duced is absent.

650 I say fourth: the propagation of light seems to be explained by a rectilinear

pressure of an ethereal substance endowed with vibratory motion, a pressure pro‐

ceeding from the motion of the luminous body and impelling the organ of sight.

Proof: for the ethereal matter claims for itself the affections of a corporeal substance,

and can be refracted, reflected and move the organ; and since it is most subtle, it can

receive motion from the particles of the luminous body; and since it is had diffused

everywhere, the propagation of motion through it is explained in the best possible

way. Moreover, it is established that the organ of hearing is so affected by the tremu‐

lous motion of the air alone, entering the cavity of the ears, that the sensation of

sound arises in us; but among all things there is the greatest analogy between light

and sound: therefore by the vibratory motion alone of a most subtle ethereal sub‐

stance, which penetrates the pupil of the eye, the organ of sight can be so altered

that the sensation of light is excited in us.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D.

bj. 1 against the first: the reasons on which our conclusion rests prove 651

O nothing else than that primitive light depends on the motion of the parts

of the luminous body as on a necessary condition: therefore primitive

light depends on the most agitated motion of the subtle parts of the lu‐

minous body only as on a condition, not as on its formal reason. I deny the whole ar‐

gument: since nothing whatever except a tremor is communicated to a sounding

body while it is struck and gives forth a sound, therefore, with none of the

Philosophers objecting, a tremor of this kind is not a condition prerequired for

sound, but is sound itself: therefore by the same reason, if, while a body is made lumi‐

nous, nothing else is excited but motion in its subtler parts, that motion is not a

mere condition necessarily required for the production of primitive light, but is light

itself.

652 Obj. 2 against the 2nd: it is not well proved from the reflection of light that it

is a body: therefore. Proof of the antecedent: for the reflection of light is not like the

reflection of a ball, since reflection is said of light metaphorically and improperly:

therefore. I deny the proof of the antecedent: for in order to prove that light does

not rebound in the way that is required for it therefore to be called a body, it is not

enough to show that it is not reflected from a mirror like a ball. For neither does

sound rebound like a ball when an Echo occurs, and yet those aerial particles in whose

tremor

sound

p. 206

sound consists, even according to the Peripatetics, are corporeal, and it is certain that sound is reflected because those particles are corporeal: therefore light too is reflected not metaphorically, but truly and properly, even though it does not rebound like a ball from a wall.

653 Obj. 3: the particles of light are most tenuous: therefore they cannot meet with [such resistance] that they can be reflected and refracted: for since light […] in […]: therefore refraction is said of light only metaphorically. I deny the consequence. For just as […] the tenuity of the particles of light, and […] by motion […], since among them they can […] and be reflected, since […] than they are impelled by the luminous body […]. For since those particles are corporeal, […] no one fails to see that there can be in them the texture in which the […] of bodies is placed, and on which their […] depends.

654 Obj. 4: bodies which are refracted in passing from a rare medium into a dense one recede from the perpendicular, because their motion is compounded of two, namely of the perpendicular one, which arises from gravity, and of a horizontal one impressed from without; but light is not so refracted, since it approaches the perpendicular: therefore it is not a body. I deny the consequence. For although a leaden ball, for example, is refracted in this way in passing from air into water because it is a body, it is not rightly inferred from this that light is not a body because it is not refracted in the same way as a leaden ball; but it must be said that light is not refracted toward the same side as that ball, not because the ball is a body, but because light is refracted not with a recession from, but with an approach to, the perpendicular, either for the reason already brought forward by us [§. 3…], or because it is attracted more strongly by water than by air, as the most distinguished Newton held. In order, then, to prove that the corporeality of light is not well proved by the Moderns from its refraction, the Peripatetics ought to demonstrate that only such a refraction arises from corporeality as is performed, in the passage from a rarer medium into a denser one, with a recession from the perpendicular.

655 Nor does it avail to say that light is not refracted of itself, but by reason of its subject, namely the air in which it is produced. For, first, the Peripatetics ought now to explain why illuminated air, although it is a body, is nevertheless not refracted as solid bodies are, namely with a recession from the perpendicular, while it is forced to enter water. 2. They must give the cause why air suffused with light can enter glass, while air lacking light cannot. It stands, then, that the corporeality of light is most firmly demonstrated by the Moderns against the Peripatetics from its reflection and refraction.

656 Obj. 5: light is compenetrated with the whole diaphanous body; but bodies cannot be naturally compenetrated: therefore light is not a corporeal substance.

Dist.

p. 207

I distinguish the major: it is compenetrated in such a way that it truly enters and passes through the solid particles of that body, I deny the major; inasmuch as it enters its pores and runs freely through them, I grant the major, and I deny the consequence: for the pores with which a diaphanous body abounds are set in a straight line and communicate with one another, so that light is diffused through them in such a way that it passes through the body itself and runs freely beyond it. The whole body, moreover, seems to be occupied by light, that is, there seems to be no part at all in it which is not suffused with light, because the pores of that body are not only innumerable, but also so close to one another that we ourselves can discern no interval whatever between them. And just as […] it does not follow that glass is compenetrated with water, so must it be said of light […] illuminating the glass.

657 Inst.: those parts of the glass which exist between the pores are either opaque or diaphanous. Not the first, because then the whole glass would be opaque, since the pores are not glass but empty spaces, which are nothing. But if those parts are diaphanous, they are then receptive of light: therefore light is received not only in the pores of the glass, but also in the very body of the glass. I reply that those parts are opaque, and I deny that it will therefore come about that the whole glass is opaque. For although the pores are nothing but empty spaces, yet if they are so disposed as to be set in a straight line and to communicate with one another, they constitute a diaphanous body, although they do not constitute the light which falls into it, but make the free passage of the rays. The Peripatetics themselves […] two bodies […]. A body, then, is porous, and is rightly called a body, although its pores are not a body but the empty spaces of a body, which are nothing: therefore by the same reason a body is rightly called diaphanous, although the pores, from whose right disposition its diaphaneity is derived, are not a body.

658 Moreover, although the particles which bound the pores of a body are entirely solid and the pores are not a body, the Peripatetics do not on that account infer that the body is altogether solid: therefore by the same reason a body can be diaphanous although those particles of it are not diaphanous, but opaque. […] it is necessary that the particles be solid from whose position and mutual adhesion we call a body solid […]. A body, then, can truly be, and be called, fluid, although the particles which constitute it are solid: therefore it can also be, and be called, a diaphanous body, although the particles of which it is composed are opaque; and just as from this alone, that the component particles of a body are solid, it cannot be inferred that the whole body is solid, so from this alone, that the particles of which a body is made up are opaque, it is not rightly deduced that it is opaque.

659 You will say: these reasons have no weight, since it is certain that no body is wholly porous, that none can […]

Dd

p. 208

[…] be called, just as on the contrary the whole body is called diaphanous […]. But against this: for it is asserted gratuitously and without foundation that the whole glass is diaphanous. For since, as every new experiment plainly demonstrates, […] light […] innumerable […] it is evident that light does not so pervade the whole glass that nothing […] to which light denies passage.

660 You will say: the whole glass is denominated luminous, just as the whole […] is said to receive light, which is by no means affirmed of a sieve pierced with very small holes, whose parts are not diaphanous, but receive light only through the holes. But I reply very easily: the whole glass is called luminous because both its pores, through which light passes, and the very particles which bound them and […] reflect it, are of so small a magnitude that they altogether escape the senses. But in a sieve the matter stands the other way. For however many the holes may be which […] light in it, and give it passage, they are nevertheless far […], just as also the parts in it […] by which the incident rays of light are sent back to us.

661 Obj. 6: if what has been said were true, light, being a most subtle substance, […] through the pores […] of the substance would fly away and vanish; but light […]: therefore light is not a most subtle substance. […] since […] is let in only through the pores […] water […] with a varied and diverse motion […] is refraction. For from this, that light is constantly propagated along a straight line, […] passes through the pores […] in the bodies […] in a straight line […] communicate […]. And this reply is that of […] Newton (m), […]

CHAPTER II

On the reflection and refraction of light.

he reflection of light is its going back from the surface of the opaque body 663

T on which it falls. Thus light is said to be reflected when it goes back from

the surface of a mirror toward the opposite side. The incident ray of light is

the straight line along which light is propagated in falling; the reflected ray,

on the other hand, is the straight line along which it is propagated in being reflected:

so that, if light falls on the surface A B (Fig. LXV.) along the straight line a b, and re‐

bounds along the straight line b d, the straight line a b will be the direct ray of light,

and the straight line b d the reflected ray. Recall to memory what we said when we

spoke of the reflection of motion.

664 A ray of light falling on the polished surface of an opaque body is reflected by

this constant law, that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. For it

is most evidently established that light let in through a very small hole of a darkened

room, if it is received on the polished surface of a mirror, always rebounds from it in

such a way that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence; and this proposi‐

tion is so certain that it is assumed as an axiom in Catoptrics by common consent.

Light falling obliquely on the polished surface of an opaque body makes the angles of inclination

of the direct and the reflected ray equal. So, if light falls from the radiant point a (same

Fig.) on the point b, and rebounds to d, then, the perpendicular z b being erected,

the angles a b z and d b z will be equal. For since the angles z b A and z b B are equal,

being right angles, the angles of reflection and incidence, a b A and d b B, cannot be

equal unless the angles of inclination a b z and d b z are also equal.

665 Light itself is reflected […], keeping after reflection the [celerity] with which it fell.

For if it were otherwise, the angle of reflection would not be equal to the angle of in‐

cidence. Nor does the heat which is communicated by the incident light to the bod‐

ies from which it is reflected stand in the way. For since those bodies are heated more

which […] a greater quantity of light, […] the heat arises not from that part of the

light which is reflected, but from the other part which is refracted, it is also easily un‐

derstood that […] the reflected light is propagated not with a different [celerity], and

that hence, in a perfect reflection of light, the angles of incidence and of reflection

are equal to each other.

666 The refraction of light is the departure and deflection of a luminous ray, pass‐

ing through different

Dd 2 media,

p. 210

media, from the direction which it had. This deviation has no place where the ray falls along the perpendicular; rather, obliquity of incidence is required. It is helpful to recall what we have said of the refraction of motion. The universal principle of the refraction of the rays of light is this: Light passing obliquely from a rarer medium into a denser one, namely from air into water or glass, is refracted by approaching the perpendicular: but passing from a denser medium into a rarer one, namely from glass or water into air, it is refracted by receding from the perpendicular line.

667 Proof of the first part. Let there be a glass vessel with a flat bottom D F H E (Fig. LXVI), covered with an opaque plate very finely perforated at B. Let a ray of light A B enter the vessel itself through the hole B. It is ascertained by experience that, while the vessel is filled with air alone, the ray A B proceeds straight to b, but on the contrary goes on to a if, the position of the vessel remaining entirely the same, the vessel itself is filled with water. Therefore the ray A B approaches the perpendicular B e while it passes obliquely from air into water. As to the second part, the matter is very well known: a coin A (Fig. LXVII.) placed on the bottom of the vessel C A B is seen from the spot a if the vessel is filled with water, but cannot be seen from the same spot if the vessel itself is full of air alone. The ray A B, therefore, breaking out of the vessel full of water, turns aside from the straight path and is therefore refracted by receding from the perpendicular B E while it passes from water into air: therefore light, etc.

668 But it is worth noting that, although it is most true that light is refracted in this way while it passes obliquely from air into water or glass, and conversely from water or glass into air, it is not therefore true, as is commonly said, that light is universally refracted by approaching the perpendicular, or by receding from it, while it proceeds obliquely from one medium into another of different density; nor is it universally true that light is refracted by approaching the perpendicular whenever it passes obliquely from any rarer medium into any denser one, or on the contrary is refracted by receding from the perpendicular whenever it likewise passes obliquely from any denser medium into any rarer one: for the most ingenious ’s Gravesande observed and certainly detected the contrary (n).

669 For he observed that light suffers no refraction at all, but passes in a straight path, from olive oil into borax, and from borax into olive oil, although bodies of this kind differ in density. For the density of olive oil is to the density of borax as 6 to 2. That light is refracted toward the perpendicular in the passage from alum into Danzig vitriol, although the density of these bodies is entirely the same. That light is likewise refracted by approaching the perpendicular in the passage from water into spirit of turpentine, and hence from a denser medium into a rarer one. For the density of water is to the density of spirit of turpentine as 8 to 7.

CHAPTER III

Some things pertaining to Optics, Catoptrics and Dioptrics are

set forth as briefly as possible.

ery many instruments ought to be brought into this place which com670

V mend themselves either by their usefulness or by the pleasure of the

spectacle they afford; nevertheless, since the narrowness of time does

not allow us to be more expansive about them, by this notice, just as

we express our desire to go through these things, so too, as we rightly ought, we

plead the lack of time. We shall therefore merely touch on some of them.

671 Optics is the science of direct vision, or the Physico-Mathematical science

by which we are taught by what mechanism objects which send rays of light from

all their points to the eye are seen by us. Catoptrics is the science of reflected vi‐

sion. The universal principle of the reflection of rays from polished surfaces is not

at all different from the law which other bodies keep in reflection, namely that the

angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. Further, surfaces of this kind,

in which this regular reflection of light is detected, are called mirrors. Mirrors,

moreover, are divided chiefly into plane, convex and concave: that is called plane

which is bounded by a plane surface, convex that which is bounded by a convex one,

concave that which is bounded by a concave one.

672 In order that the equality of the angles of incidence and of reflection in mir‐

rors, whether concave or convex, may become known, a straight line tangent to

the curved surface must be drawn through the point on which the luminous ray

falls. Such (Fig. LXVIII. and LXIX.) is the line F C drawn through the point D,

on which the direct ray I D, falling perpendicularly, returns into itself; but the ray

A D, falling obliquely on the same point, is so reflected to E that the angle of inci‐

dence C D A equals the angle of reflection F D E. The same is to be understood of

the other rays.

673 Dioptrics is the science of refracted vision, which considers chiefly the

bending of luminous rays in glasses. Glasses, moreover, are usually divided into var‐

ious classes, distinguished by their different figure. A plane glass is bounded by

plane surfaces parallel to each other. A lens is a glass of lenticular form: one is con‐

vexo-convex, namely that which is enclosed by a double convex spherical surface;

another plano-convex, which is bounded by one plane surface and the other convex.

A concavo-concave glass is that each of whose surfaces shows a cavity;

a

p. 212

a plano-concave one, one of whose surfaces is plane, while the other presents a cavity. Finally, a glass concave on one side and convex on the other is called a meniscus.

674 It is the task of Dioptrics to contemplate all these things distinctly, to examine the properties of the different media, and to form from glasses, having obtained either a convex or a concave form, telescopes, microscopes and spectacles, by all of which our sight is wonderfully helped, whether for the viewing of remote things, or for detecting the more minute secrets of nature, or for discerning more easily and better any new bodies whatever. We shall touch on a few things.

675 Glasses, or spectacles, for the eyes are most useful to the myopic, or those who […] see distant things confusedly; for since, owing to the too convex conformation of the eye, […] they need light with diverging rays, they therefore use concave glasses, which render parallel rays diverging: on the contrary, to presbyopes, or those who see distant things more clearly and distinctly and near things confusedly, convex glasses are of great help: for the rays from […] near objects […] are fixed in their […]; for which reason they fittingly use glasses of this kind, which gather the rays, or at least promote their convergence. The distinguished Redi (o) affirms that the [invention] of these spectacles is owed to Alessandro della Spina, and […] about the year […].

676 Further, from the combination of both kinds of glass the Telescope came forth, its author being (as seems to most) Zacharias Jansen, toward the end of the sixteenth century. It was constructed on this plan: that a convex glass should be turned toward the objects and a concave one toward the eye […]. This telescope is also called the Galilean, because […] for observing the phenomena of the heavens by Galileo. […] first perfected this instrument […]; the Astronomical telescope derived its origin from the same source, consisting of two glasses convex on both sides; but since it seemed somewhat inconvenient that […] the object […] inverted, […] added two further glasses, which should set upright what the former had inverted; and then, for viewing terrestrial objects, a telescope […] with four convex glasses […].

677 Finally, from glasses which swell out with a convex surface […], since they enlarge the images of minute objects, microscopes, or engyscopes, are constructed by the fit composition of various glasses […]. The first of those who […] this instrument is said to be, as Musschenbroek (p) [relates], Francesco Stelluti, who in the year […] published a description of the parts of the […] which he discovered with this aid. Then followed Power, Hooke, Grew,

Malpighi,

(o) Letter to Falconieri.

p. 213

Malpighi, Leeuwenhoek, Bonanni, Hartsoeker, Joblot, Réaumur and very many others, who have shown, as it were, a new world of minute things. A microscope consisting of only one lens is called simple; one of several is called compound, whose inventor is said to be Cornelis Drebbel, in the year […], as Huygens relates in his Dioptrics.

678 James Gregory in the year 1663 invented and described a catadioptric telescope composed of lenses and mirrors. A few years afterwards the most distinguished Newton (q) published a catadioptric telescope of a somewhat different structure, very well suited to celestial observations, called Newtonian from the name of its author, just as the former was named Gregorian. Both, however, at length, after an interval of some years, […] namely John Hadley brought them to perfection.

679 From the combination of a lens and a mirror the Polemoscope was likewise made: namely an instrument by whose aid one can view objects while looking in another direction. Its chief part is a plane mirror […] inclined, from which the image of the object is sent back toward the eye of the beholder, since he himself cannot have it along a straight line. In this way it will be possible to observe without danger the movements of the enemy, […] behind the defenses of bulwarks, […] and to […] who […], etc.

680 Here too belongs the camera obscura, which represents on a flat ground external objects expressed in their own colors, so that they can conveniently be drawn. The Magic Lantern, too, is reckoned among these instruments, in which, by the aid of a concave mirror, minute things are enlarged to […] form.

681 Finally, among the instruments to be referred to Optics the most distinguished Nollet (r) counts one […] in London in the year 17[…], devised not long before by D. Lieberkühn, Academician of Berlin, to which the name solar microscope […] differs from the magic lantern […] in a darkened room […] the rays of the sun […] glasses […]. But […] with P. Para [du Phanjas], who most recently published in French a very clear Physics under this title: Théorie des Êtres sensibles, ou Cours complet de Physique, à Paris 1772, from which we have excerpted a great many things.
