DISSERTATION V

CHAPTER I

On insensible Qualities.

On Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis.

hose qualities are called insensible, or occult, which do not themselves act 682

T immediately on our senses, but are known from their effects and by rea‐

son; the name of occult, however, is held to be undeservedly given to them

by the Modern Philosophers, who follow the right method of philosophizing and are

not content with abstract words wrongly used, in which the Peripatetics delight ex‐

ceedingly, namely faculty, or quality, or form, and others like them, but they inquire

into the causes of things, which can be grasped not indeed with the eyes, but with

the mind. Among qualities of this kind are reckoned Sympathy, Antipathy and all the

others mentioned above, of which we are to treat in this place.

683 Sympathy, then, is the name for that agreement of things by which it comes

about that, when one is affected, feels, is moved or suffers, the other too is affected,

feels, is moved and suffers. To this likewise is referred a certain friendship, or rather

fitness, between men, and a certain natural love. Antipathy, on the contrary, is the

name they give to a repugnance and, as it were, a certain enmity between things, such

that one rejects and turns away from the other. They speak of idiosyncrasy when we ei‐

ther turn away from harmless, nay salutary, things and cannot bear them, or seek and

easily tolerate things harmful and otherwise adverse. Antiperistasis is defined in the

Schools as the resistance of one body against a contrary body by which it is besieged on every

side, growing in strength, and the intensification of a quality on account of the contrary quality.

684 The explanation of these qualities does not seem so recondite to the Modern

Physicists that, if we turn our mind with mature and circumspect judgment to all the

attendant conditions, they cannot be set forth from genuine, clear and true princi‐

ples; observing, however, that care must be taken that, in order to be made more cer‐

tain of the thing itself, we first of all inquire accurately whether whatever is narrated

is really so under those circumstances and conditions. For very many observations of

doubtful credit, and fables, intrude themselves here, and very many things are

narrated

which,

p. 251

which, if we consult experience and investigate everything most accurately, we shall find for certain either not to be so at all, or never to happen in the way in which they are reported. This having been noted,

685 I say first: Sympathy, Antipathy, Idiosyncrasy and Antiperistasis are rightly attributed to substantial outflows, and to the motion, rest, figure and situation of the parts, and to other mechanical affections; likewise to custom, to manners, to temperament, or to imagination. Proof, part by part. First, by explaining sympathetic effects most clearly from the said principles. Thus, for example, the powder from calcined vitriol which is called sympathetic, and which, when thrown into blood freshly let out of a wound, is found to stop its flow and to heal the wound, will be conceived to produce this effect in no other way than through the corpuscles of the vitriol, which, mixed with the still warm particles of the blood and set into fermentation together with them, are carried to the wound from which the blood was pressed out (just as transpiration takes place), and indeed, like wedges, entirely block up the open passages through which the blood flows forth.

686 The reason of other effects of this kind, likewise in men and animals, is given from our conclusion. Thus, that when one yawns another yawns, that when one dog barks another barks too, that when some little birds sing others are stirred to warble, comes from this, that men and animals which have a fit disposition of body are easily stirred to the things that are done by others: for when certain ideas are excited, the members of the body conspire, and are easily stirred to motions determined according to a certain idea. The force of custom also contributes much to sympathetic effects, when through it a particular disposition and aptitude is induced in bodies. Finally, the inclination of one man toward another arises above all from the agreement of manners, the congruence of temperament, and likewise from elegance in speech, body, life and manners. For these provoke and win love, and bind men as with silent chains. Antipathetic effects have, in their own way, the opposite cause. Thus the causes of aversion between men are easily detected: for in the face, manners, life, speech or actions something is always found by which the one cannot but be averse to the other. Effects of this kind in animals too are fittingly derived from the principles already established. Thus who will deny that the flight of the lamb when the wolf is present, the wolf ’s rush upon the lamb, and the clucking of hens when the kite flies past, are brought about by certain impressions?

687 From the structure and disposition of the parts the distinguished Camerarius (t) has elegantly deduced the wonderful phenomena of the herb mimosa, or pudica (commonly la vergonzosa), which grows pale when a hand approaches, contracts its leaves and, as it were, withdraws itself from contact and shuns the hand,

Ee having

(t) In a special dissertation on the herb mimosa.

p. 216

having, namely, first set out the anatomy of this kind of plant, having noted the reticular composition of the leaves out of fibers, utricles, small vessels and little vesicles swollen with air of various kinds, and having weighed the equilibrium of the sap-bearing vessels and of the tracheae, he illustrates the matter: namely, when a hand approaches, the air contained in the vesicles is rarefied and expanded by the warm exhalations emitted, hence the sap-bearing vessels are in some measure compressed; when these are compressed, the more abundant inflow of the sap, from which the leaves obtained their vigor and extension, is checked, whence the leaves grow pale, become flaccid and contract. When the hand is then withdrawn, it is no wonder that the vigor of the herb is restored, since, the cause of the expansion ceasing, the rarefaction of the air is overcome by the sap flowing in through the vessels.

688 The chief reason of idiosyncrasies lies in this, that, owing to a singular disposition, constitution and likeness of the organs, and above all a more tender, softer, looser or more rigid etc. constitution of the nervous fibers, certain impressions affect the mind, and according as they are either agreeable or adverse to the mind, it is affected in various ways, either calmly, or unpleasantly, or impetuously; whence there follow determinate motions of the common sensorium and of the nerves which are stretched out and distributed from there to the parts and through them. It is accordingly explained why certain men fear cats, dogs, mice, and shudder at and abominate other animals, and grow pale and tremble even at their name.

689 For if infants have been frightened and offended by things of this kind by ignorant old women (as happens very often, not without great harm to health, nay even with danger to life), since the fibers of the brain, still tender in the infant, have been too much agitated and weakened by the vehement impression, therefore, through the rest of life thereafter, when a similar material idea, or imagination, is brought back and arises anew, the impression and agitation in the weakened fibers is more vehement than is right; and in the mind an immaterial idea arises that is most disagreeable and adverse. And from the foundations stated, more or less, the reason is given of idiosyncrasies that are hereditary, adventitious, or contracted in various ways after birth, and acquired by custom.

690 Likewise, if attention is paid to the different ways in which our organs, and the animal spirits diffused through the nerves, are affected by various objects, and to the fact that these spirits, by the aid of the imagination, can be moved very swiftly through the whole body, in brutes as well as in men, it will not be difficult to explain those effects which, through the nerves of the mother, on account of a lively imagination, are propagated into the tender, and hence easily changeable, little body of the fetus.

691 Those effects which are attributed by the Peripatetics to Antiperistasis as to an occult quality can just as well be explained by mechanical affections, without that metaphorical battle of qualities: as, for instance, that underground places are colder in summer than in winter. And indeed the experiments which, for the proof of this occult quality,

731 Moreover: since long-lasting twilights are drawn out for them, so that for

The systems of the world are briefly set out.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732

B tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the

motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been

celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is

fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air,

then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then

constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the

world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its

course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the

6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firma‐

ment with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that

by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space

of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth

as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon

in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining

Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discov‐

ered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally

he

(d) Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

p. 219

he added on top of all these the firmament, concentric with the earth.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

p. 220

rarefying it too much, or dissolving its natural mixture, exciting a malignant fermentation in it, or constricting too much, condensing the parts, and hence restraining their vigor and natural actions.

704 Monkshood, by excessive heat, thins and agitates the blood with which it is mixed, and burns up the delicate substance of the viscera; water hemlock, on the other hand, by excessive cold gradually halts the particles of the blood in the finer and extreme veins, so that there it grows torpid as though congealed; then, as these approach the heart little by little with rest and cold, it renders the blood stagnant in the heart itself, whence death follows. We omit what they say of the basilisk, namely that its look is deadly, and likewise of the remora, the little fish that holds ships back, things which indeed are reckoned among old wives’ tales by critics of better note. The motions, however, which are excited in certain men by the bite of the tarantula (which is a species of spider well known in Calabria near Tarentum), we shall explain later.

705 The manner of acting of Alexipharmics consists in this: either that they blunt and break the sharp points of the poison, as oily things do; or that they restore the ordered motion of the blood, by resolving the thicker parts and rousing the weak spirits, as theriac etc. does; or by receiving the poisoned corpuscles into themselves on account of the mutual proportion of the pores and parts. Thus a wound inflicted by a Scorpion (commonly alacrán) is healed if the scorpion itself, crushed, is at once laid on the wound, since the poisonous particles left in the hand by the bite are sucked out, as by a sponge, by the homogeneous particles which are found in the crushed body of the scorpion; or, finally, antidotes have their force against some particular poison placed in a motion which is opposite to the motion of the poison itself.

706 So the most effective remedy against the bite of the tarantula is the motions and vibrations of a musical instrument; for when the blood has been condensed by the poison and the little vessels obstructed, the inflow of the animal spirits is impeded, and the nerves are consequently relaxed; but by the harmonic vibrations of the music the blood is agitated, the spirits receive vigor, these run through the fibers and nerves, and the fibers and nerves, brought to a constitution in unison with the strings or sounding instruments, receive the vibrations of the strings; hence the motion of the limbs, and finally leaping; by the exertion of leaping the agitation of the blood is increased and sweat is drawn out, whence the poison too, thinned and agitated, is gradually dissipated by transpiration; and in proportion as the poison is dissipated the sick man is better, and this recovery of health spurs him on to continue the leaping, whence it comes about that all the poison breathes out and the blood recovers its fluidity and its former course.

707 Nor is it to be wondered at that a particular musical harmony, as Fr. Schott notes, is demanded to cure each person so affected. For since the animal spirits, fibers, nerves and poisonous particles have a different consistency and size in different men, a different harmonic conformation too is required to move the spirits, fibers and nerves, and hence to dissipate the poison by agitation,

and

p. 221

leaping. Whoever desires more on this subject should consult the learned volumes of

the more recent Physicians; among these the works of the distinguished Herman

Boerhaave, and of his Commentator, the most illustrious Dr. van Swieten, claim glory

for themselves.

708 From all that has been said it becomes clear that the knowledge of natural

things contributes a great deal to explaining wonderful effects, lays open many things

at which the common people are amazed, makes manifest the secrets of nature, and,

what is chief, leads to the knowledge of the Author of Nature, whom we adore in rev‐

erence with our whole mind.

T H E A R G U M E N T S A R E A N S W E R E D. 709

O bj. 1. against the first: the texture of the parts is the same in the living body as

in the dead, but most medicines or poisons in no way exert their force on

corpses: thus cantharides, e.g., raise blisters on the living body, not on the dead:

therefore the manner of acting of medicines is not fittingly deduced from the texture

of the parts etc. Reply, by denying the antec. and the conseq.: cantharides, or cauter‐

ies, kindled by the heat of the living body and diluted by its moisture, produce an ef‐

fervescence and wrinkle the skin of the living body.

710 Obj. 2. It can in no way be explained by the texture of the parts etc. why the

Peruvian bark, which is commonly called Quina, mostly either cures a quartan fever

or stops it for a time, or why cantharides injure the bladder itself and not other or‐

gans: therefore. Reply: it can easily be explained in several ways how the Peruvian

bark operates.

711 For 1. the powder of Quina either fixes that humor which causes the quartan,

and which in its powers is most like a poison, or checks its motion, or promotes a

new fermentation in the blood, or drives out that venom through an occult, or insen‐

sible, transpiration. So the powder of cantharides, as long as it is diluted with the

blood and the other humors, remains harmless; but after it has been secreted from

the mass of the blood in the kidneys, by its caustic force it ulcerates either the kid‐

neys themselves or the bladder.

712 Obj. finally: such phenomena, and very many others, are explained more con‐

veniently by the Peripatetic substantial forms than by the texture of the parts and

substantial effluvia, since it is incredible that effluvia should flow unceasingly from

hard and solid bodies: therefore. Dist. antec.: more conveniently and more suitably

to the nature of true Physics, I deny; not so, I grant. What is included in the an‐

tecedent stands answered in several places of our Physics where we spoke of effluvia.

Moreover: no one has hitherto denied that most gems, and diamonds themselves,

bodies certainly very hard, are powerful in electric force, which can by no means be

understood without a substantial efflux. What more? From the regulus of antimony

little vessels are made which give an emetic force to wine or beer poured into them,

and they are used for this purpose for many years without any sensible diminution of

their weight. So too mercury, boiled a little in water, gives it a force by which it kills

worms, to omit very many other things.

CHAPTER I

P A R T V, A N D L A S T.

O N T H E C O M P O S I T I O N O F T H E WO R L D.

O N T H E E L E M E N T A RY W O R L D,

AND TERRESTRIAL BODIES,

On the Composition of the World.

A summary doctrine of the structure of the visible world-sphere is

set forth.

hree kinds of artificial sphere are distinguished: one celestial, which dis713

T plays the heaven and the stars; another terrestrial, which displays the ter‐

raqueous mass; the third armillary, so called because it is a complex of

various circles and rings representing a globe.

714 The principal parts of this sphere, in which, as at one glance, the constitu‐

tion of the universe and the variety of the motions which the chief bodies of the

world require are beheld, are: I. The Axis, or diametral line, passing through the cen‐

ter of the sphere in such a way that the sphere turns about it; its extreme points are

called the poles. II. A small sphere set in the middle of the axis, which represents the

position of the terraqueous globe. III. Circles, partly greater, partly lesser. The greater

cut the whole sphere, as also the other greater circles, into two equal parts, and they

are these: the Equator, the Meridian, the Horizon, the Zodiac, the two Colures. The

lesser circles cut the sphere into unequal parts. Four of these are counted: the two

Tropics, and as many polar circles. All are divided into 360 parts equal among them‐

selves, or degrees;

these

p. 223

these in turn into 60 others, which are called minutes. Besides, certain points in the circuit of the whole sphere are usually considered and called cardinal. We shall go through the notions of all of these distinctly, one by one.

715 The Pole indicates the point of the world’s axis around which, itself wholly unmoved, the machine of the universe is turned. There are two such points, or poles: one the Arctic, which is also called Boreal and Aquilonian from the wind that blows from there. The other is called the Antarctic, and is also named Meridional, or Austral. Both are counted in the first place among the cardinal points.

716 The Equator, or equinoctial or equidial circle, is that in which, while the Sun is placed in it, day is equal to night. In the course of one year the Sun is in it twice: when it touches the beginning of the sign Aries, about the 20th of March, and when it enters the sign Libra, about the 23rd of September. The equator is distant from each pole of the world by a quadrant; it therefore divides the sphere into two equal parts, the Boreal and the Austral. Its use is defined in a manner by these points: I. It divides the whole world into the two hemispheres just named. II. It indicates the two equinoxes of the year, namely the vernal and the autumnal. III. It measures days and hours; for its 360 degrees pass by in the space of 24 hours, and so each 15 degrees make one hour. IV. It is the boundary from which the declinations of the Sun, the Moon and the other Stars are taken; for the declination of any star is its distance from the equator toward one or the other pole, which is measured by the arc of a circle passing through the poles of the world and the center of the Star. V. It defines the cardinal points of East and West on the horizon. VI. By its different position with respect to the horizon it brings it about that the horizon presents itself as right, oblique, or parallel.

717 The Horizon is understood to be described from the vertical point, which in Arabic is called Zenith, and from another set on the opposite side, which is called Nadir (both are counted among the cardinal points), and it cuts the sphere into equal parts, the upper and the lower, in such a way that the plane of the circle passes through the center of the world. Hence, since these diametrically opposite points, as we travel from one place to another, nay, relatively to each man, are different and different again, it is plain that the horizon changes again and again, and that there are as many different horizons as there are points that can be thought on the surface of the sphere. And this concerns the Astronomical, or rational, horizon, so called because it is considered by Astronomers observing the motions of the Heavens, and is perceived by reason only, not by sense. For there is another horizon, sensible or physical, which everyone set in some vast plain, or in the middle of a calm sea, defines by turning his sight round. Wherefore, mathematically speaking, the sensible horizon neither actually forms a greatest circle, since it in no way extends through the center of the world, nor consequently does it separate the sphere of the Heaven into equal parts; yet it is always parallel to the rational horizon.

718 The uses of the horizon are these. I. It distributes the world-sphere into two parts, and the rational horizon indeed into equal ones, or hemispheres:

Ff the

p. 224

the upper, which rises above the rational horizon, and the lower, which lies beneath that same horizon; the sensible horizon, on the other hand, distinguishes the part of the Heaven visible to us from the invisible. II. It determines the risings and settings of the stars. III. It designates, for each particular region, the stars that never rise or never set. IV. It defines the length of the artificial day and of the night: for that interval during which the Sun remains above the horizon is called the artificial day, as the night is taken to be this space during which it is depressed below the horizon. V. It is the boundary from which the altitude of the Stars is found: for the altitude of a star above the horizon is as great as the arc of the circle drawn through the poles of the horizon and the very center of the Star, comprehended between that center and the point of the horizon. The same holds of the depth of the Stars which they have below the horizon. VI. The Horizon, according to the different position of the sphere, makes it now right, now parallel, now oblique. This circle is not usually marked on Geographical Maps. In the armillary Sphere its office is performed by a broad and immovable rim, on which three things are inscribed: namely the degrees which the Sun runs through in the Zodiac, the old and the new Calendar, and the cardinal points of the winds.

719 The Zodiac is the circle under which the Planets are perpetually moved, and which cuts the equator at oblique angles in two opposite, equinoctial points, while in two others, likewise diametrically opposite, the solstitial, it touches the tropics: the summer tropic at the beginning of Cancer, the winter one at the beginning of Capricorn; its poles are therefore distant from the poles of the world and of the equator itself by a space of about 23 degrees and 30 minutes (c).

720 It is divided according to its latitude, which according to the Ancients comprises 12 degrees, according to the Moderns 16, nay even 20, into three circles, of which the middle and greatest is called the way of the Sun, the royal road, because the center of the Sun constantly describes this path by its periodic motion; it is likewise called the ecliptic from the eclipses of the Sun and Moon, which occur only in it or near that same line; the remaining two lesser circles, equidistant from the middle one, are called the limits of latitude. According to its longitude it is divided, in the order of the signs, into 12 equal parts, each of which comprises 30 degrees and takes its name from the neighboring sign. The signs of the Zodiac, further, are some called starry, others marked: the former are asterisms, and chiefly figures of animals composed of several stars, so that they symbolically signify the nature of the year through the months; the latter are their characters. The signs to which the characters are usually added are comprised in two verses, by the first of which the northern ones, by the other the southern ones are expressed, namely:

They

Pytheas, in the year 324 before the birth of Christ, fixed the declination at 23°. 52′. 41″ (that is, 23 degrees, 52 first minutes, 41 seconds); in the year after Christ 1715 the most distinguished de Louville at 23°. 28′. 24″ (that is, 23 degrees, 28 first minutes, 24 seconds). See Wolff, Elem. Astron. §. 165.

They are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo,

♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ♓

and Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces.

721 The use of the Zodiac is contained in these points: I. As the equator measures the diurnal motion, so the middle of the Zodiac, or ecliptic, measures the periodic motion of the stars, and chiefly of the sun; for the periodic motion is said to be completed when an entire revolution under the ecliptic is completed by the Stars. II. The eclipses of the Sun and Moon take place under this same circle. III. It causes the inequality of days and nights; for neither are the days equal among themselves, nor these to the nights, for the reason that the Sun is carried along in the ecliptic. IV. The constant alternation of the seasons, of which one succeeds another in turn in every yearly course, depends on the position of the ecliptic. V. The ecliptic is the boundary of the latitude of the Stars; for the latitude of a star is the arc of the circle (which is therefore called the circle of latitude, and is a greatest circle) drawn through the poles of the ecliptic and through the centers of the Stars themselves, intercepted between this center and the ecliptic itself. VI. The longitudes of the stars are numbered in it: for the arc of the ecliptic, proceeding from the beginning of Aries in consequentia, or according to the series of the signs, comprehended as far as the circle of latitude, is the longitude of the star.

722 The Meridian is the circle described from the two points of true rising and setting, or those in which, at the time of the equinox, the Sun rises and sets, which again are called cardinal, and passing through the poles both of the world and of the horizon, or the points Zenith and Nadir, and therefore cutting the horizon at right angles; when the Sun reaches it in its ascent, it makes midday. Hence all those points of the Sphere have the same meridian which are not distant from one another except along a straight line drawn from one pole of the world to the other; on the contrary, those places obtain a different one which are distant from east to west, or vice versa: so that the meridian changes while we travel from east toward west, or vice versa, but not at all when we proceed from north to south, or conversely. As many meridians, therefore, are really reckoned as there are vertical points that can be designated from east to west. Yet from one we take the beginning, which is named the first, so that from it the rest come into the count, the reckoning being made from West to East. This is fixed by some in one place, by others in another. The French had fixed it in the last of the Canary Islands, which is called the Island of Ferro, before the more recent Astronomers of that Nation established the first meridian in the Astronomical Observatory of Paris itself, as is customary today. We give the use of the meridian circle briefly.

Ff 2 723

p. 226

723 I. It divides the Heaven into two hemispheres, the Eastern and the Western. II. It measures the greatest altitude of the Stars above the horizon, for a star is raised above the horizon until it reaches the Meridian; then, receding from it, it is depressed: it is said to culminate when it reaches it. III. Throughout the whole year it determines the point of midday and of midnight: for it bisects all those circles which the Sun runs through by its diurnal motion. The other offices of the meridian, known to Astronomers, we pass over: for we go through these things not as Astronomers but by the office of Physicists.

724 The Colures are two greatest circles which, while they pass through the poles of the world, divide each other there at right angles, and divide the equator, and likewise the ecliptic, into four by an equal partition. The colure of the equinoxes is drawn through those points of the Zodiac in which, when the Sun is there, the equinoxes occur, namely through the beginnings of Aries and Libra. The colure of the solstices is drawn through the solstitial points (so called because the Sun, on reaching them, seems in some manner to stand still, or to make a station, that is: for some days not to change its declination from the equator at all), namely through the beginning of Cancer and of Capricorn.

725 The use of each colure consists in these points. I. They determine the four cardinal points of the Zodiac, namely those in which, when the Sun is placed there, the turnings of the seasons are brought about: in Aries the vernal, in Capricorn the winter, in Cancer the summer, in Libra the autumnal. Hence three signs correspond to each part of the year: to spring Aries, Taurus, Gemini, etc. II. As the colure of the equinoxes defines in the Zodiac those two points while the Sun occupies which day is equal to night, so the colure of the solstices marks two others in that same circle, in which, when the Sun is there, now the longest day and the shortest night, now conversely the longest night and the shortest day take place. III. As the colure of the equinoxes divides the signs of the Zodiac into six northern ones: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and as many southern ones: Libra, Scorpio, the Archer, the Goat, the Jar, Pisces; so the other colure separates the ascending signs, which are contained from the beginning of Capricorn to the first degree of Cancer, from the descending ones, or the rest, etc.

726 The Tropics are two lesser circles in the Sphere, at which, when the Sun reaches them, it does not run out further either to the north or to the south, but turns back to the Equator. They are also usually called Solstitial, because they are drawn through the solstitial points of the Zodiac: hence one is called the tropic of Cancer, the other the tropic of Capricorn. These circles are distant from the equator 23 deg. and about 30 first minutes, from each other 47 deg., from the nearer pole 66 deg. and about 30 first minutes. Their use is distinguished as threefold. I. They bound the path of the Sun. II. They define the longest and the shortest day on an oblique horizon. III. They close the torrid zone and begin the temperate.

727 The Polar circles are twin, likewise lesser circles; they have their name from the poles toward which they are moved, the one being of the arctic, the other of the antarctic, yet as far

removed

p. 227

CHAPTER II

removed from these as the tropics are from the equator, namely 23 deg., about 30

first min. These circles, together with the tropics and the equator itself, are common‐

ly called parallels, because all of them stand apart from one another by an equal inter‐

val at every point of their circuit. The use of the polar circles is: I. That the stars en‐

closed within the arctic circle never set for those to whom the sphere is either

oblique or parallel, and those comprehended within the antarctic never rise. II. By

their interposition the temperate Zones are distinguished from the frigid. All these

things will be understood more clearly by inspecting some armillary sphere.

On the threefold position of the Sphere.

n a threefold situation the sphere can be viewed, namely in the right, the 728

I oblique and the parallel, according as the position of the equator with respect

to the horizon is different. The sphere is right when the equator stands per‐

pendicularly over the horizon and cuts it at right angles, so that its poles are

set in the horizon. Those who dwell under the equator are said to have this position;

where, therefore, throughout the whole year the days are equal to the nights. The

sphere is oblique in which the equator is inclined to the horizon obliquely, or at un‐

equal angles. Those enjoy this whose latitude, or distance from the equator toward

one or the other pole computed on the meridian of the place, does not reach 90 de‐

grees, that is: all those who dwell between the equator and the poles; for them, there‐

fore, the days are unequal to the nights.

729 The sphere, finally, is called parallel in which the equator keeps parallelism

with the horizon. This position of the sphere is had by those whose vertex coincides

with one of the poles of the world, and so whose latitude equals 90 deg., or by those

who live under the poles: for those who dwell under it there is in the yearly course

only one day and one night, each bounded by as great an interval of time as the Sun

takes in traversing six figures of the Zodiac; for since their horizon and the equator

coincide, six signs of the Zodiac stand perpetually above the horizon, and as many lie

hidden below it; for that reason it is necessary that the Sun shine upon them above

the horizon for as long a time as is demanded for it to run through six signs of the

Zodiac, and again lie hidden below the horizon for as great an interval of time as is

required for it to be moved through as many lower signs, that is, the space of 6

months.

730 Although, however, night as well as day ought to be circumscribed for them

by the space of six months, yet for them the day is extended longer, while the night is

on the contrary diminished, namely on account of the very refraction

which

p. 228

CHAPTER III

which the solar rays undergo, by far the greatest, while they pass through the exceed‐

ingly dense atmosphere of those places; whence it comes about that the Sun seems to

shine above their horizon for some days, although it is depressed below it. Indeed the

Dutch who wintered in Nova Zembla in the year 1597 report that the Sun disap‐

peared on the 4th day of November and was visible again on the 24th day of January,

and so had anticipated the reckonings of astronomical calculation by an interval of

about six days.

731 Moreover: since long-lasting twilights are drawn out for them, so that for

about two months the rising of the Sun is as it were forestalled by the one, while the

other lasts so long after the setting of the Sun, therefore the darkness of night holds

them for no more than about two months. Nay, as Wolff observes (d), this darkness

of two months is tempered, for more than half of that space of time, by the splendor

of the Moon.

The systems of the world are briefly set out.

y the name of system Philosophers here understand the order, or disposi732

B tion, of this universe and of its principal parts, adapted to explaining the

motions and the celestial phenomena. Three systems have hitherto been

celebrated in the Schools, both astronomical and physical, and they still flourish. It is

fitting, therefore, to go through each of them briefly.

733 I. The Ptolemaic, so called from Claudius Ptolemy. His system makes first air,

then fire, surround the earth, which is placed in the middle of the universe; it then

constructs seven solid Heavens, one for each Planet, concentric with the circle of the

world, in this order: that in the 1st, that is, in the highest of all, Saturn runs its

course, in the 2nd Jupiter, in the 3rd Mars, in the 4th the Sun, in the 5th Venus, in the

6th Mercury, in the 7th the Moon. Above these Heavens, finally, it places the firma‐

ment with the fixed stars, which he called the primum mobile, because he thought that

by its motion the orbs of the lower Planets are carried from east to west in the space

of 23 hours, 56 minutes, 4 seconds.

734 II. The Tychonic system, constructed by Tycho Brahe. This, leaving the earth

as the center of the universe, together with the immobile atmosphere, sets the Moon

in the first place around it, then the Sun; around this, as the center of the remaining

Planets, he placed Mercury, Venus, Mars, then Jupiter with the four Satellites discov‐

ered by Galileo, and at length Saturn with its two attendants; finally

he

(d) Elem. Geograph. §. 131.

p. 219

he added on top of all these the firmament, concentric with the earth.

735 III. The Copernican system took its name from Nicolaus Copernicus, after the thirty years’ study which he spent on illustrating this hypothesis. According to it the Sun is set immobile in the center of the world; he holds that around it Mercury moves nearest, then Venus, next the Earth with the Moon circling about it, afterwards Mars, then Jupiter, and finally that Saturn revolves; beyond all the Planets, and indeed at an almost immense distance, he places the Sphere of the fixed Stars, wholly destitute of all motion. To the single Planets, the Sun alone excepted, which he therefore strikes out of the number of the Planets, he assigns a periodic motion, namely under the Zodiac, following the series of the signs.

736 To the Earth he assigns a threefold motion, namely: first, that of turning about its own axis from west to east, by which the Copernicans mean to explain the alternation of night and day; for once this motion is supposed, the Sun seems to us to be whirled from east to west, and the earth always presents another face to the Sun to be illuminated: this motion he calls diurnal, because it is completed in the interval of one day. The second he calls periodic, in the great orb around the Sun under the ecliptic, by which motion the earth so advances through the signs that the Sun appears to us to be in the sign which it covers, and hence, while the earth is in the northern signs, the Sun appears to us to dwell in the southern ones, and the reverse: this motion he names annual, as it is completed in the space of one year.

737 Lastly he establishes the motion of parallelism, by which the axis of the earth itself, in its revolution around the Sun, always remains parallel both to the axis of the world itself and to itself: by this motion the Copernicans unfold the phenomena of the alternation of the seasons of the year. To explain this matter, moreover, they also adopt such an inclination of the earth’s axis to the plane of the ecliptic that it makes with it an angle of 66 degrees, 30 minutes. “In this very age of ours (says the distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry) (e) very many men eminent in piety and religion, some even distinguished by the Purple, are freely permitted to hold with Galileo and with Copernicus, provided they do not call it a certain and undoubted System, but make it a hypothesis convenient for the uses of Astronomy, as was provided by the Decree of the Sacred Congregation of the Holy Office in the year 1620.” Thus far he. (Fig. LXX sets the Copernican System before your eyes.)

C H A P T E R I V.

A judgment on the systems of the world.

say: the Copernican System, as a mere hypothesis for explaining the mo738

I tions of the Stars and the phenomena, seems much more suitable than the

Ptolemaic and the Tychonic. We show this first in general. For the hypothe‐

sis of Copernicus is not opposed to Physics and Astronomy as the Ptolemaic system

is. For who could understand, in the latter, how the primum mobile carries away all the

lower spheres from east to west, while these nevertheless enjoy that motion in such a

way that, by a contrary reckoning, they at the same time advance daily from west to

east according to the series of the signs under the Zodiac? For if the surfaces by

which these spheres touch one another, namely the convex surface of the lower and

the concave of the upper, are smooth, it will come about that the upper imparts no

motion to the lower sphere, and so the former can revolve without carrying the latter

along with it; but if they are made rough, so that their projecting parts fit into one

another, it is clearly evident that one and the same motion will be effected both of

the upper and of the lower spheres, as Gassendi rightly argues (f).

739 The phenomena clearly show that the Ptolemaic system agrees very little

with Astronomical observations. For it has been found that Mercury and Venus are

seen by us from the earth now at the sides of the Sun, now above it. But in this hy‐

pothesis they ought always to appear below the Sun and nearer to us. Not to speak of

the awkward position of the fixed stars, since they are all set fixed in one surface,

whereas it is manifest among Astronomers that they are located in different planes,

some more remote than others.

740 Second: the Copernican hypothesis is more orderly, and weaves together the

position and disposition of the celestial bodies in a neater series; for in it none of the

primary Planets cuts the orbit (g) of another, as in the system of Tycho; then the rev‐

olutions of all the Planets are performed about the same center, namely the Sun, con‐

trary to what happens in the Tychonic. Moreover, the hypothesis of Copernicus, by

attributing motion to the earth while meanwhile the Sun and the fixed stars stand in

their places, explains the phenomena of the Heaven much more simply and from

fewer principles

than

(g) The orbit of a Planet is the name given to that curved line, returning into itself, which it de‐

scribes in its periodic motion.

p. 231

than the Tychonic does; for in the latter all the globes contained in the celestial spaces, the terraqueous one excepted, are set in motion, and indeed in such a way that each completes its circuit in the interval of 24 hours, so that for that reason they must be moved with an almost incredible velocity: therefore the Copernican hypothesis is to be preferred (Ax. II, §. 32).

741 For this reason it is much easier, and much more apt, for Astronomical observations and for constructing demonstrations: so that the Tychonian Astronomers too make use of the Copernican hypothesis to complete their observations and to carry out the construction of their tables. Nay, as the most distinguished Serry observes (h), it was once adopted by the Church herself for the emendation of the Roman Calendar.

742 The diurnal motion, indeed, by which the earth itself is turned from west to east, brings it about that the Sun, the Planets themselves and the fixed Stars seem to us to revolve from east to west; hence the alternation of day and night follows; for, as all who know the nature of motion are forced to admit, since all things which appear to us to be moved in place are perceived in this way because either they themselves really change their place, or the spectator proceeds in the opposite direction while those bodies are unmoved, according to that line of Virgil (i):

743 We are borne forth from the harbor, and lands and cities fall away, therefore it is necessary that all the phenomena of the diurnal motion appear to us in just the same way, whether the diurnal revolution toward the West is attributed to the Stars themselves, or the motion in the opposite direction, namely toward the East, is said to belong to the earth and to our eye, the Sun and the stars not being moved from their place. But it will be enough to have hinted at these things.

744 The Tychonians frame their chief argument against the Copernican hypothesis from the Sacred Scriptures. They contend, namely, that the doctrine of Copernicus is opposed to their words, inasmuch as these manifestly teach that the Sun moves, but that the earth stands still. Thus Genesis 19: The sun was risen upon the earth. Psalm 92: He hath established the world which shall not be moved. Ecclesiastes ch. 1: But the earth standeth for ever. The sun riseth, and goeth down, and returneth to his place; and Josue ch. 10 (when the Leader of the Jews commanded that the Sun should not move over against Gabaon): So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven, and hasted not to go down the space of one day. Isaias ch. 38: And the sun returned ten lines by the degrees by which it was gone down. And from these very many conclude that the Copernican system, which asserts the motion of the earth and the rest of the Sun, seems to be opposed to the authority of the Holy Scriptures.

745 But the Copernicans, distinguished alike in learning and in reverent piety toward the Divine word, reply that their opinion in no way conflicts with these testimonies. For they say that these and other words of the kind must be understood not in the literal, physical, proper and absolute sense, but only in the popular, optical, improper

Gg and

(h) In the place cited above.

(i) Aeneid, bk. III, v. 72.

p. 232

and according to appearance. They answer that Divine Scripture tempers itself to the capacity of the common people. The reason they give for asserting this is that “God (as the distinguished Muratori says (k)), speaking through his Scriptures, did not have this aim, to feed men’s vain curiosity about things not necessary to know, about the elements of the world and about bodies, but to hand down things truly useful for attaining eternal happiness. For He does not speak in the learned words of human wisdom, but lowers Himself to the use of those expressions which, although they are recognized as less accurate and as improper when weighed in the balance of human wisdom, yet set forth some useful and salutary truth more conveniently to an unlearned people.” For the rest, they profess that they do not wish to depart from the common ways of speaking, and that they will speak in accommodation to what appears by the testimony of the senses: The Sun rises; it is raised to the point of midday; it declines toward the West, etc.

746 The distinguished Theologian Hyacinthe Serry too, after adducing the testimonies of Sacred Letters cited above, rises up thus against the adversary of the Copernican hypothesis (l): “Do you wield the censor’s rod on account of those few little words of Scripture? Why not rather, if you are a Theologian, until the Church condemns the ingenious System, bend the words of Scripture cited to a convenient sense? So that those words which are paraded in favor of the immobile stability of the earth may be understood only of firmness, consistency and duration, in no way excluding local motion: for Divine Wisdom is also said to have established the Heavens, or the sky above, Prov. 8, though motion according to Ptolemy’s System is in no way at odds with that firmness of the heavens: while those which are brought forward from Sacred Letters in favor of the mobility of the Sun were said not according to the truth of the thing, but according to the opinion of the common people and the common manner of speaking, so that the Sacred Writers might accommodate themselves to the understanding of an unlearned people: which we have made manifest by so many other examples; and in this very one which is especially objected, about Josue, it is most certain, namely that it was said according to the opinion of the common people, if the whole narration of the deed is attended to more diligently. Move not, O sun, says Josue, toward Gabaon: and yet, since the earth is a small mass in comparison with the Sun, and Gabaon on that same globe of the earth is as a most minute point, what, I ask, is the Sun commanded, that it should not move toward Gabaon? Could the huge globe of the Sun so correspond to this point as either to move or to stand still over against it? Josue therefore alluded to the common judgment of the eyes, for to our eyes the Sun appears as a disk to be measured by two palms at most, running over a small space of the sky.

747 “It is added in the historical narration: So the sun stood still in the midst of heaven: but the celestial orbs, being spherical (if we wish to speak exactly), as they lack extremities, so also they lack a middle; and no middle can be devised in a circular path

APPENDIX

or line. That, therefore, must be interpreted according to the understanding of the

common people: that that place of the heavens seems to them the middle which is

equally distant from the East and the West. The narration is finally closed with these

words: there was not before nor after so long a day. Has then no longer day ever shone in

the whole world? But it is well ascertained by those who travel through the regions

situated under either Pole that the Sun shines longer there and that longer days oc‐

cur: nay, it is most certain that this very thing is proved by a demonstrative and most

evident reasoning by those skilled in Astronomical Science. The narration, therefore,

was accommodated to the Jewish people, to whom the effects of the Sun in the polar

regions were unknown.

748 “Unless we say this, and confess that the Sacred Writers, in these formulas of

speech concerning the motion of the Sun and the stability of the Earth, spoke ac‐

cording to the custom of the common people, there is danger lest, with equal license

and an equal abuse of the Divine Scriptures, some morose exactor of the Sacred

Words should set about demonstrating this very system of Copernicus and Galileo

on the mobility of the Earth, which most of the more recent Theologians brand with

their inconsiderate censures. For since the world is so often said in Sacred Letters to

be set upon its cardines [poles, hinges]: 1 Kings ch. 2: For the poles of the earth are the Lord’s;

Proverbs 8: He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the poles of the world; and since

cardines, if we wish to speak strictly, denote a turning and movable thing set upon

them, which is revolved and turned upon them: what, I ask you, will follow from this,

except that the earth is movable and turning, which, set upon its hinges, is revolved

and driven by a fixed law? All the more because in Job ch. 9, v. 6, God is said to move

the earth out of its place; which the morose exactor of words will want to have been

said without figure and katalexis (a certain manner of speaking accommodated to the

common people).” Thus far the distinguished Serry.

749 But let these things be said in passing, not so that we may hold the system of

Copernicus and Galileo as ratified and fixed, since we said from the very beginning

that we adopt it only as a mere hypothesis for explaining the phenomena.

What is to be thought of the influence of the Stars?

ublicly debated is the question whether the stars concur in producing the 750

P effects observed on the earth, or, as it is commonly put, whether they influ‐

ence sublunary things. The Sun chiefly, and the Moon, seem to some to

share a communion of effluvia with our earth: an argument which they ex‐

tend from these two Stars to the rest; nor are they content to say that the stars act on

sublunary things through heat and light, but they think that various other influences

Gg 2 are

p. 234

are exerted upon the earth, while they attribute different specific properties to the Stars: that the Moon, being exceedingly moist, excites the humors on the earth; that Saturn is cold; Mars dry and hot, etc.; so that, accordingly, the rising of some brings on rain, that of others induces drought, etc. It is not our pleasure to pursue these and more things of the kind any further: we shall set forth our view of the influence of the Stars in brief. Wherefore the conclusion follows.

751 Apart from the action of light we acknowledge no other influence of the stars upon the earth: except, however, the Sun, which by its heat, sensible enough, warms our earth, and also the Moon, which, if not by heat or cold, yet certainly by its weight upon the atmosphere beneath it, can press upon our globe variously according to its varying position. For, in the first place, certain substantial effluvia, moist, dry, etc., cannot be transmitted from the stars to the earth; for what cause can be adduced by which such effluvia should be propelled through the longest spaces beyond the atmosphere of their star, which extends only some miles? Certainly about terrestrial effluvia all agree that they by no means run out beyond the atmosphere into the region of the Moon: then, even if effluvia were thrust out, what can be imagined that would direct them to our earth rather than to some other space and celestial body? Finally, if the Moon, in which our adversaries place the greatest force, scattered its effluvia spherically, then, since these diverge from one another the more, the further they recede from the lunar body, and at so great a distance as the Moon has from the earth can and must be spread very far apart, those effects which are attributed to the influence of the moon can by no means be produced by so stingy and meager a dew of effluvia.

752 It is shown, secondly. The action of light can be the cause of all the effects; for light consists in the rectilinear pressure of the ethereal substance, propagated all the way to us. Therefore a different motion of the smallest particles can be excited, namely a vehement, varied and perturbed one; and once this motion is posited, one effect follows, and when it ceases, again another, without any need to have recourse, in order to explain the moisture of the nights, to I know not what outflowings of the Moon. Wherefore, when we see the whole of nature cherished and propagated, plants growing up, grain turning yellow, fruits ripening, in a word, generations, alterations and augmentations promoted; when we experience the seasons of the year recurring with a fixed regulation, and more particular changes of the air, often very diverse, taking place according to the concurrence of other causes, it is necessary that we attribute these things to the action of the Sun; but to the Sun acting in no other way than by its light and the heat consequent upon it.

753 Hence, although there is in the other stars a force of striking and agitating the slender fibrils of the optic nerves, and so, since particles thinner than these fibrils and more apt for motion are contained in the air, water and earth, a force of agitating and moving these particles, and consequently of producing some effects (how far these will fall under sense, each will judge from the almost immense distance of the fixed stars, and from the

faint

p. 235

faint light of the planets), nevertheless none at all is to be ascribed to them ex‐

cept in proportion to their light, whose action must be held as demonstrated.

And since the light of the Sun alone is stronger than the light of all the stars to‐

gether, therefore the cause of all these effects is chiefly to be attributed to it. But

if it should perhaps be observed that the temper of the air is not the same when‐

ever the Sun darts its rays upon the earth in the same way, this is to be referred

not to the other heavenly bodies, but to some peculiar condition, at that time, of

the air or of the earth. From these things it follows:

C O RO L L A RY I .

754

J udicial astrology is to be repudiated as a most empty imposture, unworthy of a

Philosopher, both because it is reproved by the Sacred Scriptures, condemned

by the Councils of Braga and Toledo, censured by the Fathers, and forbidden by

the authority of the Supreme Pontiffs and by the canon and civil laws, and be‐

cause it is hissed off with laughter by all the wise. Certainly that division of the

Heaven into 12 houses, on which the horoscope is founded, or the figure of the

celestial configuration that exists at the moment of birth, is a fiction. Moreover,

neither do the same fates befall all who are born under the same star, as is plain

from the example of the twins Esau and Jacob, who had the most different

propensity and fortune; nor do those who experience similar fates enjoy the

same horoscope, as is manifest: since many perish together by shipwreck, fire,

plague, or battle, although they were brought into the light at the most different

times. Not to mention that the whole supposition of this art, taken from the

septenary number of the planets and from the situation of the celestial houses, is

false. The first is shown by the satellites of Jupiter and Saturn, indeed even by

the single one of Venus; the second, because the constellations to which they

gave the name of the 12 Signs of the Zodiac, in whose order they hold that their

12 houses are found in the Heaven, have long since already receded 30 degrees

from their original place. But there is no leisure to dwell on trifles.

C O RO L L A RY I I .

755

A eroscopic astrology, or that which foretells storms and changes of the air from

the stars, is to be rejected by the Philosopher: for this art is confirmed nei‐

ther by any reason nor by experience; for soothsayers of this kind posit certain

properties in the planets: Saturn cold and dry, Venus a hot and moist planet, etc.,

which suppositions are not philosophical conjectures but fabulous ones; for why

should one be hot, another moist, when all are opaque masses not much unlike

our earth? By experience they cannot establish their art;

for

p. 236

for this rests on frequently repeated observation, whereas the astrologers neither

have nor can have an observation in which, from a similar position of the stars, a sim‐

ilar event has followed in sublunary things: since it is certain from the astronomers

that the same aspect of the same stars does not return within many millions of years;

and even if such a position had returned, it would have been unknown, as regards all

the stars, to those unskilled men, since until the past century they were ignorant of

the secondary planets.

756 Nor do predictions that sometimes come true do anything for a presumption

of truth; for who is there, says Cicero, who, hurling darts all day long, does not some‐

times hit the mark? Besides the fact that the far more numerous false ones carry very

great weight toward detracting from the astrologers’ credit, there are innumerable

examples of this. Thus in the year 1524, on account of great conjunctions of the plan‐

ets in Aquarius, entire and certain deluges were predicted, yet the year was most

serene; in the year 1586, winds and storms on account of conjunctions of all the plan‐

ets, although the whole year was passed in calm. Certainly the astrologers themselves

do not agree among themselves in their predictions: hence a certain Frenchman

bought himself so many calendars that for each single day he could choose one con‐

formable to the heavens, whereby it came about that he said his calendar was con‐

formable to the heavens the whole year round; and although these prophecies are

sometimes inserted in calendars, it is by no means proved that this is done by the

counsel of the wise, or that credence is given by them to these follies, since one will

hardly find in the whole world a learned astronomer who does not indignantly reject

this simplicity, unworthy of a learned man, as Amort says. (m)

757 These things, namely, are done so that custom may be served, not otherwise

than as physicians themselves accommodate themselves to the phlebotomic table,

whose foundation is nothing other than the numerical order of the days counted

from the new moon, which has no force at all. Certainly Amort says: the table for the

letting of a vein, which is usually in calendars, is only for boys, rustics, and the simple

common people. On account of the same inefficacious relation of numbers, the opin‐

ions about critical days and climacteric years are to be counted among fables.

C O RO L L A RY I I I .

758

E ffects are falsely, and with excessive credulity, attributed to the Moon. Thus the

Moon is believed to corrode stones by a certain peculiar force; the bones of ani‐

mals are thought to be full of marrow while the Moon is waxing, but empty of mar‐

row while it is waning, and almost filled with blood. Lobsters, oysters, and many oth‐

er fish are judged to be fuller at the new or the full moon than at the half moon. But

these things are deservedly placed among things rashly spread abroad; for it is most

likely, says the distinguished Rohault

(n)

(m) Phys. Partic., pt. 1, q. 10.

p. 237

DISSERTATION II

CHAPTER I

(n), that the heat of the sun in the space of many years can torrefy and consume these

stones, which are consumed by fire in a few hours; and when this happens, it ought to

seem no wonder at all if the moisture of the air reduces these stones, just as it does

lime, to powder. Similarly, he continues, it is falsely thought that the bones of animals

are full of marrow while the Moon waxes and empty while it wanes; for when he had

observed this for more than 25 years, he always found some bones full of marrow and

others empty, both while the Moon was waxing and while it was waning.

759 Wherefore another cause is to be assigned: it is most likely that the bones of

certain animals are empty of marrow either because the animals have lacked nourish‐

ment or because they have been worn out by labor. Falsely too, and wholly against ex‐

perience, has it been believed that the Moon, according to her various phases, fills

out or thins lobsters, oysters, etc. If the bodies of fish sometimes seem diminished,

this happens either from a lack of nourishment, or because they are too much agitat‐

ed, the waves being stirred up by a storm, or even by their own exertion; which will

seem most likely to those who know that the fish caught in the Strait of Calais,

where the water is most agitated, are generally less full than those caught near

Boulogne, where the sea rests somewhat more tranquil. Finally, the other effects are

to be attributed not to a moist influence of the Moon, but to the constitution of the

atmosphere present at the time, filled, namely, either with excessive moisture or with

other noxious effluvia.

O N T H E E L E M E N TA L E A RT H .

On the Nature of the Earth.

760

A s we are about to treat of the nature of the Elements, the Earth first presents it‐

self to us; for it is she that, as Pliny says, receives us when we are born, nourishes

us once born, and, once we are brought forth, sustains us. Let the conclusion there‐

fore be:

761 The earth is in all likelihood a body composed of coarser particles, less apt

for motion, affected for the most part with an irregular figure. Proof: from the fact

that this seems to agree best with the inertia, gravity,

and

(n) Phys., pt. II, ch. 27.

p. 238

REMARK

CHAPTER II

and solidity of the earth. Further: since the earth is dissolved with the greatest

difficulty by the force of fire, and its particles cannot be blown off into the air,

they must be coarser; and since, united together, they make a consistent and

fixed mass and shut off the passage of light, they are in all likelihood of an irregu‐

lar figure, such as to be variously entangled with one another and to form wind‐

ing passages. Finally, since the earth is held to be, as it were, the basis and foun‐

dation of the other miscible bodies, and since the hardness, fixity, solidity, and

gravity of bodies is derived in great part from the earth, it is fitting that its parti‐

cles be not only coarser and more entangled with one another, but also less apt

for motion.

762

D escartes composes the earth from parts of the third element, namely from

striated corpuscles entangled among themselves and twisted together [§.

44.]. Gassendi, with the Epicureans, would have it made up, like the other firm

and dry bodies, of little rings and hooked atoms mutually adhering to one anoth‐

er. Fr. Regnault asserts that the particles of earth are branching, such as do not

transmit light and make a consistent mass. The distinguished da Brescia says that

we cannot divine with certainty of what figure the primitive corpuscles of earth

are. It is probable, he then adds, that the primitive particles are affected with a

cubic figure: since this, as Plato says, possesses the firmest and safest bases, and

therefore seems most proper to those corpuscles which are destined by nature to

constitute a dry, inert, and fixed body. On this, however, we determine nothing

certain.

On the Figure, Situation, and Magnitude of the Terraqueous

Globe. 763

W e here contemplate the Earth as a mundane body, which is usually called

the orb, or the terraqueous globe. The Earth, then, is a mundane body compact‐

ed of earth and water, with a fiery fluid interspersed here and there, into a vast mass, sur‐

rounded on every side by air, the common habitation of men and of brutes. Under the

name of earth there comes here first of all the heap of solid and coarser bodies of

various kinds: sand, clay, fat earths of diverse colors, stones, salts, etc.: a heap

which is found in the Earth,

as

p. 239

as no one, unless he were ignorant both of history and of narratives, would deny. By water is understood that fluid and moist substance which God, Best and Greatest, in the first creation separated from the solid and dry, and gathered into the sea, which occupies a great part of the terrestrial surface.

764 That fire is diffused through the interior parts of the earth is plain, both from the fact that it is contained in mixed bodies, and from hot springs, the heat of mines, various exhalations, and fire-vomiting mountains. That the body of the Earth is compacted into a vast mass, no one is unaware; and it has its compaction and firmness from the cause of gravity, by which, namely, its parts are compressed and driven together on every side. But this is more difficult to resolve: into what figure this mass has been compacted: whether, namely, it holds a spherical one? Or a spheroidal one; and this, whether depressed at the poles and raised at the equator, or, on the contrary, rising at the poles and sinking at the equator.

765 Physicists endeavor to demonstrate that the Earth is spherical as regards sense, and physically. First, from the very eclipses of the Moon; for she suffers an eclipse because she enters the shadow of the Earth, and divides it just as if she were a plane parallel to the base of that shadow: since, namely, the Moon revolves around the Earth. But the shadow of the earth in all the lunar eclipses observed hitherto through so many centuries has always appeared round: therefore. Secondly, because all appearances, celestial as well as terrestrial, are explained most aptly and without error under a spherical figure of the Earth, as is plain in artificial globes and spheres. Thirdly, because those who travel see the summits of mountains and the tops of towers sooner than their bases, and that equally in every direction. We have said that the Earth is round in the physical sense, not the mathematical. Very high mountains in no way hinder its figure from being spherical as regards sense, for the earth, as Seneca says, is to the mountains as a huge ball to a hair. Nor does the flatness of the plains stand in the way, when the earth seems to us to stretch out into a plane: for this comes partly from its magnitude, partly from the visible horizon, which, relative to the whole globe, is a very small part and has no sensible curvature.

766 Hence the figure of the Earth, spherical as regards sense, is not hindered either by the opinion of Newton, Huygens, ’s Gravesande, and others, who think that the terraqueous mass is not formed like a sphere but presents the figure of a spheroid swelling under the equator and sinking at the poles; or by the hypothesis of both Cassinis, of Maraldi, Mairan, Eisenschmidt, and many more, by which a figure oblong toward the poles and depressed under the equator is attributed to the Earth. For besides the fact that the arguments set out above establish a round figure for the Earth in the physical sense, it is certain that neither of these opinions is greatly opposed to the physical and sensible roundness of the Earth.

767 For that excess of the greater diameter over the lesser is so slight that nothing prevents their being held as physically equal diameters, and hence the terraqueous mass as physically spherical. Newton

Hh indeed

p. 240

indeed holds that the greater diameter of the Earth is to the lesser as 230 to 229, and hence that the earth would be higher under the equator than under the poles by 17 miles and a sixth part. Huygens, on the other hand, establishes almost the same ratio of the diameters, namely that of the number 578 to 577; and if this ratio is then worked out in miles by the rules of proportion, as is usually done, it will be plain that the excess of the greater semidiameter of the Earth over the lesser does not equal even 7 miles; and so slight a difference leaves the Earth, at any rate as regards sense, spherical.

768 Nor does the argument for the first opinion, taken from the daily motion of the Earth, prove anything; from this revolution the patrons of this hypothesis think it follows that the parts, by a greater centrifugal force under the equator than toward the poles, recede farther from the axis of the Earth, and so are more elevated under the equator than under the poles, and form the spheroidal mass of the Earth. It does not, I say, prove anything: for, granting the motion of the Earth about its axis, it does not evidently follow that the parts about the equator swell out and are compressed toward the poles: for the mass of the Earth is not soft but firmly compacted, nor does it seem conformable to experience that a sphere revolved about its axis should be changed into a spheroid compressed at the poles of the revolution, with whatever speed it be turned.

769 As regards the situation of the Earth, the common opinion is that it is placed in the very center of the universe, at least as regards sense. For although, by the Copernican hypothesis, the Sun is set in the center of the universe and the Earth is turned in the great orb around the Sun, yet in the judgment of the astronomers the semidiameter of the great orb, if it is compared with the semidiameter of the starry heaven, as it were vanishes, and brings it about that the Earth is distant from the center of the universe by no sensible interval.

770 The reasons, moreover, that establish this situation of the Earth are these. The first, because at either equinox the time during which the Sun stays above the horizon exactly equals the time during which it stays below the horizon. The second, because to us who exist on the surface of the Earth, whatever region at last we may inhabit, the stars always appear of the same magnitude, whether at their rising, or at their setting, or in the middle of the heaven, provided there are absent vapors, mists, and exhalations, which impede the sight and change the figure of bodies. The third, because in whatever part of the earth, setting aside the hindrances of mountains and valleys, we always see half of the heaven: thus of the 12 signs of the Zodiac, 6 are perpetually seen above the horizon, and of stars diametrically opposite, such as are, more or less, the Eye of the Bull and the Heart of the Scorpion, when one rises on the eastern horizon, the other sets on the western.

771 The magnitude of the Earth, if it is compared with the starry heaven, is so slight that it stands to it just as a point. Its absolute magnitude, however, is altogether uncertain. Indeed, in determining the magnitude of one degree of the great circles of the terraqueous orb, authors disagree very much among themselves. Hence it is no wonder if they dissent in establishing the magnitude of the Earth: since from the value of one degree

is

p. 241

CHAPTER III

is gathered the value of the periphery of a great circle, and hence the quantity

of the diameter and of the semidiameter, as well as of the convex surface, and

finally the solidity, as geometers know. It is not possible to bring forward many

measures here; I submit one or two, worked out, nearly, to the more common

calculation. The diameter of the Earth contains nearly 1720 German miles. The

surface, nearly 92,880,000 square miles. The solidity, nearly 26,563,680,000.

One celestial degree contains 25 common leagues of France: and a common

league contains 2400 geometric paces.

On Certain Terrestrial Bodies, and First on Petrifications.

cannot fail to make mention of a certain kind of terrestrial bodies, 772

I namely of shells, oysters, and other testaceous bodies, which occur

among the strata of certain mountains. On their origin the opinion of

physicists is threefold. Woodward derives this phenomenon from the

universal deluge, namely: when all the lands were covered by the waters, then

indeed rocks, marbles, metals, all bodies were divided into minute particles and

molecules; thus divided, they were carried confusedly hither and thither by that

force of the waters, but toward the end these bodies, immersed in the water,

were precipitated according to the laws of gravity: hence it came about that

those marine testaceous shells, being somewhat heavier, sought the part that

belongs to rocks, stones, and the like, among which they are found even today

for this very reason. The second hypothesis, which Leibniz recently defended,

asserts that the sea was once in all those places in which shells and oysters are

found, but that the sea itself has at present receded from those places, leaving

the bodies there.

773 The third holds, with Lazzaro Moro, that testaceous bodies are found

among the strata of mountains because the mountains themselves, together

with those bodies, were once cast up from the bottom of the sea by the action

of subterranean fire. It is not my pleasure at present to sift and weigh these hy‐

potheses, which demand a fuller discussion. It will be enough to hint at this

one thing: that there is not one and the same cause and origin, universally, of

the oysters and testaceous bodies of this kind found in mountains and in more

prominent places. It does not seem, indeed, to stray from likelihood that those

marine spoils which the investigators of Nature find here and there on the sur‐

faces of mountains, or at no great depth,

Hh 2 are

p. 242

are to be traced chiefly to the deluge, and to seas at some time spread over those

places, as a knowledge of History and Geography will show.

774 But those which are not rarely discovered in deeper caverns were, I think,

deposited there by earthquakes, often violent ones: for in this way, the earth being

shaken, the mountains burst asunder, and swallowed up, the spoils of animals could

be buried together, and in the course of a long time be converted into stones, that is,

be petrified. But if they are of the kind of marine spoils, these were carried there, to‐

gether with a part of the sea, through subterranean passages made and hollowed out

in these motions of the earth, where the water, having dried away in the length of

time, and having been diffused into the strata of the earth or driven off into vapors,

deposited spoils of this kind.

775 Finally, that spoils of one kind are found in one mountain and those of anoth‐

er kind in another, I judge is not to be taken in a precise sense; nor, because spoils of

one kind have hitherto been found chiefly in one place, must it be said that those of

another kind do not lie hidden there or cannot be found. These things having been

briefly surveyed in general, we must say something about the magnet. For this stone,

on account of its excellent virtue and utility, is both held in admiration and valued at

a high price; so that it might accordingly seem shameful for those who inquire into

the secrets of nature to make no mention of it at all. Let it, then, be:

C H A P T E R I V.

What Is to Be Thought of the Force of the Magnet?

he magnet has its name and origin from Magnesia, a province of 776

T Macedonia, where it is dug up; but according to some, from Magnes, a

shepherd, who is said to have first discovered it on Mount Ida, when the

iron tip of his staff adhered to a stone of this kind, which is now called a

magnet. It is a stone not unlike iron, showing a blackish color, heavy, pregnant with

iron; since indeed, when subjected to fire, it exudes steel, and moreover it is dug out

of iron mines. Its force, which is called magnetic and is still wrapped in many difficul‐

ties, is reduced chiefly to three heads: to its direction, to the attraction of a magnet or

of iron, and to the communication of its virtue. The directive force consists in this, that

a magnet suspended in the air sets itself toward the meridian of the place and turns
