its southern pole toward the northern pole of the Earth, as also happens in the mag‐

netic needle. However, this direction toward the pole is not constant everywhere; for

now by more, now by fewer degrees, according to the diversity of regions, more or

less, now hither now thither (that is, now toward the east,

now

p. 243

now toward the west) the nautical needles decline; indeed, after a notable time they sometimes change their direction in the same place; and this affection is called declination.

777 To this also pertains another affection of the same, which is called inclination, various indeed, but constant, by virtue of which a magnet, or a magnetic needle freely suspended in equilibrium, preponderates toward one side and is inclined, by this law: that the inclination is more or less notable according as the tract of the earth is more remote from or nearer to the equator; for under it a perfect equilibrium is had. The attractive force is that by which a magnet draws to itself either another magnet or iron; with this difference, however, that a magnet snatches iron to itself by either of its sides, but draws a magnet to itself by one side and repels it by the other. Finally, the force communicative of itself is that by which it imbues steel or iron with the same virtue in which it is itself strong: namely, the directive and the attractive. These things set out, we inquire into the cause of these phenomena: in which altogether obscure matter we shall lay down whatever may have an appearance of likelihood and may in some fashion expound the said effects to the understanding. Before we carry this out, a preliminary hypothesis is laid down.

778 We think it not incongruous to say either, with Gilbert, that the whole terraqueous globe itself is a certain huge magnet, which that author therefore called the terrestrial magnet; or, as Fr. Zucchi holds with many others, that the nucleus of the earth itself is a true magnet.

779 This is explained, 1: because iron implements acquire a magnetic force from mere contact and application to the earth: especially if they have stood erect upon the earth for a rather long time. Hence tongs and similar iron instruments, which are usually kept standing erect beside hearths for handling the fire, acquire a force for attracting little steel needles. So too iron rods which have remained a long time, especially in the line of the meridian plane, acquire a conversive force toward the pole. Secondly, because magnetic needles suspended by a thread are inclined toward the globe of the earth just as they are observed to be inclined toward a magnet.

780 So that for this reason the tonic nisus of the magnet, or of verticity, is not toward the celestial poles but toward the terrestrial ones: hence the magnetic force resides in the terrestrial globe. Thirdly, in mines, rocks, and quarries there appear, amid huge stones, lines traced like fibers, extended very far from south to north and disposed parallel to the terrestrial axis. From this it is gathered, in all likelihood, that the magnetic force, having slipped into those tracts through effluvia, determines that disposition from pole to pole. From these, now, is deduced:

Corollary.

p. 244

C O R O L L A R Y.

781

F rom the magnetism of the terraqueous globe it is concluded that certain effluvia,

having gone out from one pole of the Earth, travel around the Earth toward its

other pole, and there, entering into it again, go out through the other pole of the

world; and thus a perpetual circulation of effluvia of this kind is set up in the Earth,

not otherwise than a perpetual circulation of subterranean water, together with the

terrestrial surface, is said to be carried on from pole to pole: although the cause by

which it comes about that the fluid bursting forth from the bowels of the earth is

borne from one pole toward the other still escapes the industry and intelligence of

physicists, and must be deduced elsewhere, at the proper time, from mechanical

principles. Moreover, these effluvia are indeed communicated also to other bodies ex‐

isting in this globe, but chiefly to those which are most earthy, such as the magnet

and iron, in which an apt disposition of the particles and pores offers itself both for

receiving and for emitting them.

782 And just as in the terraqueous globe itself the said effluvia constantly go out

from one pole and, carried around the Earth, enter again into the other pole, so too

the magnet, like a little orb, has its effluvia, namely a vortical atmosphere, which en‐

ter at one of its poles and go out from the other, and indeed always by the same law;

this is shown excellently by the iron filings into which a magnet is plunged, which

stand erect toward the poles and, in places more remote from the pole, are inclined.

Then the very disposition of the particles of the magnet can prove this, since they

are inclined more to one side than to the other, and are so disposed that they can af‐

ford ingress through one side but not, in turn, egress; that such a disposition of the

parts can come about is plain from this, that while the magnet was being formed in

its mine, the magnetic matter, crossing the earth from one pole to the other along

lines parallel to the axis and returning in a perpetual circuit, could fit the passages of

the magnet in such a way as to press down their interior little hairs toward that side

to which it was carried.

783 The distinguished Helvétius holds, with Mr. Du Fay, that the pores of mag‐

nets are furnished within with little hairs, and that these are so laid down and bent

that their points incline toward the north poles of the magnets. Those little hairs,

therefore, do not delay the motion of the magnetic matter from the pole of ingress,

that is, the one which the effluvia enter, to the pole of egress, that is, the one through

which they burst out, since they are bent toward that side; but they resist the return

of the same matter through the same passages, since they are inclined toward the op‐

posite side with the greatest difficulty, or not at all. These things laid down, let the

conclusion be:

784 I say 1. The directive force of the magnet seems to be traced to most subtle

effluvia bursting out from one pole of the Earth and breaking in through the other.

The directive force of the magnet is, namely, that by which the magnet turns itself

toward each pole of the world. But this is fittingly traced

to

p. 245

SCHOLIUM I. 786

to the effluxes set forth in the said manner; for these, moving thereafter through

the same passages of the magnet which they had made for themselves in the mine,

accordingly set the magnet, by the rule of their own motion, along lines parallel to

the axis of the earth, as is gathered from what was said a little before. Indeed, since

it is plain that no body can perpetually incline toward its due point except by the

contact of another body driven toward the same point, as Helvétius rightly says, it

is evident that there are fluids spread closely around the Earth which are driven, in

the direction of their motion, from the southern pole toward the northern.

785 Certainly this is shown manifestly also from the fact that if an iron needle,

not yet imbued with magnetic force, is placed on a pivot in a nautical box, it will be

seen in equilibrium, parallel to the horizon; but when the needle has been rubbed

on a magnet and has obtained the directive force, then in northern places the part

of the needle directed toward the north is depressed somewhat below the horizon,

so that a little ball of wax must be added to the southern point of the needle to

restore the equilibrium. At the Equator, or at an equal distance from either pole,

the needle is not depressed at all. Once the Equator is crossed toward the south,

the northern part of the point is raised and the southern is depressed. All of which

certainly confirm, not in vain, the efflux and the influx, and the circulation, of the

effluvia around the surface of the Earth.

T he phenomenon of magnetic declination is fittingly expounded in our

Hypothesis. For it is certain that the parts of the terrestrial globe are very het‐

erogeneous, and that various veins of iron occur here and there; indeed, in the same

place not only the mountains, but also the rocks and the other parts lying hid under

the earth or the sea, are now more copiously endowed with magnetic veins, now,

whether because a certain tract has been shaken by a motion of the earth and the

situation of its parts changed, or by excavations, or in some other way, are sparsely

interspersed with veins of this kind. What of the fact that in the bowels of the

lands magnets in some places lie hidden deep under the earth, and elsewhere cling

in the summits, the bowels, and the roots of mountains; that the said veins of iron

are frequently altered, diminished, and twisted, either by earthquakes, or by subter‐

ranean fires, or by floods of subterranean waters, or by diggers; and indeed that the

air itself and the corpuscles diffused in it perhaps drive the magnetic effluvia some‐

what out of their straight motion?

787 Therefore from these causes a varied declination of the same needle and

magnet can occur even in the same place, so that in places not far distant from

each other it is very notable, and in one it inclines toward the East, in another to‐

ward the West. In confirmation of this there serves the experiment reported by

Kircher and Jansonius: namely, that at Naples, after the notable conflagration of

Mount Vesuvius, a notable change of the magnetic declination was continually

observed.

Scholium

p. 246

SCHOLIUM II

SCHOLIUM III

788

T he phenomenon of inclination is also explained: for, magnetic effluvia being

supposed to burst forth from the earth, it is no wonder that the needle in‐

clines toward the terrestrial globe along that part along which the stronger and

more copious effluvia flow out, namely in the northern parts along one of its

parts, in the southern along the other, and this the more, the nearer the regions

are to the north or to the south pole. Nor is it any wonder that the needle under

the Equator, where, namely, neither effluvia prevail and the place stands off from

the poles by an equal interval, keeps a perfect equilibrium, free of all inclination.

789

F rom these principles it is illustrated why the magnet, outside the mine, on

the surface of the Earth, has a situation contrary to the situation which it

held in the mine; for if the magnetic outflows are conceived to enter through the

southern pole of the earth, they must also enter the southern pole of the magnet

turned toward the same part of the earth while it is still in the mine: but since

the effluvia flowing from south to north along lines parallel to the axis in the in‐

terior of the earth return on its surface from the northern pole to the southern,

the magnet, drawn out of the earth, must be disposed in a contrary situation for

receiving those outflows, and its southern pole must be turned toward the north‐

ern pole of the Earth, whence the effluvia are supposed to burst out.

790 I say 2. The attractive force of the magnet is derived not from the im‐

pulse of air coming in behind, but from the motion of the atmosphere surround‐

ing the magnet, in all likelihood by the same mechanical manner of acting as the

approach of homogeneous bodies. The first part is plain. In a vacuum both the

attraction of iron to the magnet and its adhesion take place: indeed, iron is

seized more quickly by the magnet when the receiver has been exhausted.

Therefore the attractive force cannot be traced to the action of the air. Besides,

if the magnetic effluvia have such force as to expel the air between the iron and

the magnet, and so to disturb the equilibrium of that column with the other col‐

umns of air, how should I think it can happen that in that intermediate space

there is a lesser resistance, compared with the air pressing on the iron and the

magnet from behind? Since into the place of the air there succeeds a stronger

body (namely, the effluvia excluding the air).

791 The second part is demonstrated. To explain the attractive force of the

magnet it is necessary that a reason be given why poles of the same name,

whether one southern and the other southern, or two northern, repel each other

not

p. 247

not only in the magnet but also in the magnetic needle; then why poles not of the same name, namely one southern and the other northern, approach each other; and finally why iron is snatched by a magnet from either side. But these things are conveniently explained by the force of the magnetic atmosphere. For if, as we laid down above [§. 781 ff.], the internal configuration of magnets and the structure of their pores is such that the smallest molecules, laid down and bent like little hairs, incline with their tips toward one pole of the magnetic body, e.g. the northern, it will come about, this contexture of the parts being supposed, that the fluid running into the southern pole can freely pervade it and be carried flowingly over the surface of the little hairs, no force being brought upon them; whereas the parts of the subtler fluid that have slipped into the northern pole will bring force upon the tips which occupy and line the paths of the little hairs. Wherefore, if one magnet is placed toward another in such a way that the northern pole of the former faces the southern pole of the latter, then, since the atmospheric fluid of the one is driven in the direction which the inflection of the little hairs has in the other, the most subtle parts of the fluid will pass along the very surface of the little hairs with no force and impression, or the least, made upon them.

792 But when those poles of the magnets are joined from which the subtler torrent of atmosphere bursts forth, then indeed the molecules of this fluid flowing out of the pole of the one will be unable to enter the pores of the like pole in the other magnet, since the points of the little hairs are stretched out and so resist: hence, force being brought upon these paths, they will strive to repel the magnet into which they rush. But if those poles of the magnets into each of which the surrounding fluid breaks in are placed not far from each other, then, besides the fact that the directions of the magnetic fluid oppose each other, repulsion must follow from this, that the twin atmospheres do not coalesce into one in such a way that all the other fluid interposed is removed and so an approach follows; and although an entrance lies open to the effluvia through each of these poles, yet because each is supposed to be endowed with such a habit of pores that only the magnetic fluid can enter through them, the commingling of the atmospheres and their conjunction, in a manner, into one vortex (other heterogeneous fluids being excluded) is for that reason impeded: hence it will come about that the magnets do not approach each other, but are repelled by the opposite directions of the effluvia on either side. The same is to be thought of the magnetic needle.

793 Finally, that iron not yet imbued, as they say, with magnetic virtue is snatched to the magnet, at whatever pole it is placed, we assert on this ground: that the structure of this metal and the conformation of its paths seem adapted for receiving and transmitting the magnetic effluvia, in such a way indeed that these can penetrate more freely through its interior surface and be carried flowingly along, no force being brought upon the walls of the pores: whereby it will be brought about that the other fluids interposed in the space between the magnet and the iron are removed; and these being moved away, since, the most subtle fluid being spread around the bodies, along that part

Ii nothing

p. 248

nothing resists, it follows that by its pressure the iron is urged toward the magnet.

794 The assertion is confirmed by an exposition of the phenomena; and first a reason is given why, besides iron or steel, no other bodies are drawn by the magnet: namely, because such is the disposition of the pores in iron, and the configuration of its parts, as in a body homogeneous with the magnet, that the effluvia penetrate it more easily than the other bodies: hence, while the torrent of effluvia crosses the pores of the iron in greater abundance, the resistance in the intermediate space is diminished, and, this being removed, these bodies are joined by the forces of the pressing fluid.

795 From this likewise the reason is drawn why a magnet, if it is clothed with steel or iron, or, as they say, armed, with well-polished steel plates placed around it, attracts far more strongly and holds fast what it has attracted: for the effluvia seem to flow more easily through steel than through air, and therefore a more abundant supply of them then bursts into the iron that is to be attracted, which before wandered more freely around the sides of the magnet and were less collected. Secondly: our opinion explains more aptly why smaller magnets sometimes sustain greater weights, whereas larger ones are often weaker, indeed why some have a portentous force; for magnets often consist of notably heterogeneous parts, through which the effluvia are not transmitted so copiously, and which accordingly possess a slight atmosphere, by whose help the attraction is effected; on the contrary it can happen that a magnet, however small, compacted of purer parts, has for its bulk a great surrounding atmosphere.

795 Thirdly: on our opinion being laid down, the motion of flight and repulsion is expounded more fittingly for Physics than in the opinion of the others, who refer this to opposite vortices but attribute attraction to the air. It can scarcely be conceived, indeed, or said, that the air between two poles of egress is not driven out when two magnets are set near each other; and yet attraction does not follow this repulsion of the air, the attraction which they say comes about when the intermediate air is expelled to the sides, and the air coming in from behind drives these two magnetic bodies toward each other, where the resistance is less.

797 I say thirdly: The magnetic force communicated to iron or steel is to be derived from magnetic outflows. For magnetic force is communicated to iron or steel when these bodies are rubbed on, or applied to, the pole of a magnet or of its armature; and it consists in this, that the iron or steel directs itself toward the poles of the world and attracts other iron. But this force without doubt proceeds from magnetic outflows; for while a nautical needle is rubbed on the pole of a magnet or of its armature, those outflows rush into the needle and incline its little fibers, or hairs, to one side, according as the iron has been drawn along the magnet, so that they form for themselves two poles in the iron or the needle, one of ingress and the other of egress, not otherwise than they are in the magnet itself; which gains likelihood from the fact that these pores are interchanged by drawing the magnet in the contrary direction: therefore.

798

p. 249

REMARK

798 That this can come about by the help of effluvia is fittingly shown; first

of all from the fact that the little fibers of iron are softer and more flexible than

those of the magnet, as the diversity of their texture suggests. Then this very

thing is explained by the analogy of mercury entering into a rod of gold; for it is

understood just as easily that the mineral effluvium of the magnet enters into

iron and confers magnetism on it, as that the effluvium of mercury enters into

gold and whitens it. What of the fact that, just as the mercury imbibed by gold

is separated from it by fire, so the magnetic force is said to be removed from

magnetic iron by fire?

799

B y no means fictitious is the circulation of the magnetic effluvia around the

Earth, and their egress from one of its poles and ingress into the other: for

what is said fittingly for explaining the phenomena of nature is not forthwith to

be deemed fictitious, if it is not destitute of foundations that afford likelihood.

Certainly for no other reason is the nautical box of no use in the places nearest

the pole than because the magnetic outflows, bursting from the pole almost

perpendicularly, direct the needle itself no more to one side than to another;

which the Dutch report that they experienced on their voyage.

800 Nor is a similar gyration around the magnet itself fictitious; for if we as‐

cribe an atmosphere to all other bodies, we should surely deny it preposterously

to the magnet. However, the effluvia are driven to perpetual motion by a most

subtle universal fluid; but by what mechanism this is accomplished remains to

be taught; and toward this circuit around the magnet they are, as it were, deter‐

mined by the very disposition of the pores and parts in the magnet, which are

apter for receiving them than any other bodies whatever, and indeed on one side

better accommodated for letting them in, on the other for emitting them. Both

points are suggested and expounded by the analogy of the juices in plants, which

insinuate themselves through fibers and do not return through the same, and by

their perennial circulation through little canals. Many more things about the

magnet are handed down by Kircher, Gaspar Schott, Lana Terzi, Wolff,

Musschenbroek, and many others.

Ii 2 Dissertation

p. 250

DISSERTATION III

CHAPTER I

O N WA T E R A S A N E L E M E N T.

On the Nature of Water.

he nature of water is made by Gassendi, with the Epicureans, to consist 801

T in smooth and round particles, which are slippery and separated by fre‐

quent little voids. Others claim that the atoms of water are cubic, because

water can scarcely be compressed. Descartes thinks they are oblong and

rounded.

802 I say: Water is more probably a substance consisting of parts that are oblong,

rounded, flexible, slippery, voluble, little entangled with one another, and oval, that

is, endowed with an egg-shaped figure.

803 For, this nature of water being supposed, the phenomena and all the proper‐

ties belonging to water can be fittingly accounted for. Thus fluidity is deduced from

slipperiness and volubility; from which likewise is derived the force of dissolving bod‐

ies that cohere more loosely. The force of moistening flows from flexibility and from

the oblong and rounded figure; for thus the particles easily insinuate themselves into

the little pores of bodies, roll around the more prominent parts on their surface, and

adhere to them. The force of washing off dirt is also understood from these things;

and this washing is done more conveniently when the body to be washed is prepared

with a viscous matter, such as soap: for since dirt is generally fatty, it adheres more

easily to the viscous matter, and then the water purges away the dirt together with

the viscous matter.

804 The force of lubricating and of flowing off depends on smoothness and on

the rounded figure, on account of which water runs off easily from polished and clean

bodies, such as glass, or from fatty ones, as happens with the feathers of birds. Quick

and swift evaporation is derived from particles little entangled. Gravity, from density,

etc.; from which also arises its aptitude for passing into ice, beyond other liquors

which are composed of finer particles: hence too it is that water is rarefied in a won‐

derful manner, but can scarcely be compressed, since its parts, touching one another

immediately and rolled over one another, cannot be joined more closely. Finally, the

lack of odor as well as of taste in water proceeds from its flexibility and volubility; for

flexible and voluble particles, or molecules, run over the organ of taste and of smell

with a gentle motion, and do not strike its papillae and fibrils with any edge. The rea‐

son of the other properties too will easily be deduced from that structure and confor‐

mation of the parts.

Scholium.

p. 251

SCHOLIUM

CHAPTER II

805

I n order to constitute the nature of water, insofar as it is a fluid substance, it is

first of all required, as is clear (from what was said on fluidity), that its parts

be divided and dissociated from one another and touch one another in few

planes. The distinguished Helvétius judges that an oval figure of the aqueous

molecules agrees better with all the effects which they produce; for these, he

says, “will not touch one another except along the smallest surfaces, and accord‐

ingly they can be carried flowingly by the least force; and yet they will congeal

into ice, because the interstices placed between them are smaller than those

which would be given if the parts of water enjoyed a spherical figure. Moreover,

the parts of water endowed with this figure can accomplish the dissolution of

bodies more easily, because their extremities are finer than their middle part.

Finally, water must be insipid and odorless, because the extremities of its parts

are blunter.” Thus he.

On Springs, Rivers, and the Other Waters. 806

T he origin of springs and rivers is what we chiefly weigh here, and on it there

is a twofold opinion. Of the Moderns, some trace their origin from the sea,

others from rains and melted snows. The first teach that the waters of the sea are

carried through subterranean passages into the mountains and the other places

in which the sources of springs are found, and that, having deposited in them

their saltness and bitterness, they then leap forth through hidden passages and

fissures. The latter contend that the part of the waters which falls down in rains

and is drunk in by the earth penetrates through the fissures and chinks of rocks

and of mountains, is received and collected in certain cavities of them and in

reservoirs, from which the waters then flow down little by little through certain

narrow outlets and give origin to springs, from which rivers are derived. What is

to be thought in this controversy our conclusion establishes.

807 Springs and rivers arise not from the sea, by a hidden route penetrating

the earth and thence welling out, as if by a road made for it, but from rains, melt‐

ed snows, and vapors. The first part is proved. If springs arose from the sea, the

sea waters would have to deposit their saltness and bitterness, and to ascend, as

it were of their own accord, to that height above the mountains at which

we

p. 252

we observe springs welling forth. But neither seems capable of being maintained; for in this way the sea water would lose its saltness and bitterness insofar as it deposited, or left behind, its salty and bitter particles in those windings which the adversaries posit; but this cannot happen: for one of two things must follow: either that at length, in the course of time, those ways and passages are obstructed by the adhering salt, or this other, that the salt is scraped off and carried away by the water coming upon it, and so the waters burst forth from the springs filled with a more potent salt, or with a greater quantity of it.

808 The other cannot be reconciled with the principles of Hydrostatics: for from these we hold it as certain that water in communicating tubes, of whatever figure and perimeter at last, does not keep equilibrium unless it has obtained the same height in them, that is, has set its surface in each tube physically parallel to a horizontal line. But the places of very many springs are higher than the surface of the sea. Therefore the sea water cannot ascend to the height from which springs well forth.

809 The second part is proved: Springs and rivers are had when vapors, rains, and melted snows are given; when these are taken away, they perish; when these are increased or diminished, they are increased or diminished. For it is proved by constant experience that those regions abound in springs in which it often rains and snows; whereas very few rivers are interspersed in those in which rain is rare; none in those on which no rain and snow ever falls. Then it has been found by experience that when rains last rather long the springs swell, and even after the rains have ceased the rivers still remain higher; that in dry weather springs are diminished, and in a long drought they disappear entirely.

810 Thus the distinguished Mariotte attests that in the year 1681, which had been very dry in France, the waters of very many springs were dried up: and he confesses that he learned by his own experience and observation that after a long drought, when the rains came on, the less deep wells received water and rose first, the deeper ones more slowly: an evident indication that a moderate rain, sufficient for replenishing the first, does not suffice for the second.

811 There is added the testimony of the same Mariotte, and also of Halley; the former of whom, having made a calculation, found that the quantity of water falling from the heavens in the places lying around the Seine (*) is far greater than that which flows from that river into the sea in the same time. Halley, on the other hand, concerning the quantity of the vapors which, chiefly by the force of the Sun, ascend daily from the Mediterranean Sea (the same is true of other waters), found, having made the trial, that their quantity is so great that the waters which daily flow into it from the Ebro, the Tiber, the Nile, and the other rivers scarcely equal one third part of that which is likewise raised into vapors from the sea itself each single day.

He

(*) The Seine, a river of France.

p. 253

812 He relates, moreover, that on the island of St. Helena, often at night on the summit of a mountain exceeding the surface of the sea by 2400 feet, he experienced so great a condensation of vapors even in clear weather that within not many minutes it had so wetted the optical glasses that they had to be wiped, and were otherwise little fit for astronomical observations. The paper, too, on which he was writing was so quickly wetted by the falling dew that the ink was diluted by the dew: whence one may understand how great a quantity of vapors is condensed on the very lofty summits of mountains.

813 Wherefore, if we join the condensed vapors with rains and melted snows, there will be water enough to feed all springs. Besides, diggers testify from their own experience that huge reservoirs of rain and snow waters are spread out beneath the earth: of such hydrophylacia Kircher enumerates four altogether memorable: one, the chief of Asia, in the Kingdom of the Mogul; another, of Europe, under the Rhaetian Alps; the third in Africa, under the Mountains of the Moon; the fourth, among the American ones, between Peru and the Kingdom of Chile. Nor does that text of Ecclesiastes, ch. 1, stand in the way: all the rivers run into the sea . . . unto the place from whence the rivers come, they return. For it suffices that the sea waters are condensed into vapors and resolved into rain or snow for it to be truly affirmed that the rivers go out from the sea.

814 Of waters there are diverse species and properties, according to that saying of Pliny: waters are such as the earth through which they pass, understanding not only earth strictly so called, but also juices, and minerals, and in general all subterranean things from which the water flowing through can take up something. Hence the origin of hot springs, of thermal baths, and of other healthful waters. From similar causes some waters and springs are metal-bearing; and very many rivers furnish gold to the washers of their sand, while, having flowed past veins and channels teeming with gold, they carry down very minute particles.

Dissertation

p. 254

D I S S E RTAT I O N I V

AND ON THE SUBLIME BODIES, OR

METEORS, AND ALSO ON PLANTS

CHAPTER I

ON THE ELEMENTS OF AIR AND FIRE,

On the Nature of Air.

hat a subtle fluid is spread round the Earth has already been said 815

T above; this fluid, though invisible, is nevertheless perceived from vari‐

ous effects, and is necessary for producing very many motions and

changes in nature and for prolonging animal life; we designate it by the

name of air. Many things about it we have indicated in the course of the Physics,

from which its properties and forces are more than sufficiently understood; here,

as in its proper place, we briefly inquire into its nature. Let the conclusion there‐

fore be:

816 Air is an aggregate of subtle particles loosely cohering, flexible with a cer‐

tain rigidity, which compose a fluid altogether different from the aggregate of va‐

pors and terrestrial exhalations.

817 That the molecules of air are subtle and minute appears from this, that

they readily insinuate themselves into the pores of bodies, which is chiefly no‐

ticed by those who attempt experiments by means of the air pump. That they co‐

here loosely, and hence that air is porous, is taught by its fluidity; then by its impu‐

rity, since it in some manner saturates itself with the particles of other bodies,

which it receives into its pores, and on account of which it very often shows itself

malignant to the animal body. Its flexibility together with rigidity is evident from

its elasticity, in which it is constantly and very greatly powerful: hence Descartes

conjectured that air is a very rare body, like soft little feathers; Guglielmini thinks

it is an aggregate of spirals twisted spherically and filled with ether, which can

penetrate into their cavity only through the narrow openings of the convolutions.

818 That the aërial fluid is different from vapors and terrestrial exhalations, and

hence that air consists of particles of its own proper kind,

is

p. 255

is evident above all from this, that it is established that vapors and exhalations as‐

cend, but that they cannot be raised unless they are thrust out by a heavier body; so

that accordingly around the globe of the Earth some other body, distinct from va‐

pors and exhalations, which is air, must necessarily be admitted. Moreover, it is as‐

certained that air enclosed in a metal vessel, and even very strongly compressed,

persists unchanged, which is not at all true of vapors. Finally, its elasticity is propor‐

tional to its density, and it occupies spaces which are reciprocally proportional to

the compressing weights, which does not belong to vapors and exhalations.

819 The properties of air are fluidity, gravity, compressibility, and finally elasticity.

And as regards this last, it is certain that compressed air exerts it in any directions

whatever; for in whatever place a vessel full of compressed air is pierced, the air will

burst out continuously; and it bursts out inasmuch as it strives to dilate itself in

every direction. It is further to be observed that the spring of compressed air equals

the force by which it is compressed; for it is compressed until the force by which it

resists the pressure has become equal to the compressing force: for then, on account

of the equilibrium, the compression is ended; and therefore the elastic force of the

lower air equals the weight of the upper air in the atmosphere.

820 Air, together with the terrestrial vapors and exhalations spread round the

Earth, is called the atmosphere of the Earth; about its height there is no agreement

among Philosophers. Nollet, having weighed all the trials that have been made by

means of the barometer, says that the height of the terrestrial atmosphere cannot be

less than 6 French leagues, nor can it exceed 15 or 20 leagues, and hence that the

height of the atmosphere lies between these measures.

821 The ancient Philosophers divided the whole air into three spheres, or re‐

gions; the first and supreme they called that which is nearest to the lunar orbit, filled

with no exhalations at all, or with very subtle ones; the lowest was held to be that

which, girding the terraqueous globe most closely, is occupied by thicker and heavier

exhalations: whence it is denser than the rest and more misty, and moreover now

hot, now cold, according as it is regarded by the Sun now directly, now obliquely: the

middle is that which is conceived as situated between the two. Hence it is deduced:

C O RO L L A R Y.

he nature and origin of the winds are to be inquired into here, since they 822

T seem to be nothing other than air flowing with force, or its force running

toward one quarter, or a more agitated motion, so that between wind and

air, as Seneca says, there is no other difference than between a lake and a

river. Their origin is various. The Sun, first of all, acting on the air, excites wind,

inasmuch, namely, as it brings about by its heat that the air directly beneath it is

greatly rarefied, and, having become rarer,

Kk by

p. 256

by that very fact becomes lighter, and hence is thrust out by the rest, which are heavier and denser, and thus, the equilibrium of the air being disturbed, wind arises.

823 Next, the Sun excites winds by rarefying vapors with its heat; similarly while, by its action, the snows with which the summits of mountains are covered melt; for then the released particles press on the air and propel it toward that very region which lies beneath the Sun, since, being rarer, it resists their dilatation less; hence at the approach of spring north winds are very frequent, and south winds at the approach of autumn, because, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Cancer, the snows lying on the northern mountains begin to melt; but on the contrary, as the Sun draws near the tropic of Capricorn, the snows lying on the southern mountains are dissolved: to which is referred another cause of the winds as well, namely the admixture of the exhalations which are rather copiously scattered in the atmosphere, and the effervescence arising thence.

824 Finally, winds can have their origin in the bowels of the earth, and burst forth from them no otherwise than from the bottom of the sea; the more probable causes of these subterranean winds are subterranean fires, copious exhalations, etc. As regards the velocity of the winds, it is various. Musschenbroek says that it is gathered from Derham’s observations that the most violent winds were driven with such rapidity that they covered 66 English feet in a second, and 45 miles in the space of an hour; and, by the same witness, they had such great force that they tore apart a stone statue 12 feet high, 5 wide and 2 thick.

825 Diverse are their properties and qualities, which arise from the diverse vapors and exhalations which the winds carry down with them, and meet in their course, and snatch away with them; so that the north wind is cold, because it carries down with it a great quantity of nitrous and cold particles; the south winds tepid and humid, because they bring hot exhalations from the torrid Zone, or from the parts nearer to it, and at the same time humid vapors from the Mediterranean Sea.

826 The diversity of the winds is manifold: besides the winds, too, which are divided variously by reason of the various quarters from which they blow, there is besides another variety, relative to the time of blowing; similarly some winds are called provincial, which prevail in certain particular places or provinces; others have their diversity from their force and swiftness, or on the contrary from a gentle breath; the former are called stormy, the latter gentle; whose names and condition there is no leisure to pursue.

Chapter

p. 257

CHAPTER II

SCHOLIUM

On the Nature of Fire.

say: Fire is a fluid consisting of most subtle, most hard, supremely 827

I mobile particles. It is demonstrated by exposition. That fire is a fluid

body is plain from this, that it communicates fluidity to other bodies,

as to metals, and in others also preserves their fluidity, and brings itself back to

equilibrium, as we observe in a room, where the heat is at length evenly dif‐

fused. That the molecules of fire are most subtle and most hard we gather from

this, that it pervades all bodies, however compact, whereas the other fluids,

even supremely volatile ones, can be kept in glasses or other vessels; then from

this, that, as a universal solvent, it so tears apart and dissolves almost all bodies

that by no industry of ours can they be restored to their former state; whence

it is proven that the greatest mobility is in fire: it is necessary too that, to effect

the motions of rarefaction, dissolution, combustion, etc., the quantity of mo‐

tion in fire be very great.

828

F ire does not consist in sulphurous and nitrous particles agitated by the sub‐

tle matter, as the Cartesians suppose; for, to pass over many things, this is

plain from this, that in the focus of a burning mirror, where the fire is so great

that the imperfect metals at least turn in a short time into glass, nothing of sul‐

phur or nitre is found; nor may one take refuge in air impregnated with these

corpuscles, since the same thing happens in an exhausted receiver; nor let an

escape be sought in the metals, since no sulphur is extracted by the chemists

from gold, flint or diamond.

C O RO L L A R Y.

829

F lame is an aggregate of little bubbles, or of sulphurous, earthy, saline, rigid

and pointed particles, agitated with a vehement and confused motion by

the most subtle igneous fluid, and condensed by the surrounding air, so that

they are not continually dissipated. For flame, relatively to other ignited bodies,

burns little, because it embraces less fire, and much foreign matter, relatively to

those ignited bodies. Its conical figure arises from

Kk 2 this,

p. 258

CHAPTER III

this, that it cleaves the air in a single place: namely, there where the air resists more

weakly and the flame is more active, since the most subtle parts are thrust out

thither.

830 The colors of flame arise from its diverse matter: the blue around the base,

from an oily humor not yet well concocted and dissipated; for the purer the flame is,

and the greater the quantity of little fires it contains, the whiter it is; in the middle,

many earthy particles mixed with the fire produce the red color, for if a small plate is

thrust into the middle of the flame, it is stained with much soot, not so at the base

and the tip. That the tip of the flame whitens is owing to the purified matter of the

flame: besides, a kind of down appears, as it were, round the flame, which seems to

be nothing else but an attenuated humor, not well kindled, and hence mixed partly

with the air, partly with the fire, no otherwise than, e.g., a drop of wine mixed with

water disperses itself, as it were, into certain filaments. No one hitherto (that I have

seen) has treated of fire better than Boerhaave, so often and never sufficiently

praised, in the Elementa Chemiae. Consult him, if you want more.

On Meteors in General.

eteor means the same as appearing on high; whence the things that 831

M are called by the Greeks meteora, or more precisely metarsia, are com‐

monly called in Latin sublimia [lofty things]. They are conveniently divid‐

ed into three kinds, or classes. The first contains the aërial or aqueous ones, in which,

namely, air or water predominates. The second embraces the fiery ones, in which

most subtle and spirituous exhalations prevail. The third class are the luminous or

emphatic meteors, in which either solely, or at least for the greater part, light and

splendor fall under consideration. A meteor, universally, is said to be an imperfect

mixture consisting of certain attenuated (or, as the Chemists speak, sublimated) ex‐

halations, and formed in the upper air. Of each we shall touch on a few things, and

we shall show this general definition and nature of a meteor in each one singly.

832 A cloud is an aggregate of vapors suspended on high. It arises from vapors

which at the beginning are so tenuous that they are not sensible, but which then, by

the accession of some particles to others, constitute larger molecules by mutual con‐

junction; and these, adhering to others, form a very vast cloud, so that a cloud is ac‐

cordingly to be called an aggregate of minute little bubbles in which aqueous vapors

consist. Mist differs from a cloud only in its degree of density and in place; for each

arises from little bubbles of humid

exhalations

p. 259

exhalations agglomerated together in great quantity: they differ, however, in this, that the little bubbles constituting a cloud are far wider, and hence lighter with respect to the air, than those which make a mist, so that they lie, as it were, upon them: mist is changed into clouds by the very fact that the lower air thrusts out the bubbles, rarefied and therefore made lighter and dissipated: hence it is plain why, as the Sun approaches the meridian, mists for the most part pass into clouds.

833 Rain arises from the broken little bubbles of the clouds, which are broken from several causes: namely, either on account of the excessive heat of the Sun, by which they are very greatly dilated; or if they collide with one another by the force of contrary winds; or if they are pressed against the sides of mountains; or, finally, if they are too much constricted by an intense cold of the air. The evening damp is a certain humor, like a most subtle and insensible rain, falling from on high as night comes on; and it arises from most tenuous aqueous little bubbles, which, carried on high, are broken and turn into insensible drops as soon as the air, after sunset, is seized by some cold: hence there is none in wintertime, but only in summer, and chiefly in spring and autumn, when, moreover, no wind is blowing. And when the sky is stormy and rainy, and in winter too, those thicker droplets are dissipated by the winds, or are not dilated by rarefaction into such minute ones.

834 The morning dew differs only in respect of time: for it falls a little before the rising of the Sun, because the air is then more humid, and hence those exhalations which remained over in the air concrete; wherefore the opinion of those is less true who think that dew is nothing else than the sweat of plants, continually breathing out from the orifice of their little vessels and congealed by the force of cold; for although we do not deny this transpiration, yet something else must be affirmed of dew, since it is established that linen and woolen cloths and other bodies, glass likewise, which transmit nothing of a sweat of this kind, are sensibly wetted if they are exposed to the open air at the time when the dew is falling. Hoarfrost is nothing other than dew frozen by a sharper cold; it scorches and sucks out the tenderer crops and leaves, such as the buds of vines, indeed not seldom the vines themselves; for the nutritive juice, which, thrust out from the earth, is diffused into all the fibers of the plant, is condensed by the cold of the hoarfrost: hence the texture of the little fibers is constricted and changed.

835 Hail is rain congealed by the very cold region of the air: it is made when thin flakes of vapors, liquefied by warm air into very small drops and already tending downward, meet another, cold air, and are at once coagulated and hardened by it, new coats, as it were, being thereupon added on account of the vapors which they touch in falling. Hence it is plain why it does not hail in winter: for then the clouds are too near the Earth for very many of those very minute droplets, into which the first ones turn, to be able to come together into one before they are seized by the cold; likewise why, the higher the cloud from whose resolution the hail is formed, the larger the grains of hail are.

836 Snow is produced if the little bubbles of a humid exhalation, while turning into rain,

are

p. 260

are frozen by cold; for the flakes of snow are nothing else than most tenuous droplets of water, which, seized by cold, are united first among themselves like threads, when they become entangled with one another in diverse ways in their descent. The figure of snow is sometimes regular, sometimes irregular; often, if it is examined with a microscope, it shows a hexagonal star, at times a lily, and not seldom a rose; which figures seem to depend on the diverse exhalations frozen together. From these things it is easily understood what honeydew, manna, and the hair of Venus, or virgin threads, which appear like spiders’ threads over hedges and grasses, are, and whence they draw their origin.

837 The fiery meteors are, first, the flash; second, thunder; third, lightning, of which enough has been said in the Electrology; fourth, Helen and Pollux, which are fires that appear to those sailing, in the lowest region of the air, and are formed from spirituous fumes, which the sea, agitated by storms, transpires, carried up little by little, gathered together and kindled. If one appeared, it was called Helen; when two were seen, Castor and Pollux. Fifth: falling and shooting stars are certain fiery globules kindled in the upper air, and so moved through it that at times they appear to us to proceed straight, at other times to glide headlong from the sky. Sixth: the licking fire, and the foolish fire, is a fat exhalation sweating out from the flesh of men or of bodies, and from fattier matter, which is kindled by compression or friction, and clings to horses or men without harm.

838 The foolish fire is a certain marshy exhalation from putrefied plants, corpses and other oily dissolved bodies, prepared by the daily heat of the Sun, which, upon the onset of friction or fermentation, is kindled, shines, and, as it were, burns. They are called foolish fires because not only do they run hither and thither by no certain law, in the manner of a foolish man, but also because they follow those who flee them, and in turn flee those who follow them; whence they are feared by simple folk, who do not understand, namely, that this happens for the reason that he who pursues the fire, both by the motion of his body and by his breath, drives the air before him, and with it the foolish fire; while he who flees from the fire draws the air after him, and with the air the foolish fire, while he yields the place left by his body to be filled by the air.

839 Seventh: nearly the same is the account of the phenomena of the aforesaid meteors, which are distinguished among themselves only by their diverse figure; for if a marshy or bituminous exhalation, gathered together with nitrous spirits and suddenly kindled in the upper air by means of fermentation, friction or compression, presents the appearance of a fiery globe, and has about it hanging flakes, as it were, and is borne with a leaping motion, it is called the Leaping Goat; if it is oblong and parallel to the horizon, the Beam; if it swells in its middle, the Dragon; if it is round and flat, the Shield; if smooth and cylindrical, the Column; if it ends in a point, the Pyramid; if it is widely dispersed and shows, as it were, kindled straws, it is named the Stubble. Eighth: the Aurora Borealis, or northern light, is

that

p. 261

that glow which in the nighttime at times appears to us in the northern quarter of the sky in such a way that the sky itself seems, as it were, to burn in that part. The history of this phenomenon is extensive; since it is found everywhere among the Moderns, for brevity’s sake I adduce only what is necessary.

840 In the first place, it has its seat in the atmosphere of the Earth, like the other fiery meteors, and is produced in it; for this light has at times been seen below the clouds, as Mayer testifies: then, if it extended beyond the atmosphere, it would be very high, and hence would be seen even from places near the equator, which, however, is contrary to experience, especially since it often happens that it is seen in one place and is not observed in another a few miles distant. Wherefore we think that this light, like the remaining fiery meteors, comes from an exhalation and vapor carried on high from the earth, or from the matter of lightning and of flashes not yet well ripened, so to speak, and not yet prepared for the effects of lightning and of flashes.

841 The luminous or Emphatic meteors are: first, the Rainbow, which is a many-colored arc formed in a dewy cloud by the refraction and reflection of the Sun opposite; whence it either brings down or naturally indicates rain, but without a great flood of waters; for clouds too heavily laden are not fit for reflecting and thus refracting the rays of the Sun. The more conspicuous colors of the rainbow are: red or crimson, yellow, green, blue, and finally purple or violet; and these in the primary rainbow hold the order mentioned and are more vivid; but in the secondary the reverse, so that in its outermost part the purple shines, then the blue, etc.; which are also seen weaker and more diluted.

842 That rainbow, moreover, is called primary which reaches the eye after two refractions of the rays and one reflection, and is seen at an angle of about 42 degrees; and the secondary, that which falls into the eye after two refractions and as many reflections, at an angle of about 52 degrees. It is to be noticed that the rainbow is not seen unless the sight is between the Sun and the dewy cloud; so when you sprinkle water from your mouth toward the light let in through windows, and stand between the Sun and the drops, you behold a rainbow, of which you also have other analogies in little leaping fountains, in spiders’ webs, on the neck of a dove, in flowers or grasses sprinkled with dew about sunrise and viewed in the due situation and place.

843 Further, why the same colors seem always to be and to remain is from this, that continually other and other parts of the dewy cloud, or new droplets again and again, succeed the earlier ones in the same situation and disposition, no otherwise than in a burning taper the same flame is believed to endure, on account of other and other particles of fire continually succeeding. Second: the Halo, or crown, or area, is a colored circle, more commonly whitish, sometimes however showing the colors of the rainbow, but more obscure, which appears now and then around the Sun, more often around the Moon; it is formed in a dewy cloud placed between the star and the eye,

with

p. 262

with a texture suited to a double refraction, by virtue of which the rays make with

the axis, or the line drawn through the center of the star and the eye, an angle of

nearly 23 degrees.

844 If the Halo is condensed ever larger and larger, it presages rain, because

the clouds gradually concrete into a shower; if it is dissipated on many sides, or

even on one side, it indicates winds arising either from several quarters or from

one; if it vanishes wholly, it foretells fair weather, for then the clouds are dissipat‐

ed by the force of heat. Third: the Parhelion and Paraselene are luminous meteors

standing beside the Sun or the Moon and showing the images of those stars; for

as often as a cloud apt to be resolved very soon into waters, diaphanous, too, to‐

ward the Sun, but terminated on the other side like a mirror, runs up to the Sun,

not below it toward the earth, nor directly opposite, but at the sides and oblique‐

ly, either toward the north or toward the south, so often the Sun impresses its

own image upon it, which, reflected thence to our eyes, represents the Sun to us

in the cloud, so that the ignorant judge that twin Suns are shining. Moreover, it

can happen that the image of the Sun, impressed in like manner on one cloud, in‐

duces again another image on a second cloud, and this again on another; the same

is to be thought, proportionally, of the Moon.

845 Fourth: Rods are formed in the air when a straight tract of clouds shows di‐

verse colors, for the same cause for which these are formed in the rainbow or the

crown. Fifth: we call it a Chasm, a Gap, or a Pit, when on a clear night exhalations

carried upward, denser in the middle and rarer in the remaining part, are placed

between the light of the stars and our eye; for if they are many, they show a

chasm; if fewer, a gap; if extended lengthwise, a pit or lake; since on account of

the density in the middle they are less illuminated, and everything dark, although

equally near and placed in the same surface, always seems more remote and more

depressed, while what is bright seems nearer and more elevated. Let it suffice to

have said this, in compendium, on a most copious matter.

C H A P T E R T H E L A S T.

What is to be said of Plants.

lants, by which name every kind of growth that bursts forth from the 846

P earth is understood, are organic bodies consisting of a varied apparatus

of organic parts most wisely co-ordinated and joined together, adhering

to the earth by their roots, and animated by the influx of a suitable

juice going round and returning in a circuit. The wonderful apparatus of these or‐

ganic bodies was investigated

and

p. 263

and explained by Malpighi the Italian and Grew the Englishman. Life, in a manner, and its actions are accomplished in plants by the continual motion, returning in a circuit, of the vital fluid through solid organs most wisely disposed; which motion the agitation, impulse and pressure of the ether and the air bring about, the elastic force mediating at the same time; so that on that account they are rightly called Hydraulic-Pneumatic machines; and that these may be understood more deeply, I subjoin a very brief Anatomy of them.

847 Of the parts of plants, some are fluid, others solid. The fluid part is that humor or juice which, like the blood in man, is diffused through the solid parts of the plant. This juice, and the true and genuine nourishment of plants, they say most probably to be saline, earthy and oily parts, which, prepared in the aqueous juice, attenuated, worked up, and distributed with this juice, as with a vehicle, into the whole structure of the plants, are carried round, so that the single parts can receive what is suitable for nourishing and increasing their substance. The solid parts constitute their organic body, and are: the trunk, roots, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits. The trunk, which in trees is called the bole and stock, in flowers and herbs the stalk, scape and thyrsus, in wheat and the like the straw or haulm, is, as it were, the body of the plant, which, bursting forth from the earth, rises above it and unfolds itself into branches, fronds, etc. The root is that part of the plant which, placed wholly below the earth and adhering to it, draws its nourishment for the plant. The branches, just as the limbs from the body of an animal, so burst forth from the body, or trunk, of the plant, for the most part without order, sometimes in an elegant order, and spread themselves in every direction; being of altogether the same nature as the trunk from which they arise, and furnished like it with bark, they contain pith in the middle, and are composed of the same little vessels, namely fibers, utricles and tracheae. The leaves embrace chiefly two parts: namely, the petiole, by which the leaf is attached to the plant, and the very body of the leaf.

848 The flowers are, as it were, the first offspring of the plant; in them four parts are distinguished, namely: the calyx, which is the base and support of the flower; the petals, which rise above the calyx, propagated from the dilated stalk, and consist of woody tubes, or fibers, of tracheae too, and at the same time of a manifold order of utricles; the stamens burst forth from the lowest part of the flower, various in number and figure: they consist of a filament and an attached capsule, which is made up of woody tubes, tracheae and utricles placed lengthwise: the style, finally, is that part of the flower which, occupying its center, hides and cherishes the seed of the plant in its cavity. The fruit is the last work of plants, to the producing and perfecting of which all the remaining parts are destined; it consists, moreover, of an envelope and the seed; the former differs according to the specific difference of the fruits, and is manifold, and of diverse consistency and firmness in diverse fruits; the seed pertains to the origin of plants: of which briefly.

849 That little grain, or kernel, is called the seed, from which, as from an egg, the plant germinates; four things are distinguished in it: the envelopes;

Ll the

p. 264

the first, or outermost of all, is harder than the rest; when it is removed, two little

skins are met, of which the exterior is thick and almost cartilaginous, the interior

very subtle, so that in a dried seed it can scarcely be separated from the exterior.

After these integuments, which are called secundines, two or even more lobes come

into view, enclosed in a certain thin and pellucid membrane, which is fourth in order;

and they embrace, in a kind of little ditch, as it were, hollowed out on either side in

the lobes, the germ of the future plant; which is nothing else than the whole plant it‐

self that is to arise from the seed, complete in all its parts, namely trunk, or stalk,

roots, branches, etc., so that the seminal plantlet lying hidden in the germ does not

differ from the adult except in the size of its parts.

850 The rising from the seed, further, is accomplished in this way: when the seed

is committed to suitable earth, the fibers of its membranes are gently loosened by the

heat of the earth and of the Sun, and their passages are dilated; whence it comes

about that the humor in which the earth abounds gradually enters them, is variously

strained in them, ferments, and is made apt for nutrition: the nutritive juice, strained

in the membranes, enters the substance of the lobes, where it is mixed with the spe‐

cific juice of the plantlet, ferments, and takes on new parts; this juice, prepared in

due manner in the lobes, enters the most subtle pores of the radicle of the germ itself

and insinuates itself into its little fibers; and the radicle, nourished and increased by

this juice, bursts forth outward, spreads out its hair, and by means of those filaments

is inserted into the earth; the root being sufficiently increased, a more lively portion

of the nutritive liquor passes into the remaining part of the germ, and, irradiating and

impelling its parts, communicates motion to them; hence are evolved and unfolded

the parts of the future plant, which lie hidden in the germ, rolled up and folded to‐

gether among themselves; then by degrees these same parts are increased and come

into view in their order: so that from this first evolution of the seed the remaining

growth of the plant is easily understood.

C O R O L L A R Y.

851

T here are therefore no plants that are not generated from seed. Certainly the pe‐

culiar disposition of plants, the collocation of their parts in wonderful order and

distinction, the little veins, utricles and tracheae, for producing flowers and fruits of

the same species, make it manifest that plants are not born from a fortuitous con‐

course of the elements, or from putrid matter. This very thing is shown by an experi‐

ment of Malpighi, who had enclosed earth dug out of a rather deep pit in a vessel in

such a way as to cover its upper part with very delicate cloths, so that entrance into

the vessel lay open to the air and the rain, but not to other very minute corpuscles

carried through the air; and so he exposed it to the rays of the Sun. He found that af‐

ter a very long time no herb, or sign of a plant, appeared; so that on that account he

inferred that, since no seed had either lain hidden before in the earth

dug

p. 265

dug out from deeper down, or could have fallen into the vessel through the air, plants have their genesis from seed.

852 As regards the nutrition and growth of plants, it is accomplished by the admission, elaboration and purification of a suitable juice, and by its continual circulation through the organs of the plant; for the roots draw in moisture; this, once received, ascends through the woody tubes of the plant, because it is urged upward unceasingly by the alternate dilatation and constriction of the tracheae which are interspersed among the woody tubes; and from these it is dispersed into the other parts. That the nutritive juice circulates is shown, first of all, because only in this way does it seem that the nutrition of plants can be accomplished; since indeed this cannot take place unless that which is useful, and is suitable nourishment for the plant, is separated from the useless, and this is thrust back again to those parts, so that it may be rendered fit for nutrition through a new purification and elaboration; and then it is plain from experience; for Malpighi, when the bark had been cut round in a circle and a ring-shaped portion torn away, found that the edge of the upper bark swelled notably and also increased, but that the lower obtained no increase, but only put forth buds in their season. And let these things, which have been excerpted from Fr. Klaus, suffice to have been said, so that we may put the finishing hand to the Physics, both General and Particular.

853 But if to anyone perhaps some of the things which I have brought forward in these Elements of the Newer Philosophy should seem briefer than was fitting, I would wish him to consider that I have written for Young Men alone. Many large volumes of learned men, far fuller ones, are available for the convenience of others. Nor yet would I think on that account that I have failed in my office, since I judged it more useful to make plain whatever could cause trouble to beginners, and with these Elements rather to help the American Youth than to burden them with a greater mass of disputations. For Philosophy is to be acquired both by meditation and by experiments, and it has nothing of great advantage placed in prolixity.

O. S. C . S. M . E . C . A . R .
